title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: Accurate positioning of multi‐leaf collimators (MLCs) is critical for ensuring the dosimetric precision of intensity‐modulated radiation therapy (IMRT). Nonetheless, daily MLC positional variations can degrade treatment accuracy, emphasizing the need for robust methodologies to detect and predict these deviations.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: This study proposes a machine learning (ML) approach to predict daily MLC positional deviations using factors contributing to positional errors, enabling daily patient‐specific quality assurance (PSQA) to assess the dosimetric impact of these discrepancies on patient treatment.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: DICOM‐RT and Dynalog files from 29 IMRT patients were collected, and 78 features were extracted, including aperture‐based features, mechanical parameters, and MLC check data. A LightGBM machine learning model was constructed to predict daily positional errors between planned and delivered MLC positions at each control point. For dosimetric analysis, nine independent IMRT plans were evaluated using dose volume histogram (DVH) parameters such as D98%, and V100% for targets and Dmax, Dmean for Organs at Risk (OARs). Moreover, the Gamma Pass Rate (GPR) was calculated for both the delivered and predicted dose distributions, with regarding the primary planned dose distribution as the reference.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: The proposed LightGBM model demonstrated accurate predictions, achieving Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 0.035 mm and 0.078 mm for the training dataset, 0.070 mm and 0.164 mm for the validation dataset, and 0.054 mm and 0.144 mm for the test dataset, respectively. Leaf velocity, with a Spearman correlation coefficient of 0.703, was the most influential feature. Evaluation on nine independent clinical cases demonstrated good agreement between delivered and predicted dosimetric deviations from the planned values, with mean differences below 0.200 Gy and approximately 1.5% for target structures, and even smaller discrepancies for OARs. The GPR (3%/3 mm criterion) was about 100% for delivered doses and 99.99% for predicted doses.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: Intensity‐modulated radiation therapy (IMRT) utilizes multi‐leaf collimators (MLCs) to generate a non‐uniform intensity distribution, thereby delivering highly conformal dose distributions to tumors while minimizing radiation exposure to surrounding healthy tissues. 1 , 2 The treatment planning system (TPS) plays an important role in the design of small, irregular segments; however, such complexity can introduce uncertainties in dose calculation. 3 , 4 Moreover, the mechanical complexity of the IMRT delivery mechanism may amplify operational variabilities in linear accelerators (Linacs), resulting in discrepancies between the intended and the delivered dose distributions. To address this challenge, several reports and guidelines issued by the American Association of Physicists in Medicine (AAPM), including Task Groups 109, 119, and 218, strongly recommend the implementation of pre‐treatment patient‐specific quality assurance (PSQA). 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 PSQA is commonly performed using Electronic Portal Imaging Devices (EPIDs) and phantoms specifically designed to be integrated with one or more two‐dimensional array detectors. 9 , 10 The gamma index is the most frequently used metric to evaluate PSQA results, typically assessed using criteria of 2–3% dose difference (DD), 2–3 mm distance‐to‐agreement (DTA), and a Gamma Pass Rate (GPR) threshold of 95–98% to ensure reliable dose delivery accuracy. 11

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: However, the PSQA is carried out exclusively after the treatment plan has been approved. In cases where the procedure fails, it may necessitate replanning and reevaluation, which can render PSQA a time‐consuming, labor‐intensive, and costly endeavor. This challenge is particularly pronounced in centers with a high workflow, as it imposes an additional burden on the staff. Identifying the sources of failure can be tricky, 12 , 13 , 14 having weak correlations observed with variations in dose‐volume histograms (DVHs). 15 , 16 Furthermore, PSQA is usually performed just once before treatment, potentially overlooking system errors that may arise during actual treatment sessions. Modern alternatives to pre‐treatment phantom‐based PSQA include computational software 17 , 18 , 19 and machine log file analysis, 19 , 20 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 which have been introduced to tackle the limitations of traditional PSQA methods. Although independent and computational‐based approaches can reduce specific issues associated with primary treatment planning system algorithms, they do not entirely replace conventional methods.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: Machine log files, which encompass information related to treatment plans and their delivered treatment, including the mechanical positions of the gantry, collimator, jaws, and leaves, facilitate comparisons between planned and daily dose distributions. Although log file analysis mitigates certain drawbacks of direct measurement, ensuring data transfer integrity and the accuracy of linear accelerator performance, it still requires loading pre‐treatment plans, imposing a comparable burden on the machine as measurements. However, this information remains unavailable until delivery completion and does not provide direct insight into the influence of planning on MLC deviations. Additionally, historical analyzes of log files intended to predict MLC failures rely on generalized plan characteristics. Consequently, they cannot effectively detect errors that may occur in specific treatment plans. 26

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: The applications of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) algorithms in radiation oncology represent an innovative approach to enhance treatment quality. 27 Valdes et al. were the first researchers to employ a weighted Poisson regression model with Lasso regularization to predict GPR across various treatment sites utilizing aperture‐based features as input variables, 28 and the model's validity was subsequently confirmed through a multi‐institutional study. 29 In addition, several studies have explored various ML models that incorporate plan parameters, complexity metrics, and dosiomics features as inputs to predict GPR values and determine pass/fail outcomes in PSQA procedures. 30 , 31 , 32 Since ML models require feature extraction using expert physicist intervention, many studies have aimed to train DL models using various inputs such as fluence maps, 33 sagittal dose distribution, 34 planar dose distribution from portal dosimetry, 35 three‐dimensional dose distribution with MLC position maps, 36 and log file delivery fluence. 37

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: Despite the advantages of ML and DL models in time efficiency, automation, and reducing staff workload, ML and DL models inherit errors from the original measurement data. 38 Additionally, these models cannot effectively illustrate the impact of individual leaf positional deviations on the three‐dimensional dose distribution delivered to the patient. 39 Furthermore, they struggle to account for recurring inconsistencies that may arise on the treatment day, complicating the reliability of the treatment delivery process.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: Previous efforts to mitigate PSQA limitations include Carlson et al., who developed ML models (Linear Regression, Random Forest, and Cubist) to directly predict deviations in MLC positions between DICOM‐RT and Dynalog files. They found that incorporating predicted MLC positions into the treatment plans increased GPR by approximately 4.17% for head and neck cases and demonstrated strong agreement between predicted and delivered DVHs. 40 Osman et al. also explored artificial neural networks (ANNs) to predict MLC positional discrepancies. 41 Additionally, several tree‐based ML models were evaluated to predict leaf positional errors, using features extracted from DICOM‐RT files as inputs. 24 , 42 Lay et al. proposed a virtual PSQA that employed tree‐based ML algorithms to assess the impact of leaf positional, using separate models for 31 IMRT plans and 85 VMAT plans. To analyze dosimetric effects, the validated model was tested on seven IMRT and ten VMAT plans, using indices such as D99%, D95%, D1%, V25‐100%, and mean dose. 43 Nevertheless, recent studies have demonstrated that MLC positions recorded in log files may not precisely represent delivered leaf positions due to mechanical malfunctions or calibration discrepancies. 43 , 44 , 45 Consequently, incorporating leaf quality control parameters into the model can enhance the accuracy of positional error assessments derived from log file data.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: It is important to note that changes in the daily operation of MLC are inevitable. The performance of MLC is routinely evaluated through daily initialization checks of Varian Clinac, which explicitly assess the functionality of the MLC. Each recorded initialization parameter can impact the daily dose distribution for each patient and should be regarded as a critical feature when evaluating daily leaf positional errors. Incorporating initialization parameters into the prediction model ensures that it is based on actual measurements, derived from MLC checks, thus mitigating the limitations of log file data. Qiu et al. evaluated the influence of spatial features and temporal variability extracted from fluence maps of 23 VMAT plans, alongside MLC‐check parameters, to forecast leaf deviations. 46 Using the Random Forest algorithm, they predicted average deviations of control points in Dynalog files for each leaf. They confirmed that incorporating log‐file‐derived leaf positions into DICOM‐RT files caused dose deviations between 12.948 cGy and 210.235 cGy.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: Despite these advances, an important gap remains in the application of machine learning to daily MLC positional error prediction. Most previous approaches have focused primarily on predicting positional errors from treatment‐plan or log‐file‐derived features, while relatively limited attention has been given to incorporating daily MLC initialization measurements that reflect the machine's condition on the treatment day. Moreover, prediction targets have often been defined as average or aggregate leaf deviations, which limits direct propagation of the predicted errors into the DICOM‐RT files for control‐point‐specific dose recalculation. 46 In this study, we proposed a novel approach to predict daily MLC positional deviations at the time of treatment, rather than just relying on generalized pre‐treatment predictions. A dataset comprising multiple IMRT plans from different treatment sites, along with the corresponding Dynalog files from a Varian Clinac 600C and daily MLC initialization logs, was used. Three categories of features were extracted: (a) aperture‐based features, reflecting the geometric characteristics of beam segments; (b) mechanical parameters, detailing MLC movements derived from DICOM‐RT files; and (c) initialization parameters, obtained from daily quality control logs of the MLC.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: These features were used to train an ML regression model designed to estimate leaf‐level positional errors for each control point. After model validation, independent clinical patient datasets were used to evaluate the dosimetric impact of predicted versus delivered MLC deviations, providing a framework for anatomy‐based daily quality assurance (QA). The study also assessed the effectiveness of the model in predicting variations in leaf positions across different treatment fractions.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: Twenty‐nine IMRT plans including 3 prostate, 17 head and neck, and 9 brain cases were collected from the Radiation Oncology department of Shohada‐e Tajrish Hospital, Tehran, Iran. All treatment plans were approved and created using the Eclipse TPS (version 13.0.33, Varian Medical Systems, Palo Alto, CA), with the Analytical Anisotropic Algorithm (AAA) dose calculation algorithm. The DICOM‐RT files were exported from TPS, and the corresponding Dynalog files, along with initialization parameters, were recorded during patient treatment sessions using a Clinac 600C linear accelerator equipped with a Millennium 80‐leaf MLC (two banks of 40 tungsten alloy leaves with 1 cm width at isocenter) from September 2022 to October 2022. The dataset comprised 34,448 control points extracted from these plans/patients across the aforementioned anatomical sites. When this number is multiplied by the number of leaves, a total of 2,755,840 input samples is obtained.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
section: MATERIAL AND METHODS > Aperture‐based features, leaf mechanical features, and daily initialization features
text: Forty‐six aperture‐based features were calculated using the Python modules Pydicom (version 2.4.4) and DVHA‐MLCA (version 0.2.3. post1) (Table 1). Additionally, twenty‐one mechanical features were defined for each control point, 40 , 43 , 47 including leaf positions, jaw positions, leaf velocity and acceleration, leaf movement direction, leaf movement status (starting, stopping, resting, or moving), leaf acceleration or deceleration status, leaf bank number, borders of each leaf (top, bottom, left, and right), collimator and gantry angle, gravity vector, 47 monitor unit values, the number of control points per beam (field), and number of beams per plan.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
section: MATERIAL AND METHODS > Aperture‐based features, leaf mechanical features, and daily initialization features
text: In addition, eleven daily machine‐specific parameters for each MLC leaf were incorporated into the machine learning model. Before patient treatment, the Linac undergoes an initialization procedure that records several parameters in “.init” files, which must remain within the predefined tolerances to enable treatment. These parameters included the backlash, the degree of leaf spring compression, the minimum and maximum raw secondary readouts of each leaf potentiometer, the maximum error during the secondary calibration of each leaf, the average Pulse Width Modulation (PWM) during the touch test, the leaf pair gap values during the touch test, and the daily, the monthly, the annual, and the lifetime traveled distance of each leaf (leaf odometer). 48 All parameters were extracted using a self‐written Python script (version 3.10). A Spearman correlation coefficient was employed to assess the correlation between these features and the signed positional discrepancy of individual MLC leaves.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
section: MATERIAL AND METHODS > Calculation of leaf positional errors between RT‐Plan and Dynalog files
text: During treatment delivery with C‐series linear accelerators, the leaf position data are recorded in Dynalog files at 50 ms intervals, resulting in multiple temporal snapshots for each leaf. In contrast, the corresponding planned leaf positions are available at discrete control points within the DICOM‐RT files. Consequently, the number of recorded leaf positions in the Dynalog files exceeds the number of control points defined in the treatment plan. To accurately quantify leaf positional discrepancies, interpolation between the planned and delivered positions is necessary. The delivered leaf positions were analyzed using the log analyzer module of Pylinac (version 3.19). Additionally, cubic interpolation was implemented using an in‐house Python script (version 3.10) to align Dynalog snapshots with the control point data and compute the signed MLC positional errors.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
section: MATERIAL AND METHODS > Model construction and evaluation
text: To ensure complete independence between model development and evaluation, the dataset was partitioned at the treatment‐plan level, with each plan corresponding to a single patient. Importantly, for each patient, the Dynalog file and MLC initialization measurements associated with the corresponding treatment plan were obtained from only one treatment fraction. All MLC initialization parameters remained within the manufacturer‐defined tolerance limits. Approximately 80% of the plans (23 plans/patients) were allocated to the training/validation cohort, while the remaining 20% (6 plans/patients) were reserved as an independent test cohort. The test cohort comprised one prostate, three brain, and two head and neck plans/patients, whereas the training/validation cohort comprised two prostate, six brain, and fifteen head and neck plans/patients. Seventy‐eight features (Section 2.3) and the positional discrepancies between the planned and delivered leaf positions were extracted for each leaf at every control point, defining a single sample. This yielded a two‐dimensional feature matrix of shape (number of samples × number of features) and a corresponding target vector of leaf positional errors with shape (number of samples,). The resulting training/validation dataset comprised 2,322,000 samples, while the independent test dataset contained 445,680 samples.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
section: MATERIAL AND METHODS > Model construction and evaluation
text: Owing to the continuous nature of the data, the LightGBM algorithm, as an advanced machine learning model, was employed to produce more generalized outcomes. LightGBM, a tree‐based algorithm, discretizes continuous features using histogram‐based methods, thereby reducing memory usage and speeding up computations. This efficiency enables LightGBM to handle large‐scale datasets efficiently while yielding a more accurate and generalized model. 56 The feature matrix served as model input, and the signed leaf positional discrepancies were used as ground‐truth targets for regression. To prevent data leakage during model development, treatment‐plan identifiers were retained during data preparation, and a treatment‐plan‐grouped three‐fold cross‐validation (GroupKFold) strategy was used. Thus, all samples originating from the same treatment plan were assigned exclusively to a single fold, and no information from a given treatment plan was shared between training and validation folds.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
section: MATERIAL AND METHODS > Model construction and evaluation
text: Hyperparameter optimization was performed on the training/validation cohort using a sequential grid‐search strategy. Predefined values were evaluated for each hyperparameter using three‐fold GroupKFold cross‐validation. This cross‐validation was used for hyperparameter selection rather than as an inner component of a nested cross‐validation framework. For each parameter value, the model was trained on two folds and evaluated on the remaining fold, and the mean validation Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) across the three folds was calculated. The value yielding the lowest mean validation RMSE was selected, fixed, and used in the subsequent optimization step. The values considered for each hyperparameter are provided in Table S1. The key hyperparameters tuned included: boosting type (e.g., gradient boosting decision tree (GBDT), random forest (RF), etc.), objective (the loss function used during training), the number of boosting iterations or trees, the maximum depth of each tree, the maximum number of leaves per tree, learning rate (the shrinkage rate per iteration), random seed (for reproducible results), data sampling strategy (e.g., bagging or Gradient‐based One‐Side Sampling (GOSS)), the subset of features used in each iteration/tree, bagging fraction (the proportion of data selected in each tree), the frequency of bagging, the minimum data in each leaf, and L1/L2 regularization parameters. 56

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
section: MATERIAL AND METHODS > Model construction and evaluation
text: After hyperparameter optimization, a second three‐fold GroupKFold cross‐validation was performed on the same training/validation cohort using the final fixed hyperparameter configuration. Mean Absolute Error (MAE) and RMSE were calculated across the three folds to characterize the performance of the optimized configuration. The optimized configuration was subsequently used to retrain the model on the entire training/validation cohort. Feature selection was then performed using the gain‐based feature‐importance scores obtained from this model. 56 Features accounting for 98% of the cumulative feature importance were retained, reducing the feature set from 78 to 25 features. The final model was subsequently retrained from scratch on the entire training/validation cohort using the selected features and the optimized hyperparameter configuration. The resulting model was saved and evaluated on the independent held‐out test cohort, which was not used during hyperparameter optimization or feature selection. Final model performance on the test cohort was assessed using MAE, RMSE, and R2 score. All computations were executed on an ASUS X415 system with an 11th Gen Intel® Core™ i5‐1135G7 processor running at 2.42 GHz. The total computation time was approximately 2 minutes.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
section: MATERIAL AND METHODS > DVH analysis and model predictability for different treatment fractions
text: Following model training, validation, and testing, an independent dataset comprising 9 additional IMRT plans from 9 unique patients (3 prostate, 2 brain, and 4 head and neck cases) was used for the clinical dosimetric evaluation. These 9 plans were completely separate from the 29 IMRT plans used for model development and were entirely excluded from the training, validation, and testing processes. The corresponding Dynalog files were collected over six consecutive treatment fractions for each plan, with the initialization and log files acquired on different treatment days from those used for model development.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
section: MATERIAL AND METHODS > DVH analysis and model predictability for different treatment fractions
text: Input features were extracted and the signed leaf positional errors were calculated for these clinical data. Then, the features fed into the model and the predicted discrepancies were acquired separately for the six treatment fractions. The dosimetric effects of these errors were analyzed for various treatment sites, with a specific focus on the first treatment fraction. To perform this analysis, the predicted leaf positions (calculated as the plan position plus the predicted error) and the delivered leaf positions, were integrated separately into the primary DICOM‐RT files. Subsequently, dose calculations for the predicted, delivered, and planned leaf positions were performed using Eclipse TPS on the selected patients' computed tomography (CT) images and RT structures, with a 2.5 mm dose calculation grid and the AAA dose calculation algorithm. From these calculations, dosimetric parameters were obtained from DVHs.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
section: MATERIAL AND METHODS > DVH analysis and model predictability for different treatment fractions
text: The dosimetric analysis focused on the extraction of DVH parameters for the Gross Tumor Volume (GTV), Clinical Target Volume (CTV), and Planning Target Volume (PTV) as targets, as well as for Organs at Risk (OARs). The considered parameters for the targets were D98%, D95%, D2% (the doses received by 98%, 95%, and 2% of the volume, respectively), Dmean (mean dose). Volume‐based metrics included V107%, V100%, and V95%, corresponding to the percentages of the target volume receiving at least 107%, 100%, and 95% of the prescribed dose, respectively. In addition, the Homogeneity Index (HI) 57 and Conformity Index (CI) 58 were calculated to assess dose uniformity within the target and the degree of conformity of the prescribed dose distribution to the target volume, respectively. For OARs, Dmax (maximum dose), Dmean, V10%, V25%, and V50% (the volumes receiving 10%, 25%, and 50% of the prescribed dose, respectively) were obtained. Moreover, the precision of the model in predicting the signed daily positional errors was evaluated across different treatment fractions for various treatment sites.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: To evaluate the agreement among the planned dose distribution and the dose distributions calculated using the delivered and predicted MLC leaf positions, GPRs were calculated for nine independent IMRT plans. Three pairwise comparisons were performed: planned versus delivered, planned versus predicted, and delivered versus predicted, with the latter providing a direct assessment of the agreement between the predicted and delivered dose distributions. The dose distributions were calculated using a 2.5‐mm dose grid. To provide finer spatial sampling for the gamma analysis, the dose distributions were interpolated to a common 1.0‐mm grid using three‐dimensional linear interpolation. Gamma analysis was subsequently performed independently on each axial slice using Pylinac (version 3.19) and represents a 2D, slice‐by‐slice gamma evaluation. Global dose normalization was used, and dose points receiving less than 10% of the maximum reference dose were excluded from the analysis. Gamma analysis was performed using the criteria of 3%/3 mm, 3%/2 mm, 2%/2 mm, and 1%/1 mm, with a passing criterion of 95%. For comparison with conventional measurement‐based PSQA, previously available GPR results from Delta4 phantom measurements (Delta4 Phantom+, ScandiDos AB, Uppsala, Sweden) were included for the nine IMRT plans. The available measurement‐based GPRs were obtained using a 3%/3 mm gamma criterion, a 10% dose threshold, and a 95% passing criterion.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: During the hyperparameter optimization procedure, the optimal hyperparameter values for the LightGBM algorithm included a boosting type of GBDT, with a Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss function (L2 regression) as the objective, a maximum depth of ‐1, 51 leaves, 500 boosting iterations, a learning rate of 0.050, a random seed of 42, and a data sampling strategy of bagging. The feature and bagging fractions were both 1.000, with a bagging frequency of 0.000. Additionally, the best results were achieved with a minimum of 120 data per leaf, and L1 and L2 regularization strengths of 0.100 and 1.030, respectively (lambda_l1 = 0.100, lambda_l2 = 1.030). The evolution of the training and validation loss functions using these optimized hyperparameters during three‐fold cross‐validation is shown in Figure 1. Because MSE was used as the objective function, the learning curves represent the MSE as a function of the number of boosting iterations. Both training and validation losses decreased progressively with increasing numbers of boosting iterations, indicating stable model convergence. The training loss decreased more rapidly and reached a lower value than the validation loss, while the validation loss decreased at a slower rate and remained consistently higher than the training loss. At 500 iterations, the final training and validation MSE values were approximately 0.006 and 0.027 mm2, respectively.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: Although the increasing separation between the training and validation curves indicates a modest degree of overfitting, the validation loss continued to decrease throughout the investigated range and did not show a clear increase or divergence. Therefore, extending the number of boosting iterations beyond 500 was not considered necessary, particularly because the additional improvement in validation loss became progressively smaller at higher iteration numbers.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: The mean and standard deviation of the performance metrics across the three cross‐validation folds at the selected model configuration were 0.035 ± 0.001 mm for MAE and 0.078 ± 0.003 mm for RMSE in the training subsets, compared with 0.070 ± 0.005 mm for MAE and 0.164 ± 0.013 mm for the validation subsets. The higher validation errors compared with the corresponding training errors are consistent with the small generalization gap observed in the learning curves. Importantly, the cross‐validation results were obtained using the complete set of 78 features and were used primarily for hyperparameter optimization and assessment of model behavior across patient/plan‐level folds. Following cross‐validation and feature selection, the optimized model achieved an MAE of 0.054 mm and an RMSE of 0.144 mm on the independent test dataset. When evaluated on a per‐plan/patient basis, the model achieved a mean MAE of 0.046 mm and a mean RMSE of 0.125 mm. Stratified by treatment site, the lowest prediction errors were observed for the prostate plan, with an MAE of 0.025 mm and an RMSE of 0.083 mm. For the brain plans, the mean MAE and RMSE were 0.041 mm and 0.120 mm, respectively, whereas the head and neck plans showed higher mean errors, with an MAE of 0.064 mm and an RMSE of 0.153 mm.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: Although these values were higher than the cross‐validation training performance, this difference is expected because the test dataset consisted of previously unseen patient/plan data. The independent test results provide the more relevant measure of the final model's generalization capability, while the learning curves demonstrate stable convergence during model development. Figure 2(a) presents a strong correlation between the predicted and actual target values of the test dataset, achieving an R2 score of 0.932. Figure 2(b) demonstrates Bland‐Altman analysis of this data with strong agreement between the predicted and delivered leaf positional errors. The mean bias between predictions and ground‐truth values is approximately 0.003 mm, indicating the absence of systematic overestimation or underestimation by the LightGBM model. The 95% limits of agreement are −0.280 mm to 0.285 mm, showing that most prediction errors remain within a relatively narrow interval. Furthermore, the majority of differences cluster around zero, reflecting high predictive consistency for the clinically prevalent small MLC deviations. Although several outliers are observed at larger positional errors, no directional trend toward consistent positive or negative deviation is identified. These findings support the capability of the proposed model to accurately estimate daily MLC positional inaccuracies.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: Figure 3 illustrates the distribution of leaf positional errors across all control points of test dataset for each leaf. Specifically, Figure 3(a) depicts the differences between the planned and the delivered positions. The mean deviations are below 1 mm (–0.026 mm to 0.718 mm), with standard deviations ranging from 0.012 mm to 1.239 mm across all leaves. Planned positions generally exceed delivered positions, with larger discrepancies particularly evident in the central leaves. Figure 3(b) presents the predicted versus delivered errors. The close alignment between the predicted and delivered positions is reflected by lower standard deviations (0.013 mm to 0.364 mm) and mean errors ranging from –0.052 mm to 0.027 mm. These results indicate that the model accurately captures the majority of positional deviations.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: According to these results, the 90th, 95th, and 99th percentiles (P90, P95, and P99) of the absolute leaf positional errors during delivery relative to the planned positions were 0.68, 1.23, and 2.81 mm, respectively, with a maximum error of 6.78 mm. The maximum error occurred at only one control point, indicating that such large deviations were rare in the test dataset, whereas the majority of observations corresponded to relatively small positional errors. Despite their low frequency, the model reproduced the upper tail of the error distribution reasonably well. These relatively large errors, including observations exceeding the whisker limits, are shown as blue dots in Figure 3(a). The corresponding predicted values for the 90th, 95th, and 99th percentiles and the maximum error were 0.70, 1.26, 2.76, and 5.92 mm, respectively. The greater discrepancy between the delivered and predicted values at the upper end of the error distribution, including the larger deviations represented by the blue dots in Figure 3(b), may be attributed to the substantial predominance of small positional errors in the dataset. This imbalance results in comparatively fewer samples representing rare, large positional deviations, potentially limiting the model's ability to accurately learn and reproduce extreme errors.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: The 25 features accounting for 98% of the cumulative feature importance during model training are presented in Table S2. Feature importance analysis identified leaf velocity, mean aperture displacement (MAD) at each control point, and the maximum raw secondary readout of each leaf potentiometer as the key predictors across the three feature categories. Spearman correlation analysis revealed that leaf velocity was the most influential feature (ρ = 0.703, p‐value < 0.001), highlighting its pivotal role in predicting positional errors. The leaf movement direction (i.e., motion toward or away from the midline) ranked as the second most important feature (ρ = ‐0.638, p‐value < 0.001), whereas MAD demonstrated moderate importance (ρ = –0.359, p‐value < 0.001). Additionally, the maximum raw secondary readout was found to be a relevant quality assurance parameter (ρ = 0.431, p < 0.001), along with the minimum raw secondary readout (ρ = 0.450, p < 0.001).

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
section: RESULTS > Model performance in daily error prediction and analysis of dosimetric indices
text: The DVH curves obtained from six consecutive treatment fractions for the three treatment sites (prostate, brain, and head and neck) are presented in Figure S1, while Figure 4 presents the DVHs from the first treatment fraction for representative cases from each treatment site. Structures exhibiting relatively large dosimetric deviations are shown. The six‐fraction analysis was performed to evaluate the consistency of the predicted daily MLC positional deviations and their corresponding dosimetric effects across repeated treatment fractions. As shown in Figure 4, the DVH curves calculated using the predicted MLC positions closely followed those obtained using the delivered MLC positions, while both exhibited deviations from the planned dose distribution. For example, in the brain case, the D98% of the PTV decreased by 0.416 Gy for the delivered distribution and 0.364 Gy for the predicted distribution relative to the planned dose. The right optic nerve exhibited increases of 0.545 Gy and 0.533 Gy for the delivered and predicted distributions, respectively. In the prostate case, the corresponding deviations in PTV prostate were −0.228 Gy and −0.188 Gy. For the head and neck case, the deviations were −0.251 Gy and −0.114 Gy for PTV66 Gy, −0.289 Gy and −0.168 Gy for PTV60 Gy, and 0.374 Gy and 0.474 Gy for PTV54 Gy.

text: To further investigate the relationship between MLC positional deviations (delivered and predicted) and their dosimetric consequences, the 95th percentile of the absolute leaf positional error was calculated for each of the six consecutive treatment fractions, and the mean of these six values was then calculated for each selected treatment case (Figure 6). Subsequently, the effects of the positional deviations on dosimetric parameters and their correlations were evaluated separately for each clinical case (Figures 7 and 8). According to Figure 6, the head and neck cases generally exhibited larger positional deviations than the prostate and brain cases, which may be related to their greater treatment complexity and more extensive and dynamic MLC motion. In particular, the mean leaf velocity, averaged across all leaves within each plan, was higher for the head and neck cases than for the prostate and brain cases, consistent with the observed correlation between leaf velocity and positional errors. In addition, the proposed model was able to closely reproduce the delivered 95th percentile of the absolute leaf positional errors across all treatment cases.

text: Figure 7(a) presents the effects of delivered and predicted leaf positional deviations on the dosimetric indices of the PTVs for the evaluated cases, averaged across the treatment fractions. Among the evaluated indices, V100% and D95% exhibited the largest discrepancies. The correlations between the 95th percentile of the absolute delivered MLC positional errors and the corresponding deviations in these two dosimetric indices for the different treatment cases are presented in Figure 7(b). No consistent relationship was observed between the 95th percentile of MLC positional errors and the corresponding dosimetric deviations across the different treatment sites. This finding suggests that the dosimetric impact of MLC positional deviations cannot be adequately characterized by a single summary measure of positional error, such as the 95th percentile. The effects of MLC positional deviations on the dosimetric indices of OARs are illustrated in Figure 8 for the ten OARs showing the largest deviations across the evaluated cases. The predicted dosimetric parameters for each OAR structure are also presented in Figure 8 and showed close agreement with the corresponding values obtained from the delivered MLC positions. These findings highlight the cumulative effect of numerous individual MLC positional deviations occurring throughout treatment delivery on different regions of the target and OAR structures, resulting in varying changes in their respective dosimetric parameters.

text: To illustrate fraction‐to‐fraction variations in MLC leaf positional deviations, the maximum deviations of the delivered and predicted leaf positions from their corresponding planned positions for each leaf over six consecutive treatment fractions were evaluated for a head and neck case and are presented in Figure 9. A case exhibiting relatively large fraction‐to‐fraction fluctuations was selected for this analysis. The pattern of delivered leaf positional discrepancies relative to the planned positions for this plan across the six treatment fractions indicates that the day‐to‐day variations were generally small, although the maximum positional deviations from the planned positions reached approximately 6–7 mm for some leaves during each treatment fraction. A similar pattern was observed for the predicted positional deviations relative to the planned positions. Accordingly, their direct impact on the daily DVHs was relatively limited, as also demonstrated in Figure S1. Nevertheless, small inter‐fraction positional variations across multiple leaves can cumulatively produce measurable dosimetric changes during different treatment fractions relative to the plan. In the selected head and neck case, the cumulative effect of these variations resulted in a dosimetric deviation of up to approximately 1.5% in V100%.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: In this study, we proposed using the LightGBM machine learning algorithm to predict daily MLC errors between planned and delivered positions at each control point of IMRT plans. The proposed approach was designed to address some challenges of conventional PSQA while complementing, rather than replacing it. By providing plan‐specific information on expected MLC positional deviations and their potential dosimetric consequences, it enables daily PSQA and plan‐specific evaluation of dose distributions and DVH parameters. Given that, disagreement between delivered and calculated dose distribution is more strongly related to aperture‐based metrics in IMRT, 28 we included these parameters to represent the deliverability of irregular apertures produced in IMRT plans alongside MLC initialization and mechanical parameters.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: Among previous studies focused on predicting MLC leaf positional errors, the ANN model developed by Osman et al. achieved an MSE of 0.0001 mm2 and an R2 score of 0.9999 for leaf‐position prediction. 41 The best‐performing model in the study by Lay et al. achieved an MAE of 0.004 mm for IMRT and 0.021 mm for VMAT. The robustness analysis demonstrated good agreement between the predicted and delivered values, with R2 scores of 0.966 for IMRT and 0.906 for VMAT. 43 Although these studies demonstrated the feasibility of machine learning approaches for MLC positional‐error prediction, they did not account for daily variations in leaf performance throughout a treatment course. Qiu et al. attempted to address this limitation by incorporating MLC‐check parameters to predict the average leaf‐position deviations across control points. Using a random forest algorithm, they predicted the average positional deviations of each leaf across the control points recorded in Dynalog files, achieving an MSE of 0.059 mm2 for validation and 0.074 mm2 for test datasets. Their results demonstrated that deviations in delivered leaf positions were associated with dosimetric deviations and revealed a substantial correlation between leaf positional deviations and both GPRs and dose deviations, with correlation coefficients ranging from −0.506 to −0.720 for GPRs and from < 0.498 for dose deviations, respectively.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: 46 Despite the advantages of the proposed method, as they predicted average leaf positional errors, predicted deviations cannot be integrated into RT‐Plan files to calculate the dose for different structures. The present model addresses this limitation by predicting daily MLC positional discrepancies at the individual leaf and control‐point levels, allowing the predicted leaf positions to be incorporated into the RT‐Plan and subsequently used for daily dose calculation and structure‐specific dosimetric evaluation. The lower MAE in Lay et al.’s results can be attributed to their larger dataset and lower leaf positional deviations (0.13 mm for total differences in test datasets). Similarly, Osman et al.’s favorable outcomes can be associated with a maximum deviation of 1.2 mm. Though Qiu et al. reported a maximum deviation of 2.21 mm, comparable to the ∼3 mm maximum deviation at the upper whisker limit (Q3 + 1.5×IQR) observed in our dataset, our model still achieved an MSE of 0.020 mm2 for the test dataset. The differences between studies may also arise from variations in linear accelerators, MLC models, ML algorithms, dataset size, feature definitions, error distributions, and treatment modalities.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: Feature importance analysis from our model highlighted the critical role of initialization parameters in capturing daily discrepancies, with the maximum raw secondary as the most crucial initialization feature. In contrast, Qiu et al. identified PWM as the most correlated feature in their study, which may be attributed to differences in feature contributions during training with different models. Previous studies have demonstrated a linear correlation between individual leaf velocity and the magnitude of positional errors. 59 , 60 , 61 Consistently, our findings identified leaf velocity as the most influential feature during model training, supported by the highest Spearman correlation coefficient. Additionally, the notable contribution of aperture‐based features to loss function reduction reinforces the impact of plan complexity on positional errors. Analysis of central leaves, as shown in Figure 3, revealed greater positional errors compared to peripheral leaves. This can be attributed to their critical role in intensity modulation and the creation of small apertures, which increase positional uncertainties.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: The model demonstrated robust performance on the test dataset, with a maximum absolute positional discrepancy of 3.60 mm between the model predictions and the delivered MLC leaf positions, occurring at a single control point in a brain case. Across the entire test dataset, only 0.02% of the samples showed an absolute prediction error greater than 2 mm, whereas 32% showed an absolute prediction error between 1 and 2 mm. The model also yielded accurate predictions for clinical data spanning six consecutive treatment days, achieving an MAE ranging from 0.051 mm to 0.056 mm and an RMSE between 0.144 mm and 0.150 mm for nine IMRT patients, underscoring its consistent precision in forecasting daily positional errors. As illustrated in Figure 4, the DVHs consistently showed a trend toward target underdosage, particularly in the steep dose‐gradient region. For OARs, both increases and decreases in dose were observed. For example, in the head and neck case, the planned mean dose for the right parotid was already elevated (30.160 Gy), likely due to competing PTV coverage priorities, whereas the recommended Dmean constraint for single gland is < 20 Gy. 62 An additional increase of approximately 1 Gy could further exacerbate parotid dysfunction.

A 2 mm error in leaf positioning could cause an increase of 0.88%‐1.9% in PTV. 65

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: The predominance of negative deviations in the target dose metrics shown in Figure 5 indicates lower dose coverage during delivery in comparison to the planned expectations. Dose reduction can decrease the tumor control probability (TCP), while excessive radiation to OARs may increase the risk of toxicity, particularly in tissues with limited repair capacity. The findings summarized in Table 2 indicate that the average differences in dosimetric indices, except for V100%, are not clinically noticeable. For instance, the mean dose reduction for the delivered plan (–0.350 Gy) and the predicted plan (–0.274 Gy) represents only a slight decrease in target irradiation compared to the primary plan. However, in individual cases, the observed minimum and maximum deviations in D98% and D95% indicate that reductions can compromise target coverage, whereas increases may affect nearby OARs. These findings underscore the importance of careful, case‐by‐case evaluation of dosimetric discrepancies.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: As shown in Figure 6, the P95 of the absolute MLC positional errors was generally higher for the head and neck plans than for the prostate and brain plans. In the present dataset, the head and neck plans also exhibited higher mean leaf velocities, which may reflect their greater modulation and dynamic leaf‐motion requirements and suggest a potential relationship between treatment‐plan complexity and MLC delivery performance. However, as shown in Figure 7, no clear correlation was observed between the P95 and the dosimetric parameters most affected by MLC positional deviations, namely V100% and D95%. This finding suggests that the dosimetric impact of MLC positional deviations is not determined solely by their magnitude but may also depend on their spatial distribution, the local dose gradients, and the anatomical structures affected. For example, prostate case 2 exhibited a substantial reduction in V100% (83%) and an approximately 0.7 Gy change in D95% of the CTV corresponding to the dose fall‐off region of the DVH curve, despite having a P95 of only 0.6 mm. Therefore, the present results suggest that a single threshold based solely on the magnitude of MLC positional error may not adequately represent the clinical importance of the resulting dosimetric changes.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: As shown in Figure 9, the maximum positional deviations of delivered MLC leaf positions from their planned positions reached up to 7.33 mm, while the inter‐fraction variations were generally small. The cumulative effect of these daily positional fluctuations is illustrated in Figure 11, which shows the variations in V100% associated with the predicted and delivered leaf positional deviations over six consecutive treatment fractions. These results demonstrate that small fraction‐to‐fraction variations can contribute to observable differences in the delivered dose distribution. The model's limitation in predicting inter‐fraction changes is also reflected in the variation range of V100%, which was approximately 2% for the predicted values compared with 4% for the delivered values. In parallel, the most influential initialization feature, maximum raw secondary, also exhibited fluctuations across treatment days (Figure 10), suggesting that changes in daily MLC initialization conditions may contribute to the observed variations in positional errors.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: Daily analysis of dose distribution is essential to adaptive radiotherapy planning, which can be modified to account for observed deviations. The advantages of the proposed daily process include improvement of efficiency, reduction of staff workload, plan verification on the treatment day, the ability to analyze dosimetric parameters, and the assessment of the impact of the Linac's daily performance on patient dose. Regarding expected MLC positional deviations and their potential dosimetric consequences before or during a course of treatment, a potential clinical workflow would involve establishing a dosimetric baseline for each individual treatment plan and subsequently evaluating the predicted MLC‐related dose deviations during treatment. If the predicted dose distribution remains within clinically acceptable limits established by the institution and treating physician, treatment could proceed according to the existing QA protocol. Conversely, an unacceptable predicted dosimetric deviation could trigger additional evaluation, such as repeat PSQA, treatment‐plan review, or investigation of MLC performance. This approach could also provide an early warning of potential leaf‐specific performance changes that may warrant further evaluation, calibration, or Periodic Machine Inspection (PMI).

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: Importantly, the proposed approach is intended to provide plan‐specific surveillance rather than replace established patient‐specific and machine QA procedures. Accurate MLC calibration and robust QA processes remain essential for reliable IMRT delivery, with a 1‐mm tolerance for MLC leaf positioning recommended by AAPM Task Group 142 and Budgell et al, 71 , 72 which is also used for Picket Fence test analysis at our institution. However, predefined test patterns used in conventional MLC QA may not fully characterize the plan‐specific dosimetric consequences of MLC deviations during highly modulated IMRT delivery. The proposed approach therefore evaluates MLC positional behavior and its potential dosimetric consequences within the context of the actual treatment geometry, providing information that may not be captured by standardized QA tests alone.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: The high GPRs observed across the four criteria (1%/1 mm, 2%/2 mm, 3%/2 mm, and 3%/3 mm) are consistent with the findings of Benjamin et al., who reported a weak correlation between the gamma index and dosimetric errors in patient anatomies. 12 These findings highlight a limitation of relying solely on gamma analysis, as a high GPR may not necessarily reflect the magnitude or spatial distribution of dose deviations within specific patient structures. In the present study, the measurement‐based PSQA GPRs were slightly lower, ranging from 97.00% to 100% under the 3%/3 mm criterion, which may be partly attributable to additional measurement and procedural uncertainties associated with phantom‐based verification. Therefore, structure‐specific dosimetric evaluation using the proposed ML model may provide additional insight into clinically relevant dose deviations that are not readily apparent from GPR alone. Several limitations should be considered. First, the study was performed using a limited number of IMRT plans from a single treatment system and MLC configuration which were collected over a relatively short period of time. The model is therefore preliminary, institution‐specific and machine‐specific, and its performance may not generalize to other treatment planning systems, dose‐calculation algorithms, linear accelerators, MLC models, or treatment modalities. External validation using larger, multi‐institutional datasets is required.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: Second, although daily initialization parameters were incorporated into the model, their relatively low feature importance suggests that the available measurements may not fully capture fraction‐to‐fraction variations in MLC behavior, potentially limiting the model's sensitivity to subtle temporal changes in MLC performance. To address this, it is recommended that additional daily quality control parameters be incorporated into the prediction models. For example, geometrical and beam evaluations during the daily Machine Performance Check (MPC) of Varian TrueBeam machines can serve as more comprehensive daily quality control features. Nevertheless, these findings suggest that daily initialization measurements provide useful information but may not capture all transient, stochastic, or abrupt changes in MLC behavior. Consequently, the proposed model should not be regarded as a standalone machine‐failure detection system. Considering the varying complexity and delivery characteristics of different treatment plans, treatment‐site‐specific models may potentially improve predictive performance. Future research should also investigate integration of the model into dose calculation workflows and evaluate the clinical and radiobiological consequences of dose discrepancies, particularly in hypofractionated treatments.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: Prospective studies involving larger datasets, systematically varied treatment complexity, multiple MLC and accelerator platforms, and documented changes in machine performance are required before the proposed approach can be considered for routine clinical implementation.

title: Daily Multi-Leaf Collimator positional error prediction using machine learning: A Dynalog-based approach for patient specific quality assurance.
text: In this study, we developed a predictive model to estimate daily MLC positional discrepancies and assess corresponding daily dose‐volume histograms (DVHs) and dosimetric indices. By incorporating MLC daily check parameters alongside aperture‐based and mechanical leaf parameters, the proposed LightGBM model demonstrated robust performance, achieving an MAE of 0.054 mm, an RMSE of 0.144 mm and an R2 score of 0.932 for the test dataset. The model's high accuracy in predicting dosimetric indices and daily DVHs further validated its precision. While notable variations in dosimetric parameters were observed due to MLC positional errors, the GPR analysis especially using the 3%/3 mm gamma index, confirmed the feasibility of treatment plan delivery. Therefore, the proposed approach may serve as a plan‐specific surveillance tool, rather than replacing established patient‐specific and machine QA procedures, and could provide a basis for further investigation of its potential role in future adaptive radiotherapy workflows.

title: Analysis of IMRT patient specific quality assurance using EPID measurement data from the Halcyon linear accelerator.
text: This study investigated the characteristics of electronic portal imaging device (EPID)-based perpendicular field-by-field patient-specific quality assurance (PFF-PSQA) on the Halcyon linear accelerator by comparing them with the true composite (TC)-PSQA performed using the Delta4 Phantom+ (ScandiDos, Sweden) system. Both methods demonstrated excellent dose agreement under the AAPM TG-218 gamma criteria and strong correlations were observed between their results across prostate, nasopharynx, and breast cases. However, gamma passing rate (GPR) reductions due to treatment isocenter displacements were more pronounced in TC-PSQA, whereas EPID-based PFF-PSQA consistently showed relatively higher and more stable GPR values. A two-way repeated measures ANOVA analysis confirmed a significant difference in sensitivity to displacement-induced errors, supporting the clinical robustness of EPID-based PFF-PSQA. In addition, EPID-based PFF-PSQA yielded tolerance and action limits of 99.5% and 99.4%, respectively, which exceed the conventional 95% and 90% thresholds specified in the report of American association of physicists in medicine (AAPM) TG-218, highlighting the necessity of refining evaluation criteria for this approach. Overall, these findings indicate that EPID-based PFF-PSQA can serve as a reliable and clinically alternative to TC-PSQA.

title: Analysis of IMRT patient specific quality assurance using EPID measurement data from the Halcyon linear accelerator.
text: Intensity modulated radiation therapy (IMRT), which enables the delivery of a highly conformal prescription dose distribution to the tumor target while minimizing dose to surrounding normal tissues, requires verification of dosimetric accuracy by measuring the actual dose distribution delivered by the treatment machine and comparing it with the calculated distribution in the treatment planning system (TPS) before starting patient treatment. This verification procedure is referred to as IMRT patient-specific quality assurance (PSQA). In the early stages of IMRT implementation, PSQA was primarily performed by measuring doses with film and ionization chambers [1,2]. However, due to a time-consuming and single-use consumable in these methods, dose distribution measurements are now predominantly conducted using diode and ionization chamber array devices [3–6]. Various research has been conducted on IMRT PSQA methods, and studies have been established to propose appropriate evaluation criteria for PSQA [7, 8].

title: Analysis of IMRT patient specific quality assurance using EPID measurement data from the Halcyon linear accelerator.
text: One of PSQA methods is to measure the dose distribution using an electric portal imaging device (EPID) installed in a linear accelerator and many studies have been conducted in this regard [9]. Although this approach allows only perpendicular field-by-field (PFF) measurements and cannot analyze the true composite (TC) dose distribution of all treatment beams used in IMRT, it is widely employed in clinical practice because it does not require the setup of additional QA devices and allows for relatively straightforward comparison and analysis with treatment planning results. In particular, the Halcyon (Varian Medical Systems, USA) linear accelerator (LINAC), with its O-ring design, has the advantage that treatment beams are consistently measured by a fixed EPID. As a result, the utilization of EPID measurement data for dose verification is more convenient compared to conventional C-arm linear accelerators, in which the EPID operates on a robotic arm.

title: Analysis of IMRT patient specific quality assurance using EPID measurement data from the Halcyon linear accelerator.
text: In this study, we aimed to evaluate whether there is a significant difference between IMRT PSQA results obtained using the EPID of the Halcyon linear accelerator and the true composite dose analysis results obtained with conventional detector array devices. Through this approach, we attempted to validate the feasibility of EPID-based PSQA for IMRT using Halcyon LINAC and to establish reference standards for clinical application by calculating the tolerance limits (TL) and action limits (AL) which serve as the evaluation criteria for PSQA results.

title: Analysis of IMRT patient specific quality assurance using EPID measurement data from the Halcyon linear accelerator.
section: Materials and methods > Preparation of IMRT PSQA plans with the Halcyon LINAC
text: Test IMRT plans were generated to analyze the characteristics of PSQA results using the EPID of the Halcyon LINAC. In this study, IMRT plans were generated for a total of 30 patients, including 10 with prostate cancer, 10 with nasopharynx cancer, and 10 with breast cancer, using the volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT) technique. This study conducted PSQA for VMAT plans instead of fixed-beam IMRT, reflecting the widespread clinical use of VMAT-based IMRT. The intention was to evaluate PFF-PSQA results under dynamic arc conditions, where the gantry rotates during irradiation, rather than under static fixed-angle measurements. VMAT plans were generated using two full arcs for prostate cancer, four full arcs for brain cancer, and four partial arcs for breast cancer patients. The VMAT plans were created using the Eclipse 16.1 (Varian Medical Systems, USA) planning system. For each VMAT plan, two types of PSQA plans were generated. One was based on the conventional TC dose verification method with a diode detector array, employing the Delta4 Phantom+ (ScandiDos, Sweden) system, while the other was generated using the PFF dose measurement method with an EPID and subsequently analyzed through the portal dosimetry 16.1 software (Varian Medical Systems, USA). The portal dose was calculated using the anisotropic analytical algorithm (AAA).
