text: 3D printing further expands the therapeutic potential of polymeric cervical scaffolds by allowing geometry, porosity, mechanical properties, and drug-loading patterns to be designed according to patient anatomy and treatment goals [52]. Instead of acting as passive fillers, 3D-printed polymeric scaffolds can integrate anatomical adaptation, mechanical compliance, mucosal compatibility, and controlled release within a single construct. However, this field remains at an early translational stage [53]. Current studies mainly support feasibility in personalized cervical implants, nanoparticle-releasing hydrogels, and printed bio-adhesive drug-delivery systems, while robust clinical evidence for long-term safety and therapeutic benefit is still lacking. Therefore, scaffold-based approaches should currently be viewed as experimental polymer-enabled local therapy platforms that may complement, rather than replace, established cervical cancer treatments. The current research on 3D-printed polymeric therapeutic scaffolds for cervical-cancer-related applications remains limited, but several representative directions have already emerged. These studies can be broadly classified into patient-specific cervical implants for post-conization tissue support, drug-loaded scaffolds for prolonged antiviral delivery, nanoparticle-eluting hydrogels for local oncological therapy, and printed bio-adhesive films for mucosal drug retention.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
section: 2. Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management > 2.2. 3D-Printed Therapeutic Scaffolds for Cervical Cancer > 2.2.2. Research in 3D-Printed Polymeric Therapeutic Scaffolds
text: A first research direction focuses on patient-specific cervical implants designed to restore local geometry and provide mechanical support after conization. Zhao et al. developed a personalized cervical tissue implant with protein-release function using polyurethane and low-temperature deposition manufacturing [43]. The implant was designed as a cone-shaped porous structure according to the depth and geometry of cervical conization. The use of polyurethane was important because this elastomeric polymer could provide flexibility and mechanical compliance closer to soft cervical tissue, while the porous architecture increased the available surface area for protein loading and release. In this system, anti-HPV protein was loaded into the implant after printing. The study demonstrated the feasibility of combining anatomical adaptation, soft-tissue support, and local antiviral protein delivery within a single printed construct. However, the protein was mainly loaded by post-printing adsorption, leading to rapid release within a short time window, which limited its ability to meet longer therapeutic requirements.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
section: 2. Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management > 2.2. 3D-Printed Therapeutic Scaffolds for Cervical Cancer > 2.2.2. Research in 3D-Printed Polymeric Therapeutic Scaffolds
text: To address this limitation, Ji et al. further developed 3D-printed cervical implant scaffolds incorporated with drug-loaded carboxylated chitosan microspheres for long-term anti-HPV protein delivery [54]. In this design, polyurethane still served as the main structural scaffold, while carboxylated chitosan microspheres were introduced as functional drug reservoirs. Compared with directly mixing or adsorbing protein onto the scaffold, microsphere-based loading helped protect protein bioactivity and prolonged release. The authors also compared different incorporation strategies, including microsphere embedding and microsphere surface modification. This work is important because it shifts the scaffold from a simple porous carrier toward a composite polymeric delivery system, in which the structural polymer determines the macroscopic support and the polysaccharide microspheres regulate the protein-release behavior. From a materials perspective, this design illustrates how combining an elastomeric scaffold with bioactive polysaccharide-based microspheres can decouple mechanical support from drug-release control.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
section: 2. Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management > 2.2. 3D-Printed Therapeutic Scaffolds for Cervical Cancer > 2.2.2. Research in 3D-Printed Polymeric Therapeutic Scaffolds
text: A second strategy involves 3D-printable hydrogels for localized nanoparticle delivery. Kiseleva et al. developed an AuNP-loaded hydrogel based on Pluronic F127 and alginate for cervical-cancer-related local therapy [55]. The two polymers provide complementary functions: Pluronic F127 enables thermoresponsive sol–gel transition near physiological temperature, whereas alginate allows Ca2+-mediated ionic crosslinking and improves structural stability. As illustrated in Figure 3a–c, the AuNP-containing formulation can be extrusion-printed into a defined geometry and subsequently stabilized by calcium-induced alginate crosslinking. This combination integrates printability, thermoresponsive gelation, structural fixation, and local nanoparticle delivery within a single polymeric system.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
section: 2. Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management > 2.2. 3D-Printed Therapeutic Scaffolds for Cervical Cancer > 2.2.2. Research in 3D-Printed Polymeric Therapeutic Scaffolds
text: In addition to demonstrating printability, the study evaluated AuNP release and transport across porcine vaginal mucosa using PET imaging. The representative images and time-dependent radioactivity profiles in Figure 3d,e show progressive release from the hydrogel, pronounced accumulation within the vaginal membrane, and comparatively limited transport into the acceptor compartment. These findings suggest that the system favors local mucosal retention rather than extensive transmembrane diffusion, an advantageous feature for localized nanoparticle-based treatment. Nevertheless, the evidence remains primarily preclinical, and further studies are required to establish in vivo retention, safety, therapeutic efficacy, and the reproducibility of patient-specific printed constructs.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
section: 2. Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management > 2.2. 3D-Printed Therapeutic Scaffolds for Cervical Cancer > 2.2.2. Research in 3D-Printed Polymeric Therapeutic Scaffolds
text: A third group of studies used printing technology to fabricate bio-adhesive drug-delivery films for cervical administration. Varan et al. first reported inkjet printing of antiviral polycaprolactone (PCL)-based nanoparticles and anticancer cyclodextrin inclusion complexes onto a bio-adhesive hydroxypropyl-cellulose film for cervical administration [56]. Paclitaxel was complexed with cyclodextrin to overcome poor aqueous solubility, while cidofovir was encapsulated in PCL or poly(ethylene glycol)-polycaprolactone nanoparticles to enable controlled antiviral release. Although this system is better described as a printed bioadhesive film rather than a true 3D scaffold, it is highly relevant to scaffold-like mucosal platforms because it demonstrates dose and geometry control on a polymeric substrate. In a follow-up study, the same group performed mechanical and ex vivo evaluation of these printed films [57]. Inkjet printing did not negatively affect film thickness and increased mechanical strength and surface free energy; the printed anticancer formulation was retained on sheep cervix tissue for more than 12 h. These findings support the broader concept that polymeric mucosal platforms can be engineered not only for drug loading, but also for adhesion, mechanical integrity, and local residence.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
section: 2. Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management > 2.2. 3D-Printed Therapeutic Scaffolds for Cervical Cancer > 2.2.2. Research in 3D-Printed Polymeric Therapeutic Scaffolds
text: Taken together, these studies indicate that therapeutic scaffold-like systems for cervical cancer are moving in three complementary directions. Rigid or semi-flexible porous implants are being explored for post-conization tissue support and local anti-HPV delivery [43,54]. Composite polymeric scaffolds incorporating microspheres are being developed to prolong protein release while preserving bioactivity [54]. Printable hydrogels and bio-adhesive films are being used to improve mucosal contact, nanoparticle retention, and spatial control of drug administration [55,56,57]. Across these systems, the central advantage of polymers lies in their tunable structure–property relationships: elasticity can be matched to soft cervical tissue, porosity can regulate protein loading and cell contact, hydrophilicity and swelling can influence mucosal interaction, and degradation or diffusion properties can shape release kinetics. However, the field is still at an early proof-of-concept stage. Most studies remain in vitro or ex vivo, and there is still limited evidence regarding in vivo retention, long-term mucosal safety, reproductive outcomes, degradation products, sterilization stability, and clinical efficacy. Future work should therefore move from material feasibility toward clinically relevant validation models and standardized performance metrics.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
section: 2. Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management > 2.3. Bioprinted Research Platforms for Cervical Cancer Modeling > 2.3.1. Research Application Scenarios and Limitations of Conventional Cervical Cancer Models
text: Beyond direct therapeutic devices, polymer-based additive manufacturing has also been used to construct in vitro research platforms for cervical cancer modeling. In this context, a research platform refers to an engineered experimental model designed to reproduce selected features of cervical tumor tissues under controllable laboratory conditions. These platforms are mainly used for studying tumor cell behavior, tumor–matrix interactions, drug response, epithelial–mesenchymal transition (EMT), hypoxia, molecular diffusion, and other microenvironment-dependent biological processes [58,59]. They are therefore distinct from implantable scaffolds or radiotherapy-assisting devices: their primary role is not clinical intervention, but disease modeling and preclinical evaluation.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
section: 2. Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management > 2.3. Bioprinted Research Platforms for Cervical Cancer Modeling > 2.3.1. Research Application Scenarios and Limitations of Conventional Cervical Cancer Models
text: The need for such platforms arises from the intrinsic limitations of conventional cervical cancer models. Two-dimensional cell culture remains useful for basic molecular assays, but it poorly represents the spatial architecture of tumor tissue. Cells grown as monolayers lack the three-dimensional organization, cell–matrix interactions, diffusion barriers, oxygen and nutrient gradients, and multicellular spheroid formation that shape tumor behavior in vivo [60,61]. Consequently, two-dimensional models may underestimate or distort key cancer phenotypes, including proliferation, invasion-related protein expression, EMT response, and chemoresistance. Animal models provide higher biological complexity, but they are limited by interspecies differences, ethical constraints, cost, low throughput, and reduced control over local matrix composition and tumor geometry [62].

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
section: 2. Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management > 2.3. Bioprinted Research Platforms for Cervical Cancer Modeling > 2.3.1. Research Application Scenarios and Limitations of Conventional Cervical Cancer Models
text: Three-dimensional spheroids, hydrogel embedding, porous scaffolds, and microfluidic systems have partly addressed these limitations by introducing spatial structure and matrix-associated signaling [63]. However, these approaches often remain constrained by limited control over construct geometry, cell distribution, spheroid size, and reproducibility [64]. These parameters are not merely technical details, because tumor size and architecture directly influence oxygen availability, metabolic gradients, drug penetration, and treatment response. Therefore, cervical cancer modeling requires a platform that is both biologically more relevant than monolayer culture and more structurally controllable than conventional three-dimensional culture systems. 3D bioprinting provides such an intermediate strategy by enabling the deposition of cervical cancer cells and polymeric bioinks into predefined three-dimensional constructs. By combining living cells with hydrogel matrices such as alginate, gelatin, fibrinogen, Matrigel, hydroxyethylcellulose, and related polymeric systems, bioprinting allows cervical tumor-like models to be fabricated with controlled architecture and experimentally adjustable matrix properties [32,64,65,66,67]. This makes 3D-bioprinted cervical cancer models particularly suitable for investigating how tumor cells respond to a defined three-dimensional microenvironment, before moving toward more complex in vivo or patient-derived validation systems.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
section: 2. Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management > 2.3. Bioprinted Research Platforms for Cervical Cancer Modeling > 2.3.2. Research Progress in 3D-Bioprinted Cervical Cancer Models
text: The first representative attempt to construct a 3D-bioprinted cervical tumor model was reported by Zhao et al., who printed HeLa cells within a gelatin/alginate/fibrinogen hydrogel system to generate an in vitro cervical tumor-like construct [32]. This study is important because it established the basic material–cell–printing logic for subsequent cervical cancer bioprinting work. Gelatin, alginate, and fibrinogen were selected as extracellular matrix-mimicking hydrogel components: gelatin contributed thermoresponsive processability and cell-interactive protein-derived cues, alginate provided ionic crosslinking and construct stabilization, and fibrinogen introduced a fibrin-like matrix component after thrombin-mediated crosslinking. The resulting bioink allowed HeLa cells to be directly incorporated into a printable hydrogel matrix and arranged into a designed three-dimensional grid structure.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
section: 2. Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management > 2.3. Bioprinted Research Platforms for Cervical Cancer Modeling > 2.3.2. Research Progress in 3D-Bioprinted Cervical Cancer Models
text: This study systematically connected material preparation, printing optimization, and biological validation. Figure 4A illustrates the overall fabrication process, in which HeLa cells were mixed with gelatin, alginate, and fibrinogen; extruded into a predefined construct; and subsequently stabilized through sequential crosslinking. Figure 4B shows the designed architecture of the printed cervical tumor model, emphasizing a grid-like geometry rather than a bulk hydrogel block. This design was functionally relevant because the interconnected channels could facilitate nutrient transport, oxygen exchange, and metabolic waste removal during culture. Figure 4C presents the experimental timeline, in which the printed 3D constructs and two-dimensional controls were cultured in parallel and then evaluated with or without paclitaxel exposure. This layout enabled direct comparison between conventional monolayer culture and the printed 3D tumor model. Figure 4D shows the temperature-dependent viscosity of the hydrogel formulation. Because gelatin-containing hydrogels become more viscous at lower temperature, printing temperature directly affected extrusion behavior and structural fidelity. Figure 4E further links this processing variable to cell survival, showing that lower nozzle temperature reduced post-printing viability, probably due to increased viscosity and shear stress during extrusion.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
section: 2. Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management > 2.3. Bioprinted Research Platforms for Cervical Cancer Modeling > 2.3.2. Research Progress in 3D-Bioprinted Cervical Cancer Models
text: Therefore, Figure 4D,E together demonstrate that bioink rheology and printing parameters must be balanced rather than optimized independently. Finally, Figure 4F shows the macroscopic appearance of the printed constructs during culture. The constructs maintained a recognizable grid structure from the initial stage to later culture time points, supporting the feasibility of using this hydrogel-based printed system as a stable cervical tumor model [32]. Biologically, the printed 3D model produced behaviors that were not reproduced by standard two-dimensional culture. HeLa cells maintained high post-printing viability, proliferated within the hydrogel matrix, and gradually formed multicellular spheroids. Compared with monolayer culture, cells in the printed 3D constructs showed stronger proliferative activity, increased matrix metalloproteinase expression, and higher resistance to paclitaxel treatment [32]. These findings indicate that 3D bioprinting did not merely change the physical format of culture, but altered tumor-relevant phenotypes by providing a spatially confined hydrogel microenvironment. From a cervical cancer modeling perspective, this study provided the first proof-of-concept that polymeric bioinks could be used to fabricate reproducible HeLa-based tumor constructs with spheroid formation, invasion-associated protein expression, and drug-response differences.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
section: 2. Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management > 2.3. Bioprinted Research Platforms for Cervical Cancer Modeling > 2.3.2. Research Progress in 3D-Bioprinted Cervical Cancer Models
text: Building on this foundation, Pang et al. further used a 3D-printed HeLa/hydrogel model to investigate TGF-β-induced epithelial–mesenchymal transition [64]. In this study, HeLa cells were printed in a composite hydrogel containing gelatin, alginate, and Matrigel. The printed grid construct supported rapid cell proliferation and spheroid formation. After TGF-β stimulation, the spheroids began to lose their compact epithelial-like organization, and some cells acquired a spindle-like morphology. Molecular analyses confirmed downregulation of the epithelial marker E-cadherin and upregulation of mesenchymal markers including Snail, vimentin, and N-cadherin. Importantly, the EMT response differed between 3D and 2D systems, suggesting that matrix embedding, spheroid organization, and diffusion-limited exposure to soluble factors can modulate EMT signaling. The authors also showed that disulfiram and the EMT pathway inhibitor C19 attenuated TGF-β-induced EMT in this model [64]. This work expanded the function of 3D-bioprinted cervical cancer models from phenotypic comparison to mechanistic interrogation of tumor invasion and metastasis-related programs.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
section: 2. Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management > 2.3. Bioprinted Research Platforms for Cervical Cancer Modeling > 2.3.2. Research Progress in 3D-Bioprinted Cervical Cancer Models
text: Subsequent studies shifted greater attention toward bioink formulation and construct design. Gospodinova et al. developed hydroxyethylcellulose/sodium alginate bioinks for extrusion bioprinting of HeLa-based cervical tumor constructs [65]. This work was less focused on a specific oncogenic pathway and more focused on the material requirements for reliable bioprinting. By varying the relative alginate content, the authors correlated rheological behavior, printability, cell viability, residence time in the bioink, and post-printing proliferation. The study showed that HeLa cell viability was strongly affected by extrusion-related stress and by the viscosity of the bioink under printing-relevant shear conditions. A formulation containing hydroxyethylcellulose with lower alginate content supported better post-printing viability and subsequent proliferation, whereas excessive alginate compromised cytocompatibility [65]. This study is valuable because it clarified a central design rule for cervical tumor bioprinting: a bioink must provide sufficient viscosity and stability for printing, but excessive resistance to extrusion can damage cells and reduce model quality.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
section: 2. Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management > 2.3. Bioprinted Research Platforms for Cervical Cancer Modeling > 2.3.2. Research Progress in 3D-Bioprinted Cervical Cancer Models
text: Othman et al. introduced another strategy by printing preformed HeLa spheroids rather than only dispersed single cells [66]. The authors prepared alginate–gelatin bioinks and optimized a multilayer hexagonal scaffold loaded with HeLa microtissues. The use of gelatin was intended to provide protein-derived cell-supportive cues, whereas alginate contributed printability and calcium-mediated stabilization. Compared with single-cell encapsulation, spheroid loading can preserve stronger cell–cell interactions and reduce direct exposure of isolated cells to shear stress during printing. The optimized alginate–gelatin formulation supported high-fidelity printing of multilayer constructs, and the embedded HeLa microtissues maintained high viability after culture. This work is conceptually important because it moved cervical cancer bioprinting from “printing cells that later form spheroids” toward “printing pre-assembled tumor microtissues into a designed scaffold,” which may better preserve multicellular architecture at the beginning of the experiment.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
section: 2. Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management > 2.3. Bioprinted Research Platforms for Cervical Cancer Modeling > 2.3.2. Research Progress in 3D-Bioprinted Cervical Cancer Models
text: Most recently, Becconi et al. advanced 3D-bioprinted cervical tumor modeling by combining alginate-based bioprinting with nano-electrochemical characterization [67]. In this study, HeLa cells were bioprinted in an alginate-based matrix supplemented with mannitol, and the formulation was optimized to improve filament uniformity and post-crosslinking shape stability. The printed system generated spheroids over time and allowed evaluation of spheroid size, cellular organization, E-cadherin expression, oxygen concentration, and molecular diffusion. A particularly important aspect of this work was the use of scanning electrochemical microscopy with platinum nanoelectrodes to measure oxygen gradients inside HeLa spheroids and quantify the diffusion of a model molecule through the three-dimensional matrix [67]. This moved the field beyond conventional assessments of morphology and cell viability toward quantitative mapping of microenvironmental parameters [67]. For cervical cancer drug-screening platforms, such information is crucial because oxygen availability and molecular diffusion directly influence hypoxia-associated biology, therapeutic penetration, and apparent drug sensitivity.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
section: 2. Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management > 2.3. Bioprinted Research Platforms for Cervical Cancer Modeling > 2.3.2. Research Progress in 3D-Bioprinted Cervical Cancer Models
text: Taken together, these studies demonstrate a clear progression in 3D-bioprinted cervical cancer modeling. The field began with proof-of-concept fabrication of HeLa/hydrogel constructs and comparison with two-dimensional culture [32], and then expanded toward EMT modeling and pathway inhibition [64], bioink rheology and cytocompatibility optimization [65], spheroid-laden scaffold construction [66], and finally spatially resolved analysis of oxygen and diffusion within the printed tumor microenvironment [67]. Across these studies, polymeric materials were not passive carriers. Their rheology determined printability and shear exposure; their crosslinking mechanisms stabilized the printed architecture; their stiffness and biochemical composition influenced cell survival, spheroid formation, and cell–matrix interaction; and their permeability regulated the transport of nutrients, oxygen, metabolites, and drug molecules. Therefore, the main advantage of polymers in 3D-bioprinted cervical cancer models lies in their tunable balance between processability and biological relevance. By adjusting polymer type, concentration, blending ratio, crosslinking strategy, viscosity, degradation behavior, and bioactive components, polymeric bioinks provide a controllable matrix framework for constructing reproducible cervical tumor models that are more physiologically informative than two-dimensional culture while remaining more experimentally tractable than animal models.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
section: 2. Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management > 2.4. Patient-Specific Anatomical Models and Educational Guidance Tools
text: In addition to therapeutic devices and in vitro tumor models, polymer-based additive manufacturing has also been applied to patient-specific anatomical visualization and educational guidance in cervical cancer. This application is clinically relevant because cervical cancer management requires accurate understanding of the spatial relationship among the cervix, uterus, tumor mass, vaginal fornix, parametrial tissues, bladder, rectum, and pelvic sidewall. Although CT and MRI provide essential diagnostic information, their two-dimensional display may be difficult for patients, trainees, and even multidisciplinary teams to interpret intuitively. Physical 3D-printed models can therefore serve as tangible tools for surgical planning, procedural simulation, patient education, and interprofessional communication.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
section: 2. Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management > 2.4. Patient-Specific Anatomical Models and Educational Guidance Tools
text: Baek et al. reported one of the earliest applications of patient-specific 3D printing in early-stage cervical cancer management [68]. In their case report, morphometric data were extracted from CT images to fabricate a physical model of the uterus, cervix, and tumor. The model was used during consultation with a young patient who initially wished to preserve fertility, and it helped her understand the tumor extent and treatment options before choosing radical hysterectomy. The model also supported surgical planning by helping the team evaluate tumor shape, location, and resection margins. This study showed that 3D-printed anatomical models may contribute not only to physician-side planning, but also to patient-centered decision-making.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
section: 2. Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management > 2.4. Patient-Specific Anatomical Models and Educational Guidance Tools
text: The educational value of 3D printing was further illustrated by Bartellas et al., who developed a hemorrhagic cervical cancer model for postgraduate gynecological simulation training [69]. Unlike patient-specific surgical models, this model was designed as a reusable teaching tool for practicing clinical recognition and management of cervical tumor bleeding. Campelo et al. extended this concept to radiation oncology by developing a multi-material modular pelvic phantom for intracavitary and interstitial high-dose-rate brachytherapy training [70]. By simulating pelvic organs and cervical tumor conditions with different printed materials, the phantom provided a structured environment for teaching applicator placement and interstitial needle procedures without exposing patients to trainee-related procedural risk. More recently, Scherer-Quenzer et al. evaluated individualized 3D-printed cervical cancer models across FIGO stages I–III and reported their perceived value for examination, diagnosis, treatment planning, and multidisciplinary communication [71]. This study is important because it moved beyond single-case demonstration and assessed how different medical disciplines may use patient-specific models in gynecologic oncology.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
section: 2. Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management > 2.4. Patient-Specific Anatomical Models and Educational Guidance Tools
text: Overall, 3D-printed anatomical and educational tools occupy a complementary position in cervical cancer management. They do not directly treat tumors and should not be overinterpreted as evidence-based therapeutic interventions. Their value lies in improving spatial comprehension, procedural training, treatment discussion, and communication among clinicians and patients. From a materials perspective, printable polymers and resins are particularly suitable for this application because they enable low-cost fabrication, rapid model production, color-coded anatomy, variable stiffness, and repeatable training models. Future studies should focus less on demonstrating visual feasibility and more on measurable outcomes, such as training performance, decision quality, patient understanding, procedural accuracy, workflow efficiency, and cost-effectiveness.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
text: Polymer-based additive manufacturing is emerging as a versatile enabling technology for cervical-cancer-related management. Current evidence indicates that its value is not limited to the fabrication of isolated devices, but extends across several interconnected application domains, including brachytherapy assistance, therapeutic scaffolds and local delivery systems, bioprinted cervical cancer research platforms, and patient-specific anatomical models for education, planning, and communication. Across these scenarios, the central contribution of additive manufacturing lies in its ability to translate imaging data, anatomical requirements, and material design into customized three-dimensional structures. This is particularly relevant to cervical cancer, where disease management is strongly affected by complex pelvic anatomy, heterogeneous tumor geometry, cervicovaginal tissue characteristics, and the need for precise local intervention.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
text: In brachytherapy, 3D-printed polymeric devices have shown clear procedural relevance. Patient-specific templates, applicator accessories, and needle-guidance systems can convert preoperative imaging and treatment plans into physical tools that improve anatomical adaptation and needle-placement reproducibility. Printable polymers are well suited to this role because they can be lightweight, low-cost, structurally precise, sterilizable, and compatible with CT- or MRI-based workflows. Therefore, in this field, polymers mainly contribute through geometric fidelity, workflow adaptability, and procedural safety rather than through direct biological activity. In therapeutic scaffold and local delivery systems, the function of polymers is more biologically active. Polyurethane implants, chitosan-based microsphere composites, Pluronic F127/alginate hydrogels, polycaprolactone-based nanoparticles, and bioadhesive cellulose-derived films illustrate how polymeric systems can be engineered to provide mechanical support, local retention, controlled release, mucoadhesion, swelling, degradation, and tissue-interface regulation. These properties are highly relevant to the cervicovaginal environment, where fluid drainage, mucus turnover, tissue softness, acidic pH, and anatomical variability can compromise conventional formulations. In this domain, polymer-based additive manufacturing provides a route to integrate anatomical conformity with localized therapeutic function.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
text: In bioprinted cervical cancer models, polymeric bioinks serve as artificial extracellular matrix platforms. Alginate, gelatin, fibrinogen, Matrigel-containing hydrogels, hydroxyethylcellulose, and alginate–gelatin systems have been used to support HeLa cell printing, spheroid formation, EMT modeling, drug-response testing, and quantitative analysis of oxygen and molecular diffusion. Here, the polymer matrix is not merely a structural support; it defines printability, shear exposure, cell viability, stiffness, permeability, matrix interaction, and long-term culture behavior. These models remain simplified compared with patient tumors, but they offer controllable platforms for studying cervical cancer biology under defined three-dimensional conditions. In anatomical models and educational guidance tools, polymer-based printing provides a low-risk and practical approach for improving visualization, training, and communication. Rigid and flexible resins, multi-material phantoms, and color-coded anatomical models can represent patient-specific tumor anatomy, pelvic organs, procedural pathways, and training scenarios. Their main value lies in spatial comprehension, patient-centered explanation, procedural rehearsal, and trainee education. Although these tools do not directly improve tumor control, they may support better decision-making and safer clinical workflows.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
text: To facilitate cross-study comparison, the representative literature is systematically summarized in Table 1 according to application category, polymer composition, key contribution, major limitations, and translational stage. Collectively, these studies encompass four major cervical-cancer-related applications of polymer-based additive manufacturing: brachytherapy guidance, therapeutic scaffolds and local delivery, bioprinted tumor models, and anatomical or educational models. The available evidence reveals a clear difference in translational maturity among these applications. Brachytherapy-guidance devices have achieved the greatest clinical proximity, with several studies demonstrating feasibility, procedural reproducibility, and potential dosimetric benefits. In contrast, therapeutic scaffolds remain predominantly preclinical, while bioprinted cervical tumor models are still largely restricted to in vitro research. Anatomical and educational models have shown practical value for visualization, training, and clinical communication, but their impact on objective clinical outcomes remains insufficiently established. Collectively, these findings indicate that the major strength of polymer-based additive manufacturing lies in combining material tunability with patient-specific structural design, although further standardized validation is required before broader clinical translation.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
text: Future development should move from feasibility demonstration toward application-specific validation: For brachytherapy, the next priority is not simply printing more individualized templates, but establishing standardized image-to-print workflows, quality-control criteria, sterilization protocols, mechanical accuracy testing, and prospective clinical evaluation. Polymeric materials used for this purpose should be assessed not only for print fidelity, but also for biocompatibility, sterilization tolerance, dimensional stability, imaging compatibility, and radiation-related safety. Further integration with MRI-guided adaptive brachytherapy, automated treatment planning, and artificial-intelligence-assisted trajectory design may expand the role of 3D-printed polymeric devices in complex primary and recurrent cervical cancer.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
text: For therapeutic scaffolds and local delivery systems, the key challenge is biological translation. Future polymeric scaffolds should be designed according to the specific clinical scenario rather than as generic drug carriers. Post-conization implants, cervicovaginal mucosal delivery systems, postoperative recurrence-prevention platforms, radiosensitizer depots, and immunomodulatory local delivery systems may require very different material properties. Important design parameters include elasticity, degradation rate, drug-loading method, release kinetics, mucoadhesion, swelling behavior, local immune compatibility, and reproductive safety. In this context, biodegradable and bioadhesive polymers, stimuli-responsive hydrogels, microsphere-loaded composites, and multi-layered scaffolds may provide more clinically relevant platforms than single-function materials.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
text: For bioprinted research platforms, future progress should focus on improving biological representativeness. Current cervical cancer models are mostly based on HeLa cells and relatively simple hydrogel matrices. More advanced systems should incorporate patient-derived cervical cancer cells, organoid-like epithelial structures, cancer-associated fibroblasts, endothelial cells, immune components, extracellular matrix gradients, and controllable oxygen or drug-diffusion profiles. Polymer design will be central to this process because bioink stiffness, degradability, ligand presentation, porosity, and permeability directly affect tumor cell behavior. A major future direction is the construction of standardized yet customizable polymeric bioinks that can support disease modeling, drug screening, radiotherapy-response testing, and personalized treatment evaluation.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
text: For anatomical and educational tools, broader implementation will depend on whether 3D-printed models can demonstrate measurable benefits. Future studies should assess objective outcomes such as trainee performance, procedural accuracy, planning time, patient understanding, informed consent quality, multidisciplinary communication, and cost-effectiveness. Multi-material polymer printing may allow models with more realistic tactile properties, flexible cervicovaginal anatomy, puncture-compatible tissues, bleeding simulation, and replaceable tumor modules. These models may be particularly useful in gynecologic oncology training, brachytherapy education, rare anatomy simulation, and patient-specific preoperative planning.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
text: From a broader materials perspective, the future of polymer-based additive manufacturing in cervical cancer will likely depend on four directions. First, printable polymers must become more clinically standardized, with clearer information on sterilization, mechanical performance, degradation products, and regulatory classification. Second, multi-material and multi-functional printing should be used to integrate mechanical support, drug release, imaging visibility, and biological interaction within the same construct. Third, digital workflows should be linked more closely with clinical imaging, treatment planning systems, and patient-specific anatomical data. Fourth, translational studies should include clinically meaningful endpoints rather than only technical feasibility or morphological similarity.

title: Polymer-Based Additive Manufacturing in Cervical Cancer Management: A Review.
text: In the long term, polymer-based additive manufacturing may support a more personalized model of cervical cancer management. A single patient-specific workflow could theoretically connect MRI- or CT-derived anatomy, individualized brachytherapy guidance, customized local drug delivery, ex vivo bioprinted tumor testing, and patient-specific educational models. This vision remains distant, but it illustrates the broader potential of polymers as adaptable, printable, and functionally tunable materials. The most realistic path forward is not to present 3D printing as a replacement for established cervical cancer treatment, but to develop polymer-based additive manufacturing as a complementary technology that improves precision, local functionality, experimental modeling, and clinical communication.

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
text: This study aimed to evaluate the impact of rectal gas evacuation on organ‐at‐risk (OAR) volumes, dose‐volume histogram (DVH) parameters, and applicator displacement during cervical cancer brachytherapy.

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
text: Twenty‐one cervical cancer patients who received three‐dimensional brachytherapy at our center between November and December 2024 and presented with rectal gas were retrospectively included. Planning computed tomography (CT) images were acquired before and after rectal gas evacuation to evaluate changes in rectal and bladder volumes, as well as radiation dose variations to OARs (bladder, rectum, sigmoid, and small intestine). Dosimetric parameters analyzed comprised D 0.1cc, D 1cc, D 2cc, and D 5cc (minimum doses delivered to the most irradiated 0.1, 1, 2, and 5 cm3 of the OARs, respectively), as well as D max (maximum dose) and D mean (mean dose). Displacements of the applicator tip and cervical stopper were quantified using a coordinate system based on pelvic bony landmarks.

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
text: Rectal volume decreased by 40.1% after gas evacuation, while bladder volume increased by 18.2%. D 0.1cc, D 1cc, D 2cc, D 5cc, and D max in the rectum decreased significantly (P < 0.001) after gas evacuation, whereas no significant changes were observed in the DVH parameters of the other OARs. The mean displacements of the applicator tip and cervical stopper were 5.86 ± 3.64 mm and 4.23 ± 3.30 mm, respectively.

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
text: Rectal gas evacuation results in a statistically significant and clinically relevant reduction in rectal volume and rectal dose, underscoring its importance as a routine clinical procedure. However, as it may induce millimeter‐level applicator displacement with clinically measurable dosimetric consequences, careful monitoring is warranted, with post‐evacuation replanning or, if necessary, applicator adjustment.

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
text: Cervical cancer is the fourth most common malignancy among women worldwide. According to the statistical report released by the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), nearly 660 000 women were newly diagnosed with cervical cancer, and cervical cancer caused approximately 350 000 deaths globally in 2022. 1 Brachytherapy is a key component of definitive radiotherapy for patients with primary cervical cancer. It delivers a high dose of radiation directly to the primary tumor and surrounding high‐risk regions, resulting in a higher tumor control rate while sparing normal tissues. 2 , 3 However, complete sparing of adjacent organs is not always feasible, particularly for radiosensitive organs such as the rectum. Rectal dosimetric accuracy is highly influenced by anatomical variability. Volume changes in the bowels due to rectal gas are a major source of dosimetric uncertainty. Clinical data have shown that rectal gas is present in approximately 24% of patients with cervical cancer undergoing radiotherapy, resulting in increased rectal radiation exposure. 4 , 5 The National Comprehensive Cancer Network (NCCN) guidelines recommend maintaining rectal D 2cc below 65–75 Gy. 6 Higher rectal D 2cc values are associated with an increased cumulative incidence of rectal treatment‐related events. Values exceeding 75 Gy are generally considered unacceptably high and may increase the risk of intestinal fistula. 7 , 8

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
text: Currently, two main clinical strategies are employed to minimize rectal radiation exposure: reducing rectal volume through enemas and increasing the anatomical space between the rectum and target area by hydrogel injection or placement of an adjustable balloon. 9 , 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 However, these conventional methods are technically complex and invasive, potentially increasing patient discomfort and the risk of procedure‐related complications. In this context, image‐guided monitoring and evacuation of rectal gas during brachytherapy may provide a practical and effective method to improve rectal dosimetry accuracy. Several preliminary studies have demonstrated that rectal gas evacuation can significantly reduce rectal radiation exposure, thereby lowering the risk of grade 2–4 rectal treatment‐related events. 15 , 16 However, these studies have limitations. They compared only the changes in rectal dose‐volume histogram (DVH) parameters before and after gas evacuation, without comprehensively evaluating concurrent changes in rectal and bladder volumes or the potential impact on applicator position.

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
text: Given these limitations, this study aimed to systematically assess changes in rectal and bladder volumes and corresponding DVH parameters before and after rectal gas evacuation to evaluate its impact on organs at risk (OARs). Additionally, the effect of gas evacuation on applicator displacement was investigated. These findings may inform the development of more precise and clinically feasible strategies for rectal protection in cervical cancer brachytherapy.

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
text: This retrospective study was approved by the institutional review board (Approval ID: CZLS2023085‐A). The requirement for informed consent was waived by the institutional review board due to the retrospective nature of the study. All patient data were fully de‐identified prior to analysis, and the study was conducted in accordance with institutional data protection policies and the Declaration of Helsinki. Between November and December 2024, a total of 130 patients with cervical cancer underwent high‐dose‐rate (HDR) brachytherapy at our center. Rectal gas was identified in 29 patients. Of these 29 patients, 25 underwent rectal gas evacuation, whereas the remaining four declined the procedure due to personal preference (e.g., hemorrhoid‐related discomfort) or other clinical considerations. Four of the 25 patients were subsequently excluded: one due to applicator repositioning and three because of incomplete imaging data. Ultimately, 21 patients were included in the analysis (Figure 1). Among them, 17 patients underwent a single gas evacuation procedure and four patients underwent two procedures. Baseline patient characteristics are summarized in Table 1. All patients received external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) with a total dose of 45 Gy in 25 fractions, combined with concurrent weekly cisplatin monotherapy (40 mg/m2, 4–5 cycles).

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
section: MATERIALS AND METHODS > Brachytherapy procedure > Patient preparation and imaging
text: Before brachytherapy, patients were instructed to empty their bladder and rectum. An indwelling Foley catheter was then placed with the patient in the lithotomy position. The Fletcher Williamson Asia Pacific applicator set was inserted based on pre‐brachytherapy diagnostic computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and gynecological examination. When clinically indicated, interstitial needles were used to optimize target dose coverage. For treatment planning, an initial planning CT scan with a slice thickness of 3 mm was acquired on a CT simulator (Philips Brilliance Big Bore, Version 3.5.4) from the iliac crest to the ischial tuberosity with the applicator in situ. No slice thickness reduction or secondary image reconstruction was applied. When rectal gas was detected on the initial planning CT scan, evacuation was performed using a disposable enema wash package. The enema tube was inserted 15–30 cm into the rectum via the anus and removed after gas evacuation. A repeat CT scan was subsequently obtained using the same slice thickness (3 mm) as the initial planning CT and was used for final treatment planning. The indwelling Foley catheter remained clamped during the interval between the two CT acquisitions to maintain bladder filling. All patients tolerated the procedure without reported discomfort.

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
section: MATERIALS AND METHODS > Brachytherapy procedure > Target and OAR delineation
text: CT images acquired before and after gas evacuation were imported into the Oncentra Brachy planning system (Elekta, Version 4.6.0). The high‐risk clinical target volume (HR‐CTV) and OARs were delineated on both image sets by a single experienced radiation oncologist in accordance with the ICRU Report No. 89 and the IBS‐GEC ESTRO‐ABS guidelines. 17 The HR‐CTV encompassed the entire cervix and residual gross tumor. OARs included the bladder, rectum, sigmoid, and small intestine. The bladder was delineated from the dome to the proximal urethra, encompassing all identifiable bladder wall structures. The rectum was delineated from the superior margin of the anal canal to the rectosigmoid junction, following the outer rectal wall. The sigmoid was delineated from the rectosigmoid junction to the level at which the uterine body was no longer visible. The small intestine was delineated to include the intestinal loops and mesentery, extending to the superior margin of the uterine body. In routine clinical practice, final treatment planning was performed based on post‐gas evacuation images.

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
section: MATERIALS AND METHODS > Brachytherapy procedure > Treatment planning and optimization
text: Brachytherapy planning was performed by a single experienced medical physicist on pre‐ and post‐evacuation CT image sets to ensure accurate and consistent applicator reconstruction. All plans were prescribed 600 cGy to the HR‐CTV. Importantly, each plan was independently reoptimized. Optimal treatment parameters were achieved through graphical optimization or manual adjustment of source dwell patterns (e.g., times and positions). Dose constraints recommended by the EMBRACE II study were followed. 18 Treatments were delivered using the Flexitron HDR afterloader (Elekta AB, Stockholm, Sweden) with an Ir‐192 source.

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
text: DVH parameters before and after rectal gas evacuation were extracted, including HR‐CTV D90% and D 98% (doses received by at least 90% and 98% of the HR‐CTV, respectively); OARs D 0.1cc, D 1cc, D 2cc, and D 5cc (minimum doses to the most irradiated 0.1 cm3, 1 cm3, 2 cm3, and 5 cm3 of each OAR, respectively); and D max, D mean, as well as rectal and bladder volumes. The time interval between the two CT scans (Time_interval) was also recorded.

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
section: MATERIALS AND METHODS > Factors associated with post‐evacuation bladder volume
text: Univariate and multivariate regression models were constructed to assess the effects of age, bladder volume before gas evacuation (Pre_volume), and the time interval between the two scans (Time_interval) on the bladder volume after gas evacuation (Post_volume). The multivariate regression model was defined as follows: Post_volume=β0+β1Age+β2Pre_volume+β3Time_interval+ε where β0 is the intercept, β1 to β3 are the regression coefficients for the independent variables, and ε is the error term.

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
section: MATERIALS AND METHODS > Coordinate system definition and applicator displacement assessment
text: A bone‐based coordinate system was established individually for each patient using pelvic landmarks (e.g., the pubic symphysis and bilateral anterior superior iliac spines). 19 , 20 This system ensured stable and reproducible quantification of applicator displacement within the same patient and treatment fraction. Different patients, as well as different fractions within the same patient, were analyzed using independent coordinate systems. The procedure was performed as follows. First, the coordinates of pelvic landmarks on CT images before and after gas evacuation were recorded. Next, rigid registration of these landmarks was performed to minimize global positional deviations caused by patient repositioning or interscan variations. A local coordinate system was then established after gas evacuation, with the x‐, y‐, z‐axes oriented in the left–right, cranial–caudal, and ventral–dorsal directions, respectively. The anatomical position of the sacrum before and after gas evacuation was used to validate the accuracy of coordinate system registration, ensuring that deviations remained within an acceptable threshold (< 2–3 mm). 21

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
section: MATERIALS AND METHODS > Coordinate system definition and applicator displacement assessment
text: As shown in Table 1, applicators used in this study were classified into five types: types 1–3 included a tandem, whereas types 4–5 did not. Accordingly, displacement assessment was tailored to the applicator configuration. For applicators containing a tandem (types 1–3), the “tip” was defined as the distal end of the tandem. In addition, the midpoint of the cervical stopper was recorded both before and after gas evacuation. For applicators without a tandem (types 4–5), the “tip” was defined as the distal end of the applicator component (e.g., vaginal cylinder or interstitial needle) that was closest to the geometric center of the HR‐CTV. Coordinates of these key positions were evaluated within the registered coordinate system to accurately quantify applicator displacement before and after gas evacuation.

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
text: Statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS version 26.0. Categorical variables were presented as counts (n) and percentages (%). Continuous variables were presented as mean ± standard deviation. Differences in DVH parameters before and after gas evacuation were analyzed using the Wilcoxon signed‐rank test, given the paired design and the non‐normal distribution of the data. These parameters were predefined and limited in number, and the analyses focused on planned within‐subject comparisons of primary endpoints. Therefore, formal adjustment for multiple comparisons (e.g., Bonferroni or Holm correction) was not applied. Due to the retrospective nature of the study, no a priori sample size or power calculation was performed, and the sample size was determined by the number of eligible patients meeting the predefined inclusion criteria during the study period. Model validity was assessed by evaluating multicollinearity using variance inflation factors (VIF). A p‐value less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
text: A total of 21 patients were included in the study, and their baseline characteristics are shown in Table 1. Rectal gas was predominantly observed during the early fractions of brachytherapy (the first and second fractions). Gas evacuation was required in 25 treatment fractions, resulting in 50 treatment plans (25 before and 25 after gas evacuation). The tandem was employed in 84% of all treatment procedures, with the specific applicator configurations detailed in Table 1. The mean time interval between the pre‐ and post‐gas evacuation CT scans was 453.56 ± 220.09 seconds.

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
section: RESULTS > Volumetric and dosimetric changes before and after rectal gas evacuation
text: Figure 2 illustrates the comparison of CT images before and after rectal gas evacuation. HR‐CTV volume showed no significant difference before and after gas evacuation (30.88 ± 20.07 vs. 30.92 ± 20.09 cm3, P > 0.05). Rectal volume decreased significantly by 25.11 ± 16.26 cm3 (62.67 ± 23.26 vs. 37.56 ± 13.10 cm3), whereas bladder volume increased significantly by 16.22 ± 17.09 cm3 (88.96 ± 26.68 vs. 105.18 ± 37.21 cm3). No significant differences were observed in HR‐CTV D 90% or D 98% (D 90%: 600.46 ± 0.22 vs. 600.45 ± 0.20 cGy; D 98%: 478.51 ± 22.06 vs. 473.97 ± 38.38 cGy). In the rectum, D 0.1cc, D 1cc, D 2cc, D 5cc, and D max decreased significantly (P < 0.001), while the reduction in D mean was not significant (P = 0.109). For the bladder, all DVH parameters except D 5cc decreased slightly without statistical significance (P > 0.05). D 5cc for the sigmoid colon and D mean for the small intestine decreased, whereas other parameters exhibited minor increases, all without statistical significance (Figure 3).

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
section: RESULTS > Predictors of post‐evacuation bladder volume
text: Univariate regression analysis revealed a significantly positive correlation between the bladder volume before gas evacuation (Pre_volume) and the bladder volume after gas evacuation (Post_volume) (P < 0.001). No statistically significant correlations were observed for the other variables, including age (Age) and the time interval between the two CT scans (Time_interval). The multivariate regression analysis confirmed that Pre_volume was the sole significant predictor of Post_volume (β2 = 1.304, P < 0.001). For every 1 cm3 increase in Pre_volume, Post_volume increased on average by 1.304 cm3. Age (β1= 0.108, P = 0.770) and Time_interval (β3= 0.017, P = 0.323) were not significant independent predictors of Post_volume (Table 2). The multivariate regression model was expressed as Post_volume = –24.894 + 0.108 Age + 1.304 Pre_volume + 0.017 Time_interval. The model demonstrated a high goodness of fit (R 2 = 0.834, adjusted R 2 = 0.81) and was statistically significant [F(3,21) = 35.1, P < 0.001]. All predictors showed VIF values below 5, indicating no significant multicollinearity.

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
section: RESULTS > Applicator displacement following rectal gas evacuation
text: After coordinate system registration, the sacral displacement error between the pre‐ and post‐gas evacuation CT scans ranged from 0.51 to 2.84 mm, with a mean of 1.50 ± 0.68 mm. These values were within the target registration error (TRE) range (< 2–3 mm) recommended in the TG‐132 report. 21 The displacement of the applicator tip ranged from 0.99 to 15.44 mm, with a mean of 5.86 ± 3.64 mm. The displacement in the ventral–dorsal direction was greater than that in the left–right and cranial–caudal directions, predominantly in the dorsal direction (16/25, 64%). In the left–right direction, displacement occurred more frequently toward the left (17/25, 68%), whereas in the cranial–caudal direction, displacement was mainly caudal (14/25, 56%). For the cervical stopper, displacement ranged from 0.67 to 12.26 mm, with a mean of 4.23 ± 3.30 mm. Cranial–caudal displacement was greater than that in the left–right and ventral–dorsal directions, with caudal movement predominating (14/21, 66.67%). In the left–right direction, displacement was more often toward the left (13/21, 61.90%), while in the ventral–dorsal direction, displacement was mainly ventral (12/21, 57.14%). Detailed displacement values for the applicator tip and cervical stopper in each direction are provided in Table 3, and the corresponding three‐dimensional displacement vectors are illustrated in Figure 4.

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
text: In this retrospective study, we evaluated the effects of rectal gas evacuation on radiation doses to the HR‐CTV and OARs, organ volume, and applicator position in cervical cancer brachytherapy. Gas evacuation significantly reduced rectal volume and rectal dose. However, it was also accompanied by bladder volume changes and applicator displacement, which warrant careful attention in clinical practice. This study demonstrated that gas evacuation significantly reduced rectal volume (from 62.67 ± 23.26 to 37.56 ± 13.10 cm3) and rectal DVH parameters (D 0.1cc, D 1cc, D 2cc, D 5cc, and D max) (Figure 3). These results align with the observations of Feree et al. 15 and Vergalasova et al. 16 According to the rectal complication model based on the EMBRACE study, the complication risk decreased from 9.5% to 6.9% after evacuation, underscoring the potential clinical value of this procedure in reducing rectal injury. 15

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
text: This study showed that bladder volume increased significantly after gas evacuation, whereas bladder DVH parameters (D 0.1cc, D 1cc, D 2cc, D max, and D mean) were slightly reduced. These findings are consistent with those reported by Feree et al. 15 and Vergalasova et al. 16 However, Sabater et al. observed an increase in bladder dose after gas evacuation, a discrepancy potentially attributable to the fact that all patients in that study had undergone prior surgery. 22 Previous studies primarily focused on changes in bladder dose before and after gas evacuation, without considering changes in bladder volume. Evidence regarding the relationship between bladder volume and radiation dose remains conflicting: most researchers suggest that increased bladder filling reduces bladder radiation dose, 23 , 24 while others have reported an increase. 25 , 26 In brachytherapy, OAR dose is strongly determined by spatial geometry relative to the applicator. Changes in bladder volume can alter both bladder morphology and its position relative to the applicator, concurrently with applicator displacement that can be induced by rectal gas evacuation. Clinically, bladder irrigation is typically performed twice to maintain consistency: before the planning CT scan and again immediately prior to treatment delivery. In the present study, the average time interval between CT scans before and after gas evacuation was only 453.56 ± 220.09 seconds.

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
text: During this brief period, only gas evacuation was performed, with no additional bladder management. Nevertheless, the regression model established in the present study showed that final bladder volume was closely related to baseline volume. Based on these findings, we recommend performing bladder irrigation after gas evacuation to maintain bladder volume consistency and minimize its impact on dosimetry.

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
text: This study is the first to quantitatively assess displacements of the applicator tip and cervical stopper in a three‐dimensional coordinate system before and after gas evacuation. The mean displacement of the applicator tip was 5.86 ± 3.64 mm, with larger movements observed along the cranial–caudal direction and ventral–dorsal direction than in the left–right direction. The position of the cervical stopper was relatively stable due to packing, with a smaller overall displacement (4.23 ± 3.30 mm) compared with the applicator tip. Its movement was more pronounced in the cranial–caudal direction, predominantly toward the caudal direction (14/21, 66.67%). This finding is consistent with previous studies on inter‐fraction uterine and cervical motion, which reported that uterine displacement was larger than the cervical displacement and was more pronounced in the ventral–dorsal and cranial–caudal directions. 27 Despite applicator fixation, intrapelvic pressure and structural changes caused by rectal gas evacuation may still induce multi‐directional displacements, including left–right, cranial–caudal, and ventral–dorsal shifts. Due to the steep dose gradients in HDR brachytherapy, even millimeter‐level deviations can meaningfully alter dose distribution. Sandun et al. simulated caudal applicator displacement while maintaining dwell times and showed that shifts exceeding 5 mm led to clinically meaningful reductions in HR‐CTV D90%, accompanied by an increase in rectal dose.

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
text: 28 In our study, although the mean tip displacement after evacuation was 5.86 mm, all post‐evacuation plans were individually reoptimized, restoring HR‐CTV D90% to the prescribed dose level. Therefore, applicator displacement on the order of 5 mm may be considered a clinically relevant threshold, and image‐guided reassessment with timely replanning is recommended whenever displacement approaches or exceeds this value. This study has several limitations. First, it was a single‐center, retrospective study with a relatively small sample size, which may limit the generalizability of the findings. Validation in multicenter studies with larger cohorts is warranted to confirm the applicability of these results. Second, the use of various applicator types among patients may have interfered with the assessment of certain dosimetric parameters when evaluating applicator displacement.

title: Impact of rectal gas evacuation on dosimetry and applicator displacement in cervical cancer brachytherapy.
text: Rectal gas evacuation results in a statistically significant and clinically relevant reduction in rectal volume and rectal dose, underscoring its importance as a routine clinical procedure. However, as it may induce millimeter‐level applicator displacement with clinically measurable dosimetric consequences, careful monitoring is warranted, with post‐evacuation replanning or, if necessary, applicator adjustment.
