title: Clinical evaluation and regression test of a commercial deep-learning auto-segmentation model.
text: This retrospective study was approved by the institutional review board of UT MD Anderson Cancer Center (protocol # RCR03‐0400) and conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. The requirement for informed consent was waived owing to the retrospective study design.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: Imaging-guided interventional radiotherapy (IG-IRT) is the standard of care for locally advanced cervical cancer but remains time-consuming and operator-dependent. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising tool to improve efficiency and reproducibility.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: A systematic review was conducted according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines, searching PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science for studies published between 2010 and 2026 investigating AI-based imaging applications in cervical IRT. Eligible studies included original research evaluating segmentation (targets and organ at risk), planning, reconstruction, image registration and applicator selection.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: Fifty-two studies were included. Deep learning–based segmentation showed variable performance across anatomical structures and studies, with Dice coefficients approaching or exceeding 0.90 for some organs at risk and target volumes in the best-performing models. Individual studies reported shorter processing times, reduced contouring variability, accurate applicator reconstruction, and potential support for applicator selection. However, the substantial methodological and clinical heterogeneity precluded direct comparisons among AI approaches.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: The available studies suggest that AI may support the automation of selected workflow steps and assist treatment-related decision-making in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy. While several applications have achieved high technical performance, most remain at the proof-of-concept stage, and robust external validation and prospective clinical evaluation are needed before routine clinical adoption.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: Cervical cancer represents a significant global health burden and remains among the leading causes of cancer-related morbidity and mortality in women worldwide (1, 2). In patients with locally advanced disease, the standard of care consists of external beam radiotherapy (EBRT) with concurrent chemotherapy ± immunotherapy followed by an interventional radiotherapy (IRT, modern brachytherapy) boost (3–5). IRT allows the delivery of highly conformal radiation doses directly to the tumor while sparing surrounding organs at risk (OARs), owing to the steep dose gradients inherent to intracavitary and interstitial techniques (6). Over the past decades, cervical IRT has evolved from two-dimensional planning to image-guided IRT (IG-IRT). In this context, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has emerged as the gold standard for target delineation due to its superior soft tissue contrast, enabling accurate definition of tumor volumes such as the gross tumor volume (GTV) and high-risk clinical target volume (HR-CTV) (7, 8). The introduction of MRI-guided IRT has significantly improved treatment outcomes, including better local control and reduced treatment-related toxicity compared to conventional approaches (9).

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: Despite these advances, MRI-guided IRT remains a complex and opera-tor-dependent procedure. Critical steps such as target delineation, segmentation of OARs, applicator reconstruction, and treatment planning are time-consuming and subject to inter- and intra-observer variability (10, 11). Furthermore, anatomical changes, including organ motion and applicator displacement, may occur during treatment, potentially affecting dose distribution and treatment accuracy (12). These limitations highlight the need for advanced tools to improve reproducibility, efficiency, and standardization in clinical workflows. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative approach in oncological imaging, with applications spanning lesion detection, segmentation, and quantitative image analysis (13, 14). In radiotherapy, deep learning models—particularly convolutional neural networks (CNN)—have demonstrated high accuracy in automatic segmentation of target volumes and OARs, reducing contouring time and variability (15, 16). In the context of cervical IRT, AI-based methods are increasingly being explored to automate key steps of the workflow, including segmentation, applicator reconstruction, and treatment planning optimization (17).

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: Beyond the AI applications currently investigated in cervical IG-IRT, radiomics represents a promising and potentially relevant approach for extracting quantitative imaging biomarkers and supporting treatment personalization (18–20). However, no studies included in the present review directly evaluated radiomics applications in this specific clinical setting; therefore, its potential role and clinical value should be specifically investigated in future studies rather than considered a currently validated approach. However, despite promising results, the clinical implementation of AI in cervical IRT remains limited. Current studies are often retrospective, based on small datasets, and lack external validation (17, 21). Additionally, challenges related to data heterogeneity, standardization of imaging protocols, and model generalizability must be ad-dressed before widespread clinical adoption can be achieved (22). The aim of this systematic review is not only to summarize current applications of artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical IRT, but also to critically assess their level of clinical maturity, distinguish technical performance from demonstrated clinical benefit, and identify the evidence gaps that currently limit their translation into routine clinical practice.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
section: Materials and methods > Study design and reporting standards
text: This systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA 2020) guidelines (23). The methodology was defined a priori to ensure transparency, reproducibility, and methodological rigor. The aim of this review was to investigate the current applications of artificial intelligence in cancer imaging within the context of image-guided cervical IRT, with a focus on segmentation (targets and OARs), planning, reconstruction, image registration and applicator selection. The review protocol was not prospectively registered. Nevertheless, the eligibility criteria, study-selection process, data items, and methodological assessment procedures were defined before the formal screening and data-extraction stages.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: Studies were selected according to predefined inclusion and exclusion criteria. Eligible studies included patients with cervical cancer undergoing image-guided interventional radiotherapy. For the purposes of this review, AI-based methods primarily included machine-learning and deep-learning approaches. Non-learning computational approaches, such as rule-based, heuristic, clustering, or optimization methods, were considered eligible only when they were explicitly developed and presented as part of an automated intelligent decision-support, planning, or reconstruction framework relevant to the cervical IG-IRT workflow. Simple deterministic automation without an AI, adaptive, predictive, or decision-support component was not considered enough for inclusion. Eligible approaches involved supervised or unsupervised machine-learning methods, artificial neural networks, convolutional neural networks, deep-learning architectures, transformer-based models, and related data-driven computational methods. These approaches could be applied directly to CT or MRI images or to imaging-derived features used for treatment-related prediction or decision support. Studies were required to evaluate at least one of the following predefined application domains: target or organ-at-risk segmentation, image registration, treatment planning or dose prediction/optimization, applicator or catheter reconstruction, or applicator/needle selection.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: Studies including mixed gynecological cancer populations were eligible only when patients with cervical cancer represented an explicitly identifiable subgroup and the investigated methodology was directly applicable to cervical IG-IRT. When cervical-specific outcome data could not be extracted separately, findings from mixed cohorts were retained only as supportive technical evidence and were not interpreted as cervical-cancer-specific estimates. Only original research articles written in English were included. Review articles, editorials, letters, and conference abstracts were excluded.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
section: Materials and methods > Information sources and search strategy
text: A comprehensive literature search was performed in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science. The search covered publications from January 2010 to May 2026, and the final search update was conducted in 31 May 2026. The search strategy was based on the same predefined core concepts across all three databases, namely artificial intelligence, cervical cancer, brachytherapy/interventional radiotherapy, and medical imaging. The same principal keywords and synonyms were used consistently across databases, while the search syntax and database-specific conventions were adapted according to the requirements of each platform. The core Boolean structure was as follows: (“artificial intelligence” OR “machine learning” OR “deep learning” OR “neural network”) AND (“cervical cancer” OR “cervix cancer”) AND (“brachytherapy” OR “image-guided brachytherapy” OR “interventional radiotherapy”) AND (“MRI” OR “magnetic resonance imaging” OR “CT” OR “computed tomography” OR “medical imaging”). This conceptual search structure was maintained across PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science, with minor adaptations in syntax as required by each database. No additional language filter was applied during the electronic search; English-language eligibility was assessed during the study-selection process. In addition, the reference lists of all included articles were manually screened to identify further relevant studies (Supplementary Table S1).

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: The selection process was carried out in two stages. Initially, titles and abstracts were independently screened by two reviewers to identify potentially eligible studies. Subsequently, the full texts of the selected articles were assessed for eligibility based on the predefined criteria. Any disagreements between reviewers were resolved through discussion, and when necessary, consultation with a third reviewer was undertaken to reach consensus. The overall study selection process was documented using a PRISMA flow diagram.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
section: Materials and methods > Data collection and data items
text: Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers using a standardized data extraction form to ensure consistency. For each included study, detailed information was collected regarding study characteristics, including authorship, year of publication and study design. Information on imaging modalities and AI methodologies was also extracted, including the type of imaging used (MRI, CT) and the specific AI approach applied. Performance metrics reported in the studies were recorded.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
section: Materials and methods > Risk of bias assessment
text: The methodological quality and risk of bias of the included studies were independently evaluated by two reviewers using prespecified task-specific frameworks. Studies of automated segmentation, applicator or catheter reconstruction, and image registration were appraised using the four-domain structure of QUADAS-2, supplemented by the AI-specific methodological considerations proposed by Sounderajah et al. as part of the QUADAS-AI initiative (24). The four original QUADAS-2 domains—patient selection, index test, reference standard, and flow and timing—were retained. The signalling questions were operationalized for AI-based imaging tasks in accordance with the AI-specific methodological considerations proposed within the QUADAS-AI framework (24). The patient-selection domain addressed the source, size, and quality of the input data, patient eligibility criteria, use of open-source datasets, reporting of training, validation, and test-set allocation, image preprocessing, and scanner information. The index-test domain assessed whether external validation was performed. The reference-standard domain assessed whether the reference standard was likely to correctly classify the target condition. The flow-and-timing domain assessed whether the time interval between the index test and the reference standard was appropriate.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
section: Materials and methods > Risk of bias assessment
text: Although segmentation, reconstruction, and image registration are not conventional diagnostic-accuracy tasks, this framework was selected because these studies compare AI-generated imaging outputs with clinician-defined or clinically approved reference standards and share methodological concerns related to input data, evaluation of the AI method, the appropriateness of the reference standard, and the relationship between the index test and reference standard. The resulting judgments were therefore interpreted as task-specific methodological assessments rather than formal diagnostic-accuracy assessments. Studies of treatment planning, dose prediction or optimization, and applicator selection were evaluated using the published 2025 version of PROBAST+AI (25). The four domains assessed were participants and data sources, predictors, outcome, and analysis. The corresponding PROBAST+AI signalling questions were applied to assess risk of bias and concerns regarding applicability. Domain-level judgments were assigned in accordance with the PROBAST+AI guidance. Assessments were performed independently by two reviewers, and disagreements were resolved through discussion or, when necessary, consultation with a third senior reviewer.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: The primary effect measures considered in this review were extracted according to the specific AI task under investigation. Segmentation studies were primarily evaluated using geometric metrics, including the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC), Hausdorff Distance/95th percentile Hausdorff Distance (HD/HD95), Average Surface Distance/Average Symmetric Surface Distance (ASD/ASSD), Mean Surface Distance (MSD), Jaccard Index (JI), Intersection over Union (IoU), Surface Dice, and other overlap-based measures. Registration studies were assessed using geometric agreement and deformation metrics, including Dice coefficient, Jaccard Index, Average Symmetric Surface Distance, Mean Distance Error, and Hausdorff Distance. Reconstruction studies were evaluated using geometric accuracy metrics, such as Dice coefficient, Hausdorff Distance, tip and shaft localization errors, reconstruction variability, and dwell position deviations.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: Planning studies were assessed using dosimetric and predictive metrics, including dose received by 90% of the target volume (D90), dose received by 98% of the target volume (D98), volume receiving 100% of the prescribed dose (V100), volume receiving 150% of the prescribed dose (V150), volume receiving 200% of the prescribed dose (V200), dose to the most exposed 2 cm³ (D2cc), dose to the most exposed 1 cm³ (D1cc), maximum dose (Dmax), Equivalent Dose in 2 Gy Fractions (EQD2), mean absolute error (MAE), mean squared error (MSE), gamma pass rate, and correlation coefficients. Applicator selection studies were evaluated using classification metrics, including accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, precision, F1-score, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), as well as dosimetric indicators of target coverage and organ-at-risk sparing. Reported values were extracted directly from the included studies and synthesized qualitatively according to the corresponding AI task. A qualitative synthesis of the results was performed. The included studies were analyzed descriptively, focusing on the clinical application of AI and its reported performance. A formal meta-analysis was not conducted. Instead, findings were summarized to identify common trends, strengths, and limitations in the current literature.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
section: Materials and methods > Assessment of reporting bias
text: Reporting bias and selective outcome reporting were assessed by comparing the outcomes specified in the methods and results sections of each included study and by evaluating the completeness of reporting of clinically relevant outcomes. Particular attention was paid to whether studies reported both technical performance metrics and clinically meaningful endpoints, such as dosimetric parameters, treatment planning outcomes, or physician acceptability assessments.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
section: Materials and methods > Certainty of evidence
text: Because the included studies evaluated heterogeneous technical tasks and outcomes, certainty was assessed separately for each application domain—segmentation, treatment planning, reconstruction, applicator selection, and image registration—rather than by combining all studies into a single certainty rating. Within each application domain, studies reporting conceptually related endpoints were considered as one body of evidence. These endpoints included geometric agreement for segmentation, reconstruction, and registration; dosimetric accuracy and plan quality for treatment-planning studies; and classification performance and dosimetric consequences for applicator-selection studies. A GRADE-informed approach was used to assess five domains: risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. Risk of bias was judged using the corresponding methodological assessment: the QUADAS-2 assessment supplemented by the AI-specific methodological considerations proposed within the QUADAS-AI framework for segmentation, reconstruction, and image-registration studies, and PROBAST+AI 2025 for planning and applicator-selection studies. Certainty was downgraded for risk of bias when important methodological limitations affected a substantial proportion of the contributing studies, particularly inappropriate patient selection, non-independent reference standards, data leakage, inadequate data partitioning, overfitting, or lack of independent evaluation.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
section: Materials and methods > Certainty of evidence
text: Inconsistency was judged according to the direction and magnitude of between-study variability in reported performance, considering differences in imaging modality, anatomical structure, AI architecture, reference standard, performance metric, and institutional setting. Because quantitative pooling was inappropriate, inconsistency was assessed qualitatively rather than using a I² statistic. Indirectness was considered present when the available evidence relied predominantly on surrogate technical metrics rather than clinical endpoints, included mixed gynecological populations without separately extractable cervical-cancer results, or was derived from narrowly selected single-center or single-vendor datasets that did not fully represent the intended clinical setting. Imprecision was judged from the number and size of the contributing studies, the amount of evaluation data, the width or availability of confidence intervals, and the stability of the reported performance estimates. Formal funnel-plot assessment was not performed because of the small number of studies within several application domains and the marked heterogeneity of outcomes and metrics. Publication bias was assessed qualitatively by considering the predominance of small, retrospective, single-center proof-of-concept studies, the availability of independent replications, and the possible underrepresentation of negative or inconclusive findings.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
section: Materials and methods > Certainty of evidence
text: Formal funnel-plot assessment was not performed because of the marked heterogeneity of the included endpoints and the limited number of studies within several application domains. Final certainty was categorized as high, moderate, low, or very low. No upgrading criteria were applied. The reasons for each final certainty rating were recorded by application domain in the corresponding Summary of Findings tables.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: The database search identified 353 records. After the removal of 127 duplicates, 226 records remained for title and abstract screening. Of these, 158 records were excluded because they did not meet the eligibility criteria or were not relevant to the review objective. The full texts of the remaining 68 articles were assessed for eligibility. Following full-text evaluation, 16 studies were excluded for specific reasons related to the predefined eligibility criteria, as detailed in the PRISMA flow diagram and Supplementary Table S2. Ultimately, 52 studies were included in the qualitative synthesis (26–77) (Figure 1).

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
section: Results > Study characteristics and results of individual studies > AI-based segmentation in high dose rate (HDR)-IRT for cervical cancer. > CTV segmentation
text: Automatic target-volume segmentation was investigated using CNN-, U-Net-, and transformer-based architectures for HR-CTV, CTV, and GTV delineation (27–29, 35, 37–39, 41, 45). Performance ranged from Dice coefficients of approximately 0.65–0.95. Among the reported results, the multimodal GSN framework achieved a Dice coefficient of 0.947 (39), while SPSeg-Dual achieved Dice coefficients ranging from 0.913 to 0.948 and showed statistically higher performance than nnU-Net and SAM-Med3D within that study (p < 0.001) (35). Significant improvements over comparator models were also reported for the dual-path CT/MRI CNN (p < 0.01) (27), ARGNet (p < 0.05) (41), and the cascaded MRI framework (p < 0.05) (45). Additional studies demonstrated promising performance using Mnet_IM (28), Diffusion-Weighted Imaging (DWI)-based U-Net ensembles (29), MRI-based nnU-Net (37), patient-specific adaptive models (38), and multimodal CT/MRI approaches (39).

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
section: Results > Study characteristics and results of individual studies > AI-based segmentation in high dose rate (HDR)-IRT for cervical cancer. > OAR segmentation
text: OAR auto-segmentation was evaluated using ResU-Net, nnU-Net, transfer-learning strategies, and attention-based U-Net architectures (32–34, 40, 49). Bladder segmentation generally showed higher reported Dice coefficients than the other evaluated organs, ranging from 0.92 to 0.96 across individual studies. Transfer learning significantly improved performance across bladder, rectum, sigmoid, and bowel structures after fine-tuning (p = 0.012–<0.001) (33). ResU-Net demonstrated significantly improved sigmoid dosimetry compared with standard U-Net (p < 0.05) (32). High geometric and dosimetric agreement with manual contours was also reported for nnU-Net–based approaches (34, 40). C2FAU-Net achieved a mean DSC of 89.7% while significantly reducing contouring time without clinically relevant dosimetric differences compared with manual contours (49).

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
section: Results > Study characteristics and results of individual studies > AI-based segmentation in high dose rate (HDR)-IRT for cervical cancer. > Combined CTV and OAR segmentation
text: Several studies simultaneously segmented target volumes and OARs using MDA-TransUNet, DCT-UNet, dual-stage CNN, DeepLabV3+/3D U-Net frameworks, large language model (LLM)-guided models, Prompt-ResUNet, AM-UNet, DSD-UNET, and SERes-U-Net architectures (26, 30, 31, 36, 42–44, 47, 48, 50). MDA-TransUNet achieved Dice values up to 94.5% for OARs and 82.4% for HR-CTV, with no significant dosimetric differences versus manual contours (26). DCT-UNet demonstrated performance comparable to human observers while substantially reducing contouring time (30). Significant improvements were reported for dual-stage CNN (p < 0.005) (31), LLM-guided segmentation (overall DSC p = 0.014, HD95 p < 0.001) (42), AM-UNet (p < 0.01–0.02) (47), SERes-U-Net (p = 0.012–0.047) (50), and 2.5D models for HR-CTV and intermediate risk clinical target volume (IR-CTV) segmentation (p = 0.031–0.001) (44). DeepLabV3+ and three-dimensional (3D) U-Net models reported favorable performance in internal and external validation cohorts, enabling online adaptive optimization with high target coverage (36). Prompt-ResUNet achieved Dice values of 0.92 for HR-CTV, 0.93 for bladder, and 0.87 for rectum, outperforming nnUNet and SAM-Med3D (43).

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
section: Results > Study characteristics and results of individual studies > AI-based segmentation in high dose rate (HDR)-IRT for cervical cancer. > Catheter segmentation
text: Catheter segmentation was addressed by Zaffino et al. using a 3D CNN on intraoperative MRI, achieving a mean Dice coefficient of 0.60 ± 0.17, a mean distance error of 2.0 ± 3.4 mm, and a false-negative detection rate of 1.5% (46). Among the segmentation approaches evaluated, individual studies reported promising performance for SPSeg-Dual in CTV/HR-CTV delineation (35), transfer-learning approaches in OAR segmentation (33), and AM-UNet, Prompt-ResUNet, and MDA-TransUNet in combined target and OAR segmentation (26, 43, 47). Within-study comparisons reported statistically significant improvements over selected benchmark architectures for SPSeg-Dual, transfer-learning frameworks, and AM-UNet (33, 35, 47). However, differences in datasets, anatomical targets, imaging modalities, comparators, and validation strategies preclude direct ranking of these architectures.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
section: Results > Study characteristics and results of individual studies > AI-based planning in HDR-IRT for cervical cancer
text: AI applications in cervical cancer interventional radiotherapy planning have focused on dose prediction, automated optimization, plan quality assurance, and adaptive planning. Multi-objective optimization with BRachytherapy via artificially Intelligent GOMEA-Heuristic based Treatment Planning (BRIGHT) improved protocol compliance, achieving 100% adherence to EMBRACE-II limits versus 88.9% in clinical plans and significantly better OAR sparing (p = 1.08 × 10-7) while maintaining comparable target coverage (p = 0.12) (51). Deep-learning frameworks were developed for plan approval prediction (52), voxel-wise dose prediction (53, 57, 59), dwell-time optimization (56, 58, 63), and independent plan verification (55), generally demonstrating high agreement with clinical plans. Dose prediction accuracy was particularly high for SE_AN, with mean absolute errors of 0.37 Gy for HR-CTV D90 and 0.23–0.28 Gy for OAR D2cc values (57), while attention-gated 3D U-Net models generated complete dose distributions within 5 seconds (53). Knowledge-based planning approaches reduced OAR doses by up to 10.7% for rectum D2cc and 10.3% for bladder D2cc (54), whereas automated planning systems generated clinically acceptable plans in 1.4–3.5 minutes with no significant differences in HR-CTV or OAR dosimetry compared with manual planning (58, 63).

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
section: Results > Study characteristics and results of individual studies > AI-based planning in HDR-IRT for cervical cancer
text: Fully automated adaptive planning further improved treatment quality, with automated plans preferred in 60/63 cases and achieving significantly lower bladder (p = 0.05) and rectum (p = 0.04) doses while increasing the proportion of patients reaching CTVHR D90 ≥ 90 Gy (14 vs 9 patients) (60). Similarly, the rule-based BiCycle system significantly reduced bladder, rectum, sigmoid, and bowel doses while being preferred by physicians in 75–76% of cases (62). Machine-learning quality-assurance tools based on overlap volume histogram (OVH) analysis (61), neural-network OAR dose prediction (64), and automated plan verification (55) also reported promising predictive performance in individual studies. Among the planning approaches evaluated, individual studies reported promising results for BRIGHT (51), automated adaptive planning systems (60, 62), and deep-learning-based dose-prediction and optimization frameworks (56–59, 63). Some studies reported clinically acceptable plans, improved OAR sparing, or shorter planning times compared with their respective conventional approaches. However, the heterogeneity of datasets, endpoints, comparators, and validation methods precludes direct comparisons or ranking of these approaches. Further prospective and independent external validation is required (Table 2).

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
section: Results > Study characteristics and results of individual studies > AI-based reconstruction in HDR-IRT for cervical cancer
text: AI-based image reconstruction studies, including more than 160 patients, have primarily focused on automated applicator, catheter, and needle digitization in CT- and MRI-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy. Several automated reconstruction studies reported submillimeter geometric accuracy and limited dosimetric differences compared with manual digitization. Thresholding and clustering algorithms achieved contour discrepancies of only 0.3 mm and dosimetric differences ≤ 1% in HDR tandem-and-ovoid applications (65), while deep learning–based approaches reported DSC values of 0.88–0.93, Hausdorff distances generally below 1 mm, and negligible differences in HR-CTV and OAR dose metrics (48, 66, 67, 69, 70). In a mixed gynecological cancer cohort that included patients with cervical cancer, MRI-based catheter reconstruction reduced reconstruction time from 46 ± 10 to 11 ± 1 minutes (68). Among the reconstruction approaches evaluated, individual studies reported promising performance for attention-gated CNN (69), nnU-Net-based models (70), and DSD-UNET approaches (48). These studies reported accurate automatic digitization and limited dosimetric differences compared with manual reconstruction. However, the absence of independent external validation and the heterogeneity of the evaluated tasks preclude conclusions regarding the relative superiority of these approaches (Table 3).

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
section: Results > Study characteristics and results of individual studies > AI-based applicator selection in HDR-IRT for cervical cancer
text: AI-based applicator selection studies included more than 260 patients and reported preliminary findings regarding the potential of machine learning to support applicator- and needle-selection decisions (71–74). In one study, a deep-learning approach achieved accuracies of 92.1–96.0% for selecting between Syed and tandem-and-ovoid applicators, 90.9% sensitivity, and 97.4% specificity (71). Machine-learning models for selecting intracavitary versus hybrid intracavitary/interstitial (IC/IS) techniques achieved accuracies up to 0.849 and AUCs of 0.903, outperforming conventional volumetric criteria, although without statistically significant differences (72). AI-assisted 3D-printed templates improved HR-CTV coverage, reduced bladder and rectum doses, and enhanced plan quality compared with free-hand insertion (73), while prospective validation demonstrated that machine learning (ML)-guided needle selection achieved 82.5% accuracy and reduced OAR doses by an average of 2.0 Gy (74). Among the approaches evaluated, individual studies reported promising performance for deep-learning-based applicator classification (70) and machine-learning-guided applicator or needle selection (72, 74). These findings suggest potential for clinical decision support, but the small number of studies, heterogeneous decision tasks, and limited independent validation preclude comparisons among approaches and require further prospective and multicenter evaluation (Table 4).

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
section: Results > Study characteristics and results of individual studies > AI-based image registration in HDR-IRT for cervical cancer
text: AI-based image registration studies included more than 200 patients and focused on applicator registration, deformable image registration, and prediction of applicator-induced anatomical deformation (75–77). A neural network–assisted registration framework achieved applicator dwell-position errors as low as 0.7 ± 0.5 mm and completed MRI-based registration in less than 30 seconds (75). Deep learning–based deformable image registration (DIR) further demonstrated high registration accuracy, with Dice coefficients of 0.89 for the cervix, 0.96 for the bladder, and 0.93 for the rectum, outperforming the conventional SimpleElastix algorithm across all evaluated metrics (76). In addition, one study reported that an AI-based model predicted applicator-induced uterine deformation from pre-interventional radiotherapy MRI, achieving Dice coefficients of 94.1% for uterine segmentation and 88.1% for deformation prediction, with a mean uterine displacement of 25.0 mm (77). Individual studies reported promising results for deep-learning-based deformable registration and deformation prediction (76, 77). These approaches showed potential to support adaptive and MRI-guided workflows; however, the small evidence base, methodological heterogeneity, and absence of independent external validation preclude conclusions regarding their comparative performance or clinical effectiveness (Table 5).

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
section: Results > Risk of bias in studies and reporting bias
text: All studies included within each application category were assessable across the applicable methodological domains. The task-adapted QUADAS-2 assessment included 25 segmentation studies, seven reconstruction studies, and three image-registration studies. The PROBAST+AI 2025 assessment included 14 planning studies and four applicator-selection studies. Overall, the methodological assessment identified substantial risk-of-bias concerns across all five application domains, with the available evidence predominantly characterized by high risk of bias. The main recurrent limitations were retrospective single-center study designs, limited sample sizes, lack of independent external validation, non-independent reference standards, and, for prediction-oriented studies, potential overfitting or data leakage.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
section: Results > Risk of bias in studies and reporting bias > Segmentation
text: The methodological assessment of the 25 segmentation studies identified an overall high risk of bias across the available evidence. Patient selection raised concerns in most studies (80.0%, n=20/25), mainly because of retrospective single-center designs and limited or selected datasets. The index-test domain represented the major source of bias, with 68.0% of studies (n=17/25) judged at high risk, primarily because of the lack of independent external validation and reliance on institution-specific datasets. The reference-standard domain also raised concerns in 72.0% of studies (n=18/25), particularly when ground-truth segmentations were generated by a single expert rather than through independent or consensus-based annotation. The flow-and-timing domain was judged at low risk of bias in all studies (100%, n=25/25). Overall, these methodological limitations indicate that the apparently high segmentation performance reported by individual studies should be interpreted cautiously, particularly about reproducibility and generalizability.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
section: Results > Risk of bias in studies and reporting bias > Planning
text: According to the PROBAST+AI 2025 assessment, the overall risk of bias of planning studies was predominantly high. The participants and data sources domain raised concerns in most studies, with 78.6% (11/14) judged at intermediate risk of bias, mainly because of retrospective single-center datasets and limited sample sizes. The predictors domain was judged at low risk of bias in all studies (100%, 14/14), as predictors were typically objectively defined and consistently assessed. The outcome domain was judged at low risk of bias in 85.7% of studies (12/14), with outcomes generally based on predefined dosimetric or clinically established planning objectives. However, the analysis domain represented the major source of bias, particularly because of limited sample sizes, inadequate or insufficiently independent model evaluation, potential overfitting or data leakage, and the frequent absence of external validation. Consequently, favorable judgments in the predictors and outcome domains did not translate into a low overall risk of bias, and the reported performance estimates should be interpreted cautiously.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
section: Results > Risk of bias in studies and reporting bias > Reconstruction
text: The methodological assessment of the reconstruction studies identified an overall high risk of bias across the available evidence. Patient selection raised concerns, mainly because of retrospective single-center designs and limited cohort sizes. The index-test domain represented the major source of bias, with most studies showing high or intermediate risk and no study including independent external validation. The reference standard was generally more robust, as ground truth was commonly derived from clinically approved treatment plans and expert annotations, while the flow-and-timing domain was consistently judged at low risk of bias. Despite favorable geometric and dosimetric performance reported by individual studies, the predominance of single-center datasets, limited sample sizes, and absence of independent external validation substantially restrict confidence in the reproducibility and generalizability of these findings.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
section: Results > Risk of bias in studies and reporting bias > Applicator selection
text: According to PROBAST+AI 2025, the overall risk of bias of the applicator-selection studies was predominantly high. Concerns in the participants and data sources domain were mainly related to single-center designs and limited sample sizes. The predictors domain was generally judged at low risk of bias because predictors were objectively defined and reproducibly assessed, while the outcome domain was judged at low risk of bias in most studies. However, the analysis domain represented the principal source of bias, particularly because of limited sample sizes, insufficient independent evaluation, potential model overfitting, and the lack of external or multicenter validation. Therefore, despite promising reported discrimination and dosimetric performance, confidence in the robustness and generalizability of these models remains limited.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
section: Results > Risk of bias in studies and reporting bias > Image registration
text: The methodological assessment of the three image-registration studies identified an overall high risk of bias across the available evidence. Patient selection raised concerns in all studies (100%, n=3/3), mainly because of retrospective single-center designs and limited sample sizes. The index-test domain represented the major methodological limitation and was judged at high risk of bias in all studies (100%, n=3/3), primarily because none performed independent external validation. The reference-standard domain was judged at low risk of bias in one study (33.3%, n=1/3) and raised concerns in two studies (66.7%, n=2/3), which relied on manual clinician delineations potentially affected by observer variability. The flow-and-timing domain was judged at low risk of bias in all studies. Overall, the high risk of bias, limited datasets, and absence of independent validation substantially restrict confidence in the reported registration performance and its generalizability across institutions and imaging systems.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: The qualitative synthesis of 52 studies indicates that individual studies of AI-based image segmentation, treatment planning, and applicator reconstruction reported promising technical performance. Segmentation performance was variable across studies, with the highest-performing models reporting Dice Similarity Coefficients above 0.90 for selected organs at risk and above 0.85 for selected target volumes. Individual automated planning studies reported plan quality comparable to their respective conventional approaches, with reductions in organ-at-risk doses (0.6–4.3 Gy) and shorter optimization times reported in selected studies. Across application domains, the evidence consistently supported technical feasibility rather than demonstrated clinical benefit. The overall evidence base was characterized by substantial methodological heterogeneity, predominantly retrospective single-center designs, limited independent external validation, and reliance on technical or surrogate endpoints, preventing conclusions regarding clinical effectiveness or generalizability.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: The certainty of evidence ranged from Low to Very Low across the five application domains. Risk-of-bias concerns were primarily related to retrospective single-center designs, non-independent reference standards, potential data leakage or overfitting, and the limited use of independent external evaluation. Inconsistency arose from substantial variability in imaging modalities, anatomical structures, AI architectures, reference standards, and reported performance metrics. Indirectness was mainly attributable to reliance on geometric or dosimetric surrogate endpoints rather than patient-relevant clinical outcomes and to the use of institution-specific datasets. Imprecision reflected small study cohorts, limited independent test samples, and the frequent absence of confidence intervals or other measures of uncertainty. Publication bias was considered possible because most of the available evidence consisted of small retrospective studies reporting favorable AI performance, while negative or inconclusive studies may be underrepresented in the published literature. Publication bias was assessed qualitatively because the small number of studies within some application domains and the substantial heterogeneity of the reported outcomes and performance metrics precluded a reliable statistical assessment.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: The final certainty rating for each application domain and the domain-specific reasons for downgrading are reported in Supplementary Tables 1-5. Correction of the risk-of-bias denominators did not change the final certainty ratings.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: This systematic review provides a comprehensive overview of artificial intelligence applications in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy, encompassing 52 studies across five major domains: segmentation (26–50), treatment planning (51–64), reconstruction (48, 65–70), applicator selection (71–74), and image registration (75–77). One study contributed to both segmentation and reconstruction analyses; therefore, the sum of studies across domains exceeds the total number of included studies (48). Overall, the available studies suggest that AI may improve selected aspects of workflow efficiency and standardization and may support treatment-related decision-making. However, the predominantly retrospective, single-center evidence base does not yet establish improvements in clinical outcomes or routine clinical effectiveness. The certainty of evidence was predominantly low to very low.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: Studies investigated automated delineation of HR-CTV, CTV, GTV, OARs, and catheters using a wide range of architectures, including CNN, U-Net derivatives, transformer-based models, attention mechanisms, multimodal frameworks, and large language model-assisted approaches (26–50). Across studies, OAR segmentation frequently showed high reported performance, with Dice coefficients frequently exceeding 0.90 for bladder delineation and demonstrating high reported agreement with expert contours in individual studies (26, 30, 32–34, 40, 43, 49, 50). Target volume segmentation was more challenging because of tumor heterogeneity, anatomical distortion, and variations in MRI interpretation, although recent models such as SPSeg-Dual, MDA-TransUNet, Prompt-ResUNet, ARGNet, and AM-UNet reported promising technical performance (26, 35, 41, 43, 47).

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: These findings are consistent with broader evidence demonstrating the growing maturity of deep-learning-based auto-segmentation in radiation oncology (15, 16). Importantly, several studies reported substantial reductions in contouring time while maintaining dosimetric equivalence with manual contours, highlighting the potential clinical utility of AI-assisted contouring in image-guided interventional radiotherapy (26, 30, 36, 43, 49). Nevertheless, the task-adapted QUADAS-2 revealed important methodological concerns. Most studies were retrospective and single-center, while only a minority incorporated independent external validation cohorts (33–36). Consequently, the index test domain demonstrated a predominantly high risk of bias, reflecting uncertainty regarding generalizability across institutions, scanners, and contouring practices. These limitations contributed to the low-to-very-low certainty of evidence assigned to segmentation applications. Treatment planning represented the second largest research area, comprising 14 studies focused on automated optimization, dose prediction, plan quality assurance, and adaptive planning (51–64). Collectively, these studies suggest that AI-based approaches can generate clinically acceptable plans with dosimetric characteristics comparable to expert-generated plans, while potentially reducing planning time. Several studies also reported improvements in OAR sparing without compromising target coverage (21, 53, 54, 56–60, 62, 63).

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: Among the approaches evaluated were the BRIGHT framework, which improved compliance with EMBRACE-II constraints (51), fully automated adaptive planning systems capable of producing physician-preferred plans (60, 62), and dose-prediction models achieving low prediction errors for both targets and OARs (57, 59, 64). These findings are consistent with broader developments in external beam radiotherapy, where AI-driven planning has been investigated as a potential approach to reduce planner variability and improve consistency. Despite these encouraging findings, methodological limitations remain substantial. Most studies were retrospective and relied on institution-specific datasets, while only a limited number incorporated rigorous blinded validation procedures (51–64). As a result, the overall PROBAST+AI risk-of-bias judgment was predominantly high, despite more favorable assessments in the predictors and outcome domains. Consequently, the certainty of evidence was graded as very low, indicating that additional validation studies are required before routine clinical implementation.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: Automated reconstruction studies focused primarily on applicator digitization, catheter localization, and interstitial needle reconstruction using CT- and MRI-based imaging (48, 65–70). Individual reconstruction studies reported favorable geometric performance, with submillimeter localization accuracy and minimal dosimetric deviations compared with expert manual reconstruction. Deep-learning-based methods, including attention-gated CNN, DSD-UNET architectures, and nnU-Net frameworks, reported Dice coefficients exceeding 0.88 in several studies (48, 65–70). One study reported the substantial reduction in reconstruction time reported in MRI-guided workflows, where AI-assisted approaches reduced reconstruction times from approximately 46 minutes to 11 minutes without compromising accuracy (68). This observation is clinically relevant because applicator reconstruction remains one of the most technically demanding components of MRI-guided interventional radiotherapy. However, the task-adapted QUADAS-2 assessment identified a recurrent methodological limitation: the complete absence of external validation. Although reconstruction tasks benefit from relatively objective reference standards derived from clinically approved treatment plans, most studies were conducted in single institutions and evaluated on limited datasets (48, 65–70). Consequently, despite the promising technical performance reported in individual studies, evidence certainty remained low.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: Applicator selection represents an emerging potential application of AI in cervical interventional radiotherapy. The four included studies investigated machine-learning and deep-learning approaches to support personalized selection of applicator type, interstitial needle use, and template configuration (71–74). Deep-learning approaches reported promising classification performance for selecting between Syed and tandem-and-ovoid applicators, while machine-learning models successfully predicted the need for hybrid intracavitary-interstitial approaches and optimized needle placement strategies (71, 72). This domain included the first prospective clinical validation study identified in the review, conducted by Stenhouse et al. (74). This study reported lower OAR doses with AI-assisted decision support while maintaining target coverage, representing an important step toward clinical translation. Similarly, AI-guided 3D-printed template approaches improved HR-CTV coverage and reduced doses to critical organs compared with conventional free-hand insertion techniques (73).

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: Nevertheless, despite promising performance, evidence remains limited by the small number of studies and the absence of independent multicenter validation. The PROBAST+AI 2025 assessment identified methodological concerns in the participants and data sources and analysis domains, particularly because of the single-center study designs, limited sample sizes, and insufficient independent external validation, thereby restricting confidence in the generalizability of these decision-support systems. Image registration was the least investigated domain, with only three studies addressing automated rigid registration, deformable image registration, and prediction of applicator-induced uterine deformation (75–77). Despite the limited evidence base, individual studies reported promising technical results. Deep-learning-based deformable registration reported higher performance than the conventional comparator evaluated within that study (75, 76). Furthermore, AI-based prediction of uterine deformation demonstrated the feasibility of estimating applicator-induced anatomical changes before interventional radiotherapy implantation (77).

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: These developments are particularly relevant in adaptive interventional radiotherapy, where anatomical variations and organ motion may influence cumulative dose delivery and treatment accuracy (12). Nevertheless, image registration studies consistently demonstrated high risk of bias within the index test domain due to the absence of external validation and the limited size of available datasets. Consequently, this remains one of the most exploratory fields within cervical IG-IRT, with very-low-certainty evidence despite promising initial results.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: Taken together, the available evidence reveals a consistent pattern across the cervical IG-IRT workflow. AI applications have predominantly focused on automating technically demanding and operator-dependent tasks, with segmentation and treatment planning representing the most extensively investigated domains, whereas reconstruction, applicator selection, and image registration remain supported by smaller evidence bases. Across these applications, the most consistent findings concern technical feasibility, geometric or dosimetric agreement with conventional approaches, and potential reductions in workflow time or inter-observer variability. However, these findings have largely been generated in retrospective, single-center studies using heterogeneous datasets, imaging protocols, reference standards, and performance metrics. Consequently, although technical performance is promising across several application domains, the overall body of evidence remains insufficient to establish generalizability, clinical effectiveness, or superiority over established clinical workflows.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: A consistent finding across all domains was the discrepancy between technical performance and clinical validation. Most studies reported geometric metrics such as Dice similarity coefficients, Hausdorff distances, localization errors, or classification accuracies, whereas relatively few investigated clinically meaningful endpoints including toxicity reduction, local control, treatment adaptation, physician acceptability, or patient outcomes. Although geometric accuracy is a prerequisite for clinical implementation, it does not necessarily translate into improved patient outcomes. Accordingly, high performance on geometric, dosimetric, or classification metrics should be interpreted as evidence of technical feasibility rather than evidence of clinical benefit. Demonstration of clinical benefit will require prospective evaluation using clinically meaningful endpoints, including workflow efficiency, treatment quality, toxicity, and oncologic outcomes.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: The methodological quality assessments further highlighted common weaknesses. Across segmentation, reconstruction, and registration studies, task-adapted QUADAS-2 assessment consistently identified a high risk of bias in the index test domain due to the absence of independent external validation. Similarly, the PROBAST+AI 2025 assessments of planning and applicator-selection studies identified recurrent concerns in the analysis domain, particularly regarding external validation and model generalizability. These findings explain the predominance of low-to-very-low GRADE ratings observed throughout the review. Explainability represents an additional challenge for clinical translation. Many of the investigated approaches, particularly deep-learning models, generate predictions without providing clinicians with transparent information on the features or decision processes underlying their outputs. This may limit clinician confidence and complicate the identification of model failures, particularly in high-stakes tasks such as target delineation, treatment planning, and applicator selection. Future studies should therefore incorporate interpretable outputs and clinically meaningful quality-assurance strategies that allow clinicians to understand, verify, and, when necessary, override AI-generated recommendations.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: Beyond model performance and explainability, successful clinical implementation will require integration into existing treatment-planning systems and clinical workflows, standardized quality-assurance procedures, and clear definition of the role of clinician oversight. Performance should also be evaluated across different institutions, imaging devices, acquisition protocols, and patient populations to determine whether models remain reliable outside the environments in which they were developed. These implementation requirements are particularly relevant in IG-IRT, where AI-generated outputs may directly influence target delineation, treatment planning, applicator reconstruction, or procedural decision-making (21, 22). The main strength of this review is its comprehensive assessment of AI applications throughout the entire cervical IG-IRT workflow. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic review simultaneously evaluating segmentation, planning, reconstruction, applicator selection, and image registration within a single framework. Furthermore, the study incorporates task-specific risk-of-bias tools (QUADAS-2, AI-specific considerations proposed within the QUADAS-AI initiative, and PROBAST+AI 2025) together with a GRADE-based certainty assessment, providing a robust evaluation of methodological quality and clinical maturity.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: Several limitations should also be acknowledged. First, substantial heterogeneity existed among studies regarding imaging modalities, AI architectures, datasets, and performance metrics, precluding quantitative meta-analysis. Second, most included studies were retrospective and single-center investigations. Third, publication bias cannot be excluded because studies reporting favorable AI performance are more likely to be published. Finally, the rapidly evolving nature of AI research means that emerging algorithms may quickly modify the current evidence landscape.

title: Artificial intelligence in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy: a systematic review.
text: The available evidence suggests that artificial intelligence may support the automation of selected labor-intensive tasks, reduce inter-observer variability, and assist treatment-related decision-making in image-guided cervical interventional radiotherapy. Segmentation was the most frequently investigated application and therefore had the largest evidence base, but substantial heterogeneity and limited external validation prevent conclusions regarding the relative superiority or clinical maturity of individual approaches. Planning and reconstruction studies also reported promising technical and workflow outcomes, whereas applicator selection and image registration remain less extensively investigated. At present, no AI approach identified in this review can be considered ready for routine clinical implementation. Across all domains, robust prospective multicenter evaluation, independent external validation, standardized evaluation methods, and assessment of clinically meaningful endpoints are required before widespread clinical adoption. Future research should prioritize standardized evaluation frameworks, multicenter collaborations, and clinically meaningful endpoints to establish the real-world impact of AI in cervical interventional radiotherapy.

title: Deep Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms for Cervical Cancer Segmentation on MRI: A Systematic Review.
text: Cervical cancer management relies heavily on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for staging and treatment planning; however, manual segmentation is time‐consuming and prone to variability. This systematic review aimed to evaluate the performance and clinical potential of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) algorithms for automated cervical cancer segmentation on MRI.

title: Deep Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms for Cervical Cancer Segmentation on MRI: A Systematic Review.
text: A systematic review guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) (PROSPERO: CRD420251247441) was conducted by searching PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar until December 2025. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies‐2 (QUADAS‐2). MRI‐based segmentation studies were primarily included, while computed tomography (CT)‐ and positron emission tomography (PET)‐based multimodal studies were analysed as complementary evidence. Due to substantial heterogeneity, findings were synthesized narratively, and certainty of evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework.

title: Deep Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms for Cervical Cancer Segmentation on MRI: A Systematic Review.
text: Thirty studies were included, mainly evaluating segmentation of tumours, high‐risk clinical target volumes, and organs at risk. DL models, particularly U‐Net variants, convolutional neural networks, and transformer‐based architectures, demonstrated promising performance, with reported Dice similarity coefficients ranging from 0.60 to 0.93. However, performance varied according to target structure, tumour characteristics, and imaging protocols. Overall risk of bias showed “some concerns,” mainly due to patient selection, reference standards, and limited external validation. GRADE assessment indicated low certainty of evidence due to heterogeneity, methodological limitations, and imprecision.

title: Deep Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms for Cervical Cancer Segmentation on MRI: A Systematic Review.
text: ML and DL algorithms show promising potential for automated cervical cancer segmentation on MRI, with potential benefits for efficiency and reproducibility. However, further multicenter studies with standardized protocols and external validation are required before routine clinical implementation.

title: Deep Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms for Cervical Cancer Segmentation on MRI: A Systematic Review.
text: Cervical cancer ranks as the fourth most prevalent malignancy among women globally, with the World Health Organization reporting approximately 660,000 new cases and 350,000 deaths in 2022, predominantly in low‐ and middle‐income countries where screening and treatment access remains limited [1, 2]. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) serves as a vital tool in cervical cancer management, providing superior soft‐tissue contrast for accurate tumour staging, assessment of local invasion, and evaluation of lymph node involvement, which inform treatment decisions [3]. Advanced MRI sequences, such as diffusion‐weighted imaging (DWI) and dynamic contrast‐enhanced (DCE) imaging, offer additional insights into tumour biology, acting as non‐invasive prognostic biomarkers [4, 5]. Image segmentation (delineating tumour boundaries and adjacent structures) is crucial for radiotherapy planning, surgical guidance, and volumetric analysis, yet manual methods are labor‐intensive, subjective, and variable across observers [6, 7]. Machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) algorithms, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and U‐Net variants, have transformed automated segmentation by effectively managing MRI complexities and enhancing accuracy [8, 9, 10].

title: Deep Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms for Cervical Cancer Segmentation on MRI: A Systematic Review.
text: Although reviews exist on DL for cervical cancer detection via cytology or colposcopy, and artificial intelligence (AI) in gynaecological cancers broadly, a targeted synthesis on ML/DL for MRI‐based cervical cancer segmentation is lacking. This systematic review, following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta‐Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, synthesizes evidence on ML and DL algorithms for cervical cancer segmentation on MRI, evaluating performance, innovations, and clinical utility in studies up to December 2025. It identifies challenges in generalizability, data availability, and workflow integration while proposing future directions for AI in cervical oncology. Although MRI is a major imaging modality for cervical cancer segmentation because of its high soft‐tissue contrast, recent AI workflows increasingly integrate complementary imaging modalities such as computed tomography (CT) and positron emission tomography (PET). Therefore, multimodal studies were considered to capture emerging AI‐assisted segmentation strategies while maintaining MRI‐based segmentation as the central focus of this review.

title: Deep Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms for Cervical Cancer Segmentation on MRI: A Systematic Review.
text: Studies were eligible if they evaluated ML or DL‐based automated segmentation approaches in cervical cancer imaging. The primary focus was MRI‐based segmentation; however, studies incorporating multimodal approaches, including PET/MRI, CT/MRI fusion, or CT‐assisted segmentation, were also included when MRI‐derived information was an essential component of the segmentation workflow or when the investigated algorithm was directly transferable to MRI‐guided clinical applications. These studies were analysed separately as multimodal extensions rather than as pure MRI segmentation studies. Therefore, multimodal and CT‐assisted studies were not pooled with MRI‐only studies but were discussed separately to avoid overestimating MRI‐specific segmentation performance. This represented a post‐protocol clarification because several eligible studies incorporated MRI‐derived information within multimodal radiotherapy workflows. These studies were retained to reflect emerging AI‐assisted multimodal segmentation strategies but were not considered equivalent to MRI‐only evidence.

title: Deep Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms for Cervical Cancer Segmentation on MRI: A Systematic Review.
text: A comprehensive literature search was conducted without date or language restrictions to identify relevant studies. The following databases were searched: PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, IEEE Xplore, and Google Scholar. Search terms were structured around the Population, Intervention, Comparator, and Outcome (PICO) framework, combined using Boolean operators (AND, OR, NOT). Table S4 outlines the PICO elements and corresponding search strategy. Database‐specific adaptations were applied. For PubMed/MEDLINE: (MRI OR “magnetic resonance imaging”) AND (segmentation OR “image segmentation” OR “tumour segmentation” OR “automatic segmentation”) AND (“cervical cancer” OR “cervix cancer” OR “cervical carcinoma” OR “cervical neoplasms”[MeSH]) AND (“diagnostic performance” OR “diagnostic accuracy” OR sensitivity OR specificity OR AUC OR ROC OR “predictive value”) NOT (review[pt] OR “systematic review”[tiab] OR “meta‐analysis”[pt] OR meta‐analysis[tiab]). Similar tailored strategies were used for Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore (full strategies available in the PROSPERO protocol).

title: Deep Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms for Cervical Cancer Segmentation on MRI: A Systematic Review.
text: Titles and abstracts were screened independently by two reviewers using predefined eligibility criteria. Full‐text articles were retrieved for potentially eligible studies, with discrepancies resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer if needed. Only published studies were considered; unpublished or grey literature was excluded.

title: Deep Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms for Cervical Cancer Segmentation on MRI: A Systematic Review.
text: Data were extracted independently by two reviewers using a standardized form. Extracted items included study characteristics, algorithm details, performance metrics, and secondary outcomes. Authors were not contacted for missing data.

title: Deep Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms for Cervical Cancer Segmentation on MRI: A Systematic Review.
text: Risk of bias and applicability concerns were assessed independently by two reviewers using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies‐2 (QUADAS‐2) tool [13]. The study‐level risk of bias summary and applicability assessments are provided in Tables S1 and S2, respectively, while detailed domain‐specific justifications are presented in Table S3.

title: Deep Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms for Cervical Cancer Segmentation on MRI: A Systematic Review.
text: If sufficient homogeneity in outcomes and metrics was present, a random‐effects meta‐analysis was planned to pool performance measures. Otherwise, a narrative synthesis was conducted, summarizing algorithm types, methodological characteristics, limitations, and clinical implications. Subgroup analyses explored influences of MRI sequences and architectures.

title: Deep Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms for Cervical Cancer Segmentation on MRI: A Systematic Review.
text: Although not predefined in the protocol, the GRADE approach was applied post hoc to assess the certainty of evidence for major outcomes. This exploratory assessment considered risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias domains.

title: Deep Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms for Cervical Cancer Segmentation on MRI: A Systematic Review.
text: The literature search yielded 1256 unique records after duplicate removal. Following title and abstract screening, 128 full‐text articles were assessed for eligibility. Full‐text assessment resulted in exclusion of 98 studies. The main exclusion reasons were non‐relevant imaging modality (n = 42), absence of quantitative segmentation outcomes (n = 31), non‐cervical cancer populations (n = 18), and review or meta‐analysis articles (n = 7), as summarized in Table S5. Ultimately, 30 studies met the inclusion criteria and were incorporated into the synthesis. The study selection process is summarized in the PRISMA flow diagram shown in Figure 1.

title: Deep Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms for Cervical Cancer Segmentation on MRI: A Systematic Review.
text: The methodological quality of the included studies was evaluated using the QUADAS‐2 framework across four domains: patient selection, index test, reference standard, and flow and timing (Figures 2 and 3). The results of this assessment are summarized in the traffic‐light plot and the overall distribution figure. Overall, the risk of bias was predominantly judged as “some concerns,” indicating moderate methodological limitations across the evidence base. Study‐level QUADAS‐2 assessments demonstrated variability across the included studies (Table S1). Concerns were most frequently related to patient selection, reference standard definition, and limited external validation of AI models. Applicability assessments were generally favourable, although several studies showed concerns related to restricted datasets, non‐representative populations, and limited generalizability (Table S2). A smaller proportion of studies were rated as low risk of bias, whereas a non‐negligible subset was classified as high risk, contributing to reduced confidence in certain findings. Across domains, flow and timing demonstrated the most favourable profile, with the vast majority of studies rated as low risk, suggesting that patient progression through the study, timing between index and reference tests, and completeness of outcome verification were generally appropriate.

title: Deep Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms for Cervical Cancer Segmentation on MRI: A Systematic Review.
text: In contrast, patient selection showed the greatest vulnerability, with a notable proportion of studies exhibiting high risk of bias, likely reflecting non‐consecutive enrollment, case–control designs, or insufficient reporting of inclusion and exclusion criteria. The index test domain was largely assessed as low risk or some concerns, implying that although MRI‐based assessments were generally implemented appropriately, blinding to reference standards and prespecification of diagnostic thresholds were not consistently reported. Similarly, the reference standard domain frequently raised some concerns, suggesting potential uncertainty regarding whether reference diagnoses were independent, uniformly applied, or sufficiently rigorous across studies. Taken together, these findings indicate that while several studies demonstrated robust methodological quality, the overall evidence is limited by variability in study design and reporting—particularly in patient selection and reference standard procedures—which should be considered when interpreting pooled estimates and conclusions.

title: Deep Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms for Cervical Cancer Segmentation on MRI: A Systematic Review.
text: The certainty of evidence was evaluated using the GRADE framework and was rated as high, moderate, low, or very low according to the presence of limitations in risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and publication bias. Overall, the certainty of evidence for AI‐based cervical cancer segmentation outcomes was judged to be low, primarily due to methodological limitations, substantial heterogeneity in imaging protocols, segmentation targets, algorithm architectures, and performance metrics, as well as limited external validation and relatively small sample sizes in several studies. Although many studies reported promising segmentation performance, including high Dice similarity coefficient values for selected targets, the variability in study design and reporting reduced confidence in the generalizability of these findings. No outcome was considered to provide high‐certainty evidence, and the available evidence should therefore be interpreted as preliminary until validated through larger, multicenter, and externally validated studies (Table 1).

title: Deep Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms for Cervical Cancer Segmentation on MRI: A Systematic Review.
text: The included studies collectively advance the application of DL for automatic segmentation in cervical cancer imaging, primarily focusing on MRI, while also including selected CT‐only and multimodal CT/PET studies (Table 2). Importantly, multimodal studies were interpreted as complementary evidence rather than direct substitutes for MRI‐only segmentation performance. These investigations address key clinical challenges such as manual contouring variability, time inefficiency, and the need for robust, generalizable models to support radiotherapy planning, brachytherapy, and tumour monitoring. Most studies evaluate segmentation performance using metrics like DSC, Hausdorff distance (HD), and surface DSC, with comparisons to expert manual delineations. Innovations span from multi‐head architectures and transfer learning to multimodal fusion and failure detection mechanisms, demonstrating a progression toward clinically viable, automated workflows (Table S6).

title: Deep Learning and Machine Learning Algorithms for Cervical Cancer Segmentation on MRI: A Systematic Review.
text: The majority of included studies evaluated artificial intelligence–based segmentation approaches using MRI as the primary imaging modality. These studies focused mainly on automated delineation of cervical tumours, gross tumour volume (GTV), high‐risk clinical target volume (HR‐CTV), and organs at risk (OARs) for radiotherapy planning and brachytherapy applications. MRI‐only studies demonstrated promising segmentation performance; however, reported accuracy varied substantially depending on tumour characteristics, imaging protocols, segmentation targets, and model architecture. For tumour segmentation, Kalantar et al. developed a multi‐head dilated deep learning framework for multiparametric MRI segmentation and achieved a median Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.823, outperforming baseline multi‐channel U‐Net models (DSC 0.788).
