title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
text: What are the main findings? Professional radiophobia is operationalised inconsistently; the evidence does not support a single pooled prevalence estimate.Knowledge, experience, perceived exposure, dosimetry, equipment usability, and safety climate were reported alongside variation in concern and protective behaviour. What are the implications of the main findings? Practice-oriented radiation-safety strategies may need to address dose literacy together with practical training, personal monitoring, usable protective equipment, and transparent risk communication.Future studies require validated multidimensional instruments separating knowledge, risk appraisal, affective anxiety, trust, protection, and avoidance.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
text: Background/Objectives: Radiation-related fear, anxiety, risk perception, reproductive concern, protective behaviour, and avoidance are conceptually related but not interchangeable. This scoping review mapped how these constructs have been operationalised among healthcare workers and health professions students. Methods: Following JBI guidance and PRISMA-ScR, PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and the Cochrane Library were searched for English-language records published from 1 January 2000 to 4 September 2026. Of 845 records, 388 duplicates were removed and 457 unique records were screened. Results: Twenty-seven reports underwent full-text assessment; one was excluded because its mixed population and radiation context did not permit a healthcare-specific occupational interpretation, leaving 26 studies. The evidence was dominated by cross-sectional studies and heterogeneous measurement instruments; therefore, study-level percentages were not treated as directly comparable prevalence estimates. Reported outcomes ranged from explicit radiophobia and affective anxiety to cognitive risk appraisal, reproductive concern, protective behaviour, and avoidance. Education was associated with differing changes across settings, while dosimetry, protective equipment, workflow, and safety climate were reported alongside occupational responses.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
text: Conclusions: The literature does not support a standardised operational definition or common measurement framework for professional radiophobia. Future research should distinguish affective fear or anxiety from contextually appropriate occupational risk appraisal and protective behaviour, and should evaluate organisational conditions alongside education.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
text: Medical ionising radiation is indispensable for diagnosis and treatment, while occupational protection is governed by justification, optimisation, and dose limitation [1,2]. These principles address exposure control, but they do not by themselves explain how workers interpret uncertain or low-dose risks. Radiation is invisible, possible effects may be delayed, and quantities such as effective dose are not intuitively understood. Consequently, objectively controlled exposure can coexist with substantial concern.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
text: Professional radiophobia has no accepted diagnostic or operational definition. Across the literature, the term has been used alongside explicit fear, anxiety, heightened perceived risk, concern about cancer or reproductive effects, and avoidance of radiation-related work. These constructs are related but not interchangeable: affective fear or anxiety concerns emotional response; perceived radiation risk concerns cognitive appraisal of probability or severity; reproductive concern concerns fertility, pregnancy, foetal, or future-child effects; protective behaviour concerns dose-reduction actions; and avoidance concerns reduction, withdrawal, or refusal of radiation-related activity because of concern. A low knowledge score is not evidence of phobia, and use of a dosimeter or protective equipment can represent appropriate safety behaviour rather than fear. For this review, these constructs were treated as analytically distinct rather than as severity levels on a single continuum, and the term radiophobia was retained only where the source itself used it or directly operationalised fear in those terms.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
text: The psychometric paradigm identifies unfamiliarity, involuntariness, delayed consequences, and limited perceived control as characteristics that intensify risk perception [3]. Ethical radiological protection also requires transparency, accountability, dignity, and stakeholder involvement [4]. In healthcare settings, these considerations extend beyond individual emotion because concern may influence participation in procedures, career decisions, communication with patients, and adherence to protection practices.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
text: Previous systematic reviews addressed related but narrower questions. Behzadmehr et al. [5] synthesised knowledge, attitudes, and practices regarding radiation protection among healthcare workers, whereas Rodrigues et al. [6] focused on radiation-protection literacy and knowledge among exposed healthcare professionals. Neither review was designed primarily to map affective fear or anxiety, reproductive concern, risk appraisal, avoidance, and organisational responses as distinct constructs. The present scoping review therefore aimed to (1) map definitions and measures of radiophobia and related radiation concern; (2) distinguish affective, cognitive, reproductive, behavioural, and organisational domains; (3) describe reported associations with knowledge, experience, demographic factors, protective behaviour, and organisational conditions; and (4) identify implications for measurement, education, and occupational-radiation protection. The operational definitions used to organise the evidence map are summarised in Table 1.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
section: 2. Materials and Methods > 2.1. Design and Reporting
text: The review followed JBI methodological guidance for scoping reviews [7] and was reported with reference to PRISMA-ScR [8] and the PRISMA 2020 flow structure [9]. A scoping design was chosen because the literature used heterogeneous populations, concepts, instruments, and study designs. The protocol was not prospectively registered because public registration was not considered mandatory for a scoping review when the study was initiated. The exact date on which the review methods were finalised was not prospectively recorded, and no publicly accessible archived protocol or review plan is available. The methods described below reflect the predefined approach used for the review.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
section: 2. Materials and Methods > 2.2. Review Question and PCC Framework
text: The review question was: How have radiophobia, radiation-related fear, anxiety, concern, and risk perception been measured among healthcare workers and health professions students in occupational or clinical-training contexts, and what factors and behaviours have been reported in association with these outcomes? Population comprised healthcare workers and students preparing for healthcare roles. The concept comprised explicit radiophobia or radiation-related fear, anxiety, concern, risk perception, or fear-linked avoidance. The context comprised occupational healthcare practice or clinical training involving ionising radiation.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
section: 2. Materials and Methods > 2.3. Information Sources and Search
text: PubMed was searched on 3 September 2026; Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and the Cochrane Library were searched on 4 September 2026. Searches covered English-language records published from 1 January 2000 to the respective search date. The strategy combined terms for radiophobia, fear, anxiety, concern, and radiation-risk perception with terms for healthcare personnel and health professions students. Complete database-specific strategies, limits, dates, and database-reported yields are presented in Supplementary Table S1. These databases were selected to cover biomedical, multidisciplinary, and evidence-synthesis literature. Resource constraints precluded Embase, PsycINFO, CINAHL, and a structured grey-literature search; consequently, studies indexed exclusively in dedicated nursing, psychological, or other subject-specific databases may have been missed. Formal backward reference-list screening, forward citation tracking, and independent peer review of the search strategy were not documented and were therefore not claimed. The final Scopus RIS and CSV exports each contained 359 records; an earlier partial 90-record Scopus export was an intermediate subset and was not counted separately. For studies published in 2026, publication year was assigned according to the bibliographic publication record, including online-first publication where applicable.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
text: Eligible reports were original quantitative, qualitative, or mixed-methods studies involving healthcare workers or health professions students that operationalised at least one substantive ionising-radiation outcome within an occupational or clinical-training context: radiophobia; radiation-related fear; anxiety or worry; occupational or reproductive concern; perceived radiation risk; protective behaviour linked to concern; or avoidance attributable to concern. Risk perception alone was sufficient for eligibility when it was a substantive ionising-radiation outcome in the relevant occupational or training context; it was not assumed to be equivalent to fear or anxiety. Studies measuring knowledge, awareness, or protection compliance alone were excluded unless these were analysed alongside an eligible affective, cognitive risk-perception, reproductive, or concern-linked behavioural outcome. Studies restricted to patients, the general public, industrial workers, non-ionising radiation, or non-clinical nuclear-accident response were excluded, as were reviews, editorials, conference abstracts without sufficient data, and unverifiable reports.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
section: 2. Materials and Methods > 2.5. Selection and Data Charting
text: The four database result sets were combined and deduplicated using exact DOI and normalised-title matching, with manual checks for ambiguous matches. The recorded retrieval comprised 845 records: PubMed 235, Scopus 359, Web of Science Core Collection 243, and Cochrane Library 8. Deduplication removed 388 records (355 exact DOI matches and 33 exact normalised-title matches), leaving 457 unique records. One reviewer screened all titles and abstracts and assessed potentially eligible full texts; a second reviewer checked potentially eligible records and full-text eligibility decisions. Disagreements were resolved through discussion and consensus. The exact proportion of records independently checked and the number of disagreements were not prospectively recorded.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
section: 2. Materials and Methods > 2.5. Selection and Data Charting
text: One primary reason was recorded for each full-text exclusion. Data were charted by country, population, design, sample, instrument or construct, main findings, and limitations affecting interpretation. One reviewer initially charted the data using a structured form. No formal pilot-testing or calibration phase of the charting form was documented, and study investigators were not contacted; extraction relied on the published reports and accessible supplementary materials. Following peer review, a second author independently rechecked the key numerical and descriptive extractions for all 26 included studies against the original reports, and source-level inconsistencies were retained rather than silently recalculated. The resulting verification dataset is provided in Supplementary Table S4. Funding sources of the included studies were not systematically charted.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
section: 2. Materials and Methods > 2.6. Synthesis and Critical Interpretation
text: Because outcome definitions and measurement scales were not commensurable, no meta-analysis or pooled prevalence estimate was undertaken. For narrative and framework synthesis, the charted findings were organised into analytically distinct domains: direct fear or source-labelled radiophobia, affective anxiety, cognitive risk and reproductive appraisal, protective or avoidance-related behaviour, and organisational modifiers. A study could contribute to more than one domain without implying that the domains represented a single latent construct. Patterns were compared across populations, measurement approaches, and study designs, and contradictory findings and source-level inconsistencies were retained. Consistent with the mapping purpose of the review, no formal risk-of-bias score was used, and no study was excluded on the basis of methodological quality. Instead, study-level limitations are systematically charted in Table 2, including sampling and response rate, instrument validation, cross-sectional design, denominator ambiguity, non-random allocation, and short follow-up. These limitations affect confidence in the magnitude and generalisability of individual associations but do not negate their value for mapping constructs, measurement problems, and hypotheses.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
section: 3. Results > 3.1. Search Results and Study Characteristics
text: The searches yielded 845 records. After removal of 388 duplicates, 457 records were screened by title and abstract; 430 were excluded and 27 reports were assessed in full text. One report was excluded because the population and radiation context were mixed and did not permit a healthcare-specific occupational interpretation (Supplementary Table S2). Twenty-six studies were included in the synthesis (Figure 1). The 26 included studies were published from 2001 to 2026. Populations included nurses, radiographers, physicians in procedure-intensive specialties, military medical personnel, radiotherapy workers, and nursing, dental, radiography, and medical students. Cross-sectional surveys predominated. Educational evidence comprised pilot pre–post, quasi-experimental, repeated cross-sectional, augmented-reality, and longitudinal designs; one French cohort linked questionnaire responses to national dosimetry records, and mixed-methods research added contextual evidence (Table 2).

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
section: 3. Results > 3.2. Direct Radiophobia and Affective Fear
text: Only a minority of studies explicitly used the term radiophobia. Pastel and Mulvaney measured radiation knowledge and attitudes before and after a three-day course; the mean attitude score shifted from 23 ± 9 to 18 ± 9, where lower scores represented more positive attitudes. The authors did not perform inferential comparisons and described the instrument as a pilot that had not been validated or tested for reliability [10]. Alotaibi and Saeed reported that 30 of 35 radiology nurses were afraid of radiation because of hazards such as cancer and infertility, while presenting 30 as 83%; this source-level arithmetic inconsistency is retained [11]. Ohno and Kaori reported that about 40% of 134 nurses had a fear of occupational-radiation exposure [12].

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
section: 3. Results > 3.2. Direct Radiophobia and Affective Fear
text: Ago et al. provided a direct source-labelled operationalisation: 174 of 274 valid survey respondents (63.5%) reported ever experiencing radiophobia during training, and 122 of these 174 (70.1%) reported first experiencing it in the first academic year [26]. The authors explicitly distinguished this occurrence/ever-experienced measure from prevalence and incidence. Shafiee et al. reported 17 nurses with radiophobia and withdrawal from fluoroscopy participation in four female nurses; however, the source reports 17/174 nurses (9.7%) in the original article’s Table 1 and later describes 17 nurses as 54.8%, creating an internal denominator inconsistency [17]. These findings support mapping of source-labelled fear constructs but do not provide a common prevalence estimate.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
text: Study-level percentages in this section are reported descriptively to characterise individual samples and should not be interpreted as directly comparable prevalence estimates. Sampling methods, response rates, denominators, populations, and measurement instruments varied substantially across studies. Among paediatric anaesthesiologists, 76.8% of respondents were concerned or very concerned, women had higher concern than men (OR 1.66, 95% CI 1.20–2.31), and 73% (151/206) of respondents who had been pregnant during practice requested not to be assigned to X-ray cases; the overall survey response rate was 21% [15]. Concern was reported by 94% of neurosurgeon respondents, although the survey response rate was 6.8%; 59% did not use a dosimeter, and only 3% correctly identified the occupational exposure limit [21]. Among orthopaedic surgeon respondents, 75 of 85 (88.2%) reported worry about occupational effects, while 39 of 85 (45.9%) reported formal fluoroscopy training [24].

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
text: Pregnancy-focused studies demonstrated behavioural consequences. Female interventional radiologists more often changed practice because of exposure concern than men (23% vs. 13%), while 6% of pregnant interventional radiologists completely abstained from fluoroscopically guided interventions [13]. In the urology survey, women more often reduced hours or changed practice because of concern (17% vs. 7%, p = 0.01); 67% of previously pregnant respondents did not know their dosimetry dose [22]. Among European radiographers and students, 30% were concerned about health effects, 24% about fertility, and 19% about children’s health, with greater reproductive concern among younger respondents and students [25].

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
section: 3. Results > 3.4. Education, Knowledge, and Risk Appraisal
text: Educational effects were not uniform. Japanese dental students showed decreased X-ray risk perception after education, whereas Indonesian students showed increased X-ray risk perception (both p < 0.05) [14]. Japanese nursing students ranked X-rays relatively highly among 30 hazards, and greater understanding was associated with lower risk perception, but cross-sectional analysis cannot determine whether knowledge changed perception [16]. In the longitudinal study by Cao et al., fear declined after coursework and declined further after onsite observation (both p < 0.001), alongside increased interest and career intention [20]. The quasi-experimental chest-equivalent-dose study included 71 nurses (Sievert-based education n = 40; CED-based education n = 31) and reported larger immediate improvements in radiation knowledge and larger reductions in radiation anxiety and radiation-related feelings in the CED group [27]. Because allocation was non-randomised and outcomes were measured immediately after education, the study supports a short-term association with communication format rather than long-term effectiveness. Wahab and Younis reported improved radiation-protection behaviour scores after a PMT-based educational intervention, but their article describes the study design inconsistently, warranting cautious interpretation [34].

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
text: Baudin et al. showed that feeling personally exposed was associated with wearing a dosimeter (OR 3.69, 95% CI 2.04–6.66) and using protective practices (OR 4.60, 95% CI 2.28–9.30) [19]. The main reported barriers to protection were unsuitable or insufficient equipment. In Kazakhstan, occupational anxiety was associated with non-use of aprons, non-use of dosimeters, and inadequate safety training, although causal direction cannot be inferred [23]. The Ghanaian mixed-methods study linked students’ source-labelled radiophobia to misinformation, limited foundational knowledge, absence of personal monitoring badges, and inconsistent safety practice at placements [26]. European radiographers described shielding discomfort, limited availability, workflow pressure, and uncertainty about long-term low-dose effects [25]. These observations show that radiation concern may coexist with deficiencies in the working or training environment and should not be interpreted automatically as an irrational individual response (Table 3).

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
section: 3. Results > 3.6. Additional Evidence on Communication, Training, and Occupational Consequences
text: Additional included studies added evidence on communication, training, and occupational consequences. Physicians ranked equivalent dose quantities differently depending on the language used to express them, while an augmented-reality-supported education study reported post-training changes in knowledge and risk rankings among nursing students [28,35]. High concern frequently coexisted with incomplete training or practice: 82% of anaesthesiology residents and 93% of interventional pain physicians reported substantial concern, while the resident dosimetry project measured low doses relative to occupational limits and the international pain-physician survey documented gaps in knowledge and practice [29,32]. These results describe co-occurring patterns rather than causal mechanisms. Radiation anxiety among Chinese medical radiation workers was associated with burnout and intention to leave [33]. In Indian radiotherapy facilities, differences in perceived risk were reported alongside variation in implementation of regulatory requirements [30]. The operating-room pilot showed that ionising radiation was ranked as a major occupational risk, with weighting varying by specialty [31]. A PMT-based intervention reported post-training changes in protective behaviour among nurses [34]. Collectively, these findings justify distinguishing affective concern, cognitive appraisal, protective behaviour, and avoidance-related responses without assuming that one necessarily causes another.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
text: A framework synthesis was applied to the charted findings. Evidence was coded into five linked but analytically distinct domains: direct fear/source-labelled radiophobia, affective anxiety, cognitive risk and reproductive appraisal, protective or avoidance-related behaviour, and organisational modifiers. The framework is a review-derived conceptual model intended to organise observed evidence and generate hypotheses for prospective testing; it is not a causal model. Organisational and individual domains are therefore shown as potential contextual inputs, and the pathways between appraisal and occupational responses are hypothesised rather than empirically established across the included studies (Table 4). The resulting review-derived conceptual framework is shown in Figure 2. For completeness, Figure 3 summarises the methodological workflow described in Section 2.1, Section 2.2, Section 2.3, Section 2.4, Section 2.5 and Section 2.6.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
section: 3. Results > 3.8. Patterns by Population and Clinical Context
text: Patterns differed qualitatively across populations and settings, although heterogeneity precluded formal subgroup meta-analysis. Student studies commonly examined knowledge, risk perception, first experiences of fear, or responses to education, whereas studies of practicing professionals more often addressed occupational concern, monitoring, protective practice, workload modification, or career consequences. Pregnancy-focused studies among interventional radiologists and urologists centred on reproductive concern, access to guidance and protective equipment, and changes in practice; these outcomes should not be conflated with generalised anxiety among students. Procedure-intensive specialties such as interventional radiology, anaesthesia, neurosurgery, orthopaedics, radiotherapy, and interventional pain medicine were represented, but exposure intensity could not be standardised because the studies did not use a common dosimetric metric. Sex/gender and pregnancy status were relevant in several reports, while younger participants or students showed greater reproductive concern in the European radiographer survey. Cross-sectional surveys predominated, so differences by profession, country, experience, or training level are descriptive patterns rather than evidence of causal subgroup effects.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
text: This review identified 26 studies but no standard definition, validated diagnostic threshold, or common measurement instrument for professional radiophobia. The evidence encompasses analytically distinct constructs: source-labelled radiophobia or explicit fear, affective anxiety or worry, cognitive risk appraisal, reproductive concern, protective behaviour, and avoidance-related responses. The broad evidence-mapping scope does not assume that these constructs are manifestations of a single latent phenomenon; they are synthesised within a common occupational-radiation context while remaining conceptually distinct. The wide numerical range in reported fear or concern should not be interpreted as variation in a single prevalence parameter. Study-level percentages describe individual samples and arose from different professions, exposure contexts, question wording, response options, time frames, denominators, and response rates. Ago et al. explicitly described their 63.5% result as occurrence/ever-experienced radiophobia rather than prevalence or incidence [26]. Alotaibi and Saeed [11] and Shafiee et al. [17] contain source-level numerical or denominator inconsistencies. Preserving these inconsistencies rather than silently recalculating them supports the conclusion that the evidence is heterogeneous and not suitable for pooled prevalence estimation.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
section: 4. Discussion > 4.2. Interpretation of Education and Experience
text: Education was generally associated with improved knowledge, but affective and risk-appraisal outcomes differed by content and context. A longitudinal student cohort reported reductions in radiation anxiety across educational time points [20], and a small quasi-experimental comparison reported larger immediate reductions in anxiety after symbolic CED communication than after Sievert-based teaching [27]. In contrast, X-ray risk perception increased after education in the Indonesian student group while decreasing in the Japanese group [14]. These observations do not establish a single educational effect. They suggest that future studies should distinguish knowledge acquisition from affective response and risk appraisal and should use prospective designs with longer follow-up. Greater experience was associated in some studies with different knowledge or risk-appraisal patterns, but the reviewed evidence does not establish a causal protective effect. Most studies were cross-sectional, and experience is entangled with profession, training, age, selection into radiation-intensive work, and local safety arrangements. Longitudinal designs using validated instruments are needed before experience can be treated as an intervention mechanism.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
section: 4. Discussion > 4.3. Distinguishing Fear and Anxiety from Contextually Appropriate Risk Appraisal and Protective Behaviour
text: The included studies do not provide validated criteria for classifying radiation-related concern as disproportionate, justified, adaptive, or maladaptive. Accordingly, this review does not assign such labels to individual behaviours. Instead, it distinguishes measured affective fear or anxiety from cognitive risk appraisal, reproductive concern, protective practice, and avoidance-related responses, and interprets each in relation to the study context. Lack of dosimetry feedback, unavailable or poorly fitting protection, inconsistent local practice, and unclear pregnancy policies provide documented contextual reasons for uncertainty [19,22,25,26]. Dosimeter use, shielding, or workflow modification may represent appropriate safety practice; conversely, avoidance or reduced participation may have different meanings depending on objective exposure, procedural requirements, available protection, and functional impact. The reviewed studies did not provide a common validated threshold with which to adjudicate these distinctions.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
section: 4. Discussion > 4.3. Distinguishing Fear and Anxiety from Contextually Appropriate Risk Appraisal and Protective Behaviour
text: Figure 2 therefore presents organisational and individual conditions as review-derived contextual domains and uses hypothesised pathways only to organise the evidence. This is consistent with international occupational-radiation guidance emphasising monitoring, education, equipment, optimisation, and quality assurance, and with published work on radiation-safety climate [36,37,38], while the included observational evidence itself does not establish causal pathways.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
section: 4. Discussion > 4.4. Implications for Practice and Research
text: For practice, the evidence supports attention to dose and risk communication, practical radiation-protection training, individual monitoring and feedback, availability and usability of protective equipment, and clear mechanisms for discussing pregnancy and occupational exposure. Because the included studies were heterogeneous and predominantly observational, this review does not rank these components or establish their comparative effectiveness. Risk communication should accurately convey magnitude and uncertainty and support informed benefit-risk discussion [39]. The need for more coherent measurement follows directly from the heterogeneity observed across the included studies. A future multidimensional instrument could separate factual knowledge, perceived probability and severity, affective fear or anxiety, perceived controllability, trust in monitoring, protective behaviour, and avoidance. Requirements such as content validity, cognitive interviewing, structural validity, internal consistency, test–retest reliability, measurement invariance, and validated thresholds are methodological recommendations for future instrument development rather than empirical findings of the present review. Prospective studies should also consider objective dosimetry, training exposure, safety-climate measures, and observed behaviour.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
section: 4. Discussion > 4.4. Implications for Practice and Research
text: The findings also have relevance for health systems in which diagnostic and interventional radiology services are expanding. Across the included studies, radiation-related concern was reported alongside potentially modifiable organisational factors, including gaps in training, dosimetry feedback, availability or usability of protective equipment, workflow constraints, and uncertainty regarding pregnancy-related practice [19,22,25,26,29,32]. Expansion of radiological services should therefore be accompanied by proportionate development of workforce radiation-safety training, individual monitoring and feedback, accessible protective equipment, and transparent risk communication. In Kazakhstan, available evidence similarly suggests that occupational anxiety may coexist with training gaps, inconsistent dosimetry use, and deficiencies in radiation-protection practices [23]. These implications are hypothesis-generating and should be evaluated prospectively in different health-system contexts.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
text: Strengths include explicit PCC criteria, database-specific search reporting, preservation of source-level inconsistencies, conceptual separation of affective, cognitive, reproductive, behavioural, and organisational domains, and independent rechecking of key extracted data against the original reports during revision. Supplementary Table S4 records the verification status and source-specific qualifications for the 26 included studies.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
text: Limitations are substantial. The English-language restriction may have introduced language bias. The search did not include CINAHL, PsycINFO, Embase, or a structured grey-literature search, and no formal backward/forward citation tracking or independent peer review of the search strategy was documented; relevant psychological, nursing, or other subject-specific evidence may therefore have been missed. This review is best understood as a structured map of evidence retrieved from the searched databases rather than an exhaustive census of all relevant literature. The protocol was not prospectively registered, the exact method-finalisation date was not recorded, and no archived public review plan is available. One reviewer performed the initial screening and charting; although potentially eligible and full-text decisions received secondary checking and all included-study extractions were independently rechecked during revision, the original extent of independent screening and disagreement frequency were not prospectively documented and no formal calibration exercise was recorded. Complete PubMed, Web of Science, and Cochrane exports and the record-level screening log were not retained, preventing full record-level reconstruction of deduplication and screening decisions.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
text: Most included studies were cross-sectional, convenience, single-centre, or low-response surveys; instruments and outcome wording differed, several measures were not validated, and intervention studies were small or had short follow-up. Formal risk-of-bias scoring was not undertaken. Consequently, the review maps constructs and generates hypotheses but does not estimate pooled prevalence, establish causality, or rank intervention effectiveness.

title: Radiation-Related Fear, Risk Perception, and Occupational Responses Among Healthcare Workers and Health Professions Students: A Scoping Review.
text: The literature does not support a standardised operational definition or common measurement framework for professional radiophobia. Included studies reported source-labelled radiophobia, radiation-related fear or anxiety, cognitive risk appraisal, reproductive concern, protective behaviour, and avoidance-related responses in different professional and student samples, but these constructs are not interchangeable and their frequencies cannot be pooled or generalised as a single prevalence estimate. Knowledge, education, experience, risk communication, dosimetry feedback, equipment usability, workflow, and safety climate were reported alongside these outcomes, but predominantly observational evidence does not establish causal pathways. Future research should distinguish radiation-related fear and anxiety from contextually appropriate occupational risk appraisal and protective behaviour, use validated multidimensional measures, and test review-derived hypotheses prospectively with objective exposure and organisational data.

title: Radiation Protection Practices Among Medical Students at Two United Kingdom Medical Schools.
text: Background Orthopaedic surgery frequently involves the use of intraoperative fluoroscopy, exposing operating theatre personnel to ionising radiation. Medical students often attend orthopaedic procedures during their clinical training, yet their education on radiation safety and access to appropriate protective equipment remain poorly understood. This study aimed to evaluate radiation safety among medical students during surgical placements, focusing on educational exposure, practical radiation protection practices, and perceived safety. Methodology A multicentre, cross-sectional, questionnaire study was conducted mainly among UK medical students from two medical schools in clinical years (n = 70). A structured nine-item questionnaire was distributed via Google Forms over a 10-day period in December 2023. Participants were recruited through university WhatsApp groups. Participation was voluntary and anonymous, and completion of the questionnaire was taken as implied informed consent. Results

title: Radiation Protection Practices Among Medical Students at Two United Kingdom Medical Schools.
text: A total of 70 medical students completed the survey (44% female, 30% male, 26% preferred not to say). Only 50% reported wearing an appropriately fitting lead apron, while 41% reported inadequate fit. Consistent use of a thyroid shield was reported by 41% of respondents, whereas 49% reported not wearing one. Formal radiation safety teaching before orthopaedic theatre attendance had been received by only 16% of participants. One-third (33%) reported feeling unsafe in operating theatres where ionising radiation was used. Conclusions The medical students surveyed who attended the theatre where ionising radiation was used demonstrated important gaps in radiation safety education and inconsistent use of appropriate protective equipment. Introducing structured radiation safety teaching before theatre exposure and ensuring access to correctly fitted protective equipment may improve student safety, confidence, and preparedness in the operating theatre. Keywords: ionising radiation, medical education, occupational radiation exposure, protective equipment, radiation safety

title: Radiation Protection Practices Among Medical Students at Two United Kingdom Medical Schools.
text: Orthopaedic surgery relies heavily on ionising radiation (IR) for intraoperative imaging and procedural guidance. Since its introduction in 1895, radiographic imaging has become integral to orthopaedic practice [1]. Despite its clinical use, occupational exposure to IR carries well-established risks. Concerns regarding the long-term health effects of radiation exposure have been raised. Female orthopaedic surgeons have been reported to have a 2.9-fold increased risk of breast cancer compared with the general population [2]. This highlights the importance of effective radiation protection measures within the surgical environment. Medical students frequently attend orthopaedic theatres during clinical placements, where they may be exposed to IR with limited formal training in radiation safety. As future clinicians, it is essential to ensure they are adequately protected and educated.

title: Radiation Protection Practices Among Medical Students at Two United Kingdom Medical Schools.
text: IR is widely used in orthopaedic surgery, particularly through fluoroscopic imaging for fracture fixation and intraoperative guidance [3]. Despite IR being essential for clinical practice, exposure is associated with cumulative stochastic risks, including malignancy and cataract information [4]. In the United Kingdom, the safe use of IR is governed by the Ionising Radiations Regulations 2017, which outline employer responsibilities for radiation protection, including training, risk assessment, and provision of appropriate protective equipment [5]. The principle of optimisation of radiation protection outlined in the 2007 recommendations of the International Commission on Radiological Protection (ICRP) is also fundamental in minimising occupational exposure [6]. It is a foundational concept which emphasises that exposure to IR should be minimised as much as possible, considering economic and social factors.

title: Radiation Protection Practices Among Medical Students at Two United Kingdom Medical Schools.
text: Research has demonstrated that orthopaedic surgeons are at increased risk due to fluoroscopically guided procedures. Increased radiation exposure to the hands, thyroid, and eyes is common during orthopaedic procedures such as intramedullary nailing and dynamic hip screw fixation [7]. However, there is still inconsistent use of personal protective equipment (PPE), including thyroid shields and lead glasses, even if available [8]. Poor compliance is likely attributed to lack of education about radiation risks, lack of formal training and time constraints [9,10]. Educational interventions can significantly improve understanding of radiation doses, and hence increase PPE use and optimise positioning during fluoroscopic procedures [11]. Furthermore, there remains a lack of focus regarding educating medical students. As temporary members of the operating theatre, they often lack formal induction and access to appropriate PPE. Hence, their understanding largely depends on inconsistent informal teaching. Surveys assessing medical student knowledge showed inadequate understanding of protective strategies and low confidence in applying these in clinical practice [12]. A cohort study assessed medical students’ knowledge after a formal lecture, which showed an increase of 31% [13].

title: Radiation Protection Practices Among Medical Students at Two United Kingdom Medical Schools.
text: Existing literature highlights three key issues, including insufficient formal teaching, variability in safe practice, and a lack of focus on undergraduate populations. This study aims to evaluate radiation safety among medical students attending theatres, with specific objectives to assess educational exposure to radiation safety, practical radiation protection practices, including PPE use and positioning, and students’ perceptions of safety during theatre attendance.

title: Radiation Protection Practices Among Medical Students at Two United Kingdom Medical Schools.
text: A quantitative, cross-sectional, questionnaire-based study was conducted among UK medical students undertaking clinical training from mainly two UK medical schools. Recruitment was primarily undertaken through medical student networks at the University of Plymouth and the University of Manchester. Data were collected over a 10-day period in December 2023 using an anonymous online questionnaire administered through Google Forms. The study aimed to assess medical students’ exposure to radiation safety education, use of PPE, education surrounding radiation protection practices, and perceptions of safety when attending operating theatres in which IR was used. Participants were eligible for inclusion if they were medical students enrolled at a UK medical school and were undertaking clinical training at the time of the survey. Students were required to have experience of, or exposure to, clinical environments in which IR could be used, particularly operating theatres. Participation was voluntary. The questionnaire was distributed using convenience sampling through university medical student WhatsApp group chats, primarily at the University of Plymouth and the University of Manchester. Students from other UK medical schools who received the survey link and met the eligibility criteria were also eligible for inclusion.

title: Radiation Protection Practices Among Medical Students at Two United Kingdom Medical Schools.
text: A total of 70 medical students completed the questionnaire and were included in the analysis. Of these, 56% (39) were from the University of Plymouth, 40% (28) were from the University of Manchester, and 4% (3) were from other UK medical schools (Cambridge, Imperial College London, and University of Lancashire). The total number of students who received the survey invitation could not be reliably established because recruitment occurred through WhatsApp group chats and the survey link could be accessed and shared within student networks. Consequently, an accurate denominator for the invited population was unavailable, and a formal response rate could not be calculated. Data were collected using a structured nine-item questionnaire developed specifically for this study by the authors, Areen Tawil and Aysha Al-Bakri, and administered electronically using Google Forms. The questionnaire was designed collaboratively by both authors in accordance with the study objectives and focused on radiation protection issues relevant to medical students attending clinical environments where IR may be used. The full questionnaire is included in the Appendices. The questionnaire was not adapted directly from a previously validated instrument and was therefore treated as a study-specific survey rather than a validated psychometric scale. The questionnaire was reviewed by clinicians with relevant experience before distribution to assess the relevance and clarity of the items.

title: Radiation Protection Practices Among Medical Students at Two United Kingdom Medical Schools.
text: The nine questionnaire items covered the following principal domains: (1) Participant characteristics, including sex and university. (2) PPE, including perceived appropriateness of lead apron fit and use of thyroid protection. (3) Radiation safety behaviour and guidance, including whether students were reminded where to stand to minimise radiation exposure. (4) Radiation safety education, including whether formal radiation safety teaching had been received before exposure to IR in theatre. (5) Perceived safety, including whether participants felt safe when attending theatres where IR was being used. Questions used categorical response formats appropriate to each item, including binary responses (e.g. yes/no) and multiple-choice categorical responses. There was one question titled additional comments, which was a free-text question. As the questionnaire assessed several distinct aspects of radiation safety rather than a single underlying construct, no overall questionnaire score was calculated. Each item was analysed independently.

title: Radiation Protection Practices Among Medical Students at Two United Kingdom Medical Schools.
text: For the purposes of this study, formal radiation safety training was defined as participants reporting that they had received dedicated radiation safety teaching before exposure to IR in the theatre environment. This definition was developed specifically for the purposes of this study, as there is currently no standardised guidance specifying the radiation safety information or formal training that medical students should receive before attending clinical environments where IR may be used. Appropriate PPE practice was assessed separately according to reported lead apron fit and thyroid shield use rather than being combined into a composite score.

title: Radiation Protection Practices Among Medical Students at Two United Kingdom Medical Schools.
text: Data collection took place over a 10-day period in December 2023. Participants accessed the questionnaire through an electronic link to Google Forms. Participation was voluntary, and questionnaire responses were anonymised to maintain confidentiality. No personally identifiable information was collected. Participants were informed about the purpose of the questionnaire, and completion and submission of the survey were taken to indicate informed consent. No formal prior sample size calculation was performed because this was an exploratory student-led survey using convenience sampling. As the study was primarily descriptive, categorical variables were summarised using frequencies and percentages. This included participant sex, university affiliation, reported lead apron fit, thyroid shield use, receipt of radiation safety teaching, reminders regarding positioning to minimise radiation exposure, and perceived safety in theatres where IR was present. The project was conducted as a student-led service evaluation and therefore did not undergo formal research ethics committee review. Participation was voluntary and anonymous, no personally identifiable information was collected, and completion of the questionnaire was taken as implied consent. The service evaluation classification should be considered when interpreting the governance and ethical oversight of the study.

title: Radiation Protection Practices Among Medical Students at Two United Kingdom Medical Schools.
text: A total of 70 medical students completed the questionnaire. Sex was reported by 52 participants. Overall, 31/70 (44%) of participants were female, 21/70 (30%) were male, and 18/70 (26%) preferred not to disclose their sex. Following standardisation of the free-text responses for medical school affiliation, the majority of participants were associated with the University of Plymouth or the University of Manchester. Overall, 39 (56%) participants were from the University of Plymouth, 28 (40%) were from the University of Manchester, and 3/70 (4%) were from other UK medical schools. Recruitment was primarily conducted through medical student WhatsApp networks associated with Plymouth and Manchester. However, as the survey link could be shared within wider student networks, three eligible responses were received from students outside the two principal institutions and were retained in the analysis. Participant characteristics are summarised in Table 1. Previous exposure to ionising radiation All 70/70 (100%) participants reported having previously been present during at least one clinical procedure involving IR. Four (6%) participants reported attending one such procedure, five (7%) reported attending two, 10 (14%) reported attending three, and eight (12%) reported attending four. The largest group, 43 (61%), reported having attended five or more procedures involving IR. Personal protective equipment

title: Radiation Protection Practices Among Medical Students at Two United Kingdom Medical Schools.
text: Only half of participants, 35 (50.0%), responded that their lead apron adequately covered their breast and axillary regions. Overall, 29 (41%) participants reported that it did not. The remaining 6/70 (9%) provided qualified responses indicating partial, inconsistent, or uncertain protection. Several of these responses specifically indicated that the breast region was covered, but the axillary region was not, while another participant reported variation in protection between different clinical settings. Thyroid shield use was similarly inconsistent. Overall, 29 (41%) participants reported wearing a thyroid shield during procedures involving IR, while 34 (49%) reported that they did not. A further seven (10%) described intermittent or conditional use, including wearing a thyroid shield only occasionally, when available, or after specifically requesting one. Radiation safety guidance and education Overall, 37 (53%) participants reported being reminded where to stand to reduce their radiation exposure, while 30 (43%) reported that they were not given such guidance. The remaining 3/70 (4%) indicated that they were reminded only sometimes. Formal preparation before theatre exposure was uncommon. Only 11 (16%) participants reported receiving an introduction to radiation safety before theatre attendance, whereas 56 (80%) reported receiving no such introduction. Three participants (4%) gave uncertain or conditional responses, including “sometimes” and “not sure.”

title: Radiation Protection Practices Among Medical Students at Two United Kingdom Medical Schools.
text: Perceived safety in theatre Overall, 66 participants answered the question regarding whether they felt safe in theatres where IR was present. Of these, 44 (67%) reported feeling safe, whereas 22 (33%) reported feeling unsafe. Four participants did not answer this question. The complete questionnaire findings are summarised in Table 2. Qualitative findings In total, five (7%) participants provided additional free-text comments. Given the small number of responses, these comments were analysed using descriptive content analysis rather than formal thematic analysis. Each response was read and coded according to the radiation safety concern or experience described. Similar codes were grouped into descriptive categories, and responses could contribute to more than one category when multiple concerns were raised. The most frequently identified category related to the availability, adequacy, fit, or anatomical coverage of PPE, which was raised by 3/5 of free-text respondents. Specific concerns included insufficient availability and sizing of lead aprons, inadequate coverage of the axillary regions, lack of thyroid protection, and absence of eye protection.

title: Radiation Protection Practices Among Medical Students at Two United Kingdom Medical Schools.
text: One participant described insufficient safety oversight during clinical placement, reporting prior awareness of radiation risks but a lack of active staff intervention to ensure appropriate protection. One participant raised a concern regarding radiation exposure associated with compulsory orthopaedic theatre attendance. These qualitative findings are summarised in Table 3.

title: Radiation Protection Practices Among Medical Students at Two United Kingdom Medical Schools.
text: This study identifies important gaps in radiation safety training, education, and protective practices among UK medical students, mainly from two institutions, during theatre exposure. Despite the well-established use of IR in orthopaedic procedures, our findings suggest that formal education and consistent implementation of safety measures at undergraduate level remain suboptimal. A key finding of this study is that one-third of respondents reported feeling unsafe in theatre environments where IR was used. This perception is clinically important, as perceived safety is closely linked to confidence, engagement in theatre-based learning, and willingness to participate in surgical specialties [14]. Feelings of insecurity may reflect inadequate preparation before clinical exposure, inconsistent supervision, or variability in the enforcement of radiation protection protocols within theatre environments. Notably, only 16% of respondents reported receiving formal radiation safety teaching before theatre exposure. This finding suggests a significant gap in undergraduate medical curricula, particularly given that orthopaedic theatres are commonly among the first surgical environments in which students are exposed to fluoroscopy and intraoperative imaging. The lack of structured teaching may contribute to poor understanding of fundamental radiation safety principles, including dose minimisation, appropriate positioning, and correct use of shielding equipment.

title: Radiation Protection Practices Among Medical Students at Two United Kingdom Medical Schools.
text: In addition, our findings demonstrate suboptimal use of PPE. Almost half of respondents reported not using a thyroid shield consistently, and 41% reported that their lead apron did not fit appropriately. This is concerning, as inadequate shielding of radiosensitive organs such as the thyroid and breast tissue may increase cumulative occupational exposure over time [15]. The issue of poor fit is particularly relevant for medical students, who may have limited access to appropriately sized protective equipment compared with permanent theatre staff. These findings are consistent with previous literature highlighting variability in radiation safety culture within surgical specialties. While most operating theatres provide protective equipment, previous studies have shown that availability does not necessarily translate into consistent use, often due to lack of training, time pressures, or insufficient reinforcement from senior staff [16]. Our findings extend this concern to medical students, who may be particularly vulnerable due to their limited clinical experience and hierarchical position within the theatre environment.

title: Radiation Protection Practices Among Medical Students at Two United Kingdom Medical Schools.
text: Furthermore, the qualitative feedback in this study highlights additional practical concerns, including insufficient availability of appropriately sized lead aprons and lack of eye protection. Although less commonly discussed in undergraduate settings, ocular exposure to scatter radiation has been recognised as a potential occupational risk in interventional specialties [17]. The absence of eye protection provision suggests that radiation safety protocols may not be fully standardised for student-level exposure. It is also notable that 43% of respondents reported not being reminded where to stand during radiation exposure. Proper positioning is a simple but highly effective method of reducing scatter radiation dose; therefore, this finding may reflect missed opportunities for informal teaching during clinical placements [18]. Reinforcement of safe positioning by theatre staff could represent a low-cost, high-impact intervention to improve safety awareness. Importantly, despite these deficiencies, two-thirds of respondents reported feeling safe in theatre environments. This discrepancy between perceived safety and objectively reported gaps in training and PPE use may indicate a lack of awareness regarding radiation risks rather than the true absence of risk. This highlights the importance of improving not only safety infrastructure but also risk awareness and education.

title: Radiation Protection Practices Among Medical Students at Two United Kingdom Medical Schools.
text: From a systems perspective, these findings suggest that radiation safety for medical students is inconsistently implemented across clinical placements. Variability between institutions, theatre teams, and supervising clinicians may contribute to unequal learning experiences. Standardisation of induction processes before orthopaedic placements, including mandatory radiation safety briefings, may help address this inconsistency. Educational interventions have been shown in other contexts to significantly improve radiation safety knowledge and behaviour among trainees [19]. Incorporating structured teaching sessions, simulation-based learning, or mandatory e-learning modules may improve both knowledge retention and compliance with safety protocols. In addition, ensuring that appropriately fitted lead protection is readily available to students should be considered a basic requirement for safe clinical exposure.

title: Radiation Protection Practices Among Medical Students at Two United Kingdom Medical Schools.
text: This study has several limitations. The sample size was relatively small and drawn mainly from two UK medical schools, which may limit generalisability to other institutions. As the survey was developed specifically for this study, its measurement properties have not been formally established. While clinical review was undertaken during questionnaire development to ensure that the questions were clear and relevant, further validation would strengthen the reliability and reproducibility of future research using this survey. The use of convenience sampling and a study-specific questionnaire may also limit the exact reproducibility of the study across different institutions and student populations.

title: Radiation Protection Practices Among Medical Students at Two United Kingdom Medical Schools.
text: In addition, the use of self-reported questionnaire data introduces potential recall and response bias. Students may have over- or under-reported PPE use or safety behaviours. Participants were recruited through university WhatsApp groups, which may have introduced selection bias, as students who chose to participate may have had a greater pre-existing interest in radiation safety. Additional participant characteristics, including year of study and the number and type of orthopaedic procedures previously attended, were not collected. These factors may influence students’ exposure to radiation safety practices and their familiarity with protective measures, and their absence limits further analysis of potential differences within the study population. Finally, the cross-sectional design limits causal inference, and the study cannot determine whether lack of training directly resulted in unsafe practices. Although previous exposure to radiation safety teaching was recorded, the questionnaire did not define or examine the format and extent of this teaching. Consequently, variation in educational exposure between participants could not be explored.

title: Radiation Protection Practices Among Medical Students at Two United Kingdom Medical Schools.
text: Despite these limitations, this study provides useful insight into an underexplored area of undergraduate surgical education. To our knowledge, few studies have specifically assessed radiation safety education among medical students in orthopaedic theatre settings. The findings therefore contribute to a growing recognition that radiation safety education should begin at the undergraduate level rather than being reserved for postgraduate training. Future research should aim to expand sample size across multiple institutions and explore differences in radiation safety practices between specialties and clinical environments. Interventional studies assessing the impact of structured radiation safety teaching on knowledge, behaviour, and confidence would also be valuable.

title: Radiation Protection Practices Among Medical Students at Two United Kingdom Medical Schools.
text: This exploratory study identified potential gaps in radiation safety education and access to appropriate protective equipment among the medical students surveyed. Structured teaching, access to appropriately fitted protective equipment, and reinforcement of safe practices may help improve students’ preparedness for clinical environments where IR is used. However, the small convenience sample, drawn predominantly from two medical schools, limits the generalisability of these findings. Further research involving larger and more representative samples is needed to determine the extent of these findings and inform future approaches to undergraduate radiation safety education.
