title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
text: However, the clinical relevance of variable RBE remains controversial. While some studies suggest that linear energy transfer-associated biological dose escalation may contribute to radiation-induced brain injury, others emphasize the uncertainty and limited clinical validation of current models [17,18]. This uncertainty is particularly relevant in paediatric patients, in whom even subtle radiation-related tissue changes may have long-term consequences. Current normal tissue complication probability models are still largely based on physical dose parameters and may insufficiently reflect the biological heterogeneity of proton beam therapy [19,20]. Consequently, there is a need for clinical data linking radiation-induced imaging changes to linear energy transfer and variable RBE-based dose parameters.

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
text: The primary objective of this study was to investigate whether RICE preferentially occurs in regions characterized by elevated LET and increased variable RBE-weighted dose following proton therapy in paediatric patients with low-grade glioma and ependymoma. Secondary objectives were to determine the incidence and radiological characteristics of RICE and to describe long-term oncological outcomes. We hypothesized that RICE would preferentially develop in regions of increased biological dose that are not adequately represented by the conventional fixed RBE approach. By integrating systematic radiological follow-up with volumetric lesion assessment and biologically informed dosimetric analyses, this study aims to provide clinical evidence for the potential relevance of LET and variable RBE in radiation-induced imaging changes and to support the future development of biologically informed proton treatment planning.

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
section: 2. Materials and Methods > 2.1. Study Design and Patient Cohort
text: This retrospective single-centre cohort study analysed data from a prospectively maintained institutional registry comprising consecutive paediatric patients treated with proton beam therapy at the HIT between January 2010 and February 2024. Patients were eligible for the overall survival (OS) analysis if they were younger than 18 years at the start of irradiation, had a histologically confirmed diagnosis of LGG or ependymoma, and underwent primary cranial proton beam irradiation. For the radiological, dosimetric, and PFS analyses, an additional requirement of at least 12 months of radiological follow-up was applied. Among 820 paediatric patients treated with PRT during the study period, 418 received cranial irradiation. Of the 132 patients diagnosed with LGG or ependymoma, all were included in the OS analysis using mortality data obtained from the German death registry. Seventy-six patients fulfilled the additional radiological follow-up criterion and were included in the radiological, dosimetric, and PFS analyses. This cohort comprised 33 patients with LGG and 43 with ependymoma. The remaining 56 patients (23 with LGG and 33 with ependymoma) were included exclusively in the OS analysis. Further clinical and radiotherapeutic characteristics of the 76 patients, stratified by tumour entity, are presented in Appendix A (Table A1).

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
text: All available follow-up magnetic resonance imaging examinations were retrospectively reviewed using a standardized dual-reader approach, with at least one reviewer being board-certified in radiology or radiation oncology. The last available pre-treatment magnetic resonance imaging examination served as the reference scan. Follow-up examinations were assessed sequentially for newly occurring or progressive contrast-enhancing lesions. RICE was defined as newly appearing contrast enhancement located outside the gross tumour volume (GTV) but within the high-dose region of the corresponding proton treatment plan. In contrast, newly detected contrast enhancement within the GTV was considered indicative of treatment-related blood–brain barrier disruption or tumour-associated imaging changes rather than RICE. Native and contrast-enhanced T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and fluid-attenuated inversion recovery sequences were evaluated where available. In cases of diagnostic uncertainty, imaging findings were reviewed jointly until consensus was reached. The observation period was limited to 120 months after treatment to ensure comparable follow-up assessment.

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
section: 2. Materials and Methods > 2.3. Dosimetric and Biological Assessment
text: Detected RICE lesions were manually contoured in RayStation version 11B and spatially correlated with the original PTV. Dose distributions were assessed using the clinically applied constant RBE value of 1.1 and three variable RBE models: Wedenberg et al. (2013), McNamara et al. (2015), and Carabe et al. (2012) [14,15,16]. The variable RBE models were implemented using scripts imported into RayStation version 11B and applied to dose and LETd data. A photon reference α/β ratio of 2.0 Gy was assumed for brain tissue. The exact mathematical formulations and numerical coefficients implemented in the scripts are provided in Appendix B (Table A2). LET-weighted dose parameters and Dose(RBE) × LET products were calculated for RICE regions and corresponding PTV at predefined dose-volume levels, including D99, D98, D95, mean dose, D50, D2, and D1. As an exploratory analysis, normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) values were estimated using the previously published model-based planning approach to compare conventional physical dose-based risk estimates with the observed occurrence of RICE [11,20].

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
text: Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 27.0.1. Continuous variables were summarized using medians and ranges, and categorical variables using absolute and relative frequencies. Non-normally distributed continuous variables were compared using the Mann–Whitney U test. Categorical variables were analysed using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test, as appropriate. Paired dosimetric comparisons between RICE regions and PTV were performed using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Overall survival and progression-free survival were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method, and group comparisons were conducted with the log-rank test. An additional exploratory descriptive comparison of overall survival and tumour progression according to RICE status was performed in the 76 patients with sufficient radiological follow-up. Although overall survival was assessed in the extended cohort of 132 patients, this comparison was restricted to patients with a systematically assessed RICE status to minimize potential misclassification. Given the small number of RICE cases, no formal statistical comparison was undertaken. A two-sided p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Because of the limited number of RICE events, multivariable regression analysis was not performed to avoid model overfitting.

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
section: 2. Materials and Methods > 2.5. Ethics, Data Availability, and Use of Generative Artificial Intelligence
text: The study was approved by the Ethics Committee of the University of Heidelberg, Germany (approval number S-377/2018). Individual-level clinical imaging and treatment data are not publicly available because of data protection regulations and institutional ethical requirements. Anonymized derived datasets may be made available by the corresponding author upon reasonable request and subject to institutional and ethical approval. No publicly deposited large-scale dataset or accession number is associated with this study.

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
text: The final radiological and dosimetric analysis cohort comprised 76 paediatric patients, including 33 patients with low-grade glioma and 43 patients with ependymoma. The cohort consisted of 43 male and 33 female patients. The median age at the start of PRT was 11 years in the low-grade glioma group and 5.6 years in the ependymoma group. In the low-grade glioma subgroup, 28 patients had World Health Organization (WHO) grade I tumours, four had grade II tumours, and one patient had low-grade glioma not otherwise specified. In the ependymoma subgroup, four patients had WHO grade II tumours and 39 patients had WHO grade III ependymomas. The median follow-up was 38.5 months, ranging from 13 to 145 months. The patient selection process is shown in Figure 1.

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
text: For overall survival analysis, the extended cohort of 132 eligible patients was evaluated using mortality data obtained from the German death registry. Median overall survival was not reached in either tumour entity. The estimated 5- and 10-year overall survival rates were 91.7% and 84.0% for low-grade glioma and 86.6% and 75.5% for ependymoma, respectively. No statistically significant difference in overall survival was observed between both entities (p = 0.41). Progression-free survival was analysed in the 76-patient cohort with available long-term data (n = 76). Five- and 10-year progression-free survival rates were 84.4% and 77.3% in patients with low-grade glioma and 69.3% and 63.0% in patients with ependymoma, respectively. Although progression-free survival tended to be lower in the ependymoma group, the difference did not reach statistical significance (p = 0.07). Tumour progression occurred in 17 of 76 patients (22.4%), including five patients with low-grade glioma (15.2%) and twelve patients with ependymoma (27.9%). Median time to progression was 27 months, with a range of 2 to 107 months. Male patients experienced significantly earlier progression than female patients, with median times to progression of 24.8 and 56.2 months, respectively (p = 0.031).

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
text: An exploratory descriptive comparison of oncological outcomes according to RICE status was performed in the 76 patients with available radiological follow-up. Among the six patients who developed RICE, no deaths and one tumour progression (16.7%) were recorded, compared with ten deaths (14.3%) and 16 progression events (22.9%) among the 70 patients without RICE. The median recorded observation times for the OS endpoint were 38 and 63 months in patients with and without RICE, respectively. Given the limited number of RICE cases, no formal statistical comparison was performed.

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
text: The median prescribed radiation dose across the entire cohort was 54 Gy, with a range of 48.6 to 68 Gy. Patients with low-grade glioma received a median dose of 54 Gy, whereas patients with ependymoma received a significantly higher median dose of 59.4 Gy (p < 0.001). Two-field irradiation was the most frequently used treatment approach in both groups, applied in 26 of 33 low-grade glioma patients and 28 of 43 ependymoma patients. PRT was predominantly administered after prior surgical intervention and represented second-line treatment in 60.6% of low-grade glioma patients and 72.1% of ependymoma patients.

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
section: 3. Results > 3.4. Incidence and Morphological Characteristics of Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancements
text: RICEs were detected in six of 76 patients, corresponding to an overall incidence of 7.9%. All affected patients belonged to the ependymoma subgroup, resulting in an incidence of 14.0% among patients with ependymoma, whereas no RICEs were observed in the low-grade glioma group. The exact 95% confidence intervals were 14.0% (6/43; 95% CI 5.3–27.9%) for ependymoma and 0% (0/33; 95% CI 0–10.6%) for low-grade glioma. The sex distribution among affected patients was balanced, with three male and three female patients. Four patients showed small transient RICE lesions that were visible in only one follow-up magnetic resonance imaging examination. Two patients developed classic periventricular RICE with persistent contrast uptake over multiple follow-up examinations. All observed lesions demonstrated spontaneous regression over time.

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
section: 3. Results > 3.4. Incidence and Morphological Characteristics of Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancements
text: A higher total prescribed radiation dose was significantly associated with the occurrence of RICE (p = 0.031). Patients with RICE had received a mean dose of 58.5 Gy, compared with 55.3 Gy in patients without such lesions. All six RICE cases occurred within the ependymoma subgroup, which received a significantly higher median prescribed dose than the low-grade glioma subgroup (59.4 vs. 54 Gy, p < 0.001). Within the ependymoma subgroup, RICE incidence varied according to the number of irradiation fields. RICE occurred in two of four patients (50.0%) treated with a single field, two of 28 patients (7.1%) treated with two fields, and two of 11 patients (18.2%) treated with three fields. Given the small number of RICE cases, these differences should be interpreted descriptively.

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
section: 3. Results > 3.5. Dosimetric and Biological Characterization of Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement Regions
text: The median volume of contoured RICE lesions was 0.16 cm3 (0.01–0.68 cm3). In comparison, the median PTV was 167.61 cm3 (45.01–419.12 cm3). To complement the voxel-wise dosimetric analyses, exploratory NTCP estimates were calculated for the five patients with periventricular RICE using our previously published risk prediction model [11,20]. Predicted NTCP values ranged from 0.05 to 0.52, with a median of 0.12. Mean Dose(RBE) × LETd products were higher in RICE regions than in PTV at low- and intermediate-dose levels (D99–D50), whereas PTV values were higher at D2 and D1 (Table 1). Direct comparison of the underlying metrics showed higher mean LETd in RICE regions, particularly at D99 and D50. In contrast, conventional RBE-weighted dose (fixed RBE = 1.1) was nearly similar between RICE regions and PTV at D99 and lower in RICE regions at D50 to D1 (Table 2). Thus, elevated combined dose–LET metrics within RICE regions were not accompanied by a consistently higher conventional RBE-weighted dose. Given the small RICE lesion volumes, dose-volume metrics were evaluated from D99 to D1. Metrics below D1 were excluded because of their increasing sensitivity to contouring, image-registration, voxel-size, and local dose-gradient uncertainties.

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
section: 3. Results > 3.5. Dosimetric and Biological Characterization of Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement Regions
text: To facilitate interpretation of the combined Dose(RBE) × LET metric, Table 2 separately presents the mean RBE-weighted dose and LET values for the eight RICE regions and six corresponding PTV. LET was higher within RICE regions, particularly at low- and intermediate-dose levels, whereas the corresponding RBE-weighted dose values were generally similar to or lower than those observed in the PTV. Application of all investigated variable RBE models, including Wedenberg, McNamara, and Carabe, resulted in higher biologically weighted dose estimates within RICE regions compared with calculations based on the conventional fixed RBE value of 1.1. Dose-volume histogram analyses demonstrated that variable RBE models predicted biologically relevant hotspots exceeding 100% of the prescribed reference dose within the target volume. The McNamara model showed the most pronounced hotspot formation and is shown in Figure 2 as an example.

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
section: 3. Results > 3.5. Dosimetric and Biological Characterization of Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement Regions
text: Across all investigated variable RBE models, relative dose differences compared with the conventional fixed RBE model (RBE = 1.1) varied across the evaluated dose-volume metrics. The most pronounced differences were observed in the low- to intermediate-dose range, particularly between D95 and D50, whereas only minor differences were present at D99, D98, and in the high-dose region (D2 and D1). Among the investigated models, the Wedenberg model generally demonstrated the largest relative deviations from the fixed RBE approach at D95–D50. Model-based dose comparisons relative to the conventional fixed RBE model are summarized in Figure 3. The robustness of these findings against potential contouring and registration uncertainty was confirmed by a margin sensitivity analysis, presented in Appendix C (Figure A1).

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
text: The present study investigated the relationship between RICE and LET-associated biological dose after proton therapy in paediatric patients. The observed spatial association between RICE and elevated biologically weighted dose across all investigated variable RBE models supports the primary study hypothesis and extends previous observations from adult glioma cohorts to a paediatric population. The primary objective of this study was to investigate the spatial association between RICE and LET-associated biological dose following PRT in paediatric patients with low-grade glioma and ependymoma. Consistent with our hypothesis, RICE regions exhibited consistently higher biologically weighted dose metrics than the corresponding PTV across all investigated variable RBE models. Relative differences between the variable RBE models and the conventional fixed RBE approach were most pronounced in the low- to intermediate-dose range, whereas only minor deviations were observed in the highest-dose regions. Together, these findings support the concept that biologically weighted dose metrics identify spatial dose heterogeneity not fully represented by the conventional fixed RBE model.

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
text: Our observations are consistent with an increasing body of clinical evidence supporting the relevance of LET-informed biological dose evaluation for radiation-induced imaging changes after PRT. Previous voxel-based studies in adult glioma patients demonstrated an increased probability of RICE in regions characterized by elevated LET and variable RBE-weighted dose [12,13,18,21]. More recently, Bregman et al. developed the first voxel-based NTCP model for paediatric posterior fossa tumours and identified the combined dose–LET metric (D·LETd), younger age, and anatomical location within the pons as independent predictors of RICE [22]. Furthermore, RICE occurred predominantly in regions combining a high absorbed dose with intermediate-to-high D·LETd, reinforcing the biological relevance of LET-associated dose metrics in paediatric patients. A complementary two-dimensional visualization of mean Dose(RBE) and LETd across RICE and PTV regions is provided in Appendix D (Figure A2), illustrating the heterogeneous Dose(RBE)–LETd characteristics of individual lesions. Although our study investigated a different tumour population and applied a region-based rather than voxel-wise analysis, the observed spatial association between RICE and biologically weighted dose is consistent with these findings. In contrast, the overall incidence of RICE in our cohort was substantially lower than that reported by Bregman et al. and also lower than rates described in adult low-grade glioma cohorts [9].

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
text: RICE was observed in 7.9% of the overall cohort and occurred exclusively in patients with ependymoma. This discrepancy is unlikely to be explained by differences in the radiological definition of RICE, as both studies adopted the definition previously proposed by our group [23], restricting RICE to newly occurring contrast-enhancing lesions outside the GTV to distinguish radiation-induced changes in normal brain tissue from intratumoural treatment-related imaging changes. Instead, differences in patient and treatment characteristics are the more likely explanation. Whereas our study exclusively included patients receiving focal cranial PRT, the cohort of Bregman et al. predominantly comprised patients with medulloblastoma, who almost invariably underwent craniospinal irradiation followed by a posterior fossa or tumour bed boost. Craniospinal irradiation exposes substantially larger volumes of the central nervous system than focal treatment alone and may therefore increase susceptibility to radiation-induced imaging changes. In addition, more than three quarters of patients in the Bregman cohort received chemotherapy, with approximately half undergoing concomitant treatment, which may have further contributed to the higher observed RICE incidence despite the inability to assess chemotherapy as an independent predictor because of the heterogeneity of treatment regimens.

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
text: Age-related differences in tissue repair capacity, vascular vulnerability, and regenerative potential may further contribute to the lower incidence observed in paediatric focal proton therapy compared with adult low-grade glioma populations [24,25,26]. Nevertheless, the concordance of the spatial dosimetric findings despite these substantial differences in patient populations and treatment approaches suggests that the association between LET-associated biological dose and RICE represents a robust phenomenon across different PRT cohorts. A central observation of the present analysis was that all investigated variable RBE models consistently identified higher biologically weighted dose estimates within RICE regions than within the corresponding PTV. Moreover, the largest deviations from the conventional RBE = 1.1 approach occurred in the low- to intermediate-dose range, whereas differences became progressively smaller towards the highest dose levels. This pattern suggests that biologically relevant dose heterogeneity may be particularly pronounced outside the high-dose core of the target volume, where physical dose distributions alone may underestimate biological effect [18,24,25,26,27]. Although the magnitude of the predicted dose differences varied between the Wedenberg, McNamara, and Carabe models, all demonstrated a comparable spatial pattern, supporting the robustness of the observed association despite differences in their underlying radiobiological assumptions.

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
text: These results contribute to the ongoing debate regarding the clinical relevance of variable RBE in PRT. The current standard of using a fixed RBE value of 1.1 provides a practical and reproducible basis for treatment planning [28,29]. However, it simplifies a complex biological process and does not account for spatial variations in LET, dose per fraction, or tissue-specific radiosensitivity. The present findings do not prove a causal relationship between LET, variable RBE, and RICE formation. Nevertheless, they provide clinical evidence that affected regions may coincide with areas of increased biological dose. This interpretation is further strengthened by the recent external validation of adult voxel-based RICE models by Palkowitsch et al. [30], who confirmed both increased periventricular sensitivity and the relevance of variable RBE for predicting radiation-induced imaging changes after PRT. Together, these studies support the view that evaluation of LET- and RBE-weighted dose complements conventional physical dose assessment, particularly for normal tissue risk characterization. At the same time, variable RBE models should be interpreted with appropriate caution. These models remain approximations of complex tissue responses, and differences between the Wedenberg, McNamara, and Carabe approaches reflect diverging assumptions regarding dose, LET, and tissue-specific parameters [23,31,32].

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
text: In small lesion volumes, model-based biological dose estimates may be sensitive to contouring uncertainty, image registration, and steep local dose gradients. Moreover, increased modelled biological dose does not necessarily imply clinically relevant toxicity. Many RICEs are asymptomatic and may regress spontaneously, suggesting that these lesions may represent transient blood–brain barrier disruption rather than irreversible parenchymal injury [33,34]. Variable RBE models should therefore currently be regarded as tools for risk exploration rather than definitive clinical decision criteria [13].

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
text: Exploratory NTCP estimates in patients with periventricular RICEs were generally low-to-moderate despite the occurrence of imaging changes. However, these results should be interpreted with caution, as the applied NTCP model was originally developed, trained, and calibrated in adult patients with low-grade glioma and was not intended for direct application to paediatric brain tumours. Paediatric patients may differ substantially from adults regarding neurodevelopment, tissue radiosensitivity, anatomical characteristics, and the spectrum and timing of radiation-induced late effects. The need for paediatric-specific normal-tissue models has been recognized by dedicated efforts such as the Paediatric Normal Tissue Effects in the Clinic (PENTEC) initiative, which addresses the limitations of extrapolating predominantly adult-derived normal-tissue data to childhood cancer populations. Consequently, the present analysis should be regarded as hypothesis-generating rather than a validation of the underlying risk model. Nevertheless, the observation that RICE occurred despite relatively low predicted complication probabilities suggests that risk estimates based primarily on physical dose and a fixed RBE of 1.1 may incompletely reflect biologically relevant tissue effects.

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
text: Our findings complement recent developments in biologically informed RICE modelling. Bauer et al. first demonstrated that incorporation of increased distal RBE and periventricular radiosensitivity into treatment planning could reduce the predicted risk of late MR-detected brain lesions in patients with low-grade glioma [35]. This concept was subsequently extended by Sallem et al., who proposed a model-based treatment planning strategy integrating biological risk estimates into proton plan optimization [20]. In parallel, Bregman et al. recently developed the first paediatric voxel-based NTCP model, demonstrating that the combined dose–LET metric (D·LETd), together with age and anatomical location, substantially improved prediction of RICE compared with absorbed dose alone [22]. Although these approaches differ in methodology and patient population, they consistently support the concept that incorporation of biological dose metrics improves characterization of radiation-induced normal tissue effects beyond conventional physical dose evaluation.

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
text: Against this background, our results provide complementary clinical imaging evidence demonstrating that RICE preferentially localized to regions characterized by increased LET-associated biological dose across multiple variable RBE models. Rather than advocating routine implementation of variable RBE-based treatment planning, our findings support continued development and prospective validation of biologically informed NTCP models and risk-adapted proton treatment planning strategies, particularly in paediatric patients, where even modest reductions in late toxicity may translate into substantial long-term clinical benefit. To confirm that these spatial associations were not attributable to image registration or contouring imprecision, we performed a margin sensitivity analysis with simulated contour shifts of up to 3 mm (Appendix C, Figure A1). This analysis demonstrated a robust, persistently elevated LET/RBE signature across all shift magnitudes, supporting the validity of our findings and minimizing the likelihood that they reflect contouring or alignment error rather than a genuine biological association. It should be noted that all observed RICE lesions were transient or self-limiting, with spontaneous regression in every case.

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
text: Rather than diminishing the relevance of our findings, we believe this favourable clinical course supports the value of identifying and addressing LET/RBE-associated dose heterogeneity proactively during treatment planning, potentially preventing even mild, transient toxicity before it manifests clinically. This is particularly relevant in paediatric patients given their long life expectancy and cumulative treatment burden. Several limitations should be considered. The retrospective design and limited number of RICE events restricted statistical power and precluded multivariable modelling of clinical risk factors. An additional limitation is the absence of spatially and dosimetrically matched non-RICE brain regions. The patient-specific PTV served as descriptive reference volumes and differed substantially from the small RICE lesions in size and spatial dose characteristics. Consequently, the observed dosimetric differences cannot establish whether LETd or variable RBE-weighted dose is independently associated with RICE localisation after accounting for anatomical location and conventional dose. Furthermore, the eight RICE regions originated from only six patients and should not be considered independent patient-level observations. Future studies incorporating appropriately matched non-RICE regions and accounting for patient-level clustering are needed to address this question.

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
text: Furthermore, the observed association between prescribed dose and RICE occurrence is univariable and may be confounded by tumour entity, as all RICE cases occurred in the ependymoma subgroup, which received significantly higher doses than the low-grade glioma subgroup. The additional descriptive comparison of oncological outcomes according to RICE status should likewise be interpreted with caution, as RICE was identified during follow-up and retrospective grouping may introduce immortal-time bias. Consequently, no conclusions regarding a prognostic association can be drawn. Given the retrospective design and the small number of observed RICE events, tumour-type-specific incidence estimates are subject to considerable statistical uncertainty, as reflected by the exact 95% confidence intervals (ependymoma: 14.0%, 95% CI 5.3–27.9%; low-grade glioma: 0%, 95% CI 0–10.6%). The overlap between the upper bound of the low-grade glioma interval and the lower bound of the ependymoma interval indicates that the retrospective cohort size limits the level of inference that can be drawn regarding a true absence of RICE in the low-grade glioma subgroup, and findings regarding tumour-type-specific risk should therefore be interpreted with caution and require confirmation in larger, ideally multicentre, cohorts.

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
text: Nevertheless, the study was based on a prospectively maintained institutional registry comprising consecutive paediatric proton therapy patients and therefore reflects routine clinical practice. MRI examinations originated partly from external institutions, introducing some heterogeneity despite standardized review procedures. Furthermore, the use of retrospective image registration and lesion contouring may have introduced spatial uncertainty, particularly in small lesions located in regions with steep dose gradients; a dedicated margin sensitivity analysis (Appendix C, Figure A1) indicated that our findings were robust to this source of uncertainty. Finally, although three established variable RBE models were evaluated, all remain approximations of complex biological processes and should currently be regarded as exploratory tools for biological dose assessment rather than definitive predictors of clinical toxicity. Despite these limitations, this study has several important strengths. It represents one of the largest homogeneous paediatric cohorts of low-grade glioma and ependymoma treated exclusively with PRT, analysed using prospectively collected clinical data and systematic MRI follow-up. By combining volumetric lesion assessment with LET-based dosimetry and multiple variable RBE models, this study provides clinically relevant evidence supporting the spatial association between biologically weighted dose and RICE.

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
text: Future multicentre studies should validate these findings in larger paediatric cohorts and investigate whether integration of LET- and RBE-weighted dose metrics into NTCP modelling and biologically informed treatment planning can further improve individualized normal tissue risk assessment without compromising tumour control.

title: Radiation-Induced Contrast Enhancement After Proton Therapy for Paediatric Brain Tumours: Association with Variable Relative Biological Effectiveness and Linear Energy Transfer.
text: Proton therapy is a safe and effective treatment modality for paediatric patients with low-grade glioma and ependymoma, demonstrating excellent oncological outcomes and a low incidence of RICE. The observed spatial association between RICE and increased LET-associated biological dose across multiple variable RBE models suggests that biologically weighted dose metrics capture clinically relevant dose heterogeneity beyond the conventional fixed RBE approach. Together with emerging evidence from biologically informed risk modelling, these findings support continued refinement of LET- and RBE-informed NTCP models and proton treatment-planning strategies to further reduce normal tissue toxicity while maintaining excellent tumour control.

title: Impact of anatomical changes on simulated proton arc therapy and intensity-modulated proton therapy for lung cancer.
text: : During lung cancer radiotherapy, inter‐fractional anatomical changes may cause the delivered dose to deviate from the primary plan, affecting tumor control and increasing the risk of normal tissue damage. This study aims to evaluate the impact of anatomical changes on the dosimetric and radiobiological performance of simulated proton arc therapy (sPAT) versus intensity‐modulated proton therapy (IMPT) for lung cancer patients under patient‐specific anatomical changes.

title: Impact of anatomical changes on simulated proton arc therapy and intensity-modulated proton therapy for lung cancer.
text: : Data from 21 lung cancer patients were retrospectively analyzed. The prescribed dose for all patients was 6000 cGy (relative biological effectiveness, RBE). Each patient with a primary planning computed tomography (pCT) and a mid‐treatment adaptive‐planning CT (aCT) acquired at a median of 29 days into treatment due to notable tumor volume changes. Primary plans for sPAT and IMPT were designed on the pCT. After rigid registration of the pCT and aCT, non‐adaptive plans (sPATp‐a, IMPTp‐a) were generated by directly recalculating the doses of the primary plans on the aCT. The comparison evaluated the dosimetric impact of anatomical changes by comparing non‐adaptive plans (sPATp‐a vs. IMPTp‐a). Dose‐volume histogram (DVH) parameters for targets and organs at risk (OARs) and tumor control probability (TCP) and normal tissue complication probability (NTCP) were evaluated.

title: Impact of anatomical changes on simulated proton arc therapy and intensity-modulated proton therapy for lung cancer.
text: : For the primary plans, sPAT and IMPT achieved similar target coverage, while the doses to OARs were generally lower in sPATp. Under anatomical changes, both non‐adaptive plans exhibited a decrease in target coverage, sPATp‐a achieved a D95% of 5567.57 cGy[RBE] compared with 5423.33 cGy[RBE] for IMPTp‐a (p < 0.001), indicating that sPAT better preserved target coverage. Compared with the primary plans, sPATp‐a and IMPTp‐a exhibited TCP reductions of 5.83% and 8.07%, respectively.

title: Impact of anatomical changes on simulated proton arc therapy and intensity-modulated proton therapy for lung cancer.
text: Proton therapy exploits the characteristic Bragg‐peak dose‐deposition property of proton beams to achieve effective tumor ablation while limiting dose deposition in adjacent normal tissues, conferring theoretical dosimetric advantages relative to conventional photon‐based radiotherapy. 1 Nevertheless, intensity‐modulated proton therapy (IMPT) remains susceptible to density variations along beam paths induced by setup uncertainties, intra‐ and inter‐fractional anatomical changes. Such perturbations may degrade delivered dose distributions, leading to insufficient target coverage or excessive irradiation of organs‐at‐risk (OARs). 2 , 3 Proton arc therapy (PAT) leverages gantry rotation to deliver irradiation across multiple beam angles. By spatially dispersing uncertainties associated with individual beam directions, PAT can theoretically yield more homogeneous target dose distributions and mitigate localized high‐dose burdens to OARs. 4 While prior investigations have contrasted baseline dosimetric performance between PAT and IMPT under robust‐optimization conditions, 5 , 6 few studies have systematically evaluated their robustness in the setting of patient‐derived inter‐fractional anatomical modifications.

title: Impact of anatomical changes on simulated proton arc therapy and intensity-modulated proton therapy for lung cancer.
text: Compared to conventional fixed‐field proton therapy, PAT is expected to demonstrate greater robustness against anatomical changes. Lung cancer patients were selected as the focus of this study for the following reasons: (1) substantial tumor shrinkage is frequently observed during conventionally‐fractionated radiotherapy, with volume reductions often exceeding 20%–40%; (2) the large density difference between lung parenchyma and soft tissue/tumor creates dramatic interfaces that amplify proton range perturbations when anatomy changes; and (3) anatomical changes including tumor regression, changes in atelectasis, and the appearance or resolution of pleural effusion are frequently observed and well‐documented. 7 , 8 In this study, we implemented simulated PAT (sPAT) using a discrete‐beam, static pseudo‐arc approach and systematically compared its dosimetric and robustness differences with IMPT under patient‐specific anatomical changes. By generating non‐adaptive, we assessed dose degradation under conditions of observed anatomical change captured on mid‐treatment repeat CT. Dose changes caused by anatomical changes may further affect clinical endpoints such as tumor control and normal tissue toxicity. To reflect these potential effects, we evaluated the clinical impact through tumor control probability (TCP) and normal tissue complication probability (NTCP).

title: Impact of anatomical changes on simulated proton arc therapy and intensity-modulated proton therapy for lung cancer.
text: This study was a retrospective dosimetric comparative analysis. Twenty‐one pathologically‐confirmed lung‐cancer patients who received conventional fractionated photon radiotherapy (60 Gy in 30 fractions) between January 2024 and July 2025 were included. Enrolment was restricted to patients exhibiting notable reduction in tumor volume who underwent clinically‐indicated mid‐treatment re‐simulation adaptive CT (aCT). The aCT scan was acquired at a median interval of 29 days following the primary‐planning CT (pCT). Patient demographic and tumor‐volume data are summarized in Table 1. Declines in clinical‐target‐volume (CTV) from median 31.99 cm3 (pCT) to 18.01 cm3 (aCT) reflect anatomical and density modifications that can perturb proton range and resultant dose distributions.

title: Impact of anatomical changes on simulated proton arc therapy and intensity-modulated proton therapy for lung cancer.
text: Both the pCT and aCT were average‐intensity‐projection CT images reconstructed from 4DCT datasets acquired during free breathing, representing the time‐averaged anatomy and mitigating respiratory motion artifacts. For each patient, primary plans (sPATp and IMPTp) were optimized on the pCT first. For the non‐adaptive plans, the CTV and OARs on the aCT were manually re‐delineated by a radiation oncologist to reflect the updated anatomy at the time of the repeat scanning. After rigid image registration of pCT onto aCT, primary‐plan beam configurations and spot weights were transferred and dose was recalculated on aCT without further plan optimization to produce non‐adaptive plans. All proton therapy plans were developed using RayStation (version 7.0, RaySearch Laboratories, Stockholm, Sweden). To eliminate inter‐planner variability, all treatment plans in this cohort were generated by a single medical dosimetrist. For IMPT plans, 3–4 beams were individually selected for each patient based on the specific tumor location and surrounding OARs, employing multi‐field optimization (MFO).

title: Impact of anatomical changes on simulated proton arc therapy and intensity-modulated proton therapy for lung cancer.
text: sPAT was implemented using a discrete‐beam, static pseudo‐arc approach, consistent with previously reported static arc‐like proton planning. 9 This implementation was an idealized, delivery‐unconstrained, discrete‐beam pseudo‐arc approximation. For each patient, beams were placed at 10° intervals, and the angular range was individually adapted to the patient's tumor geometry, spanning 120°–160° of an ipsilateral arc and yielding 13–17 beams per plan. Full 360° rotation was deliberately avoided so that no beam traversed the contralateral healthy lung. All beams and all their energy layers and spots were optimized simultaneously within a single MFO; no upper limit was imposed on the number of energy layers per beam, and the optimizer autonomously selected energy layers to satisfy target and OARs objectives. The essential difference between sPAT and multi‐field IMPT does not lie in the delivery technique but in the angular sampling: both are static fixed‐field plans, and neither simulates dynamic arc delivery. IMPT used a few clustered fixed beam directions, whereas sPAT used more numerous, denser beam directions distributed along an ipsilateral arc. Therefore, sPAT is technically equivalent to a highly multi‐field IMPT plan with dense, arc‐like angular sampling; if IMPT adopted the same angular sampling as sPAT, the two would define the same optimization problem and differ only in name.

title: Impact of anatomical changes on simulated proton arc therapy and intensity-modulated proton therapy for lung cancer.
text: Here, “arc” describes only the angular distribution of the sampled beam directions, not a continuous dynamic delivery trajectory. Dose calculation was performed using the Monte Carlo algorithm with statistical uncertainty set to 0.5%. CTV‐based robust optimization incorporated 3 mm setup‐shift uncertainty and 3% proton‐range uncertainty, parameters consistent with widely‐accepted proton‐therapy planning guidance for lung‐cancer cases. 10 A total of 21 robust‐evaluation scenarios were computed: 1 nominal scenario, 6 setup‐shift scenarios, 2 range‐error scenarios, and 12 combined setup‐ and range‐error scenarios. The relative biological effectiveness (RBE) factor was fixed at 1.1. All patients were prescribed a dose of 6000 cGy[RBE]/30 fractions. The planning objective required 95% of the CTV volume to receive prescription dose. OARs dose constraints were established according to the treatment planning guidelines recommended by the Particle Therapy Co‐Operative Group (PTCOG) and the conventional fractionated proton therapy OARs limits for lung cancer from the MD Anderson Cancer Center. 11 , 12

title: Impact of anatomical changes on simulated proton arc therapy and intensity-modulated proton therapy for lung cancer.
text: Dosimetric evaluations were performed on dose‐volume histogram (DVH) generated from the nominal dose distributions of the sPAT and IMPT. All primary‐plan dose distributions were normalized such that CTV D95% equaled 6000 cGy[RBE]. Target coverage parameters included the dose covering 98% of the target volume (D98%), the dose covering 95% of the target volume (D95%), and the dose covering 2% of the target volume (D2%). Evaluated OAR parameters encompassed lung V5, lung V20, lung mean dose, esophagus mean dose, heart mean dose, esophagus maximum dose, and spinal‐cord maximum dose. Conformity index (CI) 13 and homogeneity index (HI) 14 were computed using the following definitions: CI=(VTref/VT)×(VTref/Vref) where VTref is the target volume receiving at least the reference (prescription) dose, VT is the total target volume, and Vref is the total volume receiving at least the reference dose. A CI value closer to 1 indicates better dose conformity. The HI was calculated as: HI=(D2%−D98%)/D50% where D50% is the dose covering 50% of the target volume. A HI value closer to 0 indicates better dose homogeneity. To quantify the dosimetric impact of anatomical changes, dose differences (ΔX = Xnon‐adaptive−Xprimary, where X denotes a DVH parameter) were calculated for corresponding non‐adaptive and primary plans.

title: Impact of anatomical changes on simulated proton arc therapy and intensity-modulated proton therapy for lung cancer.
section: MATERIALS AND METHODS > TCP and NTCP calculation
text: Radiobiological outcomes were assessed with tumor‐control probability (TCP) and normal‐tissue‐complication probability (NTCP). TCP was derived by converting heterogeneous DVH data into equivalent‐uniform‐dose (EUD) values using the Niemierko model. 15 , 16 NTCP were computed using the Lyman–Kutcher–Burman (LKB) model. 17 All model parameters were derived from previously published literature and kept consistent across all radiotherapy plans; the specific parameters are summarized in Table 2.

title: Impact of anatomical changes on simulated proton arc therapy and intensity-modulated proton therapy for lung cancer.
text: Statistical analyses were performed using SPSS software (v26.0, IBM Corp, Armonk, NY, USA). The Shapiro‐Wilk test was used to assess normality of pairwise‐difference distributions. When pairwise differences satisfied normality (Shapiro‐Wilk p > 0.05), paired‐sample t‐test was applied; otherwise, the two‐tailed Wilcoxon signed‐rank non‐parametric test was used. A threshold of p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. All results are presented as mean ± standard deviation (x̄ ± SD).

title: Impact of anatomical changes on simulated proton arc therapy and intensity-modulated proton therapy for lung cancer.
text: Figure 1 displays dose distributions for one illustrative representative patient for visual demonstration. Quantitative conclusions are drawn from the cohort‐level analyses in subsequent sections. Both primary plans achieve comparable target coverage (see Figure 1a,c). Following anatomical changes simulated within non‐adaptive recalculations, the prescription‐dose region in IMPTp‐a no longer adequately overlapped with target anatomy, producing evident target‐coverage loss. In contrast, sPATp‐a maintains comparatively preserved target coverage (Figure 1b,d). Corresponding DVH comparisons are presented in Figure 1e,f.

title: Impact of anatomical changes on simulated proton arc therapy and intensity-modulated proton therapy for lung cancer.
section: RESULTS > Dosimetric evaluation of primary plans
text: The dosimetric parameters are summarized in Table 3. Both sPATp and IMPTp achieve comparable target coverage (D95% normalized to 6000 cGy[RBE]). The D2% of IMPTp is slightly higher than that of sPATp (p = 0.001), and CI and HI are both superior in sPATp compared to IMPTp (p < 0.05). For OARs, sPATp demonstrates significantly lower lung V20 and V5 (p < 0.001), and notably, the spinal cord Dmax in IMPTp is on average 415.61 cGy[RBE] higher than in sPATp (p = 0.001). The esophageal Dmean in sPATp is slightly higher than that in IMPTp, whereas the heart Dmean is marginally lower; however, these differences are not statistically significant.

title: Impact of anatomical changes on simulated proton arc therapy and intensity-modulated proton therapy for lung cancer.
section: RESULTS > Impact of anatomical changes on dosimetry
text: The dosimetric parameters for the non‑adaptive plans are summarized in Table 4. Anatomical changes, primarily tumor regression, induced dose degradation for both non‐adaptive plan techniques. sPATp‐a preserved superior CTV D98% and D95% compared to IMPTp‐a. CI and HI parameters remained more favorable for sPATp‐a. For OARs, sPATp‐a maintained lower lung V20, V5, esophageal Dmax and spinal‐cord Dmax; spinal‐cord Dmax for sPATp‐a was approximately half of IMPTp‐a. No statistically‐significant inter‐technique differences were observed for esophageal and heart Dmean among non‐adaptive plans. Dose differences relative to the primary plans are illustrated in Figure 2. Magnitudes of target‐coverage loss are substantially larger for IMPT (p < 0.05). The most pronounced OARs dose difference is observed in spinal cord Dmax, where the ΔDmax for IMPT is 2.5 times that of sPAT. For other OARs (lung, esophagus, and heart), the dose differences between the two techniques are comparable (p > 0.05).

title: Impact of anatomical changes on simulated proton arc therapy and intensity-modulated proton therapy for lung cancer.
text: TCP and NTCP results are summarized in Table 5. In the primary plans, the mean TCP values are 64.99% for sPATp and 65.58% for IMPTp. Following anatomical change modelled within non‐adaptive recalculations, TCP substantially decrease for both techniques, with average reductions of approximately 5.83% for sPAT and 8.07% for IMPT; for most OARs, sPAT exhibited smaller variations in NTCP. The result indicates that IMPT is more sensitive to anatomical changes. It should be noted that the absolute NTCP values are very low for all OARs in both techniques, and the inter‐technique differences are less than 1%. The NTCP analysis is presented primarily to complement the dosimetric findings, these small differences may have limited clinical relevance.

title: Impact of anatomical changes on simulated proton arc therapy and intensity-modulated proton therapy for lung cancer.
text: This study aimed to evaluate the impact of inter‐fractional anatomical changes on the dosimetric and radiobiological performance of sPAT versus IMPT for lung cancer patients. Our results demonstrate that sPAT exhibits a better target coverage and a smaller reduction in TCP against anatomical changes in non‐adaptive planning. This observation aligns with the hypothesis that distributing dose across a larger set of beam directions mitigates sensitivity to density alterations occurring along individual beam trajectories. PAT integrates proton physical advantages with multi‐angle gantry‐based irradiation. 21 The greater number of beam angles increases the degrees of freedom in plan optimization, potentially yielding more favorable dose distributions. 22 , 23 This can also be seen from the comparison of the primary plans in this study. For tumors exhibiting substantial motion, PAT also demonstrates superior dosimetric advantages. 6 , 24 , 25 These studies reflect the better robustness of PAT to anatomical changes in intro‐fractionation treatment. This study provides supplementary information on the robustness of sPAT and IMPT caused by inter‐fractional anatomical changes.

title: Impact of anatomical changes on simulated proton arc therapy and intensity-modulated proton therapy for lung cancer.
text: In this study, a higher spinal cord Dmax observed in IMPT plans (both primary and non‐adaptive) is attributable to the use of only 3–4 fixed beam angles. For centrally located or mediastinally adjacent tumors, one IMPT beam path may traverse or pass in close proximity to the spinal cord, resulting in concentrated dose deposition. In contrast, sPAT distributes the dose across 13–17 beam directions, substantially diluting the dose contribution from any single direction and thereby reducing the maximum point dose. We acknowledge that with appropriate beam‐angle selection, static‐field IMPT might provide improved spinal cord sparing compared with sPAT.

title: Impact of anatomical changes on simulated proton arc therapy and intensity-modulated proton therapy for lung cancer.
text: Chocan et al. 26 previously reported a lung cancer study, they found that PAT provided slightly better target coverage than IMPT but showed slightly poorer robustness for OARs, particularly the heart and esophagus. This trend also observed in our study. This organ‐specific behavior can be explained by the distinct anatomical positions of these structures relative to the beam geometry. The esophagus is located centrally and posteriorly in the mediastinum, where multiple arc beams converge, leading to a slightly higher dose bath from PAT. Conversely, the heart is positioned anteroinferiorly and is more affected by direct traversal from the limited number of fixed IMPT beams. PAT's angular dispersion reduces the per‐direction contribution to the heart. This distinction explains why the esophagus Dmean was slightly higher in PAT while the heart Dmean was marginally lower. This suggests that while PAT offers advantages in target coverage, its robustness for OARs located along the beam path may be compromised by density interfaces.

title: Impact of anatomical changes on simulated proton arc therapy and intensity-modulated proton therapy for lung cancer.
text: The PAT approach used in this study was a simulated arc plan based on discrete fields rather than true dynamic arc delivery. It should therefore be regarded as an idealized, delivery‐unconstrained, discrete‐beam pseudo‐arc approximation. In clinically deliverable spot‐scanning proton arc therapy (SPArc), gantry rotation is continuous and coupled to spot delivery; the temporal sequence of beam delivery, energy‐layer switching and beam‐on/off timing; per‐angle restrictions on the number of energy layers or spots; and machine‐specific constraints such as the minimum deliverable monitor unit per spot are explicitly modeled in planning and delivery. These delivery constraints reduce the optimization freedom relative to the present sPAT. Consequently, the robustness advantage observed for sPAT may represent an upper bound and may be attenuated under true dynamic arc delivery.

title: Impact of anatomical changes on simulated proton arc therapy and intensity-modulated proton therapy for lung cancer.
text: This study has several limitations. sPAT used a simulated arc plan based on discrete fields and was not a true dynamic arc system, so further prospective validation on clinically deliverable arc platforms is warranted. This was a single‐center retrospective analysis with a modest sample size and possible selection bias. In particular, only patients with notable tumor volume changes requiring re‐simulation CT were included, which may overestimate the typical dosimetric impact in the general lung cancer proton therapy population. Tumor shrinkage observed in the photon‐treated cohort may differ from that in proton therapy regimens. In addition, the non‐adaptive plans assumed that the entire 30‐fraction course was delivered on the changed anatomy, which overestimates the actual dosimetric impact because anatomical changes occur gradually. Furthermore, all plans were generated by a single experienced planner. Plan quality may depend on the experience and individual planning choices of the planner, which limits the generalizability of the results. Finally, the study focused primarily on dosimetric comparisons and lacked systematic evaluation of long‐term clinical outcomes. Future multicenter studies incorporating clinically deliverable spot‐scanning proton arc systems are needed to externally validate these findings.

title: Impact of anatomical changes on simulated proton arc therapy and intensity-modulated proton therapy for lung cancer.
text: This study evaluated dosimetric and radiobiological outcomes of non‐adaptive sPAT and IMPT plans for 21 lung‐cancer patients under inter‐fractional anatomical changes. sPAT maintained better stability in target coverage and TCP under anatomical changes, reflecting superior robustness against inter‐fractional anatomical changes compared with IMPT.

title: Impact of anatomical changes on simulated proton arc therapy and intensity-modulated proton therapy for lung cancer.
