The requirement for informed consent was waived due to the retrospective nature of the study.

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: Proton therapy offers a distinct physical advantage over photon radiotherapy through the Bragg peak dose concentration in target with both lower integral dose and finite path length, and sharper penumbra as compared to photons, collectively reducing radiation exposure to surrounding normal tissues and potentially improving the therapeutic ratio. However, this advantage is tempered by uncertainties, including range uncertainty and variable relative biological effectiveness. In this review, the authors summarize contemporary evidence supporting proton therapy across pediatric, central nervous system (CNS), head and neck, thoracic, breast, gastrointestinal, genitourinary, and hematologic malignancies, as well as reirradiation. The strength of evidence varies substantially by disease site. Proton therapy is well established in pediatric cancers and selected CNS tumors, where minimizing integral dose and late toxicity is especially important. Randomized trials have demonstrated clinically meaningful benefits in selected settings, including improved disease control and survival with proton craniospinal irradiation for leptomeningeal metastases and reduced toxicity with preserved disease control and survival benefit in oropharyngeal cancer. Conversely, randomized data in localized prostate cancer have not shown improved patient reported outcomes compared with intensity modulated photon therapy.

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: Ongoing phase 3 trials across multiple disease sites are expected to further define the role of protons by clarifying comparative effectiveness, toxicity reduction, and cost‐effectiveness relative to advanced photon techniques. Future progress will depend on improved patient selection, robust treatment planning, and emerging technologies including adaptive proton therapy, proton arc therapy, and FLASH radiotherapy. Keywords: comparative effectiveness, patient selection, proton beam therapy, proton therapy, radiation oncology, randomized clinical trials, treatment‐related toxicity

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: Proton therapy is distinguished by its physical dose distribution, characterized by the Bragg peak, which allows radiation dose to be deposited in a more confined region with reduced exposure to surrounding normal tissues compared with conventional photon therapy (Figure 1). This feature has the potential to improve the therapeutic ratio, particularly for tumors located near critical radiation sensitive tissues. 2 However, proton therapy subject to greater uncertainty. This includes particle range and variable energy transfer at the distal edge of the beam, necessitating robust planning, optimization, and image guidance for proton therapy planning. 3 The clinical adoption of proton therapy has been accompanied by ongoing debate. Higher treatment costs 4 , 5 , 6 and inconsistent evidence demonstrating improvements in patient outcomes compared with photon radiotherapy 7 , 8 have contributed to uncertainty regarding its optimal role across disease sites. At the same time, advances in photon therapy, including intensity modulated radiotherapy (IMRT), and specifically volumetric modulated arc therapy (VMAT), image guidance, and adaptive treatment strategies, have enabled increasingly conformal dose delivery with improved normal tissue sparing, delivered with higher efficiency. 9 As a result, the gap between photon and proton techniques has narrowed in many clinical settings.

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: The central question surrounding proton therapy is whether the physical properties of proton therapy translate into clinical benefits. These potential benefits may include reductions in toxicity, improvements in quality of life, greater tolerance of multimodality therapy, and improved survival. Recent prospective and randomized studies have begun to provide more direct evidence regarding the clinical impact of proton therapy, although the strength of evidence varies across disease sites (Table 1). In this review, we summarize the current evidence supporting the use of proton therapy across major disease sites, including pediatric malignancies, central nervous system (CNS) tumors, head and neck cancers, thoracic malignancies, breast cancer, gastrointestinal, genitourinary, and hematologic cancers (Table 2). We further discuss ongoing studies that are likely to further define the role of proton therapy in modern oncology.

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: The most widely accepted indication for proton therapy is in pediatric malignancies, where the goal is to minimize long‐term treatment‐related toxicity in patients with potentially long life expectancy. 33 Although randomized trials are lacking, a large body of dosimetric, prospective, and retrospective data consistently demonstrates that proton therapy reduces radiation exposure to normal tissues while maintaining tumor control outcomes comparable to photon‐based radiotherapy. 33 It is important to note that based on the described physical principles of proton therapy, regardless of the form of advanced photon technology that proton therapy is compared to, proton therapy will virtually always have substantially less low dose radiation collateral exposure to nontarget normal tissues (Figure 1). Where very low dose radiation may be clinically insignificant in many adults, there is often a significant risk for long‐term negative sequelae in pediatric patients.

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: The strongest clinical evidence exists in pediatric CNS tumors, especially those requiring radiation of the entire neuraxis (craniospinal irradiation), where proton therapy significantly reduces dose to the heart, lungs, thyroid, and gastrointestinal organs. Clinical studies have shown lower rates of treatment‐related toxicities, including ototoxicity, endocrine dysfunction, and cognitive decline, 34 , 35 , 36 while maintaining disease control comparable to photon‐based cooperative group trials. 10 , 36 , 37 , 38 , 39 , 40 Similar advantages have been reported in other intracranial tumors including ependymoma, 41 germinoma, 42 , 43 craniopharyngioma, 11 and low grade glioma, 44 , 45 , 46 as well as in in extracranial sites such as rhabdomyosarcoma and Ewing sarcoma, where improved sparing of surrounding normal tissues may reduce long‐term morbidity. 47 , 48

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: Physical properties of proton therapy also require special consideration and robust planning at experienced proton centers. Proton dose distributions are sensitive to anatomic changes during treatment, 49 and uncertainties related to proton range and variable relative biological effectiveness (RBE), particularly near the distal edge of the beam, 3 require careful consideration when the target abuts critical structures. These challenges are particularly relevant among patients with craniopharyngioma, where fluctuations in cyst volume during the course of radiation raise concern for geographic target misses or overdosing critical structures such as the optic chiasm. 11 , 49 Consequently, careful magnetic resonance imaging surveillance throughout treatment, robust treatment planning, and adaptive replanning when indicated are essential components of proton therapy for these patients. Early reports of brainstem imaging changes and radiation injury following proton therapy also prompted concerns regarding end‐of‐range effects and elevated RBE and linear energy transfer (LET) near the distal edge of the beam. 50 , 51 Although subsequent clinical experience and improved treatment planning techniques and conservative dose constraints have mitigated many of these concerns, 52 , 53 these observations underscore the importance of robust planning when treating tumors adjacent to critical structures.

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: Proton therapy has an important role in the management of brain malignancies, where the proximity of tumors to critical neurologic structures makes normal tissue sparing particularly relevant. A substantial body of evidence has established the relationship between radiation dose to critical brain structures and subsequent neurocognitive, endocrine, and auditory toxicity. Prospective and randomized data have demonstrated that reducing radiation dose to the hippocampi and temporal lobes preserves cognitive function following cranial irradiation. 54 , 55 , 56 There are also well established radiation dose–response relationships for endocrine dysfunction following irradiation of the hypothalamic–pituitary axis 57 , 58 and sensorineural hearing loss with treatment of the cochlea, providing an additional rationale for minimizing dose to the auditory apparatus when feasible. 59

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: Among adult patients, proton therapy is considered a standard approach for skull base chordomas and chondrosarcomas, where durable local control requires high radiation doses in close proximity to the brainstem, optic pathways, and temporal lobes. 60 The strongest prospective evidence comes from PROG 85‐26, a randomized dose escalation study in patients with skull base and cervical chordomas and chondrosarcomas, which demonstrated the feasibility, safety, and efficacy of high dose proton therapy with a median follow‐up of over 29 years. 13 , 61 These data have established proton therapy as a preferred modality in this setting. Proton therapy is also frequently used in the management of meningioma and pituitary adenoma, 62 , 63 where long‐term disease control is expected among most patients and minimizing late toxicity is a central treatment goal despite the lack of randomized data.

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: The role of proton therapy continues to be investigated in diffuse gliomas, particularly among patients with grade 2 or grade 3 IDH‐mutant diffuse gliomas (Figure 1). These patients often experience prolonged survival and are therefore at increased risk for late toxicity. A prospective phase 2 study of 60 patients with low grade gliomas treated with proton therapy with median follow‐up of 7 years showed favorable tumor control and toxicity outcomes, with data suggesting preservation of neurocognitive function, neuro‐endocrine, and quality of life in the majority of patients. 14 , 64 , 65 Additional retrospective studies suggest comparable or improved outcomes with proton therapy for this patient population. 66 , 67 In contrast, a recent retrospective multi‐institutional conference abstract reported inferior next intervention‐free survival, progression‐free survival (PFS), and overall survival (OS) patients with grade 3 IDH‐mutated gliomas treated with proton therapy compared with photon therapy. 68 These findings have generated considerable interest but should be interpreted cautiously given the retrospective design, potential selection bias and unmeasured confounding, reliance on subgroup analyses, and the unexpectedly large magnitude of the reported survival differences, which lacks a clear biologic rationale. Consequently, these results should be considered hypothesis generating rather than practice changing.

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: Several randomized trials are expected to better define the role of proton therapy in diffuse gliomas. A randomized phase 2 trial comparing proton versus photon therapy with a primary end point of cognitive preservation (NRG BN005; NCT03180502) has completed accrual and is expected to provide important data. 1 Additional randomized data are expected as well for a focus on quality of life and functional outcomes. 69 , 70 , 71 In grade 4 IDH–wild‐type glioblastoma, the role of proton therapy continues to be investigated. A randomized phase 2 trial demonstrated reduced patient reported fatigue with proton therapy compared to photon therapy, but no differences in cognitive or survival outcomes. 15 Additional prospective data come from NRG BN001. BN001 was designed as a signal seeking, randomized phase 2 trial of dose intensified (75 Gy) versus standard dose (60 Gy) radiation among patients with glioblastoma. 16 An analysis of the dose intensified proton cohort demonstrated a 6.8% improvement in 2‐year OS without an increase in high grade toxicity. This encouraging survival benefit is planned for further evaluation in a phase 3 study. Additional randomized data are also expected. 72

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: Although proton therapy is generally associated with reduced integral dose and a favorable normal tissue dosimetric profile, its unique physical and biological characteristics have prompted investigation into potential proton specific toxicities within the CNS. Although clinical evidence remains inconclusive, uncertainty surrounding RBE and elevated linear energy transfer LET near the distal edge of the proton beam has been proposed as a mechanism contributing to radiation necrosis and pseudoprogression, particularly when critical structures are located adjacent to the beam end range. 47 , 73 This issue is also relevant for skull base chordomas and chondrosarcomas, where treatment places the distal edge of the beam near the brainstem or temporal lobes, and rare cases of brainstem injury or temporal lobe necrosis have been reported. 74 Similarly, in primary brain tumors, several studies have described distinctive radiographic changes following proton therapy. 75 As proton therapy continues to expand for CNS malignancies, further prospective studies integrating LET and variable RBE modeling will be essential to optimize treatment planning for patients treated with proton therapy. 3

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: Proton therapy has also gained increasing attention for the treatment of leptomeningeal disease (LMD) and other indications requiring treatment of the entire neuraxis with craniospinal irradiation (CSI). In a phase 2 randomized trial, patients with leptomeningeal metastases from solid tumors were randomized to receive proton CSI versus involved field photon radiotherapy. Proton CSI significantly improved CNS PFS, overall PFS, and OS compared with photon involved field radiotherapy without a significant increase in severe treatment‐related toxicity. The survival benefit observed in this trial was attributed to the improved CNS disease control as there was a significant reduction in the proportion of patients who died with CNS progression among those who received proton CSI. 17 The survival benefit of proton CSI is particularly notable in LMD that has historically been extremely difficult to treat due to limited effective systemic therapy options. 76 , 77 Given these encouraging results, proton CSI is increasingly being considered for selected patients with leptomeningeal metastases who have adequate performance status and controlled systemic disease. Proton CSI for LMD is currently undergoing evaluation in a randomized, phase 3 setting in NRG BN014 (RADIATE‐LM). 28

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: In head and neck cancer, the role of proton therapy has recently been informed by randomized phase 3 data. Two randomized phase 3 trials published in 2026 have evaluated proton therapy for head and neck cancer. A US‐based trial randomized 440 patients with locally advanced oropharyngeal cancer to proton versus photon (IMRT) with concurrent systemic therapy, using noninferior PFS as the primary end point. The trial showed that proton therapy had noninferior 5‐year PFS (81.3% vs. 76.2%; hazard ratio [HR], 0.88). In addition, an improvement in 5‐year OS was observed (90.9% vs. 81.0%; HR, 0.58), although this was a prespecified secondary end point. Furthermore, proton therapy was associated with lower rates of several clinically meaningful toxicities including lower rates of severe lymphopenia (76% vs. 89%), dysphagia (31% vs. 49%), xerostomia (33% vs. 45%), and significantly lower gastronomy tube dependence (26.8% vs. 40.2%, p = .018) compared with photon IMRT. Of particular clinical significance is the reduction in grade 3 or greater xerostomia because this toxicity is likely to be permanent and a detriment to quality of life. There was no difference in recurrence patterns between groups, including local, regional, and distant control. Notably, 23% of patients crossed over after randomization, largely due to issues with insurance coverage of proton therapy and systemic therapy was variable, but outcomes were similar in intention to treat and per protocol analyses.

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: The UK‐based Proton beam therapy for oropharyngeal cancer (TORPEdO) trial was also published in 2026 and offers a complementary perspective. This phase 3 study randomized 205 patients with locally advanced oropharyngeal cancer 2:1 to proton or photon therapy (IMRT) with uniform high dose cisplatin. The coprimary end points were functional outcomes including at 12 months gastrostomy dependence or severe weight loss greater than or equal to 20% and a composite patient reported quality of life score. There was no significant difference in either functional or quality of life outcomes. Both modalities showed excellent and comparable 24‐month locoregional control and OS. Proton therapy was associated with numerically lower rates of acute grade 3 or greater toxicity within the first 3 months of treatment including mucositis, dysphagia, and dysgeusia. These differences were not reflected in the primary end point because functional outcomes were assessed only at 12 months, when most acute treatment‐related toxicities had resolved. Late grade 3 toxicities were numerically higher among patients who received proton therapy despite lower incidence of early toxicity, though remained low overall, and was primarily driven by higher rates of late weight loss (14% vs. 5%). 8 Nonetheless, the 12‐month composite quality of life score was not significantly different between patients who received proton or photon therapy. 8

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: Taken together, the early results of these trials demonstrate that proton and photon therapy achieve comparable disease control and survival, whereas proton therapy is associated with a meaningful reduction in acute toxicity. This reduction is particularly relevant in the context of multimodality therapy with concurrent chemoradiation. 78 , 79 Although late toxicity differences remain less clearly defined, the overall pattern of preserved oncologic outcomes with improved early tolerability supports an enhanced therapeutic ratio with proton therapy, particularly for patients at higher risk of treatment toxicity. Long‐term data from both randomized trials with slightly different emphasis of survival toxicity will continue to help shape the role of radiotherapy for locally advanced oropharyngeal cancer. Additional randomized data are anticipated including the Danish Head and Neck Cancer Group 35 trial (NCT04607694) and the Swedish ARTSCAN V (NCT03829033).

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: Proton therapy has the potential to improve the therapeutic ratio for thoracic malignancies by maintaining target coverage while reducing radiation dose to adjacent critical organs, including the heart, lungs, esophagus, and bone marrow. These dosimetric advantages may translate into lower cardiopulmonary toxicity, improved tolerance of multimodality therapy, and reduced lymphopenia. Radiation associated lymphopenia has become increasingly relevant given integration of immune checkpoint inhibition into standard of care treatment for curative intent thoracic malignancies. 80 Retrospective evidence demonstrates that proton therapy reduces dose to circulating immune cells and the subsequent risk of radiation induced lymphopenia compared with photon therapy for patients with locally advanced lung cancer. 71 , 81 , 82 Higher lymphocyte counts are associated with improved survival and disease control. 18

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: The randomized evidence supporting proton therapy in thoracic malignancies is more limited and less definitive than in head and neck cancer. There are no completed phase 3 randomized studies to date. A randomized phase 2 study for locally advanced inoperable non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) comparing passive scatter proton therapy to photon IMRT showed no difference in the coprimary end points of rates of grade 3 or greater pneumonitis or local failure rates. 18 The field has therefore largely been awaiting results from RTOG 1308, a definitive phase 3 trial that randomized patients with inoperable stage II–IIIB NSCLC to proton versus photon chemoradiation (70 Gy with concurrent platinum doublet chemotherapy) and is powered with a coprimary end point of OS and treatment‐related cardiac toxicity/lymphopenia. 19 The biologic premise is that reducing heart and lung dose in light of prior data linking cardiac dose to survival in RTOG 0617 may translate into improved survival. 84 The trial opened in 2014 and reached its accrual goal of 330 patients in 2023. The primary end point results are anticipated to be complete in December 2026, with secondary end point analyses expected the year afterward. 29

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: The randomized evidence supporting proton therapy in esophageal cancer is somewhat more developed than in lung cancer, although phase 3 data remain limited. A randomized phase 2 trial of 145 patients comparing proton therapy with photon IMRT in patients with locally advanced esophageal cancer showed that proton therapy was associated with a significant reduction in a composite end point of total toxicity burden (TTB) that includes acute cardiopulmonary toxicity, postoperative complications, and treatment‐related morbidity. PFS and OS were similar. 78 Two ongoing phase 3 studies are expected to define the role of proton therapy in esophageal cancer including: the US‐based NRG‐GI006 (NCT03801876) 30 and European PROTECT trial (NCT05055648). 31

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: The evidence supporting proton therapy in breast cancer is evolving, with the strongest rationale centered on cardiac and lung dose reduction. Multiple dosimetric and early prospective studies have consistently demonstrated that proton therapy can substantially reduce mean heart dose, left anterior descending artery dose, and lung exposure compared with modern photon techniques. 85 This is clinically relevant given well established data linking even low doses of cardiac radiation to adverse cardiac events. 86 , 87 Early prospective single arm studies showed low rates of acute toxicity and favorable early disease control, with emerging data suggesting reduced cardiac dose without compromising target coverage including for regional nodal irradiation. 88 , 89 , 90 Proton therapy is also an important option for anatomically challenging scenarios including patients requiring regional nodal irradiation including the internal mammary nodes, 91 treatment of patients with a pectus excavatum, 84 and patients requiring synchronous bilateral breast irradiation. 90

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: The Radiotherapy Comparative Effectiveness (RADCOMP) trial is a phase 3 randomized clinical trial comparing proton versus photon radiation therapy for patients with locally advanced breast cancer who require regional nodal irradiation. RADCOMP randomizes patients to receive standard of care photon radiotherapy (3D or IMRT) or to proton therapy. The primary end point is reduction in 10‐year major cardiac events (myocardial infarction, coronary revascularization, cardiovascular death, or major cardiac hospitalization). Key secondary end points include locoregional control, any recurrence, OS, and patient‐reported health‐related quality of life outcomes. 21 , 92 A challenge in interpreting the potential benefit of proton therapy in this setting is the long latency of radiation associated cardiac toxicity, requiring extended follow‐up. 85 RADCOMP represents the only large phase 3 randomized effort in breast cancer, and its results will be pivotal in determining the role of proton therapy in this setting. RADCOMP is closed to accrual 93 with primary end point results expected to be reported between 2028 and 2032. 94

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: Proton therapy has emerged as a promising modality for the treatment of hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), where preservation of uninvolved liver parenchyma is critical given the high prevalence of underlying cirrhosis and limited hepatic reserve. Furthermore, retrospective evidence suggests that higher doses of radiation are associated with improved local control and survival in selected patients. 95 , 96 Compared with photon radiotherapy, proton therapy can substantially reduce radiation dose to normal liver due to the absence of exit dose, which may lower the risk of radiation induced liver disease and enable safe dose escalation. Multiple prospective and retrospective series have reported excellent local control rates with proton therapy for HCC with favorable toxicity profiles even for tumors located near critical structures or in patients with borderline liver function. 97 , 98 , 99 The randomized phase 3 NRG‐GI003 (NCT03186898) trial is currently comparing proton versus photon radiotherapy for patients with unresectable or locally recurrent HCC with OS as the primary end point.

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: In genitourinary malignancies, the largest body of clinical experience with proton therapy is in localized prostate cancer. Dosimetric studies have demonstrated reductions in integral dose and low to intermediate dose exposure to surrounding normal tissues, including the bladder, rectum, and pelvic bone marrow. 100 , 101 , 102 These reductions are associated with lower rates of gastrointestinal and genitourinary toxicity in retrospective studies. 103 , 104 , 105 Multiple cohort studies have reported safety and efficacy of proton therapy for localized prostate cancer with outcomes comparable to modern photon therapy. 106 , 107 , 108 , 109 More recently, randomized evidence has begun to clarify the relative benefits of proton therapy in this setting. The phase 3 Prostate Advanced Radiation Technologies Investigating Quality of Life (PARTIQoL) trial compared proton radiation to photon IMRT. The trial included 450 patients with low to intermediate risk prostate cancer. The primary end point was change in baseline bowel quality of life at 24 months. Secondary end points included changes in urinary and sexual function as well as treatment efficacy. 110 , 111 With a median follow‐up of 60.3 months, there was no difference between proton therapy and photon IMRT in bowel function at 24 months with excellent outcomes in both groups. Similarly, there was no difference in urinary function, sexual function, or PFS at 5 years.

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: 24 These findings suggest that despite advantage of a steeper dose fall off, proton therapy does not confer a measurable improvement in patient reported outcomes in an unselected population of patients. Future work is needed to identify patient subgroups most likely to benefit, potentially based on anatomy or baseline function. Proton therapy may also offer advantages for patients requiring pelvic nodal irradiation in the definitive or postoperative setting. Compared with photon techniques, proton therapy can substantially reduce low and intermediate dose exposure to surrounding bowel, bladder, pelvic bone marrow, and other normal tissues in these settings. 112 , 113 Prospective clinical data support the safety and efficacy of proton therapy in these settings, including for pelvic node–positive prostate cancer requiring high doses of radiation therapy in the pelvis. 114 , 115 , 116 , 117 Beyond prostate cancer, proton therapy has also been explored in other genitourinary malignancies, including as a stereotactic ablative approach for primary renal cell carcinoma in medically inoperable patients, although clinical data in these settings remain limited. 118

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: The rationale for proton therapy among patients with hematologic malignancy is driven by the goal of minimizing long‐term toxicity in a population with high cure rates and prolonged survivorship. For patients requiring mediastinal or thoracic radiation, proton therapy reduces dose to nontarget structures such as the heart, lungs, and breast tissue compared with modern photon techniques. 25 , 119 The reduction in breast dose is particularly relevant for children and young adults receiving mediastinal radiation for lymphoma who are at a high lifetime risk of secondary breast cancer. 120 The dosimetric advantages of proton therapy are estimated to meaningfully reduce lifetime risk of secondary breast cancer. 121 , 122 Furthermore, prospective phase 2 123 and pooled multi‐institutional data 124 have demonstrated the feasibility and efficacy of proton therapy among patients with mediastinal lymphoma, with low rates of acute toxicity and disease control outcomes comparable to historical photon based series.

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: Proton therapy can be particularly well suited for reirradiation scenarios where prior radiation exposure limits the tolerance of adjacent normal tissues and the steeper dose fall off of protons are most clinically meaningful. Evidence varies and includes retrospective and single arm prospective studies. For example, a multi‐institutional prospective registry study led by the Proton Collaborative Group evaluated proton radiotherapy for reirradiation among patients with recurrent glioblastoma (NCT01255748) showed that proton reirradiation was safe and feasible despite prior high dose intracranial irradiation. 26 Similar, retrospective series have observed good safety and efficacy in recurrent breast cancer. 125 , 126 In head and neck cancer, both retrospective 26 , 146 and ongoing prospective efforts (NCT01973179 and NCT03981068) are informing the role of proton therapy in the setting of reirradiation including curative intent treatment.

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: Emerging technological advances may further expand the role of proton therapy in oncology and improve the therapeutic ratio for patients. Ultra‐high dose rate radiotherapy, termed FLASH radiation, has demonstrated the potential to reduce normal tissue toxicity while maintaining tumor control in preclinical studies. Proton radiation currently represents one of the most promising platforms for clinical translation of FLASH radiotherapy. 128 , 129 , 130 , 131 Early human clinical studies of proton FLASH radiation for patients with painful bone metastases have demonstrated feasibility and safety. 132 , 133 Advances in imaging and treatment planning have also facilitated the possibility of adaptive proton therapy, which allows for reoptimization of proton radiation planning during the course of treatment based intrafractional motion (such as breathing and organ motion) and interfractional motion (such as tumor shrinkage or weight loss). 134 , 135 , 136 In addition, proton arc therapy is an emerging radiation delivery technique allowing for radiation from a large number of gantry angles or even continuous delivery rather than a small number of fixed beam angles, thereby improving conformality 137 , 138 , 139 with encouraging results from the first in human studies among patients with head and neck cancer.

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: 140 Finally, technological advances in planning techniques, including RBE or LET informed planning that more accurately takes into account biological damage per unit of dose, may further reduce toxicity risk risks of proton therapy. 3 Several advances may improve access to proton therapy. Although the number of proton facilities has increased rapidly, there remain only approximately 120 proton centers worldwide compared with more than 8000 photon radiotherapy facilities. 141 Most proton centers are located in the United States, Europe, and Asia, creating geographic barriers to access for patients living in rural areas or low‐ and middle‐income countries. 141 , 142 One potential innovation to improve access is upright proton therapy, in which proton therapy is delivered while a patient is seated or standing rather than supine. 141 By eliminating the need for a massive rotating proton gantry, upright proton therapy would significantly reduce the cost of new facility construction and may improve access to care. 143

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: Proton therapy has been in use for over 60 years with the expectation of target dose escalation and surrounding normal tissue sparing as the combined means to improve disease control and reduce treatment toxicity. Parallel advancements in photon technology have occurred so quickly that the margin of benefit of proton therapy is less clear. Nonetheless, with advancements in proton technology as well, it is expected that the physical advantage of the Bragg peak and finite beam length of proton beams will lead to true future clinical gains. Future directions in proton therapy will depend on demonstrating clinically meaningful benefit beyond dosimetric advantages. Ongoing and recently completed randomized trials across disease sites, including RADCOMP, RTOG 1308, and NRG GI006, are expected to provide critical data regarding the impact of proton therapy on survival, toxicity, and patient reported outcomes. Long‐term follow‐up will be essential, particularly in disease sites where late effects drive morbidity.

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology
text: As these data mature, the role of proton therapy is likely to evolve toward a more selective application, focused on patient populations in whom reductions in normal tissue dose are most likely to translate into meaningful clinical benefit. A key question is how to identify which patients are most likely to derive meaningful clinical benefit from proton therapy. Although randomized trials remain the gold standard, patient selection will likely become increasingly individualized through integration of dosimetric, clinical, and biologic factors. Normal tissue complication probability modeling and model‐based selection may identify patients in whom the anticipated reduction in treatment‐related toxicity justifies proton therapy. 144 , 145 , 146 In parallel, expected survival, competing risks of late toxicity, patient comorbidities, age, and baseline functional status should all inform treatment selection, as the greatest benefit from reduced integral dose may accrue to patients with longer life expectancy or heightened susceptibility to radiation‐induced complications. Advances in artificial intelligence may further refine patient selection by integrating dosimetric and clinical data to predict individualized benefit. 12 , 147

title: Evolving role of proton therapy in contemporary oncology

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: Objective. Limited-angle cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) is attractive for image-guided radiotherapy and imaging-guided procedures when full-arc acquisition is impractical, but the incomplete angular sampling leads to severe streaking, shading, and structural distortion. This study aimed to develop a physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction framework for recovering anatomically faithful volumetric CBCT from short-arc limited-angle projections. Approach. We propose a physics-constrained and geometry-aware network (PCGA-Net), a dual-domain reconstruction framework that combines projection completion, analytic geometric reconstruction, and image-domain refinement within a unified cross-domain design. Specifically, a projection completion module first estimates missing-angle information from the measured limited-angle projections. A geometry-aware reconstruction module then maps the completed projections into image space using differentiable cone-beam forward and backward-projection operators. Finally, a volumetric refinement module suppresses residual artifacts and restores anatomical detail under geometry-guided cross-domain consistency supervision. The framework was evaluated on three clinically distinct cohorts: gynecologic (GYN) high-dose-rate (HDR) brachytherapy, abdominal liver four-dimensional computed tomography (4DCT), and head-and-neck (H&N) CBCT. Main results.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: Across all three cohorts, fully adapted PCGA-Net consistently outperformed conventional limited-angle Feldkamp–Davis–Kress (FDK) reconstruction and the compared learning-based baselines, a conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) and PatRecon-Net, in both qualitative and quantitative evaluation under matched patient-specific adaptation conditions. On the GYN HDR brachytherapy cohort, PCGA-Net achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 34.47 ± 6.28 Hounsfield units (HU), a structural similarity index measure (SSIM) of 0.87 ± 0.04, and a peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) of 35.79 ± 0.95 dB, compared with 178.63 ± 31.58 HU, 0.51 ± 0.03, and 18.97 ± 1.31 dB for FDK. On the abdominal liver 4DCT cohort, PCGA-Net achieved 39.27 ± 6.10 HU MAE, 0.82 ± 0.03 SSIM, and 36.85 ± 1.16 dB PSNR, versus 195.21 ± 40.08 HU, 0.50 ± 0.06, and 18.50 ± 1.50 dB for FDK. On the H&N CBCT cohort, PCGA-Net achieved 28.42 ± 4.88 HU MAE, 0.91 ± 0.05 SSIM, and 38.52 ± 0.95 dB PSNR, compared with 165.30 ± 25.40 HU, 0.61 ± 0.05, and 21.13 ± 1.14 dB for FDK. In all three cohorts, PCGA-Net also exceeded cGAN and PatRecon-Net across all evaluated metrics. Significance. These results indicate that jointly enforcing projection-domain completion, analytic imaging geometry, and image-domain refinement is an effective strategy for limited-angle CBCT reconstruction.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: PCGA-Net provides a robust short-arc reconstruction framework across multiple anatomical sites and clinical workflows, supporting its potential utility in constrained image-guided therapeutic and procedural settings.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: In contemporary image-guided therapy, the practical question is often not whether volumetric x-ray imaging is desirable, but whether a full cone-beam orbit can be executed without compromising the treatment or procedure itself. In external beam radiotherapy, cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) is routinely needed for setup verification, anatomy-of-the-day assessment, and motion-aware image guidance; in brachytherapy and other intracavitary or interstitial procedures, volumetric imaging is equally valuable for applicator-based target localization and peri-procedural verification; and in CBCT-guided interventional or surgical workflows, three-dimensional visualization must often be obtained without disrupting instrument placement or sterile workflow (Jensen et al 2019). Yet across these settings, full-arc acquisition is frequently constrained by prolonged gantry rotation, intrafraction anatomical change, patient discomfort or limited tolerance, gantry–couch clearance, immobilization hardware, anesthesia equipment, sterile draping, and the physical footprint of needles, applicators, or other procedural devices (Hueso-González et al 2020, Lei et al 2024). Under such conditions, continuous short-arc acquisition is not merely a reduced version of standard CBCT, but a more realistic and often safer imaging mode that better fits crowded treatment environments and time-sensitive procedural workflows while remaining compatible with existing onboard or C-arm systems.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: However, the clinical appeal of short-arc acquisition is inseparable from a substantially harder reconstruction problem. When the gantry traverses only a limited angular range, the resulting projection set no longer provides the complete directional information assumed by conventional cone-beam reconstruction, and the missing angular coverage propagates into the image as structured artifact rather than simple noise (Feldkamp 1984, Barutcu et al 2021). In practice, this incomplete angular support leads to characteristic degradation patterns, including streaking, shading, blurring, and local geometric distortion, which can obscure soft-tissue boundaries and compromise volumetric fidelity (Bhadra et al 2021). These errors are especially problematic in anatomy-dependent image guidance, where subtle boundary shifts or low-contrast soft-tissue changes may carry direct clinical relevance. Therefore, limited-angle CBCT should not be viewed as simply a lower-dose or faster variant of standard acquisition, but as an intrinsically more ill-conditioned reconstruction setting in which incomplete projection information must be compensated without violating the physical consistency of the measured data.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: Within this broader landscape of geometry-constrained volumetric reconstruction, our prior studies have examined two clinically meaningful but highly specific acquisition regimes: single-view reconstruction and orthogonal-view reconstruction. The single-view setting represents the most extreme discrete geometry, in which a three-dimensional CBCT volume is inferred from one arbitrary projection under strong patient-specific conditioning (Pan et al 2025). However, many real clinical workflows are not governed by an isolated single view or a strictly biplanar snapshot pair. Instead, they more often yield a continuous short arc of projections, which preserves local angular continuity while still leaving a substantial missing-angle burden. In this sense, continuous limited-angle acquisition constitutes a more general and clinically prevalent geometric constraint, positioned between highly discrete special cases and conventional full-arc CBCT, and therefore requires a reconstruction framework designed specifically for its distinct balance of continuity, incompleteness, and geometric fidelity.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: A substantial body of prior work has attempted to mitigate limited-angle degradation, but the remaining gap is not solely one of image quality; it is the difficulty of jointly preserving artifact suppression, geometric fidelity, and anatomical realism under incomplete angular sampling. On the model-based side, Shi and Qu (2022) developed an ultra-limited-angle reconstruction algorithm based on reweighting and edge-preserving regularization, Jia et al (2022) proposed a superiorization-inspired unrolled simultaneous algebraic reconstruction technique framework with learned perturbations for sparse-view and limited-angle computed tomography (CT), and Lee and Baek (2024) further explored iterative reconstruction with implicit neural representations; these approaches benefit from explicit use of the forward model, yet they still rely on iterative optimization or fixed update structures whose performance remains sensitive to the severity of angular truncation and the acquisition setting (Ritschl et al 2011, Adler and Öktem 2018, Huang et al, 2020, Wu et al 2021).

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: In parallel, image-restoration strategies have shown that post-reconstruction learning can visibly reduce wedge artifacts: Wang et al (2020) combined a Feldkamp–Davis–Kress (FDK)-based neural network with a U-Net for limited-angle CT, Hu et al (2023) proposed SEA-Net for limited-angle CBCT reconstruction from clinical projection data, Zhang et al (2023) developed TIME-Net for limited-angle artifact removal in dual-energy CBCT, and more recently hybrid U-Net/transformer designs have been reported for limited-angle cardiac CT. However, these methods remain largely image-centric by construction, and therefore may improve visual appearance without fully resolving the projection inconsistency induced by missing angles. Generative reconstruction has opened a further direction. Liu et al (2023) introduced DOLCE to combine diffusion sampling with an explicit physical measurement model for limited-angle CT, Zhang et al (2024) proposed a wavelet-inspired multi-channel score-based model to better address directional artifact structure, Wang et al (2024) developed a time-reversion fast-sampling score-based model to reduce the sampling burden of score-based reconstruction, and a recent physics-informed score-based diffusion model incorporated primal-dual hybrid gradient-based data consistency for limited-angle cardiac CT Han et al (2024).

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: These studies indicate that generative priors can recover sharper and more realistic structures, but they also underscore that, under incomplete projections, anatomical plausibility alone is insufficient unless the reconstruction is tightly anchored to scanner geometry and measured data. Accordingly, continuous short-arc CBCT still lacks a framework that can simultaneously reconcile incomplete-projection compensation, explicit geometric consistency, and anatomically faithful volumetric reconstruction.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: To address these challenges, we propose a physics-constrained and geometry-aware network (PCGA-Net) framework that treats continuous short-arc CBCT reconstruction as a coordinated projection-to-image inference problem rather than a single-domain correction task. The central idea is that limited-angle reconstruction requires simultaneous recovery of missing projection information and refinement of the corresponding volumetric anatomy under the true cone-beam acquisition geometry. Accordingly, PCGA-Net integrates three tightly coupled components within one unified pipeline. A projection completion module (PCM) first completes the unmeasured views from the available short-arc projections, providing a data-driven estimate of the missing angular information. The completed projection set is then passed through a geometry-aware reconstruction module (GARM), implemented with analytic cone-beam forward- and back-projectors, to map projection-domain inference into image space while preserving scanner-specific geometric fidelity (Feldkamp 1984, Ho et al 2020, Kim and Champley 2023). On this basis, a volumetric refinement module (VRM) further suppresses residual limited-angle artifacts and restores fine anatomical detail in the reconstructed volume.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: Finally, a projection-image-projection cycle-domain supervision strategy enforces consistency between synthesized projections, reconstructed volumes, and the originally measured data, thereby constraining the generative process with explicit physical geometry. Through this dual-domain, geometry-integrated design, PCGA-Net extends our prior geometry-aware reconstruction framework to the clinically important setting of continuous limited-angle CBCT and is intended to provide artifact-reduced, anatomically faithful volumetric images from short-arc acquisitions.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: Building upon these considerations, the contributions of this work are as follows: 1.As a clinically important and geometrically constrained imaging problem, we try to formulate the continuous limited-angle CBCT reconstruction as a unified framework, in which a short acquisition arc provides locally continuous projections but still leaves substantial missing-angle information to be recovered. This setting extends beyond highly discrete sparse-angle acquisition scenarios and better reflects a broad range of practical image-guided therapeutic and procedural workflows.2.We propose PCGA-Net, a geometry-integrated dual-domain framework that jointly combines missing-angle projection completion, analytic cone-beam geometry transformation, and volumetric refinement within a unified projection-image-projection cycle. By coordinating inference across projection and image domains, the proposed framework is designed to address incomplete angular sampling more effectively than single-domain reconstruction strategies.3.In contrast to conventional image-domain artifact reduction methods, fixed iterative reconstruction schemes, and purely generative approaches, PCGA-Net explicitly incorporates scanner-specific geometric consistency into the reconstruction process.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: This design enables the model to improve artifact suppression and anatomical detail restoration while reducing the risk of losing image fidelity that are insufficiently supported by the measured data.4.Relative to our previous preprint version (Gao et al 2025), the present study substantially expands the validation scope beyond a single pelvic application and evaluates the proposed framework across multiple anatomical sites with different structural complexity and workflow characteristics, including pelvis, abdomen, and head-and-neck (H&N) cases. This broader evaluation strengthens the evidence for the cross-site robustness under site-specific population pretraining and the specified longitudinal patient-adaptation protocol, and clinical relevance of PCGA-Net in diverse short-arc CBCT settings.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: We propose PCGA-Net, a dual-domain generative framework for reconstructing high-fidelity CBCT volumes from continuous limited-angle projections. The design is motivated by the denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM), which formulates generation as a reverse denoising process from Gaussian noise, and by the long-established use of analytic cone-beam reconstruction operators, such as the FDK algorithm, for geometry-based volumetric recovery. Rather than treating short-arc CBCT as a purely image-domain restoration problem, PCGA-Net formulates reconstruction as a coordinated projection-to-volume inference task under explicit cone-beam acquisition geometry. Consistent with the current PCGA-Net framework, the pipeline couples three differentiable components: a PCM to estimate the missing views from the measured short-arc projections, a GARM implemented with analytic cone-beam forward- and backward-projectors to map projection-domain inference into image space, and a VRM to further suppress residual limited-angle artifacts and recover anatomically relevant detail in the reconstructed volume (Feldkamp 1984, Kim and Champley 2023). This projection–geometry–image formulation also follows the broader logic established in prior geometry-integrated CBCT reconstruction work from our group, in which dual-domain generative modeling and explicit scanner geometry were used to strengthen data fidelity under severely restricted acquisition conditions (Pan et al 2024, Pan et al 2025).

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: Overall, PCGA-Net is designed to integrate complementary priors from projection and image spaces while constraining the reconstruction with analytic imaging physics, thereby extending geometry-aware diffusion-based CBCT reconstruction to the clinically important setting of continuous short-arc limited-angle acquisition.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: To evaluate PCGA-Net under clinically distinct but complementary imaging conditions, we used three datasets spanning abdominal liver four-dimensional CT (4DCT), H&N CBCT, and gynecologic (GYN) high-dose-rate (HDR) brachytherapy CT. This combination was selected to probe limited-angle reconstruction across markedly different workflow demands, motion patterns, and structural compositions rather than within a single anatomical niche. The abdominal liver 4DCT cohort represents an upper-abdominal radiotherapy setting in which respiratory motion is a dominant source of anatomical variability, and 4DCT is routinely used to characterize motion envelopes and support motion-aware target definition in liver radiotherapy. The H&N CBCT cohort represents a daily image-guided and adaptive radiotherapy scenario in which on-board CBCT is clinically relevant for setup verification, surveillance of treatment-induced anatomical change, and adaptive decision-making. The GYN HDR brachytherapy CT cohort represents a procedure-oriented pelvic setting in which volumetric imaging is required for applicator or needle verification, target localization, and peri-procedural assessment, often under severe workspace and clearance constraints.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: Consistent with prior geometry-integrated CBCT reconstruction studies from our group, the liver 4DCT and GYN HDR brachytherapy CT datasets were used to generate simulated cone-beam projections under known acquisition geometry, whereas reconstructed clinical on-board CBCT volumes were used as source volumes for matched forward-projection simulation in the H&N cohort. For CBCT reconstruction research, CT-based forward simulation provides a cleaner reference standard because the underlying CT volumes are anatomically resolved and quantitatively stable, allowing the generated projections and reconstructed volumes to remain exactly paired under a prescribed cone-beam geometry. In contrast, real CBCT images already contain scatter contamination, noise, truncation effects, and system-dependent artifacts, which can obscure the anatomical ground truth and confound algorithmic evaluation. For this reason, CT- or 4DCT-based projection simulation is particularly suitable for the liver and GYN cohorts, where the goal is to assess how accurately the model recovers volumetric anatomy from incomplete angular measurements under controlled physical conditions, while the H&N CBCT cohort complements this design by evaluating controlled re-projection/reconstruction performance on clinically derived on-board CBCT anatomy where matched planning CT was not uniformly available.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: All projection-domain inputs in this study were generated under a prescribed cone-beam geometry. For the GYN and liver cohorts, CT or 4DCT volumes were forward-projected to generate paired full-view and limited-angle data. For the H&N cohort, reconstructed clinical on-board CBCT volumes served as the source volumes and reference targets. Because vendor raw detector projections were not available, each reconstructed H&N CBCT volume was forward-projected with LEAP-CT to generate a synthetic 360-view projection stack, from which the fixed 90-view short arc was retained as the model input. Therefore, the H&N experiment uses clinically acquired reconstructed CBCT anatomy but simulated projection measurements; it is not an evaluation on original raw detector data.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: These three datasets also provide a test for model robustness. Liver 4DCT emphasizes low-contrast soft tissue under respiration-driven deformation; H&N CBCT emphasizes complex bone-air-soft-tissue interfaces, immobilization-related geometry, and fine structural detail; and GYN HDR brachytherapy CT emphasizes crowded pelvic anatomy together with metallic applicators or interstitial needles that complicate limited-angle reconstruction. Evaluating all three therefore allows us to assess whether PCGA-Net remains effective across dynamic abdominal anatomy, anatomically intricate H&N image guidance, and device-heavy interventional radiotherapy, which is more informative than validation in a single pelvic-only context. This broader multi-site design is aligned with the clinical motivation of the present study, namely, to develop a short-arc CBCT reconstruction framework that is robust to anatomical heterogeneity, workflow variability, and challenging imaging conditions encountered in real image-guided therapeutic procedures.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: The PCM is designed to recover a complete projection representation from the measured limited-angle input and serves as the first generative stage of the PCGA-Net framework. Its role is not to reconstruct the CBCT volume directly, but to infer the missing angular information in projection space so that the downstream GARM can operate on a physically more complete projection set. In this way, the projection-domain task is formulated as a conditional inpainting problem under limited-angle acquisition, where the model learns to synthesize full-view projections from incomplete measured views while remaining guided by the available short-arc data. This design follows the same dual-domain logic established in our previous geometry-integrated CBCT frameworks, while adapting it here to the continuous short-arc setting of limited-angle CBCT. As illustrated in figure 1(a), the PCM takes the measured limited-angle projections as conditional input and predicts the corresponding full-view projection representation for subsequent geometric reconstruction.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: A key practical feature of the PCM is that it explicitly separates the task of missing-angle recovery from the later task of volumetric artifact refinement. By first restoring the projection domain, the framework allows the missing angular information to be addressed where it arises physically, before image-domain refinement is performed. This ordering is consistent with the overall dual-domain philosophy of PCGA-Net and is particularly important in limited-angle CBCT, where the incompleteness originates in the projection measurements rather than in the reconstructed image alone. In this sense, the PCM provides the data-completion stage of the framework, while the downstream GARM and VRM convert that completed projection information into a geometry-consistent and anatomically refined CBCT volume.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Methodology > PCGA-Net framework > Geometry-aware reconstruction module (GARM)
text: The GARM serves as the physical bridge between the projection-domain synthesis and the image-domain refinement stages of PCGA-Net. Its purpose is to transform the completed projection set generated by the PCM into a volumetric representation that is explicitly consistent with the cone-beam acquisition geometry, rather than allowing the subsequent image reconstruction to rely solely on data-driven inference. In the proposed framework, the GARM is implemented as a differentiable analytic imaging operator composed of cone-beam forward projection and backward reconstruction modules. This design allows the synthesized projections to be mapped into image space through a physics-defined transformation, while also enabling reconstructed volumes to be re-projected back into projection space during cycle supervision. As illustrated in figure 1(b), the GARM receives the synthesized full-view projections from the PCM and produces an intermediate reconstruction, which then serves as the geometry-initialized input for the VRM. During inference, the same module also supports the reciprocal projection-image interaction shown in figure 2, enabling information exchange between the two domains throughout the generation process.

This geometric coupling is essential because the missing information originates in projection space, whereas the final anatomical fidelity must be realized in image space.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Methodology > PCGA-Net framework > Geometry-aware reconstruction module (GARM)
text: An important function of the GARM is that it provides a stricter conditioning signal for the VRM than a purely image-domain initialization would allow. The reconstructed intermediate volume \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{upgreek} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document} ${I^{\mathrm{rec}}}$\end{document}Irec is derived from the synthesized full-view projection through the known cone-beam geometry and therefore contains anatomically organized spatial information that is already aligned with the acquisition model. This geometry-initialized reconstruction is then used as a strong condition for downstream volumetric refinement, reducing the ambiguity that would otherwise arise if the VRM were asked to infer the CBCT volume directly from incomplete measurements alone. In the reverse direction, forward-projecting the image-domain output back to projection space provides a physically interpretable mechanism for checking whether the generated anatomy remains compatible with the synthesized and measured projections. This bidirectional role of the GARM is consistent with the geometry-integrated design established in our prior CBCT reconstruction frameworks, while here it is specifically adapted to the continuous short-arc limited-angle setting.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Methodology > PCGA-Net framework > Geometry-aware reconstruction module (GARM)
text: In practice, the GARM was implemented using LEAP-CT under a predefined cone-beam geometry matching the simulation setup. The source-to-detector distance and source-to-isocenter distance were set to 1500 mm and 1000 mm, respectively. The x-ray detector size was 768 × 1024 with a detector spacing of 0.78 mm, and projection views were uniformly defined over 0°-360°. The reconstruction diameter was 495 mm, with an in-plane pixel spacing of 0.9668 mm, slice thickness of 1.0 mm, and matrix size of 512 × 512. Under this configuration, the GARM provided matched forward- and backprojection operators for projection synthesis, intermediate reconstruction, and cycle-domain supervision, thereby ensuring that both domains were coupled through the same acquisition geometry rather than through loosely aligned learned mappings alone.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Methodology > PCGA-Net framework > Geometry-aware reconstruction module (GARM)
text: Another key advantage of the GARM is differentiability. Because both the forward and backward operators are embedded into the training graph, supervision can propagate across domains during optimization. This allows the PCM to benefit from image-domain feedback and the VRM to benefit from projection-domain consistency, rather than training the two branches as isolated generators. In practice, the GARM therefore enables the cycle-domain supervision used in PCGA-Net by enforcing that synthesized projections, reconstructed intermediate volumes, and refined image outputs remain mutually compatible under a unified cone-beam imaging model. This is particularly important for limited-angle CBCT, where preserving geometric fidelity is as critical as reducing visible artifacts. By anchoring both generation branches to explicit scanner physics, the GARM helps ensure that the final reconstructed volume is not only visually improved but also physically plausible with respect to the underlying acquisition process.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: The VRM constitutes the volumetric refinement stage of PCGA-Net and is designed to improve the intermediate reconstruction generated by the GARM into a high-fidelity CBCT volume. Unlike the PCM, which operates in acquisition space to compensate for missing angular information, the VRM operates in image space and focuses on suppressing residual limited-angle artifacts, restoring anatomical structures, and improving volumetric fidelity. Its role is therefore not to infer the entire anatomy from scratch, but to refine the geometry-initialized reconstruction \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{upgreek} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document} ${I^{\mathrm{rec}}}$\end{document}Irec into a cleaner and anatomically more accurate image representation. This design is consistent with the dual-domain philosophy of the framework, in which missing-angle completion is first addressed in projection space and then followed by image-domain restoration under explicit geometric guidance. As illustrated in figure 1(c), the VRM receives the GARM-based intermediate reconstruction as a strong condition and progressively denoises the volumetric sample toward the target CBCT distribution.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: This reciprocal design is important because it prevents the VRM from behaving as an isolated post-processing network; instead, it refines the volume while remaining coupled to the projection evidence through the GARM and cycle-domain feedback. A key practical consequence of this design is that the VRM and PCM have complementary but non-redundant roles. The PCM addresses incompleteness where it physically originates, namely in projection space, whereas the VRM addresses the residual anatomical and textural errors that persist after geometric reconstruction into image space. By conditioning the image-domain diffusion process on \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{upgreek} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document} ${I^{\mathrm{rec}}}$\end{document}Irec rather than on the raw limited-angle input alone, the framework provides the VRM with a substantially stronger and more structured initialization. This division of labor makes the overall PCGA-Net pipeline easier to interpret and better aligned with the physics of limited-angle CBCT reconstruction, where data incompleteness and image degradation arise in related but distinct domains.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Methodology > PCGA-Net framework > Cross-domain geometric coupling and cycle supervision
text: A central component of PCGA-Net is that the PCM and VRM are not trained as two isolated modules. Instead, they are coupled through a geometry-guided cross-domain cycle supervision strategy, which uses the GARM to establish a closed projection-to-image-to-projection loop under the same cone-beam acquisition geometry. The goal of this design is to ensure that the synthesized full-view projections generated by the PCM can be reconstructed into anatomically meaningful CBCT volumes, while the refined image-domain outputs produced by the VRM remain physically compatible with the projection measurements. As illustrated in figures 1(a)–(c), this supervision is introduced during training by linking projection synthesis, GARM-based reconstruction, and image refinement into one unified optimization framework. During application, the same cross-domain interaction is maintained in the iterative generation procedure shown in figures 2(c)–(a).

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: Figures 1 and 2 describe different stages of PCGA-Net. Figure 1 summarizes supervised training and therefore includes clean ground-truth targets, forward-diffusion training states, and optimization losses. Figure 2 contains none of these training-only quantities; instead, it unrolls one application-time transition from the current reverse timestep s to the subsequent timestep s-1, showing how deterministic estimates provide geometry-mediated cross-domain feedback while stochastic states advance the reverse diffusion trajectories. The trained model is therefore applied iteratively rather than as a single-pass PCM–GARM–VRM cascade.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: After training, PCGA-Net reconstructs limited-angle CBCT through an iterative application process that alternates between the PCM, the GARM, and the VRM. Unlike a one-pass feedforward pipeline, the proposed application strategy preserves the same cross-domain geometric linkage used during training, allowing the projection and image branches to progressively support one another during reverse diffusion. As illustrated in figures 2(c)–(a), the generation starts from noisy projection and image variables and then proceeds through reciprocal refinement in projection space and image space under GARM guidance. This design is particularly important for limited-angle CBCT, because the missing-angle information recovered in projection space and the anatomical structures refined in image space must remain compatible throughout the sampling trajectory rather than only at the final output.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Experimental setup > Datasets, split, and preprocessing
text: We evaluated PCGA-Net in three clinically distinct cohorts with different anatomical complexity, motion characteristics, and image-guidance workflows: GYN HDR brachytherapy pelvic CT, abdominal liver 4DCT, and H&N CBCT. This multi-site design was intended to assess whether the proposed framework remains effective across procedure-oriented pelvic imaging, respiration-affected upper-abdominal imaging, and anatomically intricate on-board H&N imaging, rather than in a single disease site alone. Consistent with the overall goal of balancing cross-patient generalizability and patient-specific reconstruction fidelity, we adopted a two-stage training strategy for all three cohorts: a population-level pretraining stage to learn anatomy- and geometry-related priors shared across patients, followed by a patient-specific few-shot adaptation stage to tailor the model to the target patient. In our design a global prior is first learned from a broader cohort and then refined for patient-specific reconstruction.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Experimental setup > Datasets, split, and preprocessing
text: For the GYN HDR brachytherapy cohort, data from 30 patients were used for population-level pretraining, and an additional 30 patients were reserved for adaptation and evaluation. For each patient in the adaptation cohort, 2 early fractions were used for patient-specific fine-tuning, and the remaining 3 fractions were used for testing. This cohort represents a challenging pelvic reconstruction scenario in which volumetric imaging is closely associated with applicator or needle verification, target localization, and peri-procedural assessment. Each fraction contained 229 slices with an in-plane matrix size of 512 × 512. The original scans were acquired on a Siemens Healthineers SOMATOM go. Open Pro CT system (120 kVp, 126 mA, 157 mAs), with 1.0 mm slice thickness and pixel spacing of 0.3774 × 0.3774 mm2. The corresponding geometric parameters used to define the simulated cone-beam configuration were SDD = 1113 mm and source-to-axis distance (SAD) = 610 mm. For this cohort, CT volumes were used to generate simulated cone-beam projections under a predefined geometry, enabling controlled evaluation against artifact-free volumetric references.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Experimental setup > Datasets, split, and preprocessing
text: For the abdominal liver 4DCT cohort, 50 patients were included in the pretraining stage, with 10 respiratory phases per patient used to capture shared respiratory-motion priors. The adaptation cohort consisted of 15 patients, for whom 3 phases/fractions were used for patient-specific fine-tuning and 6 phases/fractions were used for testing. This cohort was selected because limited-angle reconstruction in the upper abdomen is complicated by low soft-tissue contrast and respiration-driven deformation, making accurate recovery of volumetric anatomy particularly demanding. Each volume contained 178 slices with a 512 × 512 in-plane matrix. The 4DCT scans were acquired on a Siemens SOMATOM Definition Edge scanner (120 kVp) with 2.0 mm slice thickness and pixel spacing of 0.9766 × 0.9766 mm2. The corresponding geometric parameters were SDD = 1085.6 mm and SAD = 595 mm. As in the GYN cohort, the 4DCT volumes were used as artifact-reduced volumetric references from which cone-beam projections were simulated. This strategy is advantageous for CBCT reconstruction research because it provides exactly paired projection-volume data under known acquisition geometry, which is difficult to guarantee using real CBCT alone.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Experimental setup > Datasets, split, and preprocessing
text: For the H&N cohort, 40 patients were used for pretraining and 16 patients for patient-specific adaptation and testing. Because this cohort contains the most complex osseous-air-soft-tissue interfaces and is strongly influenced by immobilization-related geometry, a deeper adaptation setting was used: 10 fractions per patient were used for fine-tuning and the remaining 5 fractions were used for evaluation. This cohort represents a realistic daily on-board image-guided radiotherapy setting, where CBCT is clinically used for setup verification, monitoring of treatment-induced anatomical changes, and adaptive decision-making. Each fraction contained 106 slices with a 512 × 512 in-plane matrix. The CBCT scans were acquired on a Varian Medical Systems P2VA system (100 kVp, 154 mA, 889 mAs), with slice thickness of 1.9964 mm, pixel spacing of 0.5655 × 0.5655 mm2, SDD = 3700 mm, and SAD = 2700 mm. Unlike the GYN and abdominal cohorts, this dataset was evaluated directly in the CBCT domain because matched planning CT volumes were not consistently available for all cases. This complementary design allowed us to test PCGA-Net in both CT-based projection simulation settings and real clinical CBCT acquisitions.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Experimental setup > Datasets, split, and preprocessing
text: All projection–domain inputs in this study were generated under a prescribed cone-beam geometry. For the GYN and liver cohorts, CT or 4DCT volumes were forward-projected to generate paired full-view and limited-angle data. For the H&N cohort, reconstructed clinical on-board CBCT volumes served as the source volumes and reference targets. Because vendor raw detector projections were not available, each reconstructed H&N CBCT volume was forward-projected with LEAP-CT to generate a synthetic 360-view projection stack, from which the fixed 90-view short arc was retained as the model input. Therefore, the H&N experiment uses clinically acquired reconstructed CBCT anatomy but simulated projection measurements; it is not an evaluation on original raw detector data.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Experimental setup > Datasets, split, and preprocessing
text: All datasets underwent consistent preprocessing prior to model training. First, both projection data and volumetric images were intensity-normalized to [−1, 1], to stabilize optimization and match the operating range of the diffusion model. During inference, the reconstructed outputs were mapped back to the original Hounsfield unit (HU) scale for quantitative evaluation. Second, all images were resampled and cropped to a unified in-plane matrix size of 512 × 512. The slice direction was downsampled or standardized to fit graphics processing unit (GPU) memory while preserving the major anatomical structures, resulting in an anisotropic resolution close to 1 × 1 × 2 mm3. Third, a body mask was applied to remove background air and restrict analysis to the patient body region, thereby reducing irrelevant background variation during training and evaluation. For the CT-based cohorts, patient-specific cone-beam geometry was constructed from the corresponding Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine (DICOM) metadata, and full-view projections were simulated using the same geometric configuration employed by the GARM. Limited-angle inputs were then generated by retaining only the designated short-arc views for model input, while the full-view projections were used as supervision targets.
