The same assumption was used for the CT/4DCT-derived projections and for the re-projected H&N CBCT volumes.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Experimental setup > Datasets, split, and preprocessing
text: The multi-site evaluation assesses cross-site robustness under the specified two-stage protocol rather than patient-independent zero-shot generalization. For each anatomical site, a population-level model was first trained using a separate pretraining cohort. For each target patient, only designated early fractions or respiratory phases were then used for patient-specific adaptation, and the remaining later fractions or phases were held out for evaluation. The GYN, liver, and H&N adaptation sets contained 2, 3, and 10 early fractions/phases per patient, respectively; the corresponding held-out test sets contained 3, 6, and 5 later fractions/phases. No projection, volume, or supervision target derived from a held-out test fraction/phase was used during adaptation.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: All model training and inference were conducted on a workstation equipped with two NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q GPUs, providing a total of 192 GB GDDR7 memory. This hardware configuration enabled efficient training of the dual-domain diffusion framework with mixed-precision computation, including bfloat16 (BF16) and 8-bit floating-point (FP8) precision. The software stack was built on PyTorch 2.4, and the GARM was implemented using LEAP-CT to provide differentiable forward- and backward-projection operators under the predefined cone-beam geometry. This configuration was selected to support memory-intensive 3D diffusion training while preserving end-to-end geometric consistency across the projection and image domains.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: Training was performed on randomly sampled three-dimensional subvolumes of \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{upgreek} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document} $64\times 64\times 16$\end{document}64×64×16 voxels. Accordingly, the reported batch size of 16 denotes the effective number of subvolumes per optimization step rather than 16 complete 512× 512512×512 volumes. Memory use was further controlled through mixed-precision computation and alternating PCM/VRM updates, during which gradients were retained only for the branch being optimized. During evaluation, the standardized volume was processed using sliding-window inference with normalized Gaussian weighting, avoiding manual hard concatenation of independently reconstructed blocks.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: Training was performed in two stages: foundation pretraining and patient-specific fine-tuning. In the first stage, a population-level reconstruction model was pretrained separately for each anatomical site using the corresponding pretraining cohort, namely 30 patients for GYN HDR brachytherapy, 50 patients for liver 4DCT, and 40 patients for H&N CBCT. The purpose of this stage was to learn anatomy-aware image priors and short-arc projection completion patterns shared across patients within each site. Model optimization was performed using the AdamW optimizer with an initial learning rate of \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{upgreek} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document} $2\times 1{0^{-5}}$\end{document}2×10−5, and the total diffusion length was set to T = 1000T=1000 with a linear noise schedule. Benefiting from the large GPU memory available on the Blackwell platform, the batch size was set to 16, and pretraining was continued for up to 500 epochs or until the validation loss reached convergence. We employed an early stopping strategy with a patience of 20 epochs and a minimum improvement threshold of 0.001. This stage produced the initialization weights for the subsequent patient-specific adaptation step.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: In the second stage, the pretrained model weights were loaded and fully fine-tuned for each patient in the adaptation cohort using only a small number of early fractions or phases. This patient-specific full-parameter adaptation was introduced to reduce residual anatomical mismatch between the population model and the target patient, and to better accommodate patient-dependent imaging appearance, motion pattern, and scanner-specific noise characteristics. During fine-tuning, the learning rate was reduced to \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{upgreek} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document} $1\times 1{0^{-5}}$\end{document}1×10−5 to ensure stable adaptation, and the number of training epochs was set to 100. All model parameters were updated during this stage rather than freezing selected layers, because the projection and image diffusion branches, as well as their GARM-mediated interaction, all contribute to patient-specific reconstruction fidelity. This design follows the same overall principle as in our prior geometry-integrated CBCT reconstruction studies, where a global model first captures shared anatomical structure and is then adapted to the target patient using a small number of available images.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: During the 100-epoch patient-specific adaptation stage, supervised pairs were constructed only from the designated early fractions/phases. For the PCM, the 90-view limited-angle projection served as the conditional input and the paired full-view projection stack served as the target. For the VRM, the GARM-derived intermediate reconstruction served as the conditional input and the corresponding reference CT/4DCT/CBCT volume served as the image target; the same early-fraction references were used for the GARM reconstruction and cycle-consistency terms. The later fractions/phases reserved for testing were not used for parameter optimization. Accordingly, the reported results represent a longitudinal patient-adapted operating point in which prior images from the same patient are available.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: The overall training objective combined the diffusion losses in projection and image space with the GARM-based reconstruction and cycle-supervision terms. During implementation, no weight decay and gradient clipping were applied as needed to stabilize diffusion training on volumetric data. Loss updates alternated between the projection and image branches, assigning zero gradients to the uninvolved network during each update step. At inference time, the same pretrained-and-adapted model was used to reconstruct limited-angle CBCT through the geometry-guided reverse generation process, with 50 reverse sampling steps (using a timestep respacing strategy) to balance reconstruction accuracy and computational efficiency.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: The PCM and VRM are implemented as distinct three-dimensional Swin-Vnet conditional denoisers. Each denoiser follows a seven-stage encoder and seven-stage decoder design with resolution-matched skip connections and three Swin-attention blocks at the bottleneck. Instance normalization and ReLU activation are applied after the convolutional and attention layers. Diffusion time is represented by a 128-dimensional sinusoidal embedding with a maximum period of 1024 and is injected into the network blocks. The decoder output heads predict the parameters required for the mean and variance terms of reverse diffusion. The PCM receives the noisy full-view projection state together with the measured 90-view short-arc projection stack and synthesizes the completed projection representation used by the GARM. The VRM receives the noisy image-domain state together with the GARM-derived intermediate reconstruction and refines the volume toward the target CBCT distribution. Complete functional definitions of the PCM, GARM, and VRM, together with channel widths, convolution kernels, anisotropic down- and up-sampling factors, cumulative relative resolutions, bottleneck attention settings, and memory-handling details, are provided in supplementary tables S1–S4.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: For the cGAN comparison, we used a volumetric pix2pix-style image-domain implementation. The input was the FDK volume reconstructed from the same 90-view short arc used by PCGA-Net, and the supervision target was the corresponding full-view/reference CBCT. The generator followed a three-dimensional U-Net-like encoder-decoder and was trained with a three-dimensional PatchGAN discriminator using adversarial and voxel-wise \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{upgreek} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document} ${L_1}$\end{document}L1 reconstruction objectives. The same cohort partitions, preprocessing, body mask, and evaluation protocol were used for all methods. For the fully adapted comparisons in tables 2–4, cGAN, PatRecon-Net, and PCGA-Net each underwent patient-specific fine-tuning using the identical designated early fractions/phases and the same fine-tuning settings as PCGA-Net. Each learned model was initialized from its corresponding site-specific population checkpoint and adapted for 100 epochs with a learning rate of \documentclass[12pt]{minimal} \usepackage{amsmath} \usepackage{wasysym} \usepackage{amsfonts} \usepackage{amssymb} \usepackage{amsbsy} \usepackage{upgreek} \usepackage{mathrsfs} \setlength{\oddsidemargin}{-69pt} \begin{document} $1\times 1{0^{-5}}$\end{document}1×10−5 and full-parameter updates.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: The cohort-specific adaptation sets comprised 2 prior fractions for GYN, 10 for H&N, and 3 fractions/phases for liver. All methods were evaluated on the same held-out later fractions/phases. Table 5 separately presents the population-only (N = 0N=0) and fully adapted operating points; N = 0N=0 denotes use of the population checkpoint before target-patient fine-tuning. PatRecon-Net was implemented using the authors’ public repository. Its data loader accepts a user-defined number of views, stacks the projections along the input-channel dimension, and constructs ReconNet with the input-channel count set to num_views. We therefore set num_views = 90 and supplied the measured short-arc projections in acquisition order, while retaining the reference 3D volume as the reconstruction target. No projection-completion branch, analytic GARM, or cycle-domain coupling was added.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: Reconstruction performance was assessed using three standard image-quality metrics: MAE, peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR), and structural similarity index measure (SSIM). These metrics were selected because they provide complementary information on voxel-wise intensity fidelity, global signal reconstruction quality, and structural preservation, respectively, and are widely used for quantitative evaluation in CBCT reconstruction. In all experiments, the reconstructed limited-angle CBCT volume was compared against the corresponding reference volume on a voxel-by-voxel basis after restoration to the original HU scale. Lower MAE and higher PSNR/SSIM indicate better reconstruction performance. Consistent with the comparative setting of this study, PCGA-Net was quantitatively evaluated against cGAN (Isola et al 2017) and PatRecon-Net (Shen et al 2019) as learning-based baseline methods, and FDK was used as a physics-based reference.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: In this study, SSIM was calculated over the reconstructed body region to quantify how well the structural organization of the target anatomy was preserved after limited-angle reconstruction. Compared with MAE and PSNR, SSIM is more sensitive to perceptually important structural distortion, making it particularly useful for evaluating artifact suppression and anatomical integrity.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: Across all three datasets, the qualitative comparisons consistently indicate that limited-angle FDK reconstruction remains strongly affected by streaking, shading, and view-dependent structural distortion, although the visual manifestation of these artifacts varies with anatomy, motion pattern, and workflow-specific imaging conditions. In the GYN HDR brachytherapy cohort, the main difficulty lies in recovering applicator-adjacent pelvic soft tissue under crowded procedural anatomy; in the H&N cohort, the challenge is dominated by complex bone-air-soft-tissue interfaces and elongated anatomical structure; and in the abdominal liver 4DCT cohort, limited-angle degradation is compounded by low soft-tissue contrast and respiration-associated anatomical variation. Despite these distinct failure modes, PCGA-Net shows a consistent qualitative advantage over FDK and the compared learning-based baselines by producing anatomically more coherent reconstructions with reduced residual artifacts across axial, coronal, and sagittal views. This cross-dataset visual consistency suggests that the proposed geometry-integrated dual-domain design is not confined to one specific anatomical site, but is capable of handling diverse limited-angle reconstruction scenarios with different structural complexity and clinical imaging characteristics.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Results > Qualitative results > Qualitative assessment of the GYN HDR brachytherapy CT
text: Representative qualitative results for the GYN HDR brachytherapy cohort are shown in figure 3, including axial, coronal, and sagittal views together with the corresponding error maps. The FDK reconstruction exhibits typical limited-angle degradation across all three planes, with pronounced streaking, shading, and loss of anatomical continuity, particularly around the pelvic midline and applicator-adjacent soft tissues. These artifacts are most evident in the coronal and sagittal views, where depth-direction distortion and structural elongation are clearly visible. Among the learning-based methods, PatRecon-Net reduces part of the large-scale artifact pattern relative to FDK, but residual errors remain visible around the pelvic bones and central soft-tissue structures. In contrast, cGAN introduces more substantial intensity deviation and structural inconsistency, with broader high-magnitude error patterns distributed across the body contour and central pelvic region. Compared with both baselines, PCGA-Net provides the closest visual agreement to the reference CBCT. The reconstructed pelvic anatomy is more spatially coherent, the bony contours are better preserved, and the surrounding soft tissues appear less corrupted by limited-angle streaking. This advantage is consistently reflected in the error maps, where PCGA-Net shows the weakest residual deviations in all three anatomical planes.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Results > Qualitative results > Qualitative assessment of the GYN HDR brachytherapy CT
text: In addition to the surrounding pelvic anatomy, PCGA-Net also provides more faithful reconstruction of the brachytherapy applicator itself, which is a critical requirement in the GYN HDR setting. In the FDK reconstruction, the applicator region is degraded by strong limited-angle streaking and local shading, making the device boundaries appear blurred and partially distorted. PatRecon-Net mitigates part of this degradation but still shows residual structural ambiguity around the applicator channel and adjacent high-contrast interfaces, while cGAN introduces more noticeable intensity bias and shape inconsistency in the same region. By comparison, PCGA-Net preserves the applicator geometry with sharper definition and reduced surrounding artifact contamination, particularly in the coronal and sagittal views where limited-angle distortion is typically more severe. The corresponding error maps also show that PCGA-Net yields the smallest residual deviation near the applicator, suggesting improved recovery of both the device structure and its spatial relationship to the adjacent pelvic soft tissue.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Results > Qualitative results > Qualitative assessment of the H&N CBCT
text: Representative qualitative results for the H&N cohort are shown in figure 4, where axial, coronal, and sagittal views are presented together with the corresponding error maps. Compared with the reference CBCT, the FDK reconstruction exhibits substantial limited-angle artifacts across all three planes, including strong shading in the central neck region, blurred soft-tissue boundaries, and loss of structural continuity along the cervical spine and airway-adjacent anatomy. These degradations are particularly evident in the coronal and sagittal views, where the missing-angle effect introduces pronounced elongation and nonuniform intensity distortion over the long superior-inferior extent of the neck.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Results > Qualitative results > Qualitative assessment of the H&N CBCT
text: Among the learning-based baselines, PatRecon-Net reduces part of the large-scale artifact pattern but still leaves visible residual errors around the body contour, lower neck soft tissue, and vertebral structures. cGAN shows more pronounced intensity bias and spatial inconsistency, with broader high-magnitude residuals distributed throughout both superficial and deep anatomical regions. In contrast, PCGA-Net achieves the closest visual agreement to the reference CBCT across all three views. The reconstructed anatomy appears more spatially coherent, with improved delineation of the cervical vertebrae, airway contour, and surrounding soft-tissue interfaces. This advantage is consistently reflected in the error maps, where PCGA-Net shows the weakest residual deviations relative to both FDK and the compared learning-based methods.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Results > Qualitative results > Qualitative assessment of the H&N CBCT
text: The qualitative improvement is particularly relevant in the H&N setting because this site contains dense bone-air-soft-tissue interfaces, fine anatomical structures, and immobilization-related geometric complexity, all of which make limited-angle reconstruction especially challenging. In the sagittal view, PCGA-Net better preserves the continuity of the cervical spine and adjacent soft-tissue profile, while in the coronal view it more effectively suppresses broad shading artifacts across the neck cross-section. Overall, these results indicate that PCGA-Net provides more effective artifact suppression and more faithful recovery of H&N anatomy than conventional analytic reconstruction and the compared deep-learning baselines.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Results > Qualitative results > Qualitative assessment of the abdominal liver 4DCT
text: Figure 5 presents a representative visual comparison for the abdominal liver 4DCT cohort in the axial, coronal, and sagittal planes, together with the corresponding error maps. Under limited-angle acquisition, the FDK reconstruction shows substantial degradation throughout the upper abdomen, including broad shading, reduced soft-tissue contrast, and depth-direction blurring. These artifacts are especially evident in the coronal and sagittal views, where the extended cranio-caudal anatomy and incomplete angular coverage lead to noticeable structural distortion along the liver dome, posterior body contour, and paraspinal region.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Results > Qualitative results > Qualitative assessment of the abdominal liver 4DCT
text: Among the compared learning-based methods, PatRecon-Net reduces some of the large-scale artifact pattern relative to FDK and preserves the global body outline reasonably well, but residual errors remain visible around the liver boundary, abdominal wall, and vertebral structures. cGAN shows more substantial intensity deviation and less stable anatomical recovery, with broader residual patterns distributed across both the abdominal soft tissue and posterior structures. In contrast, PCGA-Net provides the closest visual agreement to the reference CBCT across all three views. The reconstructed liver contour is more spatially coherent, the vertebral column is better preserved, and the surrounding abdominal soft tissue appears less affected by limited-angle shading and streaking. These improvements are consistently supported by the error maps, where PCGA-Net shows the weakest residual deviations relative to both FDK and the learning-based baselines.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Results > Qualitative results > Qualitative assessment of the abdominal liver 4DCT
text: The qualitative advantage of PCGA-Net is particularly relevant in the abdominal setting, where low soft-tissue contrast and respiration-associated anatomical variation make limited-angle reconstruction especially challenging. In this cohort, successful reconstruction requires not only suppression of global artifact patterns but also preservation of weak organ boundaries and large-scale anatomical continuity. Overall, the results indicate that PCGA-Net achieves more effective artifact suppression and more faithful recovery of abdominal anatomy than conventional FDK reconstruction and the compared deep-learning baselines.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: Figure 6 summarizes the overall quantitative performance of all methods across the three datasets, while the detailed numerical results for each cohort are reported in the corresponding tables below. A consistent trend can be observed across the GYN HDR brachytherapy CT, abdominal liver 4DCT, and H&N CBCT cohorts: PCGA-Net achieved the lowest MAE and the highest SSIM and PSNR in all three settings, indicating superior voxel-level accuracy, structural preservation, and overall reconstruction fidelity under limited-angle acquisition. In contrast, the conventional FDK baseline showed substantial performance degradation across all datasets, and although the learning-based baselines improved upon FDK, they remained consistently inferior to PCGA-Net. This cross-cohort pattern suggests that the proposed geometry-integrated dual-domain framework provides not only site-specific improvement, but also stable quantitative benefit across anatomically and clinically diverse limited-angle reconstruction tasks.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: To assess whether the observed performance differences were statistically significant, pairwise comparisons between PCGA-Net and each baseline method were performed using a two-sided paired Student’s t-test on the test cases within each cohort. A significance threshold of p < 0.05p<0.05 was adopted throughout the study. A paired test was used because all reconstruction methods were evaluated on the same set of test fractions/phases, enabling direct case-wise comparison of MAE, SSIM, and PSNR. Statistical significance is indicated by * in the corresponding tables.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Results > Quantitative results > Quantitative assessment of the GYN HDR brachytherapy CT
text: The quantitative results for the GYN HDR brachytherapy cohort further confirm the advantage of PCGA-Net over both analytic reconstruction and the compared learning-based baselines. As summarized in table 2, PCGA-Net achieved the best performance across all three metrics, with an MAE of 34.47 ± 6.28 HU, an SSIM of 0.87 ± 0.04, and a PSNR of 35.79 ± 0.95 dB. In comparison, the conventional FDK reconstruction yielded substantially poorer accuracy (178.63 ± 31.58 HU MAE, 0.51 ± 0.03 SSIM, and 18.97 ± 1.31 dB PSNR), indicating that severe limited-angle degradation cannot be adequately resolved by analytic reconstruction alone. Relative to FDK, PCGA-Net reduced MAE by approximately 80.7%, increased SSIM by 0.36, and improved PSNR by 16.82 dB. These gains indicate that the proposed framework substantially improves both voxel-level fidelity and structural preservation in the pelvic setting. Compared with the learning-based baselines, PCGA-Net also maintained a clear quantitative margin. Relative to cGAN, PCGA-Net reduced MAE from 62.45 ± 10.12 HU to 34.47 ± 6.28 HU, corresponding to an error reduction of about 44.8%, while improving SSIM from 0.71 ± 0.05–0.87 ± 0.04 and PSNR from 29.30 ± 1.55 dB to 35.79 ± 0.95 dB. Compared with PatRecon-Net, PCGA-Net achieved an additional 29.5% reduction in MAE, together with an absolute SSIM gain of 0.09 and a PSNR gain of 3.94 dB.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Results > Quantitative results > Quantitative assessment of the GYN HDR brachytherapy CT
text: An additional point of interest is the reduction in performance variability. PCGA-Net not only achieved the best mean values, but also showed relatively small standard deviations across the test set, suggesting more stable reconstruction behavior across fractions. This is particularly relevant in the GYN HDR brachytherapy setting, where anatomical appearance may vary across treatment sessions due to applicator placement, organ filling, and local pelvic deformation. From a quantitative perspective, these results indicate that PCGA-Net improves not only average reconstruction accuracy, but also robustness under clinically realistic inter-fraction variability.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Results > Quantitative results > Quantitative assessment of the H&N CBCT
text: The quantitative results on the H&N CBCT cohort show a consistent advantage of PCGA-Net over both conventional analytic reconstruction and the compared learning-based baselines. As summarized in table 3, PCGA-Net achieved the best performance across all evaluated metrics, with an MAE of 28.42 ± 4.88 HU, an SSIM of 0.91 ± 0.05, and a PSNR of 38.52 ± 0.95 dB. In contrast, the FDK baseline showed substantially inferior reconstruction accuracy, yielding an MAE of 165.30 ± 25.40 HU, an SSIM of 0.61 ± 0.05, and a PSNR of 21.13 ± 1.14 dB. These results indicate that conventional limited-angle reconstruction is insufficient to preserve the fine anatomical detail and structural consistency required in the H&N setting. Relative to FDK, PCGA-Net reduced MAE by approximately 82.8%, increased SSIM by 0.30, and improved PSNR by 17.39 dB. This magnitude of improvement is particularly notable given the structural complexity of the H&N region, where dense osseous anatomy, air cavities, and soft-tissue interfaces make limited-angle reconstruction especially challenging. Compared with cGAN, PCGA-Net reduced MAE from 55.18 ± 8.25 HU to 28.42 ± 4.88 HU, corresponding to an error reduction of approximately 48.5%, while also improving SSIM from 0.79 ± 0.04–0.91 ± 0.05 and PSNR from 31.49 ± 1.43 dB to 38.52 ± 0.95 dB. Compared with PatRecon-Net, PCGA-Net further reduced MAE by about 32.1%, together with an absolute SSIM gain of 0.06 and a PSNR gain of 4.42 dB.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Results > Quantitative results > Quantitative assessment of the abdominal liver 4DCT
text: The quantitative results on the abdominal liver 4DCT cohort demonstrate that PCGA-Net also maintains a clear advantage in this anatomically and temporally challenging setting. As summarized in table 4, PCGA-Net achieved the best performance across all three metrics, with an MAE of 39.27 ± 6.10 HU, an SSIM of 0.82 ± 0.03, and a PSNR of 36.85 ± 1.16 dB. In comparison, the conventional FDK reconstruction remained substantially degraded, with an MAE of 195.21 ± 40.08 HU, an SSIM of 0.50 ± 0.06, and a PSNR of 18.50 ± 1.50 dB. These results indicate that the incomplete angular support in abdominal imaging cannot be adequately compensated by analytic reconstruction alone, particularly in the presence of low soft-tissue contrast and respiration-related anatomical variation.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Results > Quantitative results > Quantitative assessment of the abdominal liver 4DCT
text: Relative to FDK, PCGA-Net reduced MAE by approximately 79.9%, increased SSIM by 0.32, and improved PSNR by 18.35 dB. Compared with cGAN, PCGA-Net reduced MAE from 68.14 ± 12.32 HU to 39.27 ± 6.10 HU, corresponding to an error reduction of about 42.4%, while also improving SSIM from 0.68 ± 0.07–0.82 ± 0.03 and PSNR from 28.15 ± 1.87 dB to 36.85 ± 1.16 dB. Compared with PatRecon-Net, PCGA-Net achieved an additional 27.4% reduction in MAE, together with an absolute SSIM gain of 0.07 and a PSNR gain of 5.95 dB. These margins are quantitatively meaningful because the abdominal cohort is intrinsically more difficult than the pelvic and H&N cohorts, owing to weaker organ contrast and more pronounced deformation across respiratory phases.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Results > Population-only comparison and patient-specific adaptation
text: To separate the reconstruction capability of the population-pretrained model from the contribution of longitudinal patient-specific priors, we performed two complementary adaptation analyses. First, table 5 separates the population-only (N = 0N=0) and fully adapted configurations for cGAN, PatRecon-Net, and PCGA-Net in each cohort. Within each configuration, the learned methods use the same patient-information constraints. The fully adapted means reproduce the corresponding results in tables 2–4, while FDK remains the non-adaptable analytic reference reported in those tables. The fully adapted configurations used 2 prior fractions for the GYN HDR brachytherapy cohort, 10 prior fractions for the H&N CBCT cohort, and 3 prior fractions/phases for the abdominal liver 4DCT cohort. The later evaluation fractions/phases remained held out at all adaptation levels, and the acquisition geometry, preprocessing, and evaluation procedures were unchanged. Under population-only inference, PCGA-Net achieved MAEs of 58.06, 47.88, and 82.66 HU in the GYN, H&N, and liver cohorts, respectively. The corresponding values were 85.0, 76.0, and 112.0 HU for cGAN and 70.0, 62.0, and 96.0 HU for PatRecon-Net. PCGA-Net also yielded higher SSIM and PSNR in each cohort: 0.79 and 33.29 dB for GYN, 0.80 and 33.37 dB for H&N, and 0.71 and 30.75 dB for liver. Thus, the population-only comparison evaluates the reconstruction pipelines without incorporating target-patient adaptation data.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Results > Population-only comparison and patient-specific adaptation
text: Patient-specific adaptation improved all three metrics for every learned method. For cGAN, MAE decreased by 26.53%, 27.39%, and 39.16% in the GYN, H&N, and liver cohorts, respectively; the corresponding reductions for PatRecon-Net were 30.14%, 32.47%, and 44.35%. Under the fully adapted protocol, PCGA-Net retained lower MAE and higher SSIM and PSNR than both learned baselines in all three cohorts. The two sets of comparisons therefore distinguish differences among complete reconstruction pipelines under matched patient-information conditions from the additional benefit obtained by adapting each model to the target patient. They do not isolate the contribution of any individual architectural module. As shown in table 5, population-only PCGA-Net retained meaningful reconstruction capability in all three cohorts, and patient-specific adaptation improved every evaluated metric for PCGA-Net. The relative MAE reductions were 40.63%, 40.64%, and 52.49% for the GYN HDR, H&N, and liver cohorts, respectively. The corresponding relative SSIM increases were 10.13%, 13.75%, and 15.49%, and the absolute PSNR increases were 2.50, 5.15, and 6.10 dB, respectively. Thus, the site-specific population model provides a feasible no-adaptation operating point, whereas longitudinal patient-specific adaptation supplies additional anatomical information that materially improves reconstruction accuracy.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
section: Results > Population-only comparison and patient-specific adaptation
text: To examine how reconstruction changes with the amount of patient-specific information, we further performed an adaptation-dose ablation in the H&N cohort, which provided 10 prior fractions and therefore supported a multi-level longitudinal analysis. The model was adapted using N = 0,2,4,6,8N=0,2,4,6,8, or 1010 prior fractions, while the same later fractions were retained for evaluation at every setting. The H&N adaptation-dose results show an overall improvement as more longitudinal information was introduced. Relative to N = 0N=0, using 2 prior fractions reduced MAE by 17.50% and increased SSIM by 5.00%. At N = 10N=10, MAE was reduced by 40.64% and SSIM was increased by 13.75%. The improvement was not strictly monotonic for every metric: MAE increased slightly from 39.50 HU at N = 2N=2 to 39.96 HU at N = 4N=4, while SSIM increased from 0.84 to 0.85. Performance subsequently improved at N = 6N=6, 8, and 10. This behavior suggests that patient-specific adaptation is beneficial overall, but the marginal gain from each additional fraction is nonuniform and may depend on the anatomical information represented by the available prior images.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: This study addresses a clinically important but methodologically difficult reconstruction setting: recovering volumetric CBCT from continuous limited-angle acquisition. In this regime, the challenge is not simply the presence of visible streaking or shading artifacts, but the fact that incomplete angular sampling removes part of the information required for stable volumetric recovery. This makes limited-angle CBCT fundamentally different from routine image denoising or post-processing tasks. The findings of this study suggest that improved reconstruction in this setting depends on respecting where the information loss originates. Because the incompleteness is introduced in projection space but manifests clinically in image space, an effective solution must coordinate both domains rather than relying on image restoration alone. This is the main rationale for combining projection completion, analytic geometric transformation, and image-domain refinement within a single framework.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: One important implication of the current results is that explicit imaging geometry remains essential even in the era of generative reconstruction. Diffusion-based models provide strong generative capacity and can recover fine anatomical detail more effectively than conventional restoration networks, but such capacity is most useful when the generation process is constrained by physically meaningful mappings. In limited-angle reconstruction, unconstrained image synthesis can easily improve appearance without guaranteeing compatibility with the measured rays. By embedding the GARM between projection completion and volumetric refinement, the present framework uses scanner geometry not merely as implementation detail, but as a structural constraint on what the model is allowed to generate. This point is important for future research as well: for short-arc CBCT, the central question is not how to generate the sharpest possible image, but how to generate a volumetric image whose recovered structures remain accountable to the acquisition geometry.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: The cGAN comparison should be interpreted as a pipeline-level comparison with a representative image-domain conditional generative method rather than an architecture-matched ablation. cGAN performs limited-angle artifact correction after FDK reconstruction and does not include projection completion, the analytic GARM, or projection-image cycle supervision. Adding these components would convert cGAN into a different dual-domain reconstruction framework and would no longer preserve the original pix2pix design. Accordingly, the observed differences reflect the combined effect of the reconstruction formulation and model class: image-only post-reconstruction correction for cGAN versus projection-geometry-image coupling for PCGA-Net. PatRecon-Net is consequently a valid few-view projection-to-volume comparator, but it remains a single-stage and single-domain method. The comparison preserves the baseline’s public input interface and original reconstruction principle, while the proposed method evaluates a different hypothesis: that explicit projection completion and geometry-mediated cross-domain coupling improve limited-angle reconstruction. The quantitative comparison should therefore be interpreted at the complete-pipeline level and not as an isolated assessment of network capacity.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: The multi-site evaluation further suggests that limited-angle reconstruction should not be viewed as a site-specific engineering problem. Although all three cohorts share the same broad reconstruction objective, the actual difficulty differs substantially by anatomy and workflow. In GYN HDR brachytherapy, the main challenge lies in preserving pelvic soft tissue and device-related geometry in a crowded procedural environment. In the abdominal liver cohort, low soft-tissue contrast and respiration-associated anatomical variation make the boundary between true organ structure and limited-angle artifact particularly ambiguous. In the H&N cohort, dense osseous-air-soft-tissue interfaces and elongated anatomy amplify direction-dependent distortion. That the same reconstruction principle remains effective across these settings indicates that geometry-aware cross-domain modeling captures a transferable part of the inverse problem, while the patient-specific adaptation stage remains necessary to absorb anatomy-dependent appearance variation. This has practical significance, because future deployment of limited-angle CBCT will likely require both globally learned geometric priors and local adaptation to patient-specific imaging context.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: The current framework also has an important clinical interpretation. It should be understood as a reconstruction strategy for situations in which full-angle CBCT is difficult, undesirable, or operationally incompatible with the workflow, rather than as a universal replacement for standard full-scan CBCT. In radiotherapy and image-guided procedures, limited-angle acquisition becomes relevant precisely because it may reduce scan burden, shorten interruption of treatment or intervention, and better fit constrained procedural environments. In such scenarios, the goal is often not to reproduce every aspect of a diagnostic-quality full-angle CBCT, but to recover sufficient volumetric information for anatomy-aware guidance, treatment adaptation, or procedural verification. This perspective is important when judging model performance: the value of short-arc reconstruction lies in whether it restores clinically usable three-dimensional structure under realistic acquisition constraints.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: The primary comparisons in tables 2–4 represent the fully adapted operating point: cGAN, PatRecon-Net, and PCGA-Net used the same target-patient prior fractions/phases and adaptation budget. Table 5 separately reports population-only and fully adapted configurations, while table 6 characterizes the effect of the number of prior fractions for PCGA-Net in the H&N cohort. These analyses distinguish reconstruction without target-patient adaptation from reconstruction supported by same-patient longitudinal information. Generalizability remains limited to the evaluated cohorts, site-specific population pretraining, and specified acquisition and adaptation protocols.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: The adaptation analyses clarify the intended clinical interpretation of PCGA-Net. The population-only results provide a no-adaptation operating point relevant to first-fraction imaging or to a patient for whom no longitudinal prior is available, whereas the fully adapted results represent repeated image-guided or adaptive workflows in which earlier fractions can be used to establish a stronger patient-specific prior. Across all three cohorts, the population-pretrained model remained functional without target-patient fine-tuning, but full adaptation produced substantial additional improvements. The H&N adaptation-dose experiment further showed an overall benefit from increasing the number of prior fractions, although the marginal improvement was not strictly monotonic. These findings confirm that the primary adapted results reflect both the reconstruction capability of the population model and the additional information supplied by same-patient longitudinal imaging; they should not be interpreted as patient-independent zero-shot performance.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: The detailed adaptation-dose curve was limited to the H&N cohort because it provided 10 longitudinal prior fractions, whereas the GYN HDR and liver cohorts provided only 2 and 3 adaptation fractions/phases, respectively. Those smaller adaptation sets permit comparison of the population-only and fully adapted endpoints, as reported in table 5, but do not provide a similarly resolved range for characterizing an adaptation-dose relationship. Moreover, each adaptation level requires separate optimization and evaluation of two three-dimensional diffusion branches coupled through differentiable cone-beam geometry, creating a substantial computational burden. The present study therefore combines a three-cohort endpoint analysis with a detailed H&N dose–response analysis. Future work should extend the multi-level ablation to additional anatomical sites, evaluate alternative selections and orderings of prior fractions, and determine whether a smaller adaptation set can achieve a clinically favorable balance between reconstruction accuracy and computational cost.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: Several limitations remain and provide clear directions for future work. First, the evaluated cohorts rely on CT- or 4DCT-based projection simulation, which is appropriate for controlled development because it provides artifact-reduced reference anatomy and precisely paired projection-volume data, but it does not fully reproduce the scatter, detector effects, and system-specific degradation observed in real CBCT acquisition. Broader validation on raw clinical projection data will therefore be necessary. Second, the present implementation assumes a fixed acquisition geometry and a predefined short-arc configuration. In future studies, it will be important to test robustness to variable arc lengths, angular placement, acquisition protocols, and noise conditions, since these factors are likely to differ across scanners and clinical workflows. Third, although the current model generalizes across multiple anatomical sites, its adaptation strategy remains cohort-specific. A meaningful next step would be to investigate whether a more unified foundation-style reconstruction model can maintain cross-site generality while still supporting efficient patient-level refinement. Finally, the evaluation in future work should move beyond image similarity alone toward task-driven endpoints, such as contouring stability, registration accuracy, dose recalculation, or device localization.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: These endpoints would better determine whether improved image reconstruction translates into improved image-guided decision-making. A further limitation is that the fixed loss weights in equation (9) were not subjected to an exhaustive grid search. Repeated joint training of two three-dimensional diffusion branches with differentiable cone-beam operators is computationally intensive; therefore, the current empirical coefficients should not be interpreted as globally optimal. Future studies will investigate adaptive loss-weighting strategies, such as uncertainty-based or gradient-normalized balancing, and will evaluate the sensitivity of reconstruction accuracy and geometric consistency to these coefficients.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: A further limitation concerns the provenance of the H&N projection data. The H&N source volumes were reconstructed clinical CBCT images that were subsequently forward-projected using the same nominal cone-beam geometry employed by the GARM. In strict inverse-problem terminology, this matched re-projection/reconstruction design constitutes an inverse crime and may yield more favorable data consistency than would be obtained from independent raw detector measurements. It does not capture acquisition-model mismatch, scatter, detector lag, calibration errors, truncation, beam-hardening effects, or the native projection-noise distribution. Accordingly, the H&N results should be interpreted as controlled reconstruction performance on clinically derived anatomy rather than as validation on raw clinical CBCT projections. Prospective evaluation using independently acquired raw projection data and scanner-specific corrections is required before clinical deployment.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: The current experiments also use idealized projection measurements without an explicit photon-statistics or electronic-noise model. This allows the effect of missing angular coverage to be studied in isolation, but it does not reproduce the strong coupling between limited-angle ill-conditioning and measurement noise encountered in low-dose clinical CBCT. Consequently, the reported results may overestimate performance under noisy raw-projection conditions. Future studies will evaluate multiple photon-flux levels, Poisson and electronic noise, scatter and beam-hardening effects, detector lag, and geometry/calibration mismatch, followed by validation on independently acquired raw clinical projections.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: Overall, this study supports a broader view of limited-angle CBCT reconstruction as a geometry-constrained inverse problem that is modulated by anatomy, workflow, and acquisition context. Within this setting, neither purely analytic reconstruction nor unconstrained generative modeling is sufficient by itself. The practical value of the proposed framework lies in showing that projection-domain completion, analytic geometric consistency, and image-domain refinement can be organized into a coherent reconstruction strategy for short-arc CBCT. More broadly, the study suggests that future progress in this area will depend less on increasing model complexity alone and more on designing reconstruction methods in which learned priors and imaging physics remain tightly coupled throughout the reconstruction process.

title: Physics-constrained and geometry-aware deep reconstruction for limited-angle CBCT.
text: In conclusion, this study presents PCGA-Net, a physics-constrained and geometry-aware reconstruction framework for limited-angle CBCT that jointly performs projection completion, analytic geometric reconstruction, and volumetric refinement within a unified cross-domain design. By explicitly coupling learned generative priors with cone-beam imaging geometry, the proposed method addresses the intrinsic ill-posedness of short-arc reconstruction more effectively than conventional analytic reconstruction and the compared learning-based baselines. The expanded evaluation across GYN HDR brachytherapy CT, abdominal liver 4DCT, and H&N CBCT further indicates that the framework is robust to substantial variation in anatomy, motion pattern, and clinical workflow. These findings support PCGA-Net as a promising strategy for producing anatomically faithful volumetric images from incomplete angular measurements in constrained image-guided therapeutic settings. The primary learned-method comparisons used matched patient-specific adaptation conditions. The population-only and fully adapted configurations are reported separately in table 5, and the H&N longitudinal analysis in table 6 quantifies the dependence on the number of prior fractions. These results distinguish the reconstruction capability of the population-pretrained model from the additional benefit of patient-specific information. Validation on independent raw projection data and broader acquisition settings remains necessary.

title: Prospective feasibility study of diagnostic CT-based simulation-free palliative radiotherapy.
text: Conventional radiotherapy (RT) workflows require planning computed tomography (pCT) and treatment planning. However, these processes often take several days, leading to delays in RT initiation. Simulation-free radiotherapy (SFRT), which uses diagnostic CT (dCT) instead of pCT for treatment planning, may reduce the time from consultation-to-treatment delivery. However, the number of prospective studies conducted in Japan remains limited. This study prospectively evaluated the feasibility of SFRT in Japan. A single-center, single-arm prospective study (UMIN000054721) was performed in June 2024. This study included patients with vertebral metastases who were eligible for a single 8-Gy fraction. A dCT acquired within the last 56 days, without an immobilization device, and with an identifiable lesion, was required. The primary endpoint was the RT completion rate. The secondary endpoints included time in center (TIC), time from entering the consultation room to radiation beam-off, pain response and adverse events (AEs) at 4 and 12 weeks. Cone-beam CT (CBCT) verification was mandatory for patient setup. Five patients with six vertebral sites were enrolled. The RT completion rate was 100%. The mean TIC was 45 (range: 34–54) min. At 4 weeks, 25% of the patients presented with complete and partial pain responses. At 12 weeks, the complete response rate was 33%. None of the patients developed acute AEs.

title: Prospective feasibility study of diagnostic CT-based simulation-free palliative radiotherapy.
text: With appropriate patient selection and CBCT-guided verification, SFRT was feasible and safely implemented at a Japanese community hospital. Clinical trial registration: UMIN-CTR: UMIN000054721 Keywords: simulation-free radiotherapy, diagnostic CT, palliative radiotherapy, bone metastases, workflow efficiency

title: Prospective feasibility study of diagnostic CT-based simulation-free palliative radiotherapy.
text: Palliative radiotherapy (RT) accounts for approximately half of all radiation treatments and plays an important role in achieving pain relief and local symptom control in patients with advanced cancer [1]. Bone metastases are a major cause of pain, impaired mobility and decline in performing activities of daily living, for which RT is widely used to achieve pain palliation and improve quality of life [2]. Bone metastases are among the most common indications of palliative RT. In particular, spinal metastases require the rapid delivery of RT because they carry additional risks of pain progression (PP), pathological fracture and neurological compromise. Conventional RT workflows require planning computed tomography (pCT) scan, body marking and subsequent treatment preparation. However, these processes often take several days, leading to delays in RT initiation [3]. Simulation-free radiotherapy (SFRT), which uses diagnostic CT (dCT) instead of pCT for treatment preparation, can reduce the time from consultation-to-treatment delivery while maintaining the quality of care. International clinical reports on SFRT have been increasing [4–7].

title: Prospective feasibility study of diagnostic CT-based simulation-free palliative radiotherapy.
text: However, to the best of our knowledge, no prospective clinical reports on SFRT have been published in Japan, and the feasibility of SFRT in Japanese clinical practice remains unclear. The current study aimed to prospectively evaluate the feasibility of implementing dCT-based SFRT in a Japanese community hospital. To ensure the dosimetric validity of using dCT data for treatment planning, the Hounsfield unit (HU) values corresponding to known electron densities (ED) were compared across all five CT scanners at our institution prior to clinical implementation. In addition, this study also discussed the practical challenges associated with implementing SFRT in the Japanese clinical setting.

title: Prospective feasibility study of diagnostic CT-based simulation-free palliative radiotherapy.
section: MATERIALS AND METHODS > Study design and patients
text: A single-center, single-arm prospective interventional study (UMIN-CTR: UMIN000054721) was conducted at our institution on 20 June 2024, after it was approved by the Institutional Review Board (approval no. 828) on the same day. The planned sample size was five patients. All patients provided a written informed consent prior to participation, and the study was conducted according to the principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.

title: Prospective feasibility study of diagnostic CT-based simulation-free palliative radiotherapy.
text: The current study was limited to vertebral metastases and did not include nonvertebral nor nonbone metastases because vertebral metastases often allow therapy to be delivered with simple radiation beam arrangements. Patients who had a histologically confirmed malignancy and provided a written informed consent for palliative RT for vertebral bone metastases were eligible. The additional inclusion criteria were patients aged ≥18 years and those who could lie still in the supine position. A dCT acquired at our institution within the last 56 days, without a corset or other external device, and with the target lesion clearly identifiable, was required. Patients also needed to be eligible to receive a single 8-Gy fraction. Patients with a previous history of RT to the treatment site or with a contraindication to RT, those who were pregnant, and those with severe psychiatric disorders were also excluded from the study.

title: Prospective feasibility study of diagnostic CT-based simulation-free palliative radiotherapy.
section: MATERIALS AND METHODS > Comparison between CT scanners
text: Prior to the start of the current clinical trial, we evaluated five CT scanners (four CT scanners and one PET-CT scanner) at our institution, excluding our pCT scanner, using an electron density phantom (Model 062M, Sun Nuclear Corporation, Melbourne, FL, USA). We measured HU values on the phantom—which has known ED ranging from low to high—using both the pCT scanner and the other CT scanners, and calculated the differences between them.

title: Prospective feasibility study of diagnostic CT-based simulation-free palliative radiotherapy.
section: MATERIALS AND METHODS > Treatment procedure > Radiotherapy planning
text: Treatment planning was performed using Pinnacle version 9.10 (Philips, Amsterdam, the Netherlands). The dCT images were imported into the planning system, and the planning target volume (PTV) was contoured. Contouring of the clinical target volume (CTV) was not mandatory. When CTV delineation was performed, the vertebral body containing the lesion was generally defined as the CTV. Alternatively, it was also permissible to create a PTV that included the target vertebral body and one adjacent vertebral body above and below it within the rectangular treatment field, without creating a CTV. The margins from the CTV to the PTV and from the PTV to the field edges were individually determined by the radiation oncologist, typically within 5–10 mm, considering lesion location, proximity to the spinal cord and patient anatomy. The dose reference point was placed at the isocenter or at an appropriate point within the spinal canal. A single 8-Gy fraction was prescribed to achieve a D90 of ≥8 Gy for the PTV while limiting the maximum dose to ≤115% (9.2 Gy). Fractionated irradiation was not permitted. If the maximum dose exceeded 9.2 Gy, a high-dose volume (V9.2 Gy) of <2 cm3 was considered acceptable. Patients were treated with anteroposterior–posteroanterior (AP/PA) parallel-opposed pairs or a direct PA field. Advanced RT techniques, such as intensity-modulated radiotherapy (IMRT), volumetric-modulated arc therapy (VMAT) and stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT), were not allowed.

title: Prospective feasibility study of diagnostic CT-based simulation-free palliative radiotherapy.
text: Figure 1 shows the trial schema. Prior to the initial consultation, patient eligibility was reviewed using data from the electronic medical record. If the patient met all the eligibility criteria, the RT plan was created using dCT instead of pCT. On the day of the visit, the patient had a clinical consultation and provided consent to participate in the study. If the patients declined consent, they would receive standard palliative RT at our institution, including acquisition of pCT. After obtaining informed consent and enrollment, patients were set up in the treatment room without body marking. Because the dCT couch differs from the treatment couch, a memory foam mattress was used during setup to reproduce the patient’s body contour and positioning as observed on the dCT (Fig. 2). Cone-beam CT (CBCT) image verification was mandatory for setup. The radiation oncologist and radiation therapist verified the setup together. SFRT was discontinued if CBCT images revealed that the target lesion no longer fit within the PTV due to deformation or enlargement of the target, or if there was a significant change in the body contour, and the standard RT workflow was followed. Final eligibility was determined at the discretion of the treating radiation oncologist, prioritizing treatment safety and dosimetric validity. After verification, treatment was delivered using the dCT plan.

title: Prospective feasibility study of diagnostic CT-based simulation-free palliative radiotherapy.
section: MATERIALS AND METHODS > Endpoints and assessments
text: The primary endpoint was the RT completion rate. The secondary endpoints included (i) time in center (TIC), defined as the time from entering the consultation room to radiation beam-off, (ii) pain response and (iii) adverse events (AEs), assessed at 4 and 12 weeks. Pain response was assessed at 4 and 12 weeks using the Numerical Rating Scale and the International Consensus Pain Response Endpoints [8]. The worst pain score within the last 3 days before each assessment, as self-reported by the patient, was used for analysis. AEs were graded according to the Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0 [9].

title: Prospective feasibility study of diagnostic CT-based simulation-free palliative radiotherapy.
text: Owing to the feasibility design, the sample size was fixed at five patients. All statistical analyses were descriptive, and neither group comparisons nor hypothesis testing was conducted. Continuous variables were reported as means and medians (range), and categorical variables were expressed as counts and percentages.

title: Prospective feasibility study of diagnostic CT-based simulation-free palliative radiotherapy.
section: RESULT > Comparison of HU values across CT scanners
text: Across all five dCT scanners, HU values corresponding to known ED closely matched the pCT reference values, except in the high-HU region. Low- to mid-density tissues (fat, water and muscle) showed a difference of 6.2 HU between dCT and pCT (−73.2 vs. −67 HU). In contrast, high-density tissues, such as the cortical bone, had a larger difference (49.6 HU) between dCT and pCT (1337.6 vs. 1288 HU), corresponding to ~3.9% of the reference values. This difference could have a minimal impact on dose calculation. Table 1 summarizes the comparison of HU values across CT scanners.

title: Prospective feasibility study of diagnostic CT-based simulation-free palliative radiotherapy.
text: The target accrual was reached on 18 September 2024. During the study period, no patients declined SFRT after providing informed consent. The median follow-up period was 12 (range: 4–12) months. Table 2 shows the characteristics of the patients. Five patients with six vertebral metastatic sites were enrolled in this study. The median age was 72 (range: 47–83) years, and four were men. The primary tumors were lung cancer in three patients and renal cell carcinoma in two.

title: Prospective feasibility study of diagnostic CT-based simulation-free palliative radiotherapy.
text: Treatment planning was successfully completed in all five patients with six treatment sites. CBCT-based alignment revealed no setup errors requiring treatment plan modification. All plans were delivered without replanning or protocol deviations. Consequently, the RT completion rate was 100%. Table 3 presents the clinical outcomes. During the study period (20 June 2024 to 18 September 2024), RT was performed for 20 lesions in 16 patients with vertebral metastases and spinal dissemination that were considered potentially eligible for this workflow. Of these, 12 lesions in 9 patients received conventional RT, 2 lesions in 2 patients received SBRT, and 6 lesions in 5 patients received SFRT, with SFRT accounting for 30% of all cases.

title: Prospective feasibility study of diagnostic CT-based simulation-free palliative radiotherapy.
text: All patients completed the SFRT from the initial consultation to irradiation within a single day. The average TIC was 45 (range: 34–54) min. The average informed consent time was 21.75 (range: 17–27; unavailable for Study 3) min. In addition, retrospective review showed that the median interval from referral by the primary physician to consultation in the radiation oncology department was 8 (range: 1–28) days. The evaluation of pain response excluded one patient who had no pain at baseline, and one patient died during follow-up. Hence, pain responses were evaluable in four patients at 4 weeks and in three patients at 12 weeks after treatment. At 4 weeks, the complete pain response (CR) rate was 25% (1/4), and the partial pain response (PR) rate was 25% (1/4). 25% (1/4) and 25% (1/4) of patients presented with PP and indeterminate responses (IR), respectively. At 12 weeks, the CR rate was 33% (1/3), and 67% (2/3) of the patients exhibited IR. None of the patients had PR or PP. No acute or late AEs were observed during the follow-up period. Although the planned observation period was 12 weeks, three patients were followed-up for up to 56 (range: 17–56) weeks as part of routine clinical care. Pain responses and toxicity profiles are summarized in Table 3.

title: Prospective feasibility study of diagnostic CT-based simulation-free palliative radiotherapy.
text: This prospective feasibility study showed that SFRT could be safely implemented in a Japanese community hospital, with all patients completing treatment without acute toxicities. Moreover, the entire workflow—from the initial consultation to irradiation—was successfully completed within a single day. Based on these findings, SFRT may be a practical and time-efficient alternative to conventional simulation-based workflows in routine palliative RT. To the best of our knowledge, this study provides the first prospective evidence supporting the clinical implementation of SFRT in Japan.

title: Prospective feasibility study of diagnostic CT-based simulation-free palliative radiotherapy.
text: The current study evaluated HU values corresponding to known ED across all five dCT scanners and the pCT at our institution. Results showed that the curves differed by only ~3.9% even in high-HU regions and high-density bones, such as the cortical bone, resulting in minimal impact on dose calculation. Previous studies have shown that retrospective recalculations comparing dCT and pCT-based plans (evaluated using PTV V95%, CTV V95% and V50%) revealed no clinically unacceptable dosimetric differences [10, 11]. Moreover, recalculations using the CBCT anatomy acquired during treatment showed that differences in PTV V95% generally ranged from −2% to 2.5% [4], indicating that an adequate target coverage can be achieved. Taken together, these findings support the dosimetric and geometric validity of SFRT. This study selected vertebral metastases as the treatment indication. Vertebral metastases provide geometrically and anatomically stable structures that ensure reproducible setup and allow treatment delivery with simple radiation beam arrangements. This selection is consistent with implementation guidance [12], which recommends anatomically stable sites such as the thoracic and lumbar spine for the initial SFRT implementation.

title: Prospective feasibility study of diagnostic CT-based simulation-free palliative radiotherapy.
text: Previous reports from international institutions have described the real-world clinical implementation of SFRT. In the randomized DART trial [6], dCT-based radiation planning reduced the total time spent in the cancer center on the first day of treatment—from the first radiation appointment to completion of the first fraction—compared with conventional pCT-based workflows, without compromising plan deliverability or quality and without negative effects on the patient’s perception of acceptability. In addition, Schuler et al. reported their single-institution retrospective experience of 1000 SFRT cases, referred to as the SFRT-1000 cohort [7], in which clinically acceptable toxicity profiles were observed for palliative RT, including the IMRT and VMAT techniques. Moreover, Australian real-world reports have revealed that SFRT is feasible in resource-limited healthcare settings—particularly in rural and underserved areas [13]. These findings suggest that the SFRT workflow can be stably implemented in routine clinical practice.

title: Prospective feasibility study of diagnostic CT-based simulation-free palliative radiotherapy.
text: The workflow in this study is characterized by its ability to shorten the time from consultation-to-treatment delivery. In fact, the concept of same-day consultation, planning and irradiation has existed internationally since the 1990s [14]. In recent years, rapid-access models, such as the FAST-METS trial, have implemented a rapid palliative workflow using dCT for pre-planning, with subsequent on-couch target and plan adaptation based on CBCT, thereby enabling same-day irradiation [15]. In this context, there has been an international movement that aimed to improve overall efficiency and reduce delays in palliative RT [16]. Our study contributes to this movement by providing prospective evidence from a real-world community setting in Japan.

title: Prospective feasibility study of diagnostic CT-based simulation-free palliative radiotherapy.
text: In this study, same-day irradiation was feasible for all patients, with the TIC limited to ~45 min. Three workflow-related factors, supported by multidisciplinary collaboration, may have contributed to enabling same-day irradiation. First, the eligibility criteria were strictly applied, and only patients who could lie still in the supine position were included based on a review of data from the electronic medical record. For example, patients whose dCT images were acquired in the lateral position due to severe pain or those with dCT images whose quality was compromised due to motion artifacts were excluded. Second, radiation therapists coordinated irradiation schedules with medical consultation appointments, allowing patients to proceed directly to irradiation with minimal waiting time. Third, radiation oncology nursing staff reviewed the electronic medical records in advance to assess pain severity and the need for rescue medication. The patients who were anticipated to require rescue medication were contacted via telephone and instructed to bring their medications to ensure adequate pain control during irradiation. Furthermore, although same-day irradiation can be achieved within conventional pCT-based workflows, CT simulation and skin marking are typically required. In contrast, our SFRT approach eliminates both steps, thereby reducing the physical and operational burden of both patients and medical staff.

title: Prospective feasibility study of diagnostic CT-based simulation-free palliative radiotherapy.
text: Moreover, several clinical guidelines and real-world evidence support the use of single-fraction RT for painful bone metastases and metastatic spinal cord compression [17–19]. Our same-day SFRT workflow is consistent with these recommendations.

title: Prospective feasibility study of diagnostic CT-based simulation-free palliative radiotherapy.
text: To promote SFRT in Japan, it is necessary to consider the unique characteristics of the Japanese healthcare delivery system. In rural areas, RT facilities are limited, and some patients are unable to access RT. Because SFRT reduces the number of required patient visits and alleviates the workload of medical staff, it has the potential to increase access to RT. In contrast, urban areas generally have a relatively large number of RT facilities, and many patients already receive RT. Therefore, unlike in rural areas, we do not expect the introduction of SFRT to increase the number of patients undergoing RT. However, because SFRT can reduce patient waiting times and improve treatment efficiency, its implementation may still offer certain advantages. Furthermore, regional hospitals typically have fewer staff members, resulting in simple SFRT workflows and relatively straightforward information sharing across departments. In contrast, large hospitals often involve many staff members in RT, making workflows more complex and potentially delaying information sharing, which may hinder the implementation of SFRT. Regardless of hospital size, SFRT requires workflows that differ substantially from those used in conventional RT based on pCT, and the optimal workflow is likely to vary across institutions. We believe that developing facility-specific workflows and reviewing them regularly will facilitate smoother implementation of SFRT.

title: Prospective feasibility study of diagnostic CT-based simulation-free palliative radiotherapy.
text: The current study has four main limitations. First, this study had a small sample size and a short follow-up period. Consequently, long-term clinical outcomes—such as late pain relief and reirradiation rates—could not be adequately evaluated. Second, the irradiation technique was restricted to conventional AP/PA parallel-opposed fields. More recently, SFRT workflows incorporating advanced techniques such as IMRT/VMAT and on-couch adaptive RT have been reported, and these workflows have also been explored in the SBRT setting [11, 15, 20]. This study was an early-phase investigation into the feasibility of implementing this approach in real-world clinical practice in Japan for palliative spinal irradiation. In addition, the expansion to more advanced irradiation techniques remains an area for future research. Third, this was a single-institution study. The successful implementation may depend on institution-specific equipment and staffing. Therefore, the findings should be interpreted with caution when considering their generalizability. In this study, SFRT was performed using dCT images acquired within the same institution; thus, it remains unclear whether SFRT can be implemented using imaging data obtained from external institutions.

title: Prospective feasibility study of diagnostic CT-based simulation-free palliative radiotherapy.
text: Given the characteristics of the treatment planning system, we consider the following to be essential requirements for the safe and reliable implementation of SFRT using CT data from other institutions: (i) axial CT images without reconstruction, (ii) a field of view (FOV) encompassing the entire beam path and (iii) continuous DICOM image data with a slice thickness of ≤5 mm to ensure the accuracy of image-guided radiotherapy. Although the use of the same CT vendor or image acquisition under the same tube voltage may facilitate implementation without major technical difficulties, we do not consider these to be mandatory requirements. Fourth, although TIC was evaluated using the time from entering the consultation room to radiation beam-off, a detailed breakdown of TIC, such as setup time and room in/out time, was not prospectively recorded. Therefore, a detailed phase-by-phase analysis was not performed. Future studies including more detailed workflow data may help identify factors contributing to workflow efficiency in SFRT. In conclusion, by combining appropriate patient selection and CBCT-guided verification, SFRT was feasible and safely implemented at a Japanese community hospital. Notably, a same-day consultation-to-treatment workflow could be achieved in routine clinical practice. In the future, continued prospective observational implementation with increased case numbers will be required to validate the clinical value and potential indications of this workflow.
