text: Among them, xti represents the noisy image produced by the diffusion model, which is mathematically defined by the formula in the dashed box. x1 represents the generated fake image, that is, x1(xti) in the Figure 2. Eqϕi(xti,xi)[∥xti−xi∥2] is the mean value of the distance between the two, which is used to make the diffusion process tend to optimal transport. qϕi(xti,x1) can be expressed as: That is, qϕi(xti,x1) denotes the joint distribution of the generated fake image and the conditional distribution, and qϕi(x1) represents the distribution of the generated fake image. The discriminator estimates the probability that the fake image belongs to the target domain. The latter term of the Schrödinger bridge loss represents the information entropy of the probability of the fake image, and the entropy can be inferred indirectly from the relationship between cross‐entropy and Kullback‐Leibler (KL) divergence, since the cross‐entropy is equal to the entropy plus the KL divergence.

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: Our method performs the diffusion process in the intermediate feature space rather than directly on the image. It leverages the characteristics of deep features while reducing computational burden and improving semantic alignment across time steps. Specifically, we utilize a bidirectional stochastic framework, consisting of a forward generator qϕf(x1∣xti) and a backward generator qϕb(xti∣x1) both parameterized by neural networks. The network consists of multiple residual blocks, with features obtained from the intermediate blocks contributing to the diffusion process. During training, a noisy latent variable xti is generated at a randomly sampled time step ti using a predefined noise schedule applied to intermediate features. The forward generator learns to predict the clean representation x1, while the backward generator reconstructs xti from x1, forming a time‐symmetric stochastic process. This dual generator framework is optimized using adversarial training objectives, combined with a bidirectional consistency constraint that ensures path coherence between the forward and backward trajectories in feature space. Together, this design enforces smooth transitions across diffusion steps and enhances the reconstruction fidelity of the model.

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: In addition, we adopt a Fourier convolution frequency domain processing module. This module augments the existing spatial domain convolution feature learning with Fourier convolution frequency domain feature learning. By doing so, it enhances the network model's ability to learn discriminative features, thereby further improving the accuracy of MRI reconstruction.

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: Fourier convolution applies convolution operations to the feature map in the Fourier domain. After applying the Fourier transform and before performing the inverse transform back to the spatial domain, this approach facilitates the encoding of detailed information from different frequency domain components of the image, thereby enhancing feature extraction during the reconstruction process. Specifically, we present a diffusion Fourier residual generative network, and the structure of the generative model qϕ describing the evolution of the Schrödinger Bridge distribution path is shown in Figure 3. In the proposed architecture, the input feature maps are first passed through a 2D Fourier transform (FFT) to convert spatial features into frequency domain representations. These frequency features are then separated into real and imaginary components and processed using two parallel convolutional branches with shared or synchronized parameters. After convolution, the real and imaginary components are recombined into complex form, followed by an inverse Fourier transform (IFFT) to map features back to the spatial domain. A skip connection from the input feature is added to the output of the IFFT operation to form the Fourier residual block.

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: By adding noise embedding to the features of the Fourier residual at each time step, we form a conditional Fourier residual block. The main difference between the conditional Fourier residual block and the Fourier residual lies in the additional embedding, which exists before the inverse transformation. Specifically, a time‐dependent noise embedding vector is generated and passed through a small MLP to produce scale and shift parameters. These parameters are used to modulate the frequency features via affine transformation before the IFFT step, allowing the model to adaptively adjust feature importance at different diffusion stages. This mechanism enables the conditional Fourier residual blocks to model dynamic transformations across the diffusion trajectory, enhancing the model's capacity to preserve fine‐grained frequency components critical for high‐fidelity MRI reconstruction.

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: The proposed model was trained on an RTX A6000 (48GB) GPU. We employed the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 0.0002, and set the hyperparameters β1=0.5 and β2=0.999 to control the first and second moment estimates, respectively.

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: In this study, we collected the MRI of 22S‐duration imaging and full‐duration MRI of 31 fractional MRI scans from 14 patients. Among them, the MRI of 23 fractional scans were selected as the training set, and the MRI of 8 fractional scans were selected as the test set. The training set and test set are completely separated by patient identity, no overlapping patients exist across two subsets (23 patient fractional scans for training, 8 for testing). The predicted results on the test set were quantitatively and qualitatively compared with the state‐of‐the‐art methods to accurately evaluate the model's performance.

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: In this study, four quantitative indicators, namely MAE (Mean Absolute Error), RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error), SSIM (Structural Similarity Index Measure), and PSNR (Peak Signal‐to‐Noise Ratio), were adopted to measure the performance of the MR reconstruction model on the test set. All four quantitative metrics (MAE/RMSE/PSNR/SSIM) are computed based on full 3D volumetric images instead of randomly selected single slices. Specifically, for the data of each case in the test set, the predicted results of MR reconstruction were compared with the fully imaged data, and the quantitative indicators were calculated in the following way. MAE is a commonly used metric in statistics and machine learning to evaluate the performance of a predictive model. MAE measures the average magnitude of the errors between the predicted values and the actual values, without considering the direction of the errors. It is calculated by taking the average of the absolute differences between the predicted and actual values for a set of data points. Mathematically, if we have n data points, with predicted values ypred,i and actual values ytrue,i, the MAE is calculated as follows: A lower MAE value indicates a better performance of the model, as it means that the average difference between the predicted and actual values is small.

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: RMSE measures the square root of the average of the squared differences between the predicted values and the actual values. It takes into account both the magnitude and the direction of the errors. By squaring the differences, larger errors are given more weight than smaller ones, which makes RMSE more sensitive to outliers. Mathematically, for a set of (n) data points with predicted values (ypred,i) and actual values (ytrue,i), the RMSE is calculated as follows: Similar to MAE, a lower RMSE value implies a better‐performing model. It provides a measure of the typical deviation of the predicted values from the actual values, and is often used in comparing different models or in evaluating the performance of a model over time. PSNR is defined as the ratio of the maximum possible power of a signal to the power of the noise that affects the signal. The formula for calculating PSNR is as follows: where MAXI is the maximum possible pixel value in the image, and MSE is the Mean Squared Error between the original image (I) and the reconstructed image (K), which is calculated as: where m and n are the dimensions of the image. A higher PSNR value indicates a better quality of the reconstructed or compressed image, meaning that the processed image is more similar to the original. SSIM is a metric used to assess the similarity between two images, primarily focusing on the structural information of the images. Mathematically, the SSIM between two images I and K is calculated as follows:

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: where μI and μK are the means of images I and K respectively, σI and σK are the standard deviations of images I and K respectively, σIK is the covariance between I and K, and C1 and C2 are small constants used to avoid instability in the calculation when the denominators are close to zero. The value of SSIM ranges from ‐1 to 1. A value of 1 indicates that the two images are identical, while a value of 0 indicates that the images are completely different. In general, the higher the SSIM value, the more similar the two images are in terms of their structural characteristics.

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: In this study, the state‐of‐the‐art paired image translation method, Refusion, 24 and the unpaired image translation methods, CycleGAN 17 and CSGAN, 25 were selected as the comparative methods. The Refusion model uses the diffusion model as the basic architecture for paired image translation training. The CycleGAN model, a widely‐used unpaired image translation method, uses the generative adversarial network (GAN) as the basic architecture for unpaired image translation. Building upon CycleGAN model, CSGAN model employs the guidance of body mask and channel‐wise attention to further improve the unpaired image‐to‐image translation task.

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: Table 1 shows the quantitative comparison results between the proposed FSBD method and state‐of‐the‐art methods. The 22S‐duration baseline is used to quantify the discrepancy between the original low‐quality images captured under 22S‐duration imaging and high‐quality images acquired via full‐duration imaging. The FULL‐Fraction baseline represents the metric performance between two full‐quality standard MR images from different fractions of the same patient, which serves as clinical reference standard We note that this value is only used to provide the index fluctuation range derived from high‐quality complete images acquired in multiple fractions for the same patient, assisting in intuitively distinguishing image variations caused by the rapid reconstruction algorithm from inherent deformation deviations among different fractions. To ensure fair comparison, these image pairs of 22S‐duration and full‐duration MRI were first registered to correct for global positioning shifts before computing voxel‐wise metrics. After this preprocessing step, the reconstructed images generated by all MR reconstruction methods were spatially aligned to the full‐duration reference images, guaranteeing consistent spatial correspondence between the input data and ground‐truth labels across all methods.

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: Refusion utilizes the paired training strategy. The training data for the Refusion model consists of registered image pairs from two MRI sets (the 22S‐duration and full‐duration MRI), and each pair of images has a clear corresponding relationship. Since the registered image pair provides explicit supervision information, the Refusion model can directly learn the mapping from the source image (22S‐duration MRI) to the target image (full‐duration MRI). In comparison, CycleGAN, CSGAN and our FSBD adopt unpaired training to lower the dependency on perfectly matched image pairs.

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: As shown in Table 1, the Refusion model converged on the training set obtained MAE, RMSE, PSNR, and SSIM values of 99.95, 149.16, 26.77, and 0.870 respectively on the test set. Different from the paired training method, CycleGAN adopts an unpaired method for model training. The training dataset consists of two image sets (the 22S‐duration and full‐duration MRI), but there is no explicit correspondence between these images. Through unpaired training strategy, CycleGAN learns the latent mapping relationship between the two sets. The CycleGAN model converged on the training set obtained MAE, RMSE, PSNR, and SSIM values of 112.92, 172.55, 25.82, and 0.881 respectively on the test set, and the numerical indicators are inferior to those of the Refusion model. Based on the CycleGAN model, CSGAN model introduces the guidance of body mask to enhance the learning of unpaired image‐to‐image translation. The CSGAN model outperforms CycleGAN model by achieving the MAE, RMSE, PSNR, and SSIM values of 103.04, 162.29, 26.34, and 0.878 respectively.

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: The proposed FSBD model in this study employs the diffusion model as the basic architecture and adopts the unpaired training strategy. On the test set, FSBD obtained MAE, RMSE, PSNR, and SSIM values of 86.00, 123.42, 28.44, and 0.885 respectively. These results significantly outperform state‐of‐the‐art models (Refusion, CycleGAN and CSGAN). Above quantitative results effectively show that the proposed FSBD model, with the help of Schrödinger bridge diffusion model in Fourier frequency domain, can learn the best translation function from the 22S‐duration MRI set to the full MRI set among these state‐of‐the‐art methods, even in an unpaired training setting.

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: Figure 4 shows qualitative comparison of the visualization results of Refusion, CycleGAN, CSGAN and the proposed FSBD model. As illustrated in Figure 4, the CycleGAN and CSGAN model cannot reconstruct the internal anatomical structural details of the MRI, and many regions are incorrectly reconstructed as background regions. The Refusion model achieves better MRI reconstruction performance by restoring more detailed anatomical structure. However, it still struggles to produce consistent reconstruction results for internal structures. Nevertheless, the proposed FSBD model can accurately restore most of the internal anatomical structures. For example, for the zoom‐in organs shown in Figure 4, the CycleGAN, CSGAN and Refusion model fail to reconstruct the organ structure details. However, our proposed FSBD model accurately and consistently reconstructs the anatomical structure details. The error maps between the reconstructed MRI and full‐duration MRI are also shown in the Figure 4. Obviously, the error maps of internal organs generated by our FSBD model are the best, with closer mean error to zero, significantly smaller dispersion and fewer obvious outliers. These qualitative results further indicate the superiority of the proposed FSBD model. From above quantitative and qualitative comparison results, it is evident that the proposed model achieves significantly better MRI reconstruction results than existing state‐of‐the‐art methods, effectively demonstrating its superiority.

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: In terms of the inference speed, with the proposed FSBD model, accurate MR reconstruction results can be obtained in 20 s with the 22S‐duration MRI as input. The whole imaging time is about 42 s (22 seconds for MR imaging and 20 seconds for MR reconstruction). In this way, the whole processing time is significantly reduced from 3 min to less than one minute. As a result, the proposed method can significantly reduce scan time to enhance the patient experience, alleviating discomfort and physical fatigue for children, the elderly, and patients with claustrophobia. Additionally, it minimizes image artifacts caused by involuntary movements such as breathing and heartbeat, thereby reducing the need for repeat scans, improving examination efficiency, and optimizing clinical workflows.

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: Substituting the traditional T2‐weighted imaging which takes 360 s with the optimized T1‐weighted protocols lasting for only 120 s has effectively addressed the problem of rapid magnetic resonance (MR) imaging. Meanwhile, it ensures the image quality required for accurate contouring. These improvements not only increases patients' willingness to cooperate but also alleviates the anatomical changes that occur during the fractionated treatment. Additionally, this approach helps to reduce the burden on clinical resources, as indicated in references. 5 , 6 , 8 This study presents the first implementation of sub‐one‐minute rapid magnetic resonance (MR) imaging (< 1 min) in an MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy (ART) workflow. This implementation achieves an over 80% reduction in scan time compared to standard MR sequences. This advancement renders the image acquisition phase of MR‐guided ART more time‐efficient than conventional cone‐beam computed tomography (CBCT) or CT‐guided ART systems, effectively addressing the long‐standing limitation of prolonged MR scan times in traditional MR‐guided radiotherapy. 4 , 26

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: Although specific optimizations for the Unity MR linear accelerator have not been reported, the successful application of related technologies in similar MRI reconstruction problems 10 , 11 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 indicates that U‐Net is well‐suited for single‐frame processing of MRI sequences, cascaded CNNs are suitable for processing dynamic sequences, and GAN‐based k‐space super‐resolution can serve as a future development direction. In contrast to previously reported rapid MR techniques, which primarily focuses on MR simulation or diagnostic applications, 26 this work pioneers the integration of ultrafast MR imaging of Unity MR linear accelerator into online ART workflows. Although 22s undersampled and full‐length scans were acquired in the identical fraction, minor intra‐scan organ deformation still exists. Unpaired training helps the model learn robust anatomical transformation rather than simply memorizing pixel‐wise average mapping from paired data.

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: Methodologically, this study introduces a novel framework that combines Schrödinger Bridge theory with diffusion models to address the inherent challenges of ultrafast MR imaging, particularly noise amplification and resolution degradation caused by limited scan time. Compared to conventional denoising and image enhancement technique, such as compressed sensing, sparse reconstruction, and generative adversarial networks (GANs) 18 , 19 , 26 ), the proposed model demonstrates obvious advantages. The diffusion model's iterative noise addition/removal process enables precise learning of MRI noise distributions. Schrödinger Bridge theory optimizes the transformation pathway via optimal transport constraints, ensuring stable denoising without mode collapse or over‐smoothing observed in traditional approaches.

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: The numerical metrics demonstrate that the proposed FSBD model achieves obviously better results than current Refusion, CycleGAN and CSGAN model. Concretely, the FSBD model achieves 86.00 MAE, 123.42 RMSE, 28.44 PSNR and 0.885 SSIM. The MAE and RMSE value measures the reconstruction accuracy. Our proposed FSBD model significantly reduces the reconstruction error of Refusion, resulting in evident reduction of 13.95 MAE and 25.74 RMSE. For the comparison with CycleGAN model, FSBD also achieves clear reduction of 26.92 MAE and 49.13 RMSE. Similar results can be observed for the comparison between the CSGAN and FSBD model. Moreover, the PSNR and SSIM value reflect the quality of reconstructed MRI. Notably, our FSBD model also achieves the highest reconstruction image quality, outperforming Refusion by 1.67 PSNR and 0.015 SSIM. Similar results can be observed for the comparison with CycleGAN. Compared to CycleGAN, the FSBD model obtains the enhancement of 2.62 PSNR and 0.004 SSIM, while surpassing CSGAN by 2.10 dB in PSNR and 0.007 in SSIM. These quantitative results effectively demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed FSBD model. In addition, visualized comparison results clearly show the superiority of the FSBD model, by effectively reconstructing details of internal structures.

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: CycleGAN and CSGAN approximate the target distribution through the adversarial interplay between generators and discriminators, relying on adversarial loss functions. This makes their discriminators prone to overfitting or vanishing gradients, leading to mode collapse (repetitive generation of similar samples) and blurred details in the generated outputs. In contrast, the proposed FSBD method based on diffusion model iteratively model the data distribution via forward diffusion (gradually adding noise) and reverse denoising (learning the inverse process). Under the constraint of variational lower bound loss, the FSBD directly models the probability density of the data distribution, enabling more controllable generation processes that capture complex internal structures, such as textures and semantic consistency. As a result, FSBD achieves obviously better reconstruction accuracy, in terms of MAE and RMSE. The reconstruction error is largely decreased from the CycleGAN (112.92 MAE, 172.55 RMSE) and CSGAN (103.04 MAE and 162.29 RMSE), resulting in the MAE of 86.00 and RMSE of 123.42 for the proposed FSBD model. Visualized comparison shown in Figure 4 also clearly demonstrates the superiority of FSBD model by reconstructing the details of internal body tissue structures.

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: Several existing works have explored DSBM and Fourier‐constrained diffusion models for general medical image reconstruction; distinct from these architectures, our FSBD embeds dedicated Fourier convolution block tailored for Unity abdominal accelerated MRI under unpaired training setting.

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: The Refusion model follows the “noise‐to‐data” paradigm of traditional diffusion model, progressively transforming data into pure noise before reconstruction. Its prior distribution offers limited information about the target, resulting in suboptimal generation guidance. Conversely, the proposed FSBD model implements a “data‐to‐data” process, leveraging prior knowledge directly from the target distribution via discriminative feature learning in frequency domain. Moreover, traditional diffusion models start from pure Gaussian noise, requiring numerous sampling steps and function evaluations to generate high‐quality samples, thus limiting efficiency. The Schrödinger bridge model, however, constructs a direct diffusion path between two distributions—for example, transitioning from a structured distribution (e.g., degraded images) to the target (clean images). By starting closer to the target distribution, the model maintains performance with fewer evaluations, achieving high‐quality generation with fewer steps and improved sampling efficiency. As a result, the proposed FSBD model effectively preserves finer internal structural details in generated images. Concretely, the MAE and RMSE are significantly reduced from 99.95 to 86.00, 149.16 to 123.42, respectively.

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: As shown in the visualization results of Figure 4, MRI reconstruction result generated by the proposed FSBD model effectively retains the detailed anatomical structures, which is also validated by quantitative evaluation metrics. Using the proposed FSBD model, a fast MRI reconstruction method can be achieved, with the reconstruction time of only 20 s. In this way, the overall MR imaging time is significantly reduced from 3 min to 42 s. A 1‐min MR imaging duration enhances patient comfort and compliance—mitigating discomfort, motion artifacts, and examination failures, particularly among vulnerable populations (pediatric, geriatric, pain‐afflicted, or claustrophobic patients)—while improving equipment throughput. As the gold standard for soft tissue contrast and target/Organ‐at‐Risk (OAR) delineation, MR's traditional 3‐min acquisition previously constrained its utility in real‐time applications. However, 1‐min imaging, synergized with AI‐powered image registration and rapid dose optimization (achievable within minutes), enables Online Adaptive Radiotherapy (Online ART) workflows—encompassing positioning, imaging, plan adaptation, and treatment—to be completed within the patient‐tolerable 20–30‐min window. When integrated with MR‐Linac systems, this advancement facilitates seamless “imaging‐adaptation‐treatment” integration, overcoming the 3‐min bottleneck that historically prolonged procedures and elevated risks of motion‐related inaccuracies or delays.

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: We acknowledge several limitations to be addressed in subsequent work: (1) The full‐duration standard scan and the 22‐s rapid scan in this study were acquired sequentially. Although patient motion was limited within 5 mm using abdominal belt fixation, subtle positional shifts and physiological organ deformation between fractions are inherent limitations of this work. Such displacements inevitably introduce biases to the quantitative comparison of the two sets of images. (2) Clinical patient data contain inherent biases including organ deformation and slight respiratory movement, which cannot be isolated. It is difficult to accurately distinguish whether image differences originate from reconstruction algorithm errors or inherent deviations caused by patient motion. (3) Global volumetric metrics were adopted for reconstruction evaluation in this study, which may conceal local errors in targets and organs at risk. We note that global averaged indices smooth local distortion, artifacts and detail loss and fail to reflect regional image quality for radiotherapy. (4) All data originate from abdominal sites, leaving other anatomical regions unverified. (5) The current experiment is a single‐center test, and future research is needed to investigate the performance of the proposed method on multi‐center dataset. (6) Current FSBD model requires extended training (nearly 2 weeks), which suggests that the reported results may not yet represent the method's full potential.

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: Planned improvements include: (1) Contour‐guided regional quantitative evaluation: Computing separate local metrics for the target and each OAR based on delineated contours to precisely evaluate anatomical reconstruction accuracy for online adaptive radiotherapy. (2) Dataset expansion and generalization: Enriching training samples and extending the framework to diverse sequences (T1/T2‐weighted, Balanced, DWI) across multiple anatomical sites. (3) Training acceleration: Investigating more effective diffusion mechanisms or lightweight architectures to reduce computational demands. (4) Integration with auto‐segmentation: Linking enhanced MRIs to automated organ delineation to streamline entire ART workflows.

title: Frequency Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for fast MRI reconstruction in abdominal MR‐guided online adaptive radiotherapy
text: We developed an online MRI‐guided radiotherapy rapid‐scan reconstruction method based on a Schrödinger bridge diffusion model for image enhancement. This approach improves the clinical efficiency of MRI‐guided radiotherapy while ensuring high‐quality fast‐scan MRIs, specifically designed for 1.5 T MRI‐based radiotherapy systems. It significantly reduces scan time from 3 min to 42 s (22 seconds for MR imaging and 20 seconds for MR reconstruction) while maintaining high‐resolution MR imaging, thereby ensuring precise radiation delivery and good patient compliance. This breakthrough establishes a technical foundation for precision online ART implementation.

title: Clinical Outcomes and Prognostic Factors Following Routine CT-Based Image-Guided Adaptive Brachytherapy for Cervical Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
text: MRI-guided brachytherapy provides highly accurate treatment for cervical cancer but is not routinely available in many hospitals. CT-based brachytherapy offers a more accessible alternative, although long-term clinical evidence remains limited. We evaluated 237 patients with cervical cancer treated using routine CT-based image-guided adaptive brachytherapy. Despite more than half of the patients having stage III–IV disease, the 5-year local control and overall survival rates were 84.4% and 62.9%, respectively. Delivering an adequate brachytherapy dose to the tumor was associated with improved local control, while receiving at least four chemotherapy cycles and completing treatment within 56 days were associated with improved overall survival. These findings suggest that a standardized CT-based brachytherapy program can provide clinically meaningful outcomes in centers where routine MRI access is limited. Keywords: cervical cancer, CT-based IGABT, image-guided brachytherapy, local control, overall survival

title: Clinical Outcomes and Prognostic Factors Following Routine CT-Based Image-Guided Adaptive Brachytherapy for Cervical Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
text: Cervical cancer remains a major public health concern in Thailand and worldwide. In 2022, approximately 600,000 new cases were diagnosed globally, while Thailand recorded 8662 new cases and 4576 deaths in the same year [1]. Cervical cancer can be treated with surgery, radiotherapy, and systemic therapy, depending on disease stage and patient factors. For patients undergoing definitive radiotherapy, the standard approach consists of external beam radiotherapy, with concurrent cisplatin-based chemotherapy for those with locally advanced disease, followed by brachytherapy [2,3]. Brachytherapy is an essential component of this definitive regimen because it enables delivery of a high radiation dose to the primary tumor while limiting exposure to adjacent organs at risk. Consequently, the delivery of high-quality brachytherapy is a critical determinant of local control and survival outcomes [4].

title: Clinical Outcomes and Prognostic Factors Following Routine CT-Based Image-Guided Adaptive Brachytherapy for Cervical Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
text: The development of image-guided adaptive brachytherapy (IGABT) has substantially improved the precision of target delineation and dose delivery. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-guided IGABT provides superior soft-tissue contrast, enabling individualized target definition and adaptive dose optimization. Early clinical experience demonstrated the feasibility and clinical impact of MRI-guided IGABT [5]. Subsequent large multicenter studies, including Retro-EMBRACE and the prospective EMBRACE-I cohort, reported high rates of long-term local control and overall survival with acceptable rates of severe morbidity, establishing MRI-guided IGABT as a benchmark standard in well-resourced settings [6,7]. However, access to MRI during brachytherapy remains limited in many regions because of limited MRI availability and logistical constraints associated with obtaining MRI during brachytherapy procedures, with recent practice-pattern data identifying MRI access as a major barrier to routine implementation [8,9]. In this context, computed tomography (CT)-based IGABT has emerged as a practical alternative. CT-based planning enables three-dimensional dose optimization and volumetric evaluation of target coverage and organs at risk constraints. Although CT has inherent limitations in soft-tissue contrast, international consensus guidelines have been developed to standardize CT-based contouring, and clinical studies have reported promising outcomes with this approach [10,11,12,13].

title: Clinical Outcomes and Prognostic Factors Following Routine CT-Based Image-Guided Adaptive Brachytherapy for Cervical Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
text: At our institution, CT-based IGABT was introduced in 2008 and subsequently developed through the incorporation of CT-based treatment planning and transabdominal ultrasound guidance. Our previous studies demonstrated the feasibility of these image-guided approaches in routine clinical practice [14,15]. In December 2018, the installation of a dedicated CT scanner (Alexion, Canon Medical Systems, Japan) within the brachytherapy unit enabled the full integration of CT-based IGABT into our routine clinical workflow. Outcomes from the earlier implementation period between 2008 and 2018 have been reported, with a 4-year overall survival rate of 69.1% [16]. The present study evaluates clinical outcomes and prognostic factors in patients treated with definitive radiotherapy incorporating routine CT-based IGABT between January 2019 and December 2021, following the implementation of dedicated CT-based brachytherapy in our division.

title: Clinical Outcomes and Prognostic Factors Following Routine CT-Based Image-Guided Adaptive Brachytherapy for Cervical Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
section: 2. Materials and Methods > 2.1. Study Design and Population
text: This retrospective cohort study evaluated clinical outcomes following the implementation of routine CT-based IGABT in the Division of Radiation Oncology, Faculty of Medicine, Chiang Mai University. The study was reviewed by the Research Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Medicine, Chiang Mai University and was certified as exempt from ethical review (RAD-2568-0136). The requirement for written informed consent was waived by the Research Ethics Committee because the study involved retrospective analysis of anonymized clinical data. The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. All consecutive patients with cervical cancer treated with curative-intent external beam radiotherapy followed by CT-guided brachytherapy between January 2019 and December 2021 were included. Inclusion criteria were: (1) International Federation of Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) 2018 stage I–IVA cervical carcinoma; (2) treatment with definitive radiotherapy as the primary modality; (3) histology of squamous cell carcinoma, adenocarcinoma, or adenosquamous carcinoma; and (4) availability of complete clinical, treatment, and dosimetric data. Exclusion criteria included: (1) other histological subtypes; (2) evidence of distant metastatic disease at diagnosis; (3) treatment with non-standard external beam radiotherapy schedules; (4) incomplete medical records or absence of post-treatment follow-up data; or (5) prior pelvic radiotherapy or concurrent malignancies.

title: Clinical Outcomes and Prognostic Factors Following Routine CT-Based Image-Guided Adaptive Brachytherapy for Cervical Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
text: Clinical, treatment, dosimetric, and outcome data were extracted from institutional electronic medical records. Vital status and dates of death were verified using the hospital cancer registry. Local control was defined as the time from the start of radiotherapy to the date of documented local recurrence, with patients without local recurrence censored at their last documented disease assessment. Overall survival was defined as the time from the start of radiotherapy to death from any cause, with surviving patients censored at the date they were last known to be alive.

title: Clinical Outcomes and Prognostic Factors Following Routine CT-Based Image-Guided Adaptive Brachytherapy for Cervical Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
section: 2. Materials and Methods > 2.3. Treatments and Follow-Up
text: External beam radiotherapy was delivered to the pelvis at a dose of 45–50.4 Gy in 23–28 fractions, at 1.8–2.0 Gy per fraction, using either a four-field box technique or intensity-modulated radiation therapy (IMRT). Dose schedules included 45 Gy in 25 fractions, 46 Gy in 23 fractions, 50 Gy in 25 fractions, and 50.4 Gy in 28 fractions, which varied during the study period according to institutional practice at the time. The pelvic clinical target volume included the cervix, entire uterus, parametria, upper vagina, and regional pelvic lymph nodes for both conventional radiotherapy and IMRT. The treatment technique was selected at the discretion of the treating physician based on clinical requirements. Extended-field radiotherapy was delivered to patients with para-aortic nodal involvement and to those with common iliac nodal involvement or three or more involved pelvic lymph nodes. Involved lymph nodes received additional irradiation using either a simultaneous integrated boost or a sequential boost. Concurrent weekly cisplatin 40 mg/m2 or carboplatin AUC 2 was administered when clinically indicated. Induction chemotherapy was used selectively in patients with prolonged waiting times for radiotherapy, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic.

title: Clinical Outcomes and Prognostic Factors Following Routine CT-Based Image-Guided Adaptive Brachytherapy for Cervical Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
section: 2. Materials and Methods > 2.3. Treatments and Follow-Up
text: High-dose-rate CT-based IGABT was delivered in four fractions, with a prescribed dose of 7 Gy per fraction, following external beam radiotherapy. Intracavitary applicators were used either alone or in combination with interstitial needles (hybrid intracavitary/interstitial [IC/IS] technique), depending on tumor extent and anatomical geometry. Applicator insertion was performed under transabdominal ultrasound guidance using tandem–ovoid, tandem–ring, or tandem–cylinder applicators. A hybrid IC/IS approach was considered for patients with residual parametrial involvement or asymmetric disease, based on physician judgment. The brachytherapy approach was assessed at each fraction and could be adapted according to tumor response and anatomical findings. After each applicator insertion, CT-based contouring of the high-risk clinical target volume (HR-CTV) and organs at risk, including the bladder, rectum, and sigmoid colon, was performed in accordance with established international recommendations for three-dimensional image-guided cervical brachytherapy and CT-based contouring guidance [10,17,18,19]. The HR-CTV encompassed the entire cervix and residual macroscopic tumor at the time of brachytherapy. The intermediate-risk clinical target volume (IR-CTV) was not routinely delineated. Treatment planning and optimization were based on dose–volume histogram parameters.

title: Clinical Outcomes and Prognostic Factors Following Routine CT-Based Image-Guided Adaptive Brachytherapy for Cervical Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
section: 2. Materials and Methods > 2.3. Treatments and Follow-Up
text: External beam radiotherapy and brachytherapy doses were summed using the equivalent dose in 2-Gy fractions (EQD2) concept, applying α/β ratios of 10 Gy for tumor tissue and 3 Gy for late-responding normal tissues. Brachytherapy plans were optimized to achieve adequate target coverage while respecting organs-at-risk dose constraints. A cumulative HR-CTV dose covering 90% of the target volume (HR-CTV D90) was pursued, with further dose escalation when feasible. If an HR-CTV D90 of 85 Gy EQD2 could not be achieved, a cumulative dose of ≥80 Gy EQD2 was considered acceptable. After completion of definitive radiotherapy, patients were scheduled for follow-up at six weeks, then every three months for the first year, every four months in the second year, every six months in the third and fourth years, and annually thereafter. Treatment response was assessed at the six-week follow-up based on clinical examination, with imaging performed when clinically indicated.

title: Clinical Outcomes and Prognostic Factors Following Routine CT-Based Image-Guided Adaptive Brachytherapy for Cervical Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
text: Descriptive statistics were used to summarize baseline and treatment characteristics. Local control and overall survival were estimated using the Kaplan–Meier method, and differences between groups were assessed using the log-rank test. As an additional analysis, the cumulative incidence of local recurrence was estimated with death without prior local recurrence treated as a competing event. Prognostic factors were evaluated using univariable and multivariable Cox proportional hazards regression, reporting hazard ratios (HRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Variables were selected a priori for inclusion in the multivariable models based on clinical relevance and included age group, stage grouping, histology, tumor size, HR-CTV dose, chemotherapy exposure, overall treatment time, nodal status, external beam radiotherapy technique, and induction chemotherapy. Given the limited number of local failure events, a sensitivity analysis using a reduced multivariable model was also performed, including FIGO stage, histology, HR-CTV D90, and radiotherapy technique. The associations between FIGO stage and external beam radiotherapy technique were assessed using the χ2 test. Statistical analyses were performed using Stata version 18 (StataCorp LLC, College Station, TX, USA). A two-sided p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

title: Clinical Outcomes and Prognostic Factors Following Routine CT-Based Image-Guided Adaptive Brachytherapy for Cervical Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
text: Data from 267 patients who underwent radiotherapy between 2019 and 2021 were screened for inclusion. Of these, 30 patients were excluded: 8 without cervical cancer, 7 treated in the postoperative setting, 7 with metastatic disease, 4 with missing data, 2 with ineligible histology, and 2 treated with palliative intent. A total of 237 patients were included in the final analysis. The mean age was 58.2 ± 12.8 years, and 56.9% had FIGO stage III–IV disease. Squamous cell carcinoma was the predominant histological subtype, accounting for 83.5% of the cohort. Most patients received concurrent chemotherapy, with weekly cisplatin being the most common regimen. External beam radiotherapy was delivered primarily using conventional techniques in 184 patients (77.6%), while 53 patients (22.4%) received IMRT. At the fraction level, intracavitary brachytherapy was used more frequently than hybrid IC/IS brachytherapy, and the tandem–ovoid was the most commonly used applicator. Detailed patient, treatment, and dosimetric characteristics are summarized in Table 1.

title: Clinical Outcomes and Prognostic Factors Following Routine CT-Based Image-Guided Adaptive Brachytherapy for Cervical Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
text: At the six-week follow-up after completion of radiotherapy, 222 patients (93.7%) achieved a complete response, while 15 patients (6.3%) had persistent local disease. For the local control analysis, the median follow-up was 59.9 months (IQR, 19.5–71.1), during which 36 local failure events were observed. The 5-year local control rate was 84.4% (95% CI, 79.1–88.5%; Figure 1A). When death without prior local recurrence was treated as a competing event, the 5-year cumulative incidence of local recurrence was 15.2% (95% CI, 11.0–20.1%), corresponding to 84.8% remaining free from local recurrence. When stratified by FIGO 2018 stage, the 5-year local control rates were 100.0% for stage I, 88.8% (95% CI, 80.6–93.6%) for stage II, 85.0% (95% CI, 77.0–90.4%) for stage III, and 57.5% (95% CI, 32.2–76.3%) for stage IV. Local control differed significantly across stages (p < 0.01; Figure 2A). In the multivariable analysis, squamous histology and HR-CTV D90 ≥ 85 Gy EQD2 were independently associated with improved local control, whereas the use of IMRT was associated with poorer local control (Table 2).

title: Clinical Outcomes and Prognostic Factors Following Routine CT-Based Image-Guided Adaptive Brachytherapy for Cervical Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
text: In a sensitivity analysis using a reduced model including FIGO stage, histology, HR-CTV D90, and radiotherapy technique, the findings remained consistent: squamous histology (HR 0.43, 95% CI 0.21–0.88; p = 0.02) and HR-CTV D90 ≥ 85 Gy EQD2 (HR 0.28, 95% CI 0.14–0.58; p < 0.01) were associated with improved local control, whereas IMRT (HR 3.50, 95% CI 1.76–6.96; p < 0.001) was associated with poorer local control. For the overall survival analysis, the median follow-up was 71.1 months (IQR, 60.1–77.1), and the 5-year overall survival rate was 62.9% (95% CI, 56.3–68.8%; Figure 1B). When stratified by FIGO 2018 stage, the 5-year overall survival rates were 100.0% for stage I, 72.5% (95% CI, 62.5–80.3%) for stage II, 57.2% (95% CI, 47.4–65.9%) for stage III, and 42.9% (95% CI, 20.4–63.6%) for stage IV. Overall survival differed significantly across stages (p = 0.02; Figure 2B). In the multivariable analysis, squamous histology and receipt of ≥4 cycles of chemotherapy were independently associated with improved overall survival, whereas an overall treatment time > 56 days was independently associated with worse overall survival (Table 2).

title: Clinical Outcomes and Prognostic Factors Following Routine CT-Based Image-Guided Adaptive Brachytherapy for Cervical Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
text: To assess potential imbalance in disease stage between treatment groups, we compared the distribution of FIGO stage according to external beam radiotherapy technique. The stage distribution differed significantly between patients treated with IMRT and those treated with conventional radiotherapy (p = 0.002). Among the 53 patients treated with IMRT, none had stage I disease, 11 (20.8%) had stage II disease, 37 (69.8%) had stage III disease, and 5 (9.4%) had stage IV disease. Among the 184 patients treated with conventional radiotherapy, 2 (1.1%) had stage I disease, 89 (48.4%) had stage II disease, 78 (42.4%) had stage III disease, and 15 (8.2%) had stage IV disease. In a sensitivity analysis restricted to patients with squamous cell carcinoma, the main prognostic patterns were generally consistent with the primary analysis. HR-CTV D90 ≥ 85 Gy EQD2 was associated with improved local control, while ≥4 chemotherapy cycles and shorter overall treatment time were associated with improved overall survival. IMRT was associated with poorer local control and overall survival in this subgroup.

title: Clinical Outcomes and Prognostic Factors Following Routine CT-Based Image-Guided Adaptive Brachytherapy for Cervical Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
text: This retrospective cohort study demonstrated that routine CT-based IGABT achieved clinically meaningful outcomes among patients with cervical cancer. Among 237 patients treated between 2019 and 2021, the 5-year local control and overall survival rates were 84.4% and 62.9%, respectively. HR-CTV D90 ≥ 85 Gy and squamous histology were independently associated with improved local control. Squamous histology and receipt of at least four cycles of chemotherapy were independently associated with improved overall survival, whereas overall treatment time > 56 days was associated with inferior overall survival. IMRT use was associated with poorer local control but was more common among patients with advanced-stage disease. Compared with our previously reported cohort treated between 2008 and 2018, which had 4-year local control and overall survival rates of approximately 89% and 69%, respectively [16], the present cohort included a higher proportion of stage III–IV disease. However, comparisons between the two cohorts should be interpreted cautiously because of differences in follow-up duration and the transition to FIGO 2018 staging, which incorporates nodal status and may have resulted in stage migration.

title: Clinical Outcomes and Prognostic Factors Following Routine CT-Based Image-Guided Adaptive Brachytherapy for Cervical Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
text: Our findings support the real-world feasibility of implementing a structured CT-based IGABT program in settings where routine access to MRI-based IGABT, the preferred standard for image-guided cervical brachytherapy, remains limited. Our results suggest that well-implemented CT-based workflows can achieve outcomes broadly comparable to those reported in contemporary real-world brachytherapy series. These findings reinforce the practical role of CT-based IGABT as an achievable and scalable strategy for improving cervical cancer outcomes in settings with limited MRI access. This interpretation is supported by a recent study from India comparing MRI-based and CT-based IGABT, which demonstrated comparable outcomes after propensity score matching [20].

title: Clinical Outcomes and Prognostic Factors Following Routine CT-Based Image-Guided Adaptive Brachytherapy for Cervical Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
text: Although our local control and overall survival rates did not reach those reported in MRI-guided EMBRACE-I, the differences may partly reflect the higher proportion of stage III–IV disease in our cohort. The use of hybrid IC/IS techniques in our study (30.2%) remained lower than that in EMBRACE-I (43%) but increased substantially from 9% in our previous cohort [16]. In addition, our retrospective CT-based cohort reflects greater real-world heterogeneity in disease burden and healthcare service constraints than highly protocolized MRI-based programs. Nevertheless, our results are broadly aligned with those of the Retro-EMBRACE study [6], particularly in terms of overall survival. Furthermore, our findings are consistent with contemporary CT-based brachytherapy series from Thailand and Japan [21,22,23], further supporting the clinical feasibility and effectiveness of CT-based brachytherapy in routine practice where MRI availability remains limited (Table 3). In multivariable analysis, squamous histology was independently associated with improved local control and overall survival. This finding is consistent with previous reports demonstrating inferior outcomes in adenocarcinoma and adenosquamous carcinoma compared with squamous cell carcinoma following definitive chemoradiotherapy [24,25].

title: Clinical Outcomes and Prognostic Factors Following Routine CT-Based Image-Guided Adaptive Brachytherapy for Cervical Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
text: Dose to the HR-CTV remained an important determinant of local control. In our cohort, 60.3% of patients achieved an HR-CTV D90 ≥ 85 Gy EQD2, which was independently associated with improved local control. This finding supports the established dose–response relationship reported in large image-guided brachytherapy series [26]. Although HR-CTV D90 was not independently associated with overall survival in the multivariable model, achieving an adequate target dose remains important for optimizing local disease control. Increasing the proportion of patients who achieve an HR-CTV D90 ≥ 85 Gy EQD2, with escalation toward 90 Gy EQD2 when clinically appropriate, may further improve local control. Adequate chemotherapy delivery and timely treatment completion were also important. Receipt of at least four chemotherapy cycles was associated with improved overall survival, whereas overall treatment time > 56 days was associated with inferior survival. Although 70% of patients in our cohort completed treatment within 56 days, further efforts to minimize unnecessary delays may improve outcomes. These findings are consistent with previous evidence emphasizing the importance of adequate chemotherapy delivery and avoidance of unnecessary treatment delays during definitive chemoradiotherapy [27,28].

title: Clinical Outcomes and Prognostic Factors Following Routine CT-Based Image-Guided Adaptive Brachytherapy for Cervical Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
text: The observed association of IMRT with inferior local control should be interpreted cautiously, particularly as its association with overall survival was attenuated and no longer statistically significant after multivariable adjustment. IMRT was used more frequently in patients with advanced-stage or clinically complex disease, including those requiring extended-field or inguinofemoral irradiation. Thus, this association likely reflects confounding by indication and residual differences in disease burden. Current evidence indicates that IMRT reduces treatment-related toxicity while providing survival outcomes comparable to those achieved with conventional radiotherapy [29]. Therefore, our findings should not be interpreted as evidence of a detrimental effect of IMRT itself.

title: Clinical Outcomes and Prognostic Factors Following Routine CT-Based Image-Guided Adaptive Brachytherapy for Cervical Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
text: In the present cohort, the entire uterus was included in the CTV during EBRT. Emerging studies have explored individualized uterine EBRT, in which uninvolved portions of the uterine corpus are excluded from the target volume to reduce irradiation of surrounding normal tissues [30,31]. However, this approach relies on accurate assessment of the superior extent of disease. In predominantly CT-based settings such as ours, where routine MRI access is limited, accurate assessment of tumor extension into the uterine corpus may be challenging. Similar uncertainties apply to CT-based brachytherapy target delineation, particularly in defining the superior extent of residual disease, for which CT-based consensus recommendations advocate a more conservative target definition when MRI information is unavailable [32]. Therefore, although individualized uterine EBRT is an emerging approach of interest, its application in CT-dominant settings should be considered cautiously and requires further evaluation.

title: Clinical Outcomes and Prognostic Factors Following Routine CT-Based Image-Guided Adaptive Brachytherapy for Cervical Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
text: The strength of this study is that it reflects routine clinical practice, making the findings particularly relevant to institutions where MRI access is limited by cost, scheduling, or availability. The inclusion of a relatively large consecutive cohort and long-term outcome assessment further strengthens the reliability of the findings. Moreover, the high proportion of patients with advanced-stage disease provides clinically relevant evidence from a population often encountered in resource-limited settings. In such settings, CT-based brachytherapy represents a practical and scalable approach to improving cervical cancer care.

title: Clinical Outcomes and Prognostic Factors Following Routine CT-Based Image-Guided Adaptive Brachytherapy for Cervical Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
text: However, this study has several limitations. First, its retrospective design introduces the potential for selection and information bias. Second, the relatively small number of local failure events may limit the stability of the multivariable estimates for local control. However, the main findings remained unchanged in a sensitivity analysis using a reduced multivariable model. In addition, although Kaplan–Meier analysis may overestimate the probability of local recurrence when death is a competing event, a competing-risk analysis produced similar results. Third, the observed associations between external beam radiotherapy technique and clinical outcomes remain vulnerable to confounding by indication because IMRT was used more frequently in patients with advanced-stage or clinically complex disease. Fourth, treatment-related toxicity was not systematically evaluated, limiting assessment of the overall therapeutic benefit of this approach. Finally, the single-center design may limit the generalizability of the findings. Larger multicenter prospective studies are warranted to validate these results.

title: Clinical Outcomes and Prognostic Factors Following Routine CT-Based Image-Guided Adaptive Brachytherapy for Cervical Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
text: Future program development should focus on expanding the use of hybrid IC/IS brachytherapy, increasing the proportion of patients achieving an HR-CTV D90 ≥ 85 Gy EQD2, selectively escalating the dose toward 90 Gy EQD2 for large residual tumors, and improving treatment completion within 56 days. Further integration of transabdominal ultrasound guidance, optimized use of IMRT, and selective incorporation of MRI may also improve treatment quality. Emerging findings from the MRI-guided EMBRACE-II study support the potential benefits of these strategies within contemporary image-guided radiotherapy workflows [33].

title: Clinical Outcomes and Prognostic Factors Following Routine CT-Based Image-Guided Adaptive Brachytherapy for Cervical Cancer: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
text: Routine CT-based image-guided adaptive brachytherapy achieved clinically meaningful local control and overall survival despite a high proportion of stage III–IV disease. An HR-CTV D90 ≥ 85 Gy EQD2 was independently associated with improved local control, while receipt of at least four chemotherapy cycles and completion of treatment within 56 days were associated with improved overall survival. These findings support CT-based IGABT as a practical and scalable option for centers with limited access to MRI when delivered within a standardized adaptive brachytherapy workflow.

title: Daily image-guided carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma: paving the way for MR-guided online adaptive treatment.
text: 13 patients received 4 × 10.5 Gy (RBE-weighted dose) CISR to 14 HCC lesions in challenging locations (N = 10: liver dome, N = 3: < 1 cm from intestines). All patients underwent daily in-room CT, with forward calculation of the baseline plan. Additionally, four patients were shuttled to a 1.5 Tesla MR scanner in treatment position for MRI simulation. Based on visual review of all data, the physician decided to treat or to perform offline plan adaptation and treat another day. We compare the dosimetry properties of four scenarios per fraction: (1) baseline plan, (2) no adaptation, (3) occasional offline adaptation (OOA), (4) DOA.

title: Daily image-guided carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma: paving the way for MR-guided online adaptive treatment.
text: Baseline planning target volume (PTV) and internal target volume (ITV) coverage by the prescribed dose (median coverage: PTV: 97%, ITV: 100%) significantly decreased for no adaptation (PTV: 87.6%, p = 0.0001; ITV: 97.7%, p = 0.007) and OOA (PTV: 87.8%, p = 0.0001; ITV: 97.7%, p = 0.007), while DOA maintained high PTV coverage (PTV: 95.7%, p = 0.17; ITV: 100%, p = 0.53). Frequent violations of organs-at-risk (OAR) dose constraints occurred for no adaptation and OOA (both 20/52 fractions, 38.5%). They affected the bowel, heart and esophagus up to 6 cm from the PTV. DOA led to considerably fewer (6/52 fractions, 11.5%) and less intense violations of OAR dose constraints.

title: Daily image-guided carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma: paving the way for MR-guided online adaptive treatment.
text: Daily CT- and MR-guided CISR is feasible in the liver, and demonstrates frequent violations of initial treatment planning objectives when non-adaptive or offline adaptive approaches are followed. DOA could improve target coverage and OAR protection, while particularities of carbon ions such as overdoses far from the target should be considered.

title: Daily image-guided carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma: paving the way for MR-guided online adaptive treatment.
text: Hepatocellular carcinomas (HCC) represent the 5th most prevalent cancer disease worldwide and are associated with high mortality [1–3]. Even though HCC mostly occur in low- and middle-income countries, incidences are increasing in Northern America and Europe due to more cases of hepatitis and liver cirrhosis [1–3]. Surgical tumor resection represents the treatment of choice, but is often not feasible for technical or medical reasons. Instead, local ablative treatments including radiofrequency ablation (RFA), microwave ablation (MWA) and transarterial chemoembolization (TACE) have been established. However, they face limitations, especially with larger HCC lesions [3, 4]. In recent years, stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) has emerged as an effective alternative. Retrospective analyses and smaller prospective trials have demonstrated high local tumor control and few side effects, so that SBRT can compete with established approaches [5–10]. In specific, SBRT seems useful in larger tumors, where efficacy of other approaches declines [4, 9].

title: Daily image-guided carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma: paving the way for MR-guided online adaptive treatment.
text: Carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy (CISR) offers further promise due to its high biological effectiveness and ability to spare organs at risk (OAR) [11]. Our previous phase I trial of CISR in HCC, PROMETHEUS, indicated excellent local control and minimal side effects [10]. This agrees with previous prospective phase I/II trials from Japan [12]. CISR represents a high precision technique that delivers doses with steep distal and lateral gradients due to a narrow Bragg peak [11, 13]. Moreover, carbon ions offer a high linear energy transfer (LET) and thus high biological efficacy [11, 13]. However, CISR is sensitive to interfractional changes because even moderate anatomical alterations translate to relevant changes of the dose distribution, creating unwanted “cold-spots” in the tumor and “hot-spots” in sensitive OAR [11, 14]. Therefore, treating tumors near intestinal OAR or in the liver dome poses considerable challenges due to bowel movements and changes in the position of the diaphragm [11, 14]. Hence, we have excluded patients with HCC in these challenging locations from the previous PROMETHEUS trial [10].

title: Daily image-guided carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma: paving the way for MR-guided online adaptive treatment.
text: In the past years, our carbon ion facility was equipped with an in-room computed tomography (CT) scanner and a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scanner combined with a shuttle system [15]. Moreover, we can now re-calculate the treatment plan on the current anatomy. Hence, patients with HCC undergo daily imaging with plan re-calculation. Then, the treating physician decides to continue with treatment or to postpone treatment and perform offline plan adaptation in the meantime. These sophisticated advances have encouraged us to treat challenging cases of HCC that we would have excluded from CISR before. Recent advances in online adaptive proton radiotherapy (RT) suggest promising dosimetric improvements in situations with relevant interfractional change [16, 17] and have led to the first clinical implementation [18]. Moreover, MR-guided online adaptive photon SBRT yields superior target volume coverage and OAR protection when treating tumors in the upper abdomen [19–22]. Our vision is to combine the advantages of carbon ions, online adaptive treatment and MR-guidance, which would yield enormous potential to improve target volume coverage and spare OAR. Therefore, we are developing a daily online adaptive workflow for CISR of liver cancer that includes the above-mentioned MRI shuttle system. In the following, we will: (1) report on the clinical feasibility of daily CT- and MRI-guided CISR with occasional offline plan adaptation in challenging HCC cases;

title: Daily image-guided carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma: paving the way for MR-guided online adaptive treatment.
text: This retrospective analysis included patients with HCC who underwent CISR between December 2021 and June 2024. Typically, patients were referred to our institution through a multidisciplinary tumor board due to ineligibility for surgical intervention or other local ablative treatments such as RFA or TACE. Hence, patients presented with complex clinical and anatomical characteristics.

title: Daily image-guided carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma: paving the way for MR-guided online adaptive treatment.
text: Patients were immobilized in supine position on a vacuum pillow, and a belly press was utilized to minimize breathing motion. For treatment planning, a contrast-enhanced four-dimensional (4D) CT was acquired with eight breathing phases. Additionally, a recent contrast-enhanced liver MRI was mandatory. The gross tumor volume (GTV) was defined based on all available imaging. Then, a margin of 5 mm was added to obtain the clinical target volume (CTV), followed by the creation of an internal target volume (ITV). Finally, a margin of 5 mm (7 mm in beam direction) was applied to create the planning target volume (PTV). A total dose of 42 Gy (biologically-weighted dose) in 4 fractions was prescribed to the PTV in a homogeneous fashion. Thus, the aim was to cover at least 95% of the PTV with 95% of the prescribed dose, while limiting the maximum dose to 104%. OAR dose constraints were based on the QUANTEC guidelines [23] and mostly aligned with Timmermann et al. [24] (typical mandatory constraints: maximum spinal cord dose (Dmax) < 25.6 Gy, heart Dmax < 37 Gy, esophagus Dmax < 35.6 Gy, stomach Dmax < 33.2 Gy, bowel Dmax < 32 Gy, liver-ITV Dmean < 12 Gy, and < 700 cm³ liver volume above 10 Gy). Treatment planning was performed using RayStation® (RaySearch Laboratories AB, Stockholm, Sweden) as treatment planning software (TPS). The dose was delivered via a single lateral beam (12/14, 86%) or two angulated lateral beams (2/14, 14%) using pencil beam scanning.

title: Daily image-guided carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma: paving the way for MR-guided online adaptive treatment.
text: Treatment fractions were administered every other day. Patients were immobilized on the treatment couch with abdominal compression and underwent verification CT imaging using a mobile in-room CT scanner (AIRO® system, Brainlab, Munich, Germany). Afterwards, the treatment couch was repositioned in front of the nozzle. Two-plane radiographs were acquired to verify and, if necessary, adjust patient positioning based on bony landmarks. Simultaneously, rigid registration of the planning CT with the verification CT was conducted in the TPS, also using bony anatomy as a reference. Following this, all target volumes and OAR were rigidly registered onto the verification CT, and the baseline treatment plan was recalculated. Finally, the treating physician visually reviewed all data and decided to proceed with the treatment or to postpone treatment and perform offline plan adaptation in the meantime. For four patients, additional daily MRI imaging in treatment position was included for one or two fractions. In these cases, patients were first transferred to a 1.5 Tesla MRI scanner (MAGNETOM Sola®, Siemens Healthineers, Forchheim, Germany) using a shuttle system with a hovercraft transfer mattress (Q-Fix® Symphony patient trolley, CQ Medical, Pennsylvania, USA). They underwent a non-contrast-enhanced liver MRI (T1-weighted VIBE and T2-weighted BLADE, approx. 15 min) and were returned to the treatment room for the above-specified CT-based verification process.

title: Daily image-guided carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma: paving the way for MR-guided online adaptive treatment.
section: Methods > Analysis of intra- and interfractional changes
text: All available imaging data were imported into RayStation® version 11B. In two cases, two daily CT scans were missing small portions of the beam entry channel due to insufficient field-of-view, so that these four fractions were excluded from all subsequent analyses. The clinical registrations between the planning CT and daily verification CT were utilized to match all images. Both the baseline plan and the offline adapted plans that were used in actual treatment were re-calculated on the daily verification CTs. The GTV was manually edited on the verification CT. Given the limited lesion-to-liver contrast in many instances, two independent methods were employed for comparison: (1) deformable image registration (DIR) using RayStation’s built-in functionality (ANACONDA [25]) was applied between the CT image sets to generate a vector field that enabled consecutive automatic GTV registration (2). MR-informed manual GTV adjustment was applied in cases where daily MRI was available to leverage its superior soft-tissue contrast. The ITV and PTV were automatically transferred from the planning CT to the verification CT using the vector field between the planning and verification (manually edited) GTVs via the above-described DIR algorithm. Additionally, OAR contours were reviewed. Thus, dose volume histograms (DVH) became available to characterize the baseline plan and potentially offline-adapted plans on the daily anatomy.

title: Daily image-guided carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma: paving the way for MR-guided online adaptive treatment.
section: Methods > Analysis of intra- and interfractional changes
text: Finally, the baseline plan was re-optimized on the daily anatomy with the initial planning objectives. In six cases, re-optimization was performed both manually and via a fully automated plan optimization tool. This automated plan optimization tool is based on the “Create adapted plan function” available in RayStation® version 11B. Thus, a new plan is created on the daily CT with the same beam and optimization settings as in the baseline plan. Initially, the tool performs 25 optimization iterations, followed by another 25 iterations with robust optimization on the ITV (5 mm isotropic uncertainty). A final optimization filters the beam’s spots and energy layers. Finally, the dose is scaled to fulfill the primary prescription (median dose (D50%) of 42 Gy (RBE) on the ITV). Given the high concordance between the manual and fully-automated approaches (Supplementary Fig. 1), the automated tool was subsequently applied to all cases. Essential DVH parameters were compared across four treatment scenarios:

text: Baseline plan: The initially intended treatment plan.No adaptation: Application of the baseline plan across all fractions.Occasional offline adaptation (OOA): Occasional offline adaptations of the baseline plan could be triggered by the physician’s visual review of the current fraction images and applied in the next fraction (current clinical approach).Daily online adaptation (DOA): Daily re-optimization of the treatment plan with the patient on the treatment couch using the fully automated tool (hypothetical).

title: Daily image-guided carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma: paving the way for MR-guided online adaptive treatment.
text: DVH parameters were compared across the four treatment scenarios using descriptive statistics. Additionally, paired two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were conducted to assess potential differences between DVH parameters of the baseline plan (scenario 1) and the median values over four fractions in the remaining scenarios. p-values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant, although all findings should be considered exploratory. To accurately estimate differences in PTV coverage across the four scenarios, a Bayesian linear multilevel model (LMM) was applied. Observations were clustered within the 14 irradiated lesions, meaning that observations from different fractions applied to the same lesion were not independent. Thus, we chose a Bayesian approach that is feasible for any number of observations and data structure. The LMM assessed the correlation between the PTV coverage and the respective treatment scenario (population level effect) based on weakly informative priors for the intercept (~ Normal(80, 20)) and treatment scenario (~ Normal(0, 20)).

text: Posterior distributions were derived using Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) simulations, employing 4 chains with 8000 iterations each. Convergence of the chains was verified through R^-values, all of which were ≤ 1.01. To ensure the robustness of the results, sensitivity analyses confirmed that the findings remained consistent under reasonable variations of the prior distributions. Median follow-up was calculated using the inverse Kaplan-Meier approach, while overall survival (OS), progression-free survival (PFS) and local tumor control (LC) rates were estimated using the Kaplan-Meier method. All statistical analyses were conducted using Python version 3.12, with the Bayesian LMM calculations performed in R version 4.4.1 using the brms library.

title: Daily image-guided carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma: paving the way for MR-guided online adaptive treatment.
text: We treated 13 patients with CISR to 14 HCC lesions because one patient was treated twice within one year for a new HCC lesion. Patient characteristics are given in Table 1. Briefly, median age was 69 years [IQR 67–77 years]. Most patients were male (9 / 13 patients, 69%) and presented with advanced liver cirrhosis (Child Pugh Score A – B: 8 patients, 61%). Tumors had a median gross tumor volume (GTV) of 20.5 cm³ [7.7–70 cm³]. Most lesions had previously been treated with at least one local treatment (surgery or local ablative therapy: 8/14 cases, 57%) and were located in a challenging anatomy. Particularly, ten lesion were in the right liver dome (segments IVa, VII or VIII), with two lesions lying < 1 cm from the pericardium, while three lesions were located < 1 cm from the bowel (exclusion criterion in our previous PROMETHEUS trial [10]). In three lesions (21%), the treating physician triggered one offline plan adaptation after two fractions. Two cases (14%) included one daily MRI and another two cases (14%) included two daily MRI acquisitions.

Auto-GTV: automatically generated GTV by deformable image registration The PTV coverage was highest in the baseline plan (median 97.0% IQR [95.1–99.1]) and decreased significantly when no adaptation (87.6% [81.8–92.5], p = 0.0001) or OOA were performed (87.8% [81.8–92.4], p = 0.0001), while only a small non-significant decrease was observed for DOA (95.7% [89.8–98.4], p = 0.17). In total, 71.4% (10/14) of baseline plans covered 95% of the PTV with 95% of the prescribed dose. This aim was reached in 15.4% (8/52), 13.5% (7/52) and 55.8% (29/52) of fractions for no adaptation, OOA and DOA, respectively. The Bayesian linear multilevel model (LMM) was compatible with a baseline PTV coverage of 95% [99% compatibility interval: 88–102%] that decreased by -9% [-15 – -3%] for both no adaptation and OOA, but only by -2% [-8–4] for DOA. Accordingly, DOA would increase the PTV coverage by + 7.3%, [4–10%] compared to no adaptation and by + 7.1%, [4–10%] compared to OOA (Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3).
