text: Similarly, the ITV coverage by 95% of the prescribed dose was highest in the baseline plan (median 100.0% IQR [97.6–100]) and decreased significantly for no adaptation (97.7% [94.8–99.7], p = 0.007) and OOA (97.7% [95.3–99.7], p = 0.007), while no change was observed for DOA (100% [96.6–100], p = 0.53). ITV coverage was above 95% in 85.7% (12/14) of the baseline plans, which decreased to 71.2% (37/52), 75% (39/52) and 78.8% (41/52) of fractions for no adaptation, OOA and DOA, respectively (Fig. 1). The GTV coverage by 95% of the prescribed dose was not significantly different between the scenarios, although we observed a trend towards decreased GTV coverage for no adaptation and OOA (Table 2). Still, GTV coverage was above 95% in 92.9% (13/14) of the baseline plans, compared to 86.5% (45/52), 86.5% (45/52) and 98.1% (51/52) of fractions for no adaptation, OOA and DOA, respectively (Fig. 1).

title: Daily image-guided carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma: paving the way for MR-guided online adaptive treatment.
text: To account for the limited lesion-to-liver contrast when contouring the GTV on daily in-room CT images, we also investigated (1) fully automatic PTVs based on DIR-generated GTVs and (2) PTVs based on MRI-informed manual GTVs (Supplementary Figs. 4 and 5). Overall, the volumetric Dice similarity coefficients (DSC) and mean distance to agreement (MDA) demonstrated a good agreement of the manual CT-based PTVs with the fully automatic contours (mean DSC.92, mean MDA 1.5 mm) and a fair agreement with the MRI-informed contours (DSC 0.75–0.9, MDA 1.5–3 mm). The underlying manual CT-based GTVs and fully automatic GTVs still demonstrated good agreement (mean DSC 0.83, mean MDA 1.8 mm), whereas comparisons of the manual CT-based GTVs and MR-informed GTVs varied between good and insufficient (DSC 0.62–0.89, MDA 1.4–5 mm). Furthermore, calculation of dose volume parameters led to similar values for fully automatic PTVs (Supplementary Fig. 6), although the decrease of the PTV coverage from the baseline was overall higher and also reached statistical significance for DOA (baseline plan: 97.0% [95.1–99.1]; no adaptation: 85.6 [78.1–92.0], p = 0.0001; OOA: 85.7 [78.1–91.8], p = 0.0001; DOA: 94.8 [91.1–97.6], p = 0.0001). Accordingly, the Bayesian LMM yielded similar results when analyzing the fully automatic PTVs (Supplementary Table 1, Supplementary Figs. 7 and 8).

text: MRI-based PTVs were only available in a limited number of fractions, but suggested even stronger declines of the PTV coverage (Supplementary Fig. 9) especially for no adaptation and OOA (baseline plan: 97.0% [95.1–99.1]; no adaptation and OOA identical: 73.5 [71.1–77.7], p = 0.13; DOA: 87.1 [79.7–92.5], p = 0.13).

Nevertheless, individual violations of dose constraints were similarly frequent when no adaptation or OOA were performed (20 / 52 fractions with ≥ 1 violated constraint, 38.5%). text: Fig. 3Carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of a tumor in the liver dome. Upper left: Baseline plan with excellent planning target volume (PTV: blue) and gross tumor volume (GTV: dark green) coverage and sparing of mediastinal organs (heart: pink, esophagus: orange). Due to a caudal shift of the liver, the beam “overshoots” into the mediastinum and causes high dose exposition of heart and esophagus. title: Daily image-guided carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma: paving the way for MR-guided online adaptive treatment.
text: DOA considerably reduced individual dose constraint violations (6 / 52 fractions with 1 violated constraint, 11.5%). Only moderate violations of the heart dose constraints remained in three patients (Fig. 2, two patients: 1/4 fractions, one patient: 4/4 fractions). These violations were deemed clinically acceptable to maintain good PTV coverage. Finally, DOA led to statistically significant albeit moderate increases in the lung V10Gy (baseline: median 7.0% IQR [1.2–10.6], DOA scenario: 7.8% [0.7–16.8], p = 0.049) and mean liver dose (baseline: 8.3 Gy [5.4–9.2], DOA scenario: 8.7 Gy [5.1–9.7], p = 0.03) compared to the baseline plan (Supplementary Fig. 10).

title: Daily image-guided carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma: paving the way for MR-guided online adaptive treatment.
text: After a median follow-up of 15 months, only one lesion (7%) had progressed locally (in-field) after 17 months. Furthermore, three cases (21.4%) of out-field liver progression were observed. Consequently, the OS, PFS and LC rates were 78% (34–83%), 64% (95% CI: 46–92%) and 100% [100–100%] after 1 year. Acute adverse events occurred after eight treatments (57%) and were mostly mild, with six (43%) grade (G) 1 (erythema, fatigue, diarrhea, nausea, elevation of liver enzymes), one (7%) G2 (abdominal pain) and two (14%) G3 (cholangitis, portal vein thrombosis) toxicities. Late adverse events were observed after three treatments (21%), with two (14%) G1 (asymptomatic pleural effusion and rib fracture) and one (7%) G3 (portal vein thrombosis) toxicities. No acute or late G 4–5 toxicities were observed.

title: Daily image-guided carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma: paving the way for MR-guided online adaptive treatment.
text: Adaptive particle therapy is a developing area in radiation oncology [14, 16–18, 27–31]. Previous studies focus on repeated offline plan re-calculations and potentially adaptations based on weekly re-planning CTs, e.g. in carbon ion RT for lung cancer [32] and proton RT for esophageal and head and neck cancers [28, 31]. Very recently, clinical approaches to online adaptive proton RT have been developed [16, 17] and were translated into clinical practice for cases with rigid anatomical changes such as skull base tumors [18]. At our facility, we can already perform online plan re-calculation so that the treating physician can decide whether to treat or postpone treatment and instead perform (occasional) offline adaptation (OOA). Currently, we are refining fully automated tools for fast online re-optimization. Together with our MR-shuttle system, we possess the essential prerequisites for an MR-guided online adaptive workflow.

title: Daily image-guided carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma: paving the way for MR-guided online adaptive treatment.
text: A growing body of studies in MR-guided online adaptive photon SBRT demonstrates superior target coverage and sparing of neighboring OAR when treating tumors in the upper abdomen [19–22]. However, (online) adaptive particle treatment comes with especially high workloads and treatment times [30]. So far, only few studies have investigated the potential benefits of adaptive particle SBRT in the upper abdomen. Considering carbon ions, Molinelli et al. [14] compared different robust optimization approaches to a simulated online adaptive CISR of pancreatic cancer based on repeated pre-treatment 4D-CT images. They concluded that only efficient online adaptation strategies can maintain high target coverage in most fractions while sparing the duodenum. Considering HCC, Nenoff et al. [33] have simulated adaptive versus non-adaptive photon and proton SBRT courses in ten patients based on daily setup MR images from a photon MR-linac treatment. They found proton SBRT provided better OAR sparing over photons, but the impact of DOA seemed limited. Conversely, Moteabbed et al. [27] created daily online adaptive MR-guided, offline MR-guided and CBCT-guided proton SBRT plans based on different PTV margins. They demonstrated that transitioning from CBCT-guided to daily online adaptive MR-guided reduced PTV margins, therefore enhancing OAR sparing. Here, we present the first analysis of original treatment plans and images derived from patients who received CISR to HCC with OOA.

title: Daily image-guided carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma: paving the way for MR-guided online adaptive treatment.
text: Interfractional anatomical changes often reduce the PTV coverage, which may be tolerable as long as the PTV is a sufficient “buffer” to maintain coverage of clinical targets. However, we observed that the ITV and, to a lesser degree, the GTV were affected by interfractional changes as well. One important reason for the observed changes appeared to be variable positioning of the belly press. Target volume coverages were maintained by DOA, but not by our OOA workflow. One essential point to consider is that our OOA workflow relies on visual review of re-calculated plans on rigidly registered contours. This may allow fast and pragmatic online evaluation, but could also introduce misinterpretations compared to accurate contour editing. Previous analyses of MR-guided photon SBRT have suggested that visual reviews alone are insufficient to determine the need for online plan adaptation [19]. In specific, subjective visual review of a daily image without editing contours and re-calculation of the baseline plan could not reliably determine when plan adaptation is needed, while a workflow based on re-contouring and re-calculation yielded a sensitivity of 90% [19].

title: Daily image-guided carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma: paving the way for MR-guided online adaptive treatment.
text: This aligns well with our data because offline adaptation was only triggered once (mid-treatment) in 3/14 (21%) lesions, even though relevant deviations from planning objectives were found in more cases when using re-contouring and re-calculation (25% of fractions failed to provide high ITV coverage, > 50% of fractions with violations of heart dose constraint). Furthermore, one should bear in mind that OOA is quite different from DOA because the plan is re-optimized on past imaging. Thus, OOA mainly aims to increase the general plan robustness, while DOA copes flexibly with day-to-day interfractional changes. All in all, DOA appeared to yield superior target volume coverage. Finally, compromised GTV visibility on non-contrast-enhanced daily CT images represents an important limitation of our analyses and will impede both OOA and DOA in the future. While manual and automatic target volumes agreed well, the comparison between manual CT-only and MR-informed contours yielded good - fair agreements for the PTV but partly insufficient agreements for the GTV. This suggests that future workflows will likely benefit from MRI-guidance to yield highest contour accuracy.

title: Daily image-guided carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma: paving the way for MR-guided online adaptive treatment.
text: Similar to our results from target volume coverage, interfractional anatomical changes frequently cause violations of OAR dose constraints. DOA prevented the majority of potential overdoses to OAR, whereas OOA barely seemed beneficial. Several cases of HCC in the liver dome demonstrated dose hotspots in the mediastinum with potential overdoses in the esophagus and heart as far as 3–6 cm from the PTV. These occurred because a lower position of the liver dome opened the way for “beam overshoots” through lung tissue. It is well known that carbon ion dose distributions are not robust near tissue-air interfaces [11]. Still, our results make clear that methods from MR-guided online adaptive photon RT cannot simply be adopted in carbon ion treatment. Particularly, OAR can safely be re-contoured within 3 cm of the PTV to streamline MR-guided online adaptive photon RT [34]. Online adaptive CISR will require more extensive re-contouring, at least in beam direction. We observed small increases of mean doses inside the right lung and liver for DOA. However, these increases did not appear clinically relevant. Slightly elevated lung and liver doses as well as few residual heart dose constraint violations may also reflect the demands of efficient online re-optimization.

title: Daily image-guided carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma: paving the way for MR-guided online adaptive treatment.
text: Our image-guided CISR workflow with OOA allowed treatment of HCC in difficult locations with good clinical outcomes. After an intermediate median follow-up time of 15 months, local tumor control (in-field) was good. Therefore, the superior target coverage with DOA might not only ensure high long-term local tumor control but could also be exploited to reduce PTV margins. Consequently, doses to OAR could be further decreased, which would lower the risk of side effects in general and prevent severe toxicity in individual patients, such as the case with repeated high dose exposure of the esophagus. In this cohort, we observed moderate rates of adverse events, without any G 4–5 events. The three incidents of G3 toxicity, namely portal vein thromboses and cholangitis, were not necessarily associated with RT but could also be a consequence of the underlying liver cirrhosis. Potentially, an even wider spectrum of difficult cases could be managed using DOA.

title: Daily image-guided carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma: paving the way for MR-guided online adaptive treatment.
text: Currently, the OOA workflow already includes daily CT and potentially MRI, rigid contour registration and forward calculation of the baseline treatment plan onto the daily imaging as well as visual review by the physician. Therefore, the remaining steps towards creating a clinically feasible DOA workflow include re-contouring, plan re-optimization and quality assurance (QA). Firstly, re-contouring is usually performed manually and remains the most time-consuming step in current MR-guided online adaptive photon RT, with approximately 10–20 min in the upper abdomen [34–36]. These times could further increase because re-contouring within 3 cm of the PTV might not be sufficient in CISR. Therefore, new developments in AI-based contouring should be implemented to reduce the contouring times [37, 38]. Secondly, our automated plan optimization tool in RayStation® could already be implemented into a clinical workflow, managing a full plan re-optimization within mean 2–3 min. Finally, a clinically robust QA procedure still needs to be set up. Based on our experiences with QA for adapted proton plans as well as previous data from online adaptive MR-guided photon RT [35], it seems realistic to implement a streamlined QA workflow that requires up to 10 min.

title: Daily image-guided carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma: paving the way for MR-guided online adaptive treatment.
text: Even though our work supports the benefits of DOA in carbon ion irradiation of liver cancer, further developments, especially in imaging and re-contouring, are needed to enable full clinical application. Generating consistent GTVs was difficult from non-contrast enhanced daily CT images, which limits our analyses of target volume coverage as well as implementation of future CT-based DOA workflows. Although we found good agreement between manual and automatic contouring approaches, the comparison between CT and MR-based contours suggested potentially relevant differences. Implementing daily MRI could overcome these limitations in a transition to MR-guided DOA. However, the integration of MRI and DOA will increase treatment time and still requires significant technical refinements. Future approaches towards in-room MR-guided treatment may allow MR-based patient positioning and beam gating, which would further reduce interfractional changes and intrafractional changes.

title: Daily image-guided carbon ion stereotactic radiotherapy of hepatocellular carcinoma: paving the way for MR-guided online adaptive treatment.
text: Daily CT- and MR-guided CISR is feasible in the liver. While OOA based on visual review of online re-calculated plans demonstrated few benefits, DOA could improve target volume coverage and sparing of OAR. Future DOA implementations should consider particularities of carbon ion treatment, such as possible overdoses far from the target.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: Carbon ion radiotherapy (CIRT) offers superior dose conformity and biological effectiveness; however, its precision is highly sensitive to respiratory motion, leading to dose uncertainty and interplay effects that compromise treatment accuracy.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: A comprehensive literature synthesis was conducted on studies employing motion‐resolved imaging techniques (e.g. SMEIR), dynamic dose prediction, 4D robust planning, and hybrid adaptive methods for CIRT. The study emphasised the use of Geant4 Monte Carlo simulations combined with deep learning models, including physics‐informed neural networks, to simulate and predict dose perturbations caused by respiratory motion. This review also examined clinical treatment planning systems, radiobiological modelling, and adaptive strategies to mitigate the effects of motion.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: The integration of Geant4 with deep learning enabled high‐fidelity, computationally efficient dose prediction under respiratory motion, improving accuracy in dose localization and adaptation. Motion management techniques such as respiratory gating, rescanning, and 4D robust optimization demonstrated enhanced tumor control and normal tissue sparing. Hybrid models combining Monte Carlo data and AI inference show promise for near‐real‐time adaptive therapy. Despite these advances, challenges remain, including limited motion‐rich datasets, computational demands for real‐time recalculations, and the complexity of incorporating variable relative biological effectiveness (RBE) into adaptive planning.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: Combining Geant4‐based Monte Carlo simulations with deep learning frameworks shows emerging promise for controlling carbon ion dose distributions amid respiratory motion, though direct clinical validation for this combination remains limited. These hybrid models may enhance the precision and adaptability of CIRT, offering improved outcomes. Future efforts should focus on clinical validation, standardization, and overcoming computational and data limitations to facilitate clinical translation of motion‐adaptive CIRT. These approaches remain at Technology Readiness Levels (TRL 3–5) and require prospective clinical validation before routine implementation.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: In cancer radiotherapy, particle therapy—which includes techniques like proton and heavy ion beams—has emerged as a promising and increasingly adopted modality, supported by a growing body of clinical evidence, although robust phase III trial data remain limited and particle therapy currently treats only a small fraction of radiotherapy patients worldwide. 1 , 2 Unlike conventional photon‐based techniques, which distribute dose along the entire beam path according to an exponential attenuation profile, particle beams exploit the Bragg peak effect and can cause maximum energy deposition at a given depth with minimal total dose delivered, a considerable saving of normal tissues located out of the target. 1 , 2 Among particle therapies, carbon ion radiotherapy (CIRT) is distinguished from proton therapy by its greater linear energy transfer (LET) and relative biological effectiveness (RBE), making it specifically effective in the treatment of hypoxic, radioresistant or deeply seated tumours. 3 , 4 , 5 Long‐term clinical data from facilities in Japan, Germany, and Italy suggest potential advantages of carbon ions in treating difficult cancers such as sacral chordomas, head‐and‐neck tumours, and pancreatic cancers, although direct randomized comparisons against photon therapy remain very limited. 2

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: The therapeutic advantage of carbon ions, however, is very dependent upon accurate dose deposition. Small differences between the planned and actual dose of deliveries can result in considerable clinical impact because of large dose rates at the Bragg peak and increased biological responses at distances close to the distal edge, even in cases when there is only a small beam range uncertainty. 6 Accuracy of dose distributions, therefore, is a fundamental precondition in CIRT, which requires effective treatment planning systems and quality assurance procedures. 7 Respiratory motion presents a major challenge in thoracic and abdominal radiotherapy because it introduces time‐varying anatomical displacements in multiple spatial directions simultaneously. Diaphragm and chest‐wall excursion is commonly reported in the range of 5–25 mm, but tumor displacement itself is generally smaller and highly site‐specific: most lung tumors move less than 10 mm, whereas liver tumors—particularly those near the diaphragm—can exceed 20 mm in the superior‐inferior direction; breathing frequency (∼12–20 per min) is randomly variable, especially in stress, when sedated, or with a disease. 8 While the tumor itself does not change in volume during respiration, the surrounding anatomy deforms around it, shifting its position and the density of tissue traversed by the beam, which creates a dynamic requirement for compensation techniques.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: As an example, the superior‐inferior motion of liver tumor can be greater than lateral movement and could be greater than 20 mm, whereas direction dependent deformation of lung tumor could be present during the breathing process. 9 During respiration, the position of the tumour and the surrounding anatomical structures may undergo deformation, particularly in thoracic and abdominal regions. Modern tumour tracking systems and surface‐guided radiotherapy (SGRT) are capable of detecting abnormal respiratory patterns in real time, allowing for the interruption of beam delivery through respiratory gating. While these methods enhance geometric accuracy, they typically result in an increase in overall treatment time. Abnormal breathing patterns like sighing and coughing introduce uncertainties to the dose tracking—that is, the time‐integrated accumulation of dose across respiratory phases relative to a reference anatomy—of scanning ion beams.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: The interplay effect is considered one of the most significant dose distribution issues in CIRT, a phenomenon produced by the interaction between dynamic delivery of the beam (e.g. spot scanning) and organ motion. Since the target shifts during the respiration cycle or cardiac cycles, the accurately targeted carbon ion spots will not fall on the desired point, causing under‐ or over‐dosage in the tumor volume. 10 The research highlights the prominent nature of this interaction in particle therapy as it is especially sensitive to spatially derived changes, which makes it a major aspect in planning quality. 11 Besides the interplay, range uncertainties due to motion are still a cause of serious concern. Because carbon ions deposit the bulk of their energy sharply at the Bragg peak with minimal distal dose, any anatomical changes during breathing or digestive movements can shift the Bragg peak out of the tumour, possibly irradiating normal tissue. 9 In CIRT specifically, positional changes and set‐up errors in deep‐seated or thoracic tumours have consequences beyond simple geometric miss: because the beam range is highly sensitive to the density of tissue traversed, even small anatomical shifts can displace the high‐dose region into or out of the target volume, underscoring the need for careful pre‐treatment analysis. 12

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: Breathing and other physiological motions lead to complex patterns of dose deviations, which are not easily predicted by using simple, static 3D planning, and further highlight the necessity of incorporating temporal variations to dosimetry. These challenges have necessitated adaptive and robust planning methodologies. Multi‐phase 4D delivery approaches synchronize the beam to specific respiratory phases to minimize interplay, 13 whereas 4D‐robust optimisation techniques instead feature explicit representation of varied uncertainties (i.e. patient anatomy shift, range error) directly within the plan objective, without requiring synchronization to a specific motion phase, in an attempt to limit interplay and motion effects. 14 , 15 A comprehensive overview of motion mitigation strategies in particle therapy, spanning gating, rescanning, and robust and 4D optimization, is provided by Galeone et al. (2025). High‐end technologies (e.g., multi‐phase 4D radiotherapy, respiratory gating) are also useful in this respect because they synchronize beam delivery with patient breathing, minimizing effects of interplay and motion uncertainties. 16 There is growing interest in in‐vivo range verification strategies—including PET‐based detection of positron‐emitting fragments, prompt‐gamma imaging, and radioactive ion beams to minimise the safety margins traditionally required for range uncertainties, thus improving conformity. 7 , 17

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: Moreover, there is a growing interest in leveraging advanced computational modeling and artificial intelligence (AI). The use of Monte Carlo (MC) simulations with platforms such as Geant4 have become essential in the realistic simulation of dose distributions in complex clinical conditions, such as the presence of respiratory motion. These kinds of simulations permit high‐fidelity dose calculations which consider heterogeneities of tissues as well as the stochastic interactions of the particles. Several general‐purpose Monte Carlo toolkits—including FLUKA, TOPAS, GATE, and MCNPX—are also used in particle therapy dosimetry. Geant4 was selected as the focus of this review because it uniquely combines macroscopic dose simulation with the Geant4‐DNA extension for nanodosimetric and track‐structure modelling, and because the Geant4 collaboration maintains the G4‐Med validation platform, which benchmarks the toolkit's physics models specifically for medical applications, including carbon ion therapy. This combination of clinical‐scale dose calculation and biologically resolved modeling within a single, actively validated framework distinguishes Geant4 from other general‐purpose codes for the purposes of this review.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: In parallel, deep learning methods are being investigated to quickly propagate dose distributions from anatomical and motion information, with recent work focusing on physics‐informed neural networks that naturally produce physically valid results by applying known dosimetric constraints. Notably, hybrid methods that combine Monte Carlo data and deep learning, including CAM‐CHD U‐Net heavy‐ion plans or CNN‐based dose denoisers for proton/cyberknife systems, seek to provide the superior accuracy of physics‐based models, with the speed of AI inference, to permit real‐time and adaptive radiotherapy workflows. 18 , 19 Dedicated architectures for online adaptive particle therapy, such as DOTA and C‐DOTA, have further been proposed specifically for dose prediction under motion in carbon ion beams. It is against this background that the present review aims to critically synthesize the existing literature devoted to the development of methods of dynamical control of carbon ion dose distributions on the back of respiratory motion, with a specific focus on the use of prediction models that combine the capabilities of Geant4‐based Monte Carlo simulations and deep learning or physics‐constrained modeling frameworks.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: This review provides a critical evaluation of the methodologies, reporting of the most relevant findings, and the identification of the challenges that remain open, thereby becoming a useful source to clinicians, physicists and researchers at the intersection of particle therapy, computational modeling, and AI‐based adaptive therapy approaches. The challenges associated with FLASH radiotherapy are anticipated to intensify, given the ultra‐high dose‐rate delivery characteristic of this modality. This delivery method may exhibit heightened sensitivity to respiratory motion and interplay effects, thereby underscoring the necessity for precise motion prediction and adaptive dose control.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: This structured narrative review was informed by a systematic literature search across PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect, Google Scholar, and Web of Science, focusing on studies published from January 2010 to March 2026. The search strategy involved combining terms like “carbon ion radiotherapy” or “heavy ion therapy” with “Geant4” or “Monte Carlo simulation”, alongside “respiratory motion”, “4D”, or “interplay effect”, and “deep learning”, “machine learning”, or “artificial intelligence”. Additional keywords included “SMEIR”, “relative biological effectiveness”, and “treatment planning system”. To uncover further pertinent studies, reference lists from qualifying articles and recent reviews were manually examined. Studies were selected if they presented original data on computational, dosimetric, imaging, treatment‐planning, or clinical aspects related to Geant4‐based or similar Monte Carlo simulations, respiratory motion management, 4D dose calculation, adaptive radiotherapy, or AI‐assisted dose prediction in particle therapy, particularly focusing on carbon ion radiotherapy. Review articles were mainly used to provide methodological context and to pinpoint primary studies, but they did not serve as the main evidence for specific conclusions. Exclusions were made for non‐English publications, conference abstracts without full‐text articles, and studies that lacked adequate methodological detail.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: Due to the diverse nature of the available evidence, which included computational, phantom, imaging, treatment‐planning, and clinical studies, a formal systematic review, PRISMA‐guided quantitative synthesis, or risk‐of‐bias assessment was not conducted. Instead, the chosen literature was critically analyzed to assess recent advancements in Geant4‐based Monte Carlo simulation, motion‐resolved imaging, respiratory motion management, radiobiological modeling (LEM and MKM), deep learning‐based dose prediction, and hybrid adaptive strategies for carbon ion radiotherapy. The review was conducted as a structured narrative review and therefore did not follow PRISMA guidelines because of the heterogeneous computational, phantom, dosimetric, and clinical evidence included. A total of 312 records were identified through searching (PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect, Web of Science, and Google Scholar). After duplicate removal (n = 48), 264 publications remained for title and abstract screening. Following screening, 147 articles unrelated to carbon‐ion radiotherapy, respiratory motion management, Monte Carlo simulation, or artificial intelligence‐based dose prediction were excluded. The remaining 117 full‐text articles were assessed for eligibility; 82 publications were included in the narrative synthesis after excluding review articles, conference abstracts without details, and studies outside the scope. Quantitative meta‐analysis was inappropriate because of heterogeneity.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
section: BACKGROUND: CARBON ION RADIOTHERAPY—PHYSICS, RADIOBIOLOGY, AND MOTION CHALLENGES
text: The physics and radiobiology of carbon‐ion therapy are well established in the literature and are not, in themselves, novel findings of this review. They are summarised here only to the extent needed to interpret the motion‐management, Geant4‐based simulation, and deep learning literature that follows, and the treatment below is deliberately condensed relative to standard reference texts on the subject. Readers already familiar with Bragg‐peak physics, LET, RBE, LEM, and MKM may proceed directly to Section 3.2, which addresses the motion‐specific background most directly relevant to this review, or to Section 4, where the critical synthesis of the reviewed literature is presented.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
section: BACKGROUND: CARBON ION RADIOTHERAPY—PHYSICS, RADIOBIOLOGY, AND MOTION CHALLENGES > Principles of carbon ion radiotherapy > Physics of carbon ion radiotherapy
text: Carbon ion radiotherapy exploits the Bragg peak effect, depositing the bulk of beam energy at a precise depth and sparing surrounding tissue relative to the exponential attenuation profile of conventional photons. 20 Figure 1 demonstrates the effect of respiratory motion on this precise dose localization, which is the central motion‐related vulnerability examined throughout this review. Modern scanning‐beam technologies overlay multiple Bragg peaks to create a spread‐out Bragg peak (SOBP) with consistent dose coverage across extended tumour volumes 21 ; as discussed in Section 5, the LET—and therefore the biological effectiveness—varies considerably across this SOBP, which has direct implications for motion‐affected planning. Carbon ions attain LET values approaching ∼100 keV/µm only at the distal edge of a clinically realistic SOBP, with considerably lower LET—and correspondingly lower biological effectiveness—in the proximal and mid‐SOBP regions; this spatial LET variation, and the densely ionised, less repairable DNA damage it produces, underlies the biophysical planning approaches discussed below. 22 , 23 , 24 Nuclear fragmentation also produces a low‐dose fragmentation tail distal to the target that must be accounted for in dose calculations; this is a dosimetric liability rather than the planned therapeutic benefit some earlier literature has speculated. 25

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
section: BACKGROUND: CARBON ION RADIOTHERAPY—PHYSICS, RADIOBIOLOGY, AND MOTION CHALLENGES > Principles of carbon ion radiotherapy > Radiobiology of carbon ions
text: Carbon ions' high LET generates clustered double‐strand breaks largely independent of oxygenation status or cell cycle phase, making them effective against hypoxic or radioresistant tumours where photon therapy often underperforms. 26 , 27 Carbon‐ion RBE varies between approximately 2–5 depending on target tissue, biological endpoint, and LET, 28 and—unlike proton therapy's fixed clinical RBE of 1.1—varies spatially within the field, peaking near the distal Bragg‐peak edge. Modern planning systems accommodate this spatial variation using the Microdosimetric Kinetic Model (MKM) and Local Effect Model (LEM), 21 discussed further below, which several comparative studies link to improved tumour control in radioresistant disease. 23 , 29 A comparison of key physical and biological parameters across photon, proton, and carbon‐ion therapy is provided in Table 1.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
section: BACKGROUND: CARBON ION RADIOTHERAPY—PHYSICS, RADIOBIOLOGY, AND MOTION CHALLENGES > Principles of carbon ion radiotherapy > Clinical treatment planning
text: In clinical practice, CIRT requires biologically informed treatment planning, which is significantly more complex than that for photon or proton therapy. Treatment planning systems (TPS) must integrate both physical dose calculations and biological parameters such as LET and RBE. TRiP98, developed at GSI Darmstadt, was used during the original German pilot clinical project but is no longer licensed for routine clinical use; it was succeeded by Siemens Syngo PT, which remains operational at some centers. RayStation (RaySearch Laboratories), which supports both the LEM and MKM biophysical models, is now the dominant treatment planning system used across the majority of carbon ion facilities in Europe and Japan. For instance, in sacral chordoma patients, LEM‐based RBE‐weighted dose combined with dose‐averaged LET was shown to significantly affect local control and normal tissue sparing. 30 Critically, carbon‐ion RBE is not a function of LET alone: it also depends on dose per fraction, tissue radiosensitivity (α/β ratio), and biological endpoint, which is why LEM and MKM are needed to translate the spatially varying physical dose and LET into a clinically meaningful RBE‐weighted dose rather than simply maximizing physical dose to the target. 23 An additional source of uncertainty arises from the α/β ratio used in radiobiological models.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
section: BACKGROUND: CARBON ION RADIOTHERAPY—PHYSICS, RADIOBIOLOGY, AND MOTION CHALLENGES > Principles of carbon ion radiotherapy > Clinical treatment planning
text: Published α/β values may differ by approximately 30% depending on tumour type, experimental conditions, and model assumptions, which can substantially influence predicted RBE‐weighted dose distributions and treatment optimisation. Góra et al. 29 proved that treatment conclusions, such as dose per fraction and CTV coverage, vary significantly depending on whether LEM or MKM is used, highlighting the pragmatic implications of model choice. Mein et al. 31 validated RBE‐weighted models across three levels, revealing that outdated mid‐LET assumptions can overestimate toxicity risk, necessitating TPS modernization.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
section: BACKGROUND: CARBON ION RADIOTHERAPY—PHYSICS, RADIOBIOLOGY, AND MOTION CHALLENGES > Principles of carbon ion radiotherapy > Clinical treatment planning
text: The next frontier is multi‐objective optimization. Jointly optimizing physical and biological dose, including nanometric ionization‐cluster distributions, was explored in the 2000s; Burigo et al. 32 provided a computational protocol for simultaneous optimization of RBE‐weighted dose and nanometric distributions. At very high LET (above ∼200 keV/µm), the overkill effect must be accounted for in biophysical models, particularly near the distal Bragg peak. Precise model translation aids in treating difficult tumors like adenoid cystic carcinoma (ACC). The debate between LEM and MKM versions involves dosimetric and clinical comparisons. Molinelli et al. 33 found no clinically significant differences in ACC outcomes between LEM and MKM, underscoring the difficulty of isolating model‐specific effects. Range uncertainty remains a primary challenge, especially in motion‐affected sites, prompting increased use of adaptive re‐planning and motion‐managed delivery. There is growing interest in hybrid planning integrating photon and carbon ion plans. Bennan 34 addressed optimal LET and RBE for complex volumes, using carbon ions to increase biological effect in resistant areas and photons to manage geometric uncertainty. Weyrather and Kraft 35 established the basis for LEM‐based planning by comparing in vitro RBE data with predictive models, a contribution still applied in TPS calibration today.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
section: BACKGROUND: CARBON ION RADIOTHERAPY—PHYSICS, RADIOBIOLOGY, AND MOTION CHALLENGES > Respiratory motion in carbon ion radiotherapy
text: Respiratory motion is complex, defined by amplitude, frequency, and irregularity. These parameters impact radiation therapy, diagnostics, and biomechanics. Amplitude, the displacement of thoracic or abdominal structures, is patient‐ and region‐specific; most lung tumors move under 5–10 mm 36 . Precise quantification is vital in radiation therapy to avoid geographic miss 36 . In stroke patients, irregular amplitude disrupts breathing coordination, affecting vocalization and cough reflexes. 37

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
section: BACKGROUND: CARBON ION RADIOTHERAPY—PHYSICS, RADIOBIOLOGY, AND MOTION CHALLENGES > Respiratory motion in carbon ion radiotherapy
text: Healthy adults breathe 12–20 times per minute, though rates shift with exercise, stress, or pathology. Frequency influences chest wall and diaphragmatic movement, impacting mechanical ventilation. Altered patterns often indicate underlying pathology or brain stem dysfunction 38 , 39 demonstrated that respiration's oscillatory nature, where impedance and phase change with frequency, is essential for modeling lung diseases like asthma and COPD. Abnormal breathing may stem from neurological illness, anxiety, or cancer. Cheong et al 40 proposed the respiration regularity index (RRI) to measure amplitude and period variability, improving radiotherapy gating. In panic disorder patients, 41 linked respiratory chaos to mental health and autonomic dysregulation. Modeling confirms respiratory motion is not purely sinusoidal, involving baseline drift, phase shifts, and frequency modulations that challenge clinical gating and tracking systems. 42 Compared with breath‐hold or respiratory gating techniques, adaptive motion modelling allows treatment under free breathing and may improve patient comfort while reducing dependency on patient compliance. However, breath‐hold and gating generally increase treatment delivery time and workflow complexity.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
section: BACKGROUND: CARBON ION RADIOTHERAPY—PHYSICS, RADIOBIOLOGY, AND MOTION CHALLENGES > Respiratory motion in carbon ion radiotherapy
text: Carbon ions have a steep Bragg peak and great sensitivity to density and path‐length variations, as well as higher mass. This increases their vulnerability to misalignment and underdose or overdose, unlike photons, which have diffusive profiles of dose deposition, or even protons, which, despite their lower LET are typically planned using a fixed clinical RBE of 1.1 regardless of position—a simplification that eases planning but is increasingly questioned, in contrast to CIRT, where the higher and spatially variable LET requires explicit, position‐dependent RBE modeling. 43 In actively scanned beam delivery, interplay between tumor motion and pencil beam scanning (PBS) can cause dose distortions—called the interplay effect—where dose lines miss the tumor during respiration, reducing target conformity. Richter et al. 44 demonstrated that motion amplitudes as small as 6 mm in liver tumors could significantly degrade dose homogeneity, but increased pencil beam overlap mitigated this effect. Chi et al. 45 compared intensity‐modulated carbon ion therapy (IMCIT) to IMPT and VMAT under simulated lung tumor motion; however, respiratory gating was applied to restrict motion to ≤5 mm, and interplay effects—to which carbon ions are the most sensitive of the three modalities studied—were not modeled. Their results should therefore be interpreted cautiously and do not support a general claim of carbon‐ion robustness at amplitudes up to 20 mm. 45

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
section: BACKGROUND: CARBON ION RADIOTHERAPY—PHYSICS, RADIOBIOLOGY, AND MOTION CHALLENGES > Respiratory motion in carbon ion radiotherapy
text: The sensitivity of the dose distribution to respiratory motion varies widely across carbon ion, proton, and photon therapies, with carbon ion therapy being the most sensitive owing to its steep dose gradient and biological effectiveness (Table 2)

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
section: BACKGROUND: CARBON ION RADIOTHERAPY—PHYSICS, RADIOBIOLOGY, AND MOTION CHALLENGES > Respiratory motion in carbon ion radiotherapy
text: CIRT is clinically beneficial in lung and liver cancers (Table 3), particularly in the treatment of hypoxic or radioresistant lesions, where a high LET is desirable. Nevertheless, the respiratory‐induced displacements were greatest at these locations. The inferior‐superior movement of liver tumors, for example, exceeding 30 mm, makes it difficult to accurately target the beam during scanning of the beam. 44 In lung tumors, single‐fraction stereotactic body radiation therapy (SBRT) as well as fractionated with carbon ions have been studied. Anderle et al. 46 determined that carbon ions and photons had better normal tissue sparing even in the setting of simulated respiratory motion by utilizing carbon. This result was attributed more to a less integral dose. Motion effects are progressively addressed using adaptive approaches, including respiratory gating, beam rescanning, and 4D robust optimization. These methods either time the delivery of the beams to coincide with particular phases of respiration or stochastically average motion‐induced errors across an entire series of beam passes. 9 , 47 Clinically, respiratory gating is most commonly performed during the end‐expiration phase because respiratory motion is generally more reproducible and stable than during inspiration, thereby improving tumour localisation accuracy.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: Although numerous studies have independently investigated Geant4‐based Monte Carlo simulation, respiratory motion management, and deep learning dose prediction, relatively few studies explicitly integrate all three components into a unified carbon‐ion adaptive radiotherapy framework. Of the literature identified through our search strategy, fewer than ten studies explicitly combine Geant4‐generated or Geant4‐comparable Monte Carlo dose data with a deep learning or physics‐constrained prediction model in the specific context of respiratory motion in carbon‐ion therapy (e.g., 18 , 48 ; the DOTA and C‐DOTA architectures of Wahl et al. 2026, 2026b); a larger but still modest set of studies addresses two of the three components—for instance Geant4‐based 4D dose calculation without deep learning, 48 or motion‐resolved imaging coupled with non‐Geant4 dose engines 49 , 50 —and these are included for context rather than as direct evidence for the integrated approach. This small and heterogeneous evidence base is itself informative: it indicates that the explicit combination of Geant4, deep learning, and respiratory‐motion management for carbon‐ion therapy is an emerging rather than an established research direction, which motivates a narrative synthesis over a fully quantitative review at this stage, while also underscoring the need for further dedicated studies at this intersection.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: Respiratory motion introduces significant challenges in CIRT due to the precise dose localization associated with the Bragg peak of heavy ions. Therefore, multiple studies have explored advanced dose calculation tools, such as Geant4‐based Monte Carlo simulations, deep learning (DL) models, and the Simultaneous Motion Estimation and Image Reconstruction (SMEIR) framework, to accurately model or mitigate the effects of motion interplay during treatment (Table 4). The role of Geant4‐based Monte Carlo simulation in this context, including its 4D simulation capabilities and known limitations, is discussed in full in Section 5, which consolidates material previously split across two sections in response to reviewer feedback.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: SMEIR (Simultaneous Motion Estimation and Image Reconstruction) is an advanced imaging technique that reconstructs 4D images from cone‐beam CT data while simultaneously estimating anatomical motion. It is important to note that SMEIR is an image‐domain reconstruction algorithm, not a dose calculation engine: it provides the anatomical model on which a separate dose engine subsequently calculates dose. SMEIR can also be used in CIRT to provide clinicians with improved models of patient‐specific respiratory motion and to adjust dose calculations to the patient's respiratory motion, thereby providing a higher level of accuracy. In a study by Shrestha et al. 50 , the SMEIR for CIRT of lung cancer was assessed, and Shrestha et al. 50 demonstrated that the use of SMEIR‐generated 4D cone‐beam CT significantly enhanced motion‐resolved anatomical reconstruction in carbon‐ion radiotherapy, facilitating more precise dose accumulation throughout the respiratory cycle. Subsequent validation by Annunziata et al. 49 confirmed improved target localization and a reduction in organ‐at‐risk dose compared to conventional motion‐compensated reconstruction strategies. Nevertheless, the majority of published studies emphasize qualitative or workflow‐based improvements rather than standardized quantitative metrics, such as gamma pass rate, dose‐volume histogram (DVH) indices, target coverage (D95%), conformity index (CI), or computational efficiency.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: As a result, direct quantitative comparisons between SMEIR and Geant4‐based Monte Carlo dose calculations remain limited. Given that SMEIR is fundamentally an image‐reconstruction algorithm rather than a particle‐transport dose engine, its primary contribution lies in generating accurate motion‐resolved anatomy, upon which Geant4 or other Monte Carlo platforms can subsequently perform dose calculations. Therefore, current evidence supports SMEIR as a complementary imaging framework that enhances anatomical fidelity for adaptive carbon‐ion therapy. However, further studies reporting standardized quantitative dosimetric endpoints are necessary to fully establish its clinical benefits. Dose calculation in that study was performed using the goCMC Monte Carlo engine rather than Geant4 51 ; SMEIR and Geant4 are conceptually distinct tools—an image‐reconstruction algorithm and a particle‐transport dose engine, respectively—and direct agreement between the two is therefore not the relevant comparison. Rather, the two are complementary: SMEIR (or an analogous motion‐resolved reconstruction method) supplies the time‐resolved anatomy, while a Monte Carlo engine such as Geant4 performs the dose calculation on that anatomy.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: Motion‐resolved approaches such as SMEIR are most valuable when the planning goal is to accurately accumulate the biologically weighted dose across respiratory phases, or where interplay cannot be adequately averaged out by rescanning; a properly constructed internal target volume (ITV) with density override on a static CT, combined with beam rescanning, can already achieve adequate dose coverage in many routine scenarios without requiring full 4D imaging or reconstruction. A summary of the reported performance outcomes, computational advantages, and current limitations of recent deep learning and motion‐adaptive approaches is presented in Table 5.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
section: RESEARCH TRENDS > Deep learning and respiratory modeling
text: Deep Learning can be defined as a machine learning model that uses artificial neural networks to learn complicated patterns in a large dataset. In radiation oncology, DL has the ability to simulate non‐linear associations among anatomical movement and the amount of dose distribution, frequently in real‐time. When used together with physical modeling (e.g. physics‐informed neural networks or PINNs), DL can be used to generate clinically meaningful and physically plausible outputs. It should be clarified that Meschini et al. 52 used an optical surface‐monitoring‐derived surrogate respiratory signal to guide gated CIRT, not a deep learning model; genuinely DL‐based approaches for CIRT dose prediction include He et al. 18 , who demonstrated deep learning–based Monte Carlo dose prediction for heavy‐ion online adaptive radiotherapy with high fidelity relative to full Monte Carlo calculations at substantially reduced computational cost. Moreover, DL frameworks are being applied to designing predictive analytics, which simulate operationally expensive models, such as Monte Carlo calculations, potentially permitting real‐time treatment adjustment without sacrificing precision. He et al. achieved a high level of agreement with Monte Carlo reference doses, significantly reducing computation time from several minutes to nearly real‐time inference. However, the validation was conducted on limited datasets, and prospective clinical validation has yet to be performed.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
section: RESEARCH TRENDS > Deep learning and respiratory modeling
text: Recent advancements in deep learning methodologies have significantly decreased Monte Carlo computation times while preserving high dosimetric accuracy. This finding suggests its potential application in online adaptive radiotherapy. However, the model's development relied on relatively limited training datasets and retrospective validation, with external multi‐institutional validation still lacking. Similarly, physics‐informed neural networks and U‐Net‐based architectures have shown enhanced robustness by integrating physical dose constraints during training, thereby minimizing prediction artefacts compared to purely data‐driven models. Despite these promising results, most studies are still limited to simulation environments, and prospective clinical implementation has not yet been realized. Present limitations encompass the scarcity of motion‐rich datasets, the uncertainty in generalizing findings across different institutions, the absence of standardized benchmarking datasets, the lack of prospective clinical validation, and the ambiguity surrounding regulatory implementation within adaptive carbon‐ion radiotherapy workflows.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
section: RESEARCH TRENDS > Deep learning and respiratory modeling
text: While these studies consistently show enhanced computational efficiency and promising dosimetric accuracy, the overall readiness of the technology remains constrained. The majority of published research comprises proof‐of‐concept studies utilizing retrospective datasets or computational phantoms. To incorporate Geant4–deep learning frameworks into routine adaptive carbon‐ion radiotherapy, standardized benchmarking, prospective multicenter validation, workflow integration, and regulatory approval are necessary.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
section: RESEARCH TRENDS > Comparative and hybrid studies
text: A comparative or hybrid model that integrates multiple modelling tools is frequently required to capture the interaction between motion and treatment delivery in CIRT. 53 Such may comprise Geant4 simulations, SMEIR image‐based correction, and DL estimation devices. In a similar example, Anderle et al. 46 conducted an in silico study to compare photon therapy and carbon ion therapy using simulated breathing motion with 4DCT. They proved that CIRT, although having a better target, is more prone to respiratory motion dose distortion owing to its sharp Bragg peak.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
section: GEANT4 TOOLKIT OVERVIEW & RELEVANCE FOR CIRT
text: Accurate prediction of dose perturbations caused by respiratory motion is essential in particle therapy, especially in CIRT, which is highly sensitive to anatomical changes and intra‐fractional motion. Monte Carlo simulations, particularly those built using Geant4, offer detailed modeling capabilities to assess these perturbations with high fidelity. Geant4 is particularly well suited to simulating the interaction of high‐LET particles with tissues, which is an important aspect of CIRT due to its large physics libraries and modular capabilities. It is also complemented by its Geant4‐DNA extension to support nanodosimetric modeling and modeling of biological effects, an important consideration in analyzing cellular effects due to radiation. 54 Geant4‐DNA specifically extends the standard toolkit to simulate particle track structure at the nanometric scale, enabling stochastic modeling of clustered DNA damage and supporting microdosimetric implementations of the MKM that underlie several clinical RBE models. Relevant physics developments for CIRT include the Liege Intranuclear Cascade model coupled to quantum molecular dynamics (LIQMD) and explicit treatment of multi‐ionization processes, both of which affect the nuclear interaction cross‐sections governing secondary‐particle production and, in turn, the predicted fragmentation tail.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
section: GEANT4 TOOLKIT OVERVIEW & RELEVANCE FOR CIRT
text: Because Geant4 simulation results are strongly dependent on the specific physics list and toolkit version used, the Geant4 collaboration maintains G4‐Med, a dedicated benchmarking platform that validates Geant4 physics models against experimental data for medical applications including CIRT; reviewers and users of Geant4‐based CIRT studies should consider which version and physics list were validated against G4‐Med before drawing comparative conclusions across studies (cite Geant4 collaboration documentation; e.g.).

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
section: GEANT4 TOOLKIT OVERVIEW & RELEVANCE FOR CIRT
text: Geant4 (Geometry and Tracking), developed by CERN, models microscopic physical interactions such as electromagnetic interactions, hadronic interactions, and nuclear processes, a level of granularity essential for estimating the Bragg peak and the complex dose distributions that accompany high‐LET particles in CIRT. Dowdell et al. 48 developed a 4D Monte Carlo simulation using Geant4 to evaluate the interaction between breathing and particle beams, finding that dose smearing effects were considerably high in the absence of proper motion control, particularly in the superior‐inferior direction. This single early study, however, is illustrative of a broader gap: relatively few Geant4‐based 4D simulation studies for CIRT have been published, and direct quantitative comparisons between 4D Monte Carlo (4D‐MC) and 4D pencil‐beam algorithms (4D‐PBA) remain scarce. This is a meaningful omission, because Monte Carlo carries a particular computational advantage in 4D scenarios: 4D‐PBA requires separate analytical dose calculations for each respiratory phase or scenario, with computational effort scaling roughly linearly with the number of phases, whereas 4D‐MC can sample particle histories across the full motion envelope within a more unified simulation framework, without a proportional per‐phase increase in cost. Future Geant4‐based CIRT studies should explicitly benchmark 4D‐MC against 4D‐PBA in heterogeneous, motion‐affected anatomy to substantiate this advantage.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
section: GEANT4 TOOLKIT OVERVIEW & RELEVANCE FOR CIRT
text: Geant4‐based simulations have proven effective in dynamic environments with respiratory motion. 55 As an example, Andersson 56 was able to leverage machine learning together with Monte Carlo modeling to enhance in vivo transmission dosimetry in dynamic therapies. With this hybrid technique, it was possible to model pixel‐specific dose‐response functions under realistic motion conditions. The need for such modelling is evident when one considers the implications of motion‐induced misalignment of the Bragg peak: the tumour is severely underdosed, while healthy tissues are overdosed. A study by Chatzisavvas & Priniotakis emphasizes the maturity of Monte Carlo toolkits as general‐purpose dose calculation tools in radiation dosimetry, involving dynamic anatomical settings, such as Geant4 and MCNPX. They noted that further development of simulation‐based verification systems is essential for motion‐influenced treatments.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
section: GEANT4 TOOLKIT OVERVIEW & RELEVANCE FOR CIRT
text: In addition to respiratory motion, other perturbative factors have been studied in recent times, for example, an external magnetic field, which can potentially couple with respiratory motion in MRI‐guided CIRT. For example, Marhou et al. 57 described a dose shift under the influence of a 1.5 T magnetic field during carbon therapy. Their simulations using Geant4 told of both lateral shifts and modulations of the Bragg peak with field orientation and respiratory phase, adding to the understanding of how cumulative physical effects can further complicate motion‐informed dose prediction.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
section: GEANT4 TOOLKIT OVERVIEW & RELEVANCE FOR CIRT
text: Even though Geant4 has its advantages, it is not without shortcomings. Calculational efficiency remains its greatest hurdle. Conventional 4D Monte Carlo is computationally expensive because a much finer spatial resolution is required to obtain high statistics. This concern is particularly notable in adaptive workflows or in trying to make a real‐time dose prediction. An illustrative diagram of the Geant4 simulation pipeline, with deep learning for motion‐based dose prediction, is shown in Figure 2. Clinical implementation is limited by factors such as treatment delivery time, adaptive workflow duration, and computational latency. While GPU acceleration and AI‐based surrogate models significantly decrease calculation time, real‐time adaptive carbon‐ion therapy is still in development. These factors are anticipated to gain importance in future FLASH carbon‐ion therapy, where ultra‐high dose‐rate delivery necessitates swift motion monitoring and verification to maintain dosimetric accuracy and the intended FLASH effect.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
section: GEANT4 TOOLKIT OVERVIEW & RELEVANCE FOR CIRT
text: In an attempt to overcome this bottleneck, a number of strategies have emerged. Deep learning methods, especially convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and U‐Nets, have been used to generate approximations of the dose distributions by a selected subset of the input simulation parameters using surrogate modeling. With these models, which have been trained on Geant4 with high‐fidelity output, dose can be predicted with high accuracy and quickly across different respiratory cycles. 58 Deformable image registration (DIR) has similarly been proposed to accumulate dose across respiratory phases by mapping dose calculated on a reference anatomy onto deformed anatomical states. For carbon ions, however, this approach must be applied with caution: because the Bragg peak position is highly sensitive to the density and path length of tissue traversed, dose distributions cannot generally be deformed across anatomical states without recalculation, and full 4D‐MC recalculation on each respiratory phase remains the more reliable approach for accurate dose accumulation in CIRT.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
section: GEANT4 TOOLKIT OVERVIEW & RELEVANCE FOR CIRT
text: Combining Geant4 with fast analytic dose engines or machine learning (AI)‐aided correction layers has led to the development of hybrid simulation techniques to facilitate performance (near real‐time) without compromising physical accuracy. They consist of precomputed Monte Carlo data that are utilized in training generative AI that can dynamically predict the dose deposition patterns (it should be noted that Sarrut et al. 59 is a general review of AI applications in Monte Carlo simulation for medical physics, citing a single proton MC application and none specific to carbon ions or Geant4; similarly, Webster et al. 60 is a general review of computational radiotherapy approaches without a specific AI‐Geant4‐carbon ion connection—both are cited here for the broader methodological context they provide rather than as carbon‐ion‐specific evidence). Other studies investigate cloud and GPU‐accelerated platforms that optimize wall‐time without compromising Monte Carlo precision in four‐dimensional scenarios. 60 The use of Geant4 within the context of more general simulation pipelines that incorporate artificial intelligence, adaptive feedback, and probabilistic modeling remains a topic of ongoing interest as the field evolves, enhancing the applicability of Geant4 in CIRT. However, further efforts are needed to standardise these hybrid techniques for clinical application and to validate them on various patient anatomies. 59

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: Carbon ion radiotherapy benefits from adaptive replanning under respiratory motion owing to its sharp dose gradients and sensitivity to anatomical changes. Approaches such as respiratory gating and motion modelling have been demonstrated to accurately estimate and correct irregular motions in real time. As an example, Meschini et al 52 explain how motion predictive models could be used to guide beam gating, and Kubiak delineates the layered rescanning and tumor tracking methodologies applicable in offline adaptive replanning and the developing field of online adaptive radiotherapy during treatment delivery. 8 Integration of 4D imaging and dose computation can provide a temporally resolved understanding of dose delivery across motion cycles. 61 , 62 Techniques employing tools to synchronize beam delivery with 4D CT data sets, for example those mentioned by, 63 provide an overall picture of dose distribution throughout the phases of motion. 63 Rietzel and Bert's framework, while foundational, is now 15 years old and was developed primarily for regular, periodic respiratory motion; Steinsberger et al. 64 provide a modern extension of this motion‐management framework that explicitly addresses irregular respiratory motion, which is more representative of real patient breathing patterns. Such temporal accuracy minimizes the differences between the planned dose and the actual dose.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: Mori et al 65 have also compared the gated and ungated planning approaches on pancreatic cancer using 4D CT and indicated significant accuracy improvements with the motion‐managed approach. Real‐time verification of dose tools has also been reported, such as the one reviewed by Galeone et al., which allows moving targets to be corrected almost in a real‐time scenario 66 . Since the respiratory motion is variable, individual motion profiles necessitate margin adaptation. According to, 67 integration of the real‐time motion pattern analysis would enable clinicians to plan with customized volumes of target (PTVs), which eliminates the irradiation of healthy tissues unnecessarily. Adaptive radiotherapy frameworks, such as range‐adapted internal target volumes (raITVs), allow PTV tailoring based on motion amplitude and direction. 68 demonstrated cycle‐based respiratory guidance methods that refined beam delivery timing and margins. Furthermore, Jia et al. 69 quantified the improvements in organ‐sparing and dose conformity for patients with locally advanced NSCLC using adaptive carbon ion strategies.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: Machine learning algorithms for real‐time, motion‐ and dose‐adaptive applications require large labelled datasets to capture a wide range of respiratory dynamics. Nevertheless, this type of dataset is limited in CIRT. Fossati et al. stress that motion‐rich data should be gathered to enhance the bioinformatic learning used in clinical practice to achieve more adaptation and resilience with the help of AI. 70 Pakela et al 9 highlighted the existence of this gap, and they stressed the importance of collaborative data generation to achieve applications of robust machine learning in the field of particle therapy.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: RBE‐weighted dose is already incorporated in adaptive planning workflows at leading CIRT centers, including LEM‐ and MKM‐based implementations in RayStation, and recent studies have demonstrated real‐time RBE‐weighted dose computation; the ongoing challenge is therefore not whether RBE can be included in adaptive planning, but how accurately and efficiently spatially variable RBE can be recalculated as anatomy changes during treatment. As explained by, 23 modern models of RBE are complicated and mostly non‐linear with dynamic conditions. The LET distributions that are variable with respect to motion inevitably require a biologically‐weighted dose modeling to prevent under‐ or over‐treatment of regions. It can be stressed that work by Karger demonstrates that conventional models of RBE can underestimate biological efficacy with different modes of motion. 23 Research, such as that by, 71 is attempting to combine NTCP models with biological dose optimisation in the treatment of lung cancer.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: Such adaptive strategies as 4D dose re‐computations and optimization of relative biological effectiveness are very computationally demanding, in many cases contradicting the fast schedule of decision‐making within the clinics. As Lebbink et al. 43 note, there is a challenge in performing real‐time recalculations without adversely affecting clinical throughput. Kim et al. 72 discussed that reducing the latency in dose recalculation and beam path adaptation is essential to avoid workflow bottlenecks. Fast dose engines and GPU‐accelerated platforms are under development but remain inconsistently implemented across clinics. 73 To transition from bench to bedside, these innovations require prospective validation and regulatory approval. Motion modelling protocols and multi‐centre trials must be standardised. Chi et al. 45 highlight that the lack of rigorous clinical evidence will lead to a protracted adoption of even promising technologies, as safety and reproducibility will be at issue. Future experiments, such as those cited by Jia et al. 69 are required to confirm the safety and effectiveness of adaptive strategies. Regulatory pathways should also adapt to the complexities of biologically and motion‐guided adaptive treatment approaches, as highlighted by Pakela et al. 9 . These uncertainties have a direct impact on the routine clinical implementation of radiotherapy.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: Specifically, uncertainty in Relative Biological Effectiveness (RBE) modelling may affect the selection of prescription doses. Additionally, the limited availability of motion‐rich datasets constrains the generalisability of artificial intelligence models. Computational latency continues to pose a challenge to online adaptive radiotherapy, thereby limiting its widespread clinical application. Most integrated Geant4–deep learning adaptive carbon‐ion radiotherapy frameworks are currently at Technology Readiness Levels (TRLs) 3–5, which are primarily based on simulation or preclinical validation. Routine clinical implementation requires multicentre validation, integration into clinical workflows, regulatory approval, and prospective clinical trials.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: The studies reviewed here are, almost without exception, simulation‐based, retrospective, or preclinical, and most integrated Geant4–deep learning frameworks for motion‐adaptive carbon‐ion radiotherapy remain at Technology Readiness Levels (TRL) 3–5. Within that limit, the trajectory of the field is consistent: Geant4‐based Monte Carlo simulation provides high‐fidelity modelling of particle transport and dose deposition under respiratory motion, and deep learning approaches—particularly when constrained by physical priors, as in physics‐informed neural networks—have repeatedly been shown to approximate these Monte Carlo dose distributions with substantially reduced computation time. He et al. 18 , for example, demonstrated near‐real‐time dose prediction with high agreement to Monte Carlo reference doses, though on a limited, retrospective patient cohort, and purpose‐built architectures such as DOTA and C‐DOTA point toward further refinement of this approach rather than a solved problem. What is not yet established is direct, prospective clinical validation of these hybrid frameworks specifically under 4D respiratory motion in CIRT: published evidence to date supports feasibility and computational promise, not clinical readiness.

title: Dynamic control of carbon-ion radiation dose distribution amid respiratory motion challenges: A review of prediction research using geant4 and deep learning physics-constrained models.
text: Realising the potential of this combination—motion‐compensated, biologically weighted treatment planning delivered at clinically usable speed—will require standardised benchmarking datasets, multicentre prospective validation, integration into existing adaptive workflows, and regulatory engagement, none of which has yet been demonstrated at scale. Until these steps are taken, the appropriate framing for this body of work is one of a promising but early‐stage research direction rather than a near‐term clinical solution.
